003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.name: Five textile fragments.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.description:
Five circular woollen textile fragments each decorated with a depiction of a bird, perhaps a duck or a goose, in different sizes and colours, and woven in a non-extended weft pattern, a tapestry technique. The fragments were taken from bigger textiles, perhaps used as a counterpane or curtains, and which may have consisted of a decorative design with repetitive motifs. Upper Egypt was famous for sumptuous woven cloth such as this, with Asyut, Akhmim and the City of Fustat prominent places of production during the Tulunid period (AH 3rd / AD 9th century).  
During the Tulunid period, textiles were distinguished by the appearance of a shadow in the decorative components, where the colour was graded from light to dark, as well as for their powerful expression. They were also influenced by the Sassanid style, brought by Ahmad ibn Tulun (r. AH 254–70 / AD 868–84) from Iraq. The production of textiles in the Tulunid period represents a period of transition in Egypt between the Coptic period and the Islamic period with regard to the decorative components and their development.  
Most of the *jizya* (tribute) which Ahmad ibn Tulun sent to the court of the Abbasid caliphs consisted of textiles made in the *Tiraz* workshops, under royal decree, which produced magnificent fabrics of wool and linen. Tulun took a personal interest in the textile factories of Egypt, which were widespread in the north delta regions of Tanis, Dabik, Damietta, and other cities. These regions were famous for the manufacture of linen cloth with inscriptions woven in silk in a multitude of colours. Interest in textile manufacture increased in Egypt with the rule of the sons of Ibn Tulun: Khumarawayh (r. AH 270–82 / AD 884–96) and Harun (r. AH 283–92 / AD 896–905), who were inclined towards recording their names in inscription bands on the textile itself.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.short_description: Cotton and linen textiles were woven in various factories in Egypt: Alexandria, Damietta, Farma, Bahnasa, Akhmim and Asyut. Coptic-style decorations remained prevalent during the AH 1st–3rd / AD 7th–9th centuries. The pieces here are notable for the shadow effect in the decorations, where colour is graded from light to dark shades.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.holder: Textile Museum (One of the branches of the Museum of Islamic Art in Cairo)
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.dimensions: Diameter of the biggest piece: 20 cm.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.method_for_datation: These fragments have been dated based on a study of their decorative components that include the depiction of birds similar to those found in Tulunid *Tiraz* textiles from the Upper Egypt region, and which also resemble the depictions of birds on other Iraqi applied arts with Sassanid roots. Furthermore, the colours used in these textiles, whether it be different shades of yellow, degrees of green or blue, are colours that were customary on Tulunid textiles.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.method_for_provenance: Egypt was famed during the Tulunid period for its textile industry where magnificent woollen and linen fabrics were produced. The depiction of birds found on these textile fragments are also similar to those found in Tulunid *Tiraz* textiles from Upper Egypt.
003a4edc-0d1e-5875-9041-6715b1c36ebf.obtention: The fragments were bought in 1944 from one of the antiquities dealers in Cairo, Fukyan Jan Tano.

012b5222-da31-50c5-8bfc-eb439eea45d0.name: *Flight of the French army and retreat of the Duke of Alençon across the Ticino*
012b5222-da31-50c5-8bfc-eb439eea45d0.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the right-hand border of the tapestry; the mark can also be found on another example in the series. The presence of the weaver’s mark has also allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014). According to this perspective, the tapestry examined here, placed in the sequence suggested by Paredes, constitutes the last in the series and should be read in close continuity with the subject represented in the tapestry that precedes it, *Flight of the besieged and retreat of the Swiss who drown in great numbers in the Ticino*. In particular, from the juxtaposition of the two tapestries, the landscape south of Pavia can be recreated, distinguished by the presence of the small island of Gravellone, separated from the city by the waters of the Ticino. The tapestry represents one of the final moments of the battle, with a portrait of the Duke of Alençon – identified by the writing on the caparison of his horse – who, after having crossed the bridge of boats on the Ticino, orders its destruction to prevent the enemy from following. In the foreground, a few infantrymen are depicted, busy destroying the bridge, while a horseman and other soldiers are the last to cross it. The action of the Duke of Alençon, brother-in-law of the King of France, condemns all those who do not manage to cross the bridge to the wrath of the enemy or to the swirling waters of the river. In the distance, one can glimpse a herd of cows grazing serenely, indifferent to the war, in the rural landscape.

01c1fd3b-239c-5a49-b106-2c0d2c8ff5bf.name: Textile fragment
01c1fd3b-239c-5a49-b106-2c0d2c8ff5bf.description: This fragment of a scene depicting hunters on camels indicates the extraordinary skill of the Safavid weavers. Another fragment of this textile showing six hunters is in the Keir Collection at the Dallas Museum of Art. In the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts' piece, two turbaned riders hunting gazelles with spears stand out against an orangey red background adorned with rocks and plant designs. The subject of the scene – hunting on camelback – is borrowed from a story that the Persian poet Nizami (AD 1141–1209) told about the Sasanian King Bahram Gur (AD 420–438/39). The theme of the royal hunt figured prominently in Achaemenid and Sasanian decorative arts, providing a favourite motif for Safavid weaving and the miniatures of the period.

02324453-7acd-5e97-99f2-81813dc8f9c1.name: Yomud *chuval*
02324453-7acd-5e97-99f2-81813dc8f9c1.description:
Common among all people of Central Asia were various bags, of different size and shape, which were hung on the inside of the tent wall and served as containers for clothes and household utensils. The Turkomans called them the *chuval*, *torba* and *mafrach*.  
The rectangular central field has 3 by 3 rows of small *chuval göl*s and secondary *chemche* (spoon) motifs. The central field is framed with three borders. The main border is decorated with hexagons alternating red and white *kaikalak* (four opposing ram's horns) motifs. Minor borders are decorated with a chain of S shapes. The top elem panel is decorated with a row of *kochak* (ram's horns) motifs on blue ground. The bottom elem panel has halfs of *kelle* (head) figures and small square motifs on red ground.

048c6a9d-2f1b-5deb-80ce-ba88d1053a07.name: Milas Prayer Rug
048c6a9d-2f1b-5deb-80ce-ba88d1053a07.description: Milas region is famous for its prayer rugs. This is an outstanding example of a Milas prayer rug with intensive decoration and skillful handcraft. The prayer area of the rug is decorated with a tree of life on a ground filled with rose, carnation and tulip motifs. The border is composed of highly stylized tree and dragon motifs which are locally called “leaf” and “frog”. These continuous motifs are arranged in the form of “cattle water” which is the most important decoration element of Milas rugs.

05e51871-4d33-519c-836e-6e68090e5a80.name: Ladik Prayer Rug
05e51871-4d33-519c-836e-6e68090e5a80.description: This rug is an outstanding example of a Ladik prayer rug because of its colours and detailed decorations. Typical characteristics include, upside down tulips in the borders and three crescent motifs at the top of a triple niche *mihrab*. However, the column motifs usually present in this type of rug do not appear. This example demonstrates the variety of the Ladik prayer rugs and the broadness of its motif repertory.

0686d02e-ea89-5422-8643-7f699b666839.name: Wall hanging
0686d02e-ea89-5422-8643-7f699b666839.description:
Valerie Jorud (1902–1945) began working as a textile artist and later also in ceramic art and sculpting. In 1935 she displayed her textile work at the Grassi Fair. Here, the museum acquired the wall hanging, which was not only designed but also crafted by the artist. In the years that followed, during the Third Reich, the Jewish artist managed to hide with the help of ceramic artist Jan Bontjes van Beek and continued to create art from the underground. She died tragically in 1945 during a bomb attack in Berlin.  
Azure and cornflower-coloured ribbons (cotton, 2.5cm wide) have been applied to a black-blue cotton sheet. Through the arrangement of the ribbons, which run parallel and in right angles, geometrical figures are created and cover the entire surface. Most prominent are two wide rows consisting of 12 ribbons each, which run from the middle section at a right angle around the entire hanging. The sections between these two rows – six triangles on the outside and a square at the center – are structured by varying, closely positioned ribbons. The work gains a strong spatial presence through the strong contrast of the lighter and darker blue tones. It is signed VJ.
0686d02e-ea89-5422-8643-7f699b666839.owner: GRASSI Museum of Applied Art, Leipzig
0686d02e-ea89-5422-8643-7f699b666839.obtention: Acquired at the Grassi Fair in 1935

072908a4-0753-537a-a852-9b3ddcb4ddd6.name: Kırşehir Prayer Rug
072908a4-0753-537a-a852-9b3ddcb4ddd6.description: Kırşehir Province of Central Anatolia was an important prayer rug producing centre. This double *mihrab* prayer rug is an outstanding example of the regional style. Kırşehir prayer rugs characteristically have elaborate stepped arches above the *mihrab*, vivid colours, and detailed floral decorations. The multiple borders are filled with stylized flowers, leaves and a scrolling vine of carnations. The most important element of the decoration is the naturalist bird motif woven inside the *mihrab* area.

07917edd-ff85-5fd1-b5b8-5faef0c0f94d.name: Polish carpet
07917edd-ff85-5fd1-b5b8-5faef0c0f94d.description:
Carpets in Poland were made in manufactories founded by Polish aristocrats on their own estates. This carpet belongs to the group of five stylistically homogenous objects preserved in Polish collections, which were woven probably in Niemirów or Tulczyn, in a manufactory located on the Potocki family estate.  
In the middle of the ivory-coloured central field, there is the coat of arms of the Potocki (Pilawa) and Mniszech (Mniszech) family underneath a nobleman’s crown, displayed above trophies of combat. Looking closer at the trophies, elements characteristic of the Republic of Poland and Lithuania are recognisable: two *karabelas* ‒ sabres with an open hilt and pommel, recalling an eagle’s head ‒ and two maces with spherical heads called *bulawas*, which were the attributes of *hetman*s, the highest-ranking commanders in the Polish and Lithuanian army. There are also banners and cannons. Beneath the coat of arms are bullets, gunpowder barrels and kettledrums. Thanks to the coat of arms of the Pilawa and Mniszech, it is possible to presume that the carpet was made to mark the marriage of Stanisław Szczęsny Potocki and Józefina Mniszchówna in 1774, and to decorate their manor house in Tulczyn.  
The ornamental decoration of the rug is also very interesting. The central field is decorated with isolated palmettes and roses. The wide border is tightly filled with palmettes and flowers, among which we can find irises, typical of Islamic ornamentation. Strong geometrisation of floral motifs brings to mind Caucasian carpets. It is very probable that the Potocki manufactury employed Armenians and this easily explains the Caucasian inspiration.  
The colour green is predominant in this carpet, with the addition of red, yellow, blue and emerald-green, although the colours are somewhat faded now. The wool used to knot Polish carpets was coarser and thicker than the wool used for rugs in warmer, sunnier areas of the world.

088db2ad-2975-50d5-98f5-125c810d504b.name: *Ensi*
088db2ad-2975-50d5-98f5-125c810d504b.description: The basic design of the Turkmen rug called *ensi* (or *engsi*) features two long narrow rectangles intersecting at a right angle, which accounts for the term formerly used to designate them: *khachli* or *khachlu* (from the Armenian *khach* = cross). The arch at the upper end, which sometimes also appears on the vertical band of the cross, seems to suggest *ensi*s may have been used as prayer rugs. More recently, though, the idea has been largely abandoned, the *ensi* being currently defined only as a door cover for felt tents. Sometimes, *ensi*s have been compared to the *chahār-bāgh*\-style Persian garden, whose layout resembles the quartered format of the *ensi*’s central field. The present example dates most probably from the last decade of the 19th century; its decorative repertoire is characteristic of the Tekke rugs, with Y-shape motifs and “ram’s horns” along the secondary outer border. This remarkably well preserved rug was part of the Romanian treasure sent to Moscow in 1916.

095b7e62-f9c6-596f-a836-6ef282bea7af.name: Carpet
095b7e62-f9c6-596f-a836-6ef282bea7af.description:
As a curtain that covers a Torah Ark containing the Torah scrolls in a synagogue, this carpet contains above the arch a Hebrew inscription from Psalms CXVIII:20 that reads “This is the Gate of the Lord: Through it the Righteous Enter.” Material, technique, design elements, and coloring supply sufficient proof that the carpet was woven in a Ottoman court-controlled atelier in Cairo, Egypt, although it is unknown in the ark of which synagogue it was hung. When the Ottoman Turks conquered Egypt in 1517, there was already an established carpet-weaving industry there. This carpet, and others of its time woven in Cairo, reflect Ottoman taste in elements of the design, but they were produced for a wide raging clientele from European aristocracy to Sephardic Jewish comminities who lived in Ottoman lands.  
  
Probably, woven for a Sephardic Jewish community that settled in the Ottoman lands after their expulsion in the late fifteenth century from Iberian Peninsula, this Torah curtain shows many of the same stylistic characteristics as the two seccade hanging behind it. The artistic forms shared between the Muslim *seccade* and the Jewish *parochet* are no coincidence, for they indicate a vocabulary of symbolism: the shared meaning of door- like forms as gateway to heaven given to the Muslim *mihrab* and the Jewish Torah ark and hanging lamps and light as a metaphor for God.  
  
The contrast between styles shows especially well on the carpets produced in Egypt during the Mamluk Sultanate and afterwards during the Ottoman Empire. Curvilinear and naturalistic rendering of the floral motifs on the Ottoman carpets, such as in this example, produces a more sensuous effect than the geometric and angular patterning of the Mamluk style in which the limited colour scheme – red, blue and green – imparts a restrained and intellectual quality.
095b7e62-f9c6-596f-a836-6ef282bea7af.holder: The George Washington University Museum and The Textile Museum
095b7e62-f9c6-596f-a836-6ef282bea7af.method_for_datation: The carpet exhibits both Mamluk and Ottoman elements in its style, material, and structure, and thus could be after the Ottoman Empire took control of Egypt and the process of adopting Ottoman artistic elements into the Cairene carpet weaving tradition was underway.

09a4894e-2a26-5a8f-8c64-32e79d122187.name: Pile carpet fragment
09a4894e-2a26-5a8f-8c64-32e79d122187.description: The dark green central square is surrounded by three light-coloured borders, which in their turn are framed by thin bands in various colours. The first border is decorated with polychrome zig-zags, the second with yellow dots placed on differently-coloured bands and the third has a perimetric *kufic* inscription, which bears the name of Allah, on an abrashed red ground. The pile is in relatively good condition, apart from the areas of dark brown which are noticeably worn, so that the surface of the carpet gives the impression of having concave sections. The original dimensions of the carpet were approximately 45 cm square, as indicated by the shape of the pattern, the inscription which runs around the central decorative feature, and the fact that in technique, design and dimensions it resembles Benaki fragments 16148 and 16193, as well as no.73.726 in the Textile Museum, Washington.
09a4894e-2a26-5a8f-8c64-32e79d122187.method_for_datation: It belongs to a group of fragments attributed to Egypt and their dating between the 8th and the 11th century. In addition, the form of the *kufic* inscription belongs to this period
09a4894e-2a26-5a8f-8c64-32e79d122187.method_for_provenance: Factors that determine the provenance: 1. The use of linen, which is the basic Egyptian fibre, for both warps and wefts; 2. The left-twisting (S) spin of the materials is also an Egyptian feature. Linen warps S-spun, Z-plied are found in Coptic fabrics of the 9th-10th century. Right-twisted spinning (Z) is rarely found in Group A; 3. The technique of weaving with cut-pile loops which continues the long-standing Egyptian tradition of weaving with a pile made of loops; 4. The pattern, colouring and techniques of this group fragments bear a close resemblance to contemporaneous Coptic textiles. 5. The fragments display similarities to certain inscribed and non-inscribed fragments from Fustat.
09a4894e-2a26-5a8f-8c64-32e79d122187.bibliography: Published in Theologou, J., Ozoline, A., Sartzetakis, Y., "Fustat Carpet Fragments", *Hali*, 156 (summer 2008): 65-71.

09cdeb4b-d8af-5846-88b2-2da55fbe30d8.name: Carpet
09cdeb4b-d8af-5846-88b2-2da55fbe30d8.description:
Spanish carpet of the Crown style.  
Field: The field is formed of three full crowns of oak leaves along with a partial segment of a fourth in which a barely visible golden leaf litter stands out on the rounded bottom. The better distinguished blue flowers mark the quadrants of the wheels or crowns. Within the inner border, the field finishes off in a continuous line of the same colours.  
Border: The border is formed by candlestick motifs utilising the same colours as the field, which stand out against the dark blue background. On the larger sides they are arranged on a longitudinal axis, while on the smaller side, the same decorative motif is repeated horizontally.  
The colours of the wool used consists of molasses, gold and dark blue.  
The carpet is from the crown series which was largely produced throughout the 16th century and typical of the workshops of the Old Kingdom of Murcia.  
The laurels or crowns were a decorative element widely used in the Renaissance and can be found in numerous decorative designs. In exceptional cases they may also contain heraldic motifs or religious anagrams. However, the internal border that creates linked rhombuses is an outdated Mudejar stylistic element.  
This carpet is catalogued as belonging to the workshops of Alcaraz by several scholars, however certain stylistic elements such as its colour or composition may call into question this attribution. The range of colours (yellow, molasses and blue) as well as the arrangement of the crowns, free of any reference, would make it closer to the core of the Cuenca region, although today there are no parallels or documentary evidence.  
The carpet conforms to carpet number ten of the Weissberger collection visible in the collections acquisition catalogue, although the measures differ slightly.  
A similar carpet is found in: Ferrandis, J., 1933: Exhibition Catalog of Old Spanish Carpets. Madrid, nº 36, plate XXVIII, page 112. Another in the catalogue of the Textile Museum of Washington.

09fff21c-90f5-5324-8374-bd46dbcc09ba.name: Kurdish carpet, so-called *Şarkışlar*
09fff21c-90f5-5324-8374-bd46dbcc09ba.description: An Anatolian Kurdish carpet, most likely stemming from the middle of the 19th century and preserved in almost full size. Not much more is missing from the top and bottom of the carpet than the narrow border retained on the sides. Up to the 1990s, pile carpets formed part of the traditional tent decoration of Kurdish nomads in Anatolia. In their black goat-hair tents, the openings of which were located on the longer side, the pile carpet was accorded a central place. Only a very few examples of this type of carpet still exist. They are ascribed to the region around Şarkışla, southwest of Sivas. Characteristic here are the totem-like symbols in large, variously coloured rhomboid shapes, which, in alteration with small squares, form the carpet's tiled pattern. However, the central motif, which appears quite zoomorphic, can probably be traced back to plant shapes. The Dresden piece displays typical East Anatolian colouring and a straightforward, differentiated overall design. Despite some damage and later reworkings, this carpet makes a powerful and confident impression.
09fff21c-90f5-5324-8374-bd46dbcc09ba.holder: Museum für Völkerkunde Dresden (Ethnological Museum Dresden), Dresden State Art Collections
09fff21c-90f5-5324-8374-bd46dbcc09ba.obtention: Purchased in 1980 from a Dresden Collector, Friedrich Uhlemann, who afore acquired the piece at a stately art-dealing shop in Leipzig (VEB Leipzig). Uhlemann was very much engaged in helping Dresden painter Wilhelm Müller (1928–99) to secure oriental rugs, carpets and flatweaves of rural and nomadic tradition that were still on the territory of the GDR with building up a collection for the Ethnographic Museum of Dresden, mainly between 1979 and 1986.

0a4bee6d-d19c-5df8-85c0-343c3bb0c7b6.name: ‘Animal combat’ carpet
0a4bee6d-d19c-5df8-85c0-343c3bb0c7b6.description:
Indian carpets began to arrive in Portugal from the second half of the 16th century onwards. Despite apparently not having been introduced in significant quantities, Indian carpets constituted an alternative to the decoration present in their Turkish and Persian counterparts.  
This carpet is a beautiful example of North Indian production, with its palette dominated by tones of red, as well as by *ton sur ton* colouring. It features a rectangular field with a red background, filled by a vertically organised scene in which various felines are chasing herbivorous animals. Dense branches interspersed with floral motifs, bunches of grapes, cutout leaves and palmettes frame the scene.  
The wide border also has a red background. This is decorated with cutouts and a repeated, interlocking series of three coloured and poly-lobed cartouches, themselves filled with polychrome rosettes, which alternate with palmettes, Timurid-inspired sinuous cloudbands and floral and leaf arrangements.

0b92d7bf-5e20-5bb2-8dc2-0844969d6fc4.name: Carpet with dragon and phoenix.
0b92d7bf-5e20-5bb2-8dc2-0844969d6fc4.description:
This fragmented carpet is one of the most important animal-carpets of the early Ottoman period that have become known to the present day. Two highly stylised animals, a dragon and a phoenix, are depicted fighting, against a yellow background and within two octagonal spaces. The phoenix is swooping down onto the dragon from above. The image is clearer in the lower octagonal casing than in the upper. The outer border is composed of semi-palmette tendrils, which are framed on both sides by an edging of little rosettes. The original border appears to be missing on both the left and right sides. It is possible that the carpet was originally wider in shape, featuring a greater number of octagonal compartments. This would make it more akin to the animal-carpets that were reproduced in paintings. The dragon and phoenix motif, which originated in China – where yellow was considered to be the colour of the sovereign – was introduced into Islamic art in the AH 7th / AD 13th century with the arrival of the Mongols, as is demonstrated by its ubiquitous presence on a number of works of art, made in a variety of materials.  
Animal-carpets often appear in the paintings of Italian artists, but only a few of the actual pieces survived. The painter Domenico di Bartolo depicted a similar dragon-phoenix carpet in his fresco ‘The Wedding of the Foundlings’, which he painted in the Spedale della Scala in Siena in 1440–4. An animal-carpet featuring stylised birds on trees was found in a church in Sweden. The wide distribution of animal-carpets in Europe demonstrates that they were among the early types of carpets to be exported to Europe from the Ottoman Empire. This carpet allegedly comes from a church in central Italy and, from the results of Carbon-14 analysis, is dated to be from the AH mid-9th / AD mid-15th century.
0b92d7bf-5e20-5bb2-8dc2-0844969d6fc4.short_description: This Ottoman carpet with the pattern of a dragon being attacked from above by a phoenix is one of the most famous carpet designs. Introduced from the Far East, carpets with animal designs already occurred in numerous paintings from the European masters in the 13th and 14th centuries.

0bdd9721-3f27-532b-aa49-d29c2756dbbe.name: *Flight of the besieged and retreat of the Swiss who drown in great numbers in the Ticino*
0bdd9721-3f27-532b-aa49-d29c2756dbbe.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014). According to this perspective, the tapestry examined here should be viewed immediately after the tapestry with *The taking of Mirabello Castle*, and it precedes the last in the series, *Flight of the French army and retreat of the Duke of Alençon across the Ticino*. In particular, from the juxtaposition of the three tapestries, one can reconstruct on the left the French encampment, bordered in the foreground by the walls of the Visconti Park and by the defensive system composed of a series of gabions, which one can also distinguish in the distance. On the right, one can recreate the landscape south of Pavia, distinguished by the presence of the small island of Gravellone and by the course of the waters of the Ticino.  
Dominating the tapestry is the depiction of the city of Pavia, bordered by walls, with the Visconti Castle on the left and the Covered Bridge on the right. This is the final phase of the battle: troops commanded by Antonio de Leyva burst out of the city besieged by the imperial troops and attack the French army from behind. In the centre, soldiers and civilians come out of their shelters, trying to flee, while several men, pushed towards the Ticino by the imperial cavalry, drown in the river. In the centre of the tapestry, one of the cavaliers of François de Laval, Count of Montfort, can be identified thanks to the writing embroidered on his horse’s harness.

0c9e0529-7380-57a8-b3d5-151fa4c93eb2.name: The revenge ground of al-Mukhtar (Persian: *Dar al-entegham-e Mokhtar*)
0c9e0529-7380-57a8-b3d5-151fa4c93eb2.short_description: The tragic martyrdom of the Prophet’s grandson al-Husayn and his companions at Karbala' near Kufa, where they were massacred by an Umayyad army in 61/680, played an important role in the consolidation of the *Shi'i* ethos; it also led to the formation of radical trends among the *Shi'i*. The earliest of such trends became manifest in the movement of al-Mukhtar, who won control of Kufa in an open revolt in 66/685. Aiming to avenge al-Husayn’s murder, al-Mukhtar launched his own movement and proclaimed Ibn al-Hanafiyya, al-Husayn’s half-brother Muhammad, as the *Mahdi*, 'the divinely guided one', the messianic saviour imam and restorer of true Islam who would establish justice on earth and deliver the oppressed from tyranny.
0c9e0529-7380-57a8-b3d5-151fa4c93eb2.obtention: Purchased 1996 in Isfahan by Dr Axel Steinmann, curator at the Museum für Völkerkunde, during his fieldwork in Iran.

10698c43-c17e-5574-bbc9-4b8526898e69.name: Carpet
10698c43-c17e-5574-bbc9-4b8526898e69.description: The highly elaborate design of the red central field features richly coloured motifs – palmettes, lotus blossoms, scrolls and Chinese cloudbands – rigorously ordered along an axis of symmetry. Many such carpets, dating from the late 16th or 17th century can still be found in Europe. In what concerns the Romanian Principalities, 17th-century documents, notably those related to the Movilă princes, mention hundreds of Iranian carpets, thus attesting to their popularity in this part of the world as in the rest of Europe. In all likelihood, this carpet, unique in Romania, has come from a Moldavian monastery, to which it was donated by a rich *boyar* or by the *voivode* himself. The use of silk warp could be indicative of a royal workshop. The carpet is comparatively small, but it is precisely its size and its surprisingly well-preserved pile that make it a rare and valuable work of art.

11712c70-825f-5003-97bb-14deb92e5caf.name: Uşak Rug (Lotto type)
11712c70-825f-5003-97bb-14deb92e5caf.description: “Lotto” rugs are produced in the Uşak Province of Anatolia. Classical examples of “Lotto” rugs are generally dated to the 16th century. Lotto type rugs dated to 17th and 18th centuries are rare and they differ from the examples from the 16th century. This example from the 18th century, is part of the late Lotto group. The distinctive motif in this group of rugs are squares filled with octagons and stylized patterns which form ivy. Blue areas on the main ground are a distinctive feature of late Lotto rugs. The schema of classical early carpets is preserved while the intensive geometrical motifs has changed into sparse botanical ones.

11712c70-825f-5003-97bb-14deb92e5caf.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

13b29772-43e9-5a5f-9d0a-30a66bd89d36.name: Arraiolos rug
13b29772-43e9-5a5f-9d0a-30a66bd89d36.description: During the 17th century, oriental carpets were an important source of inspiration for production in Arraiolos. However, throughout the 18th century, the impact of Eastern patterns would gradually fade from Portuguese carpets. This rug is a good example of such a process. A highlight of the old Arraiolos production, it is wool-embroidered, in small stitches, onto burlap, with the outlines of the motifs featuring stem-stitch, characteristic of early Arraiolos rugs. Its rich chromatic scheme varies from yellow to deep blue and includes red, green and black. It is decorated with the so-called “animal pattern”, itself quite representative of that industry’s tendencies during the first half of the 18th century. In this pattern both animal figuration of erudite and popular inspiration and floral motifs abound. Both in the field, with its central medallion, and on the border, birds, quadrupeds and mythological animals are combined with winding vegetation and flower vases. These still denote the influence of other oriental textiles besides carpets, namely the *colchas* (coverlets), made in India since the middle of the 16th century for the Portuguese market.

13cbe817-137e-568a-9fe2-c1976fbb2dba.name: Wall hanging with scenes from the *Tale of Tristan and Iseult* (2 fragments)
13cbe817-137e-568a-9fe2-c1976fbb2dba.description:
The frieze in the bottom section of this wall hanging depicts the tragic love story of Tristan and Iseult (alternatively Isolde). A short introductory text and banners with caption complete the visual narrative. The story begins with the wedding of Tristan’s parents and his birth. This is followed by the young hero's first deeds at the behest of his uncle, King Mark of Cornwall, and his subsequent journey to Ireland to propose to princess Iseult for his uncle. The last part of the tale, depicting their return to Cornwall, the wedding of Iseult and Mark, and the tragic ending of Tristan and Iseult, is missing, due to the fragmentary condition of the hanging.  
The décor in the upper section of the hanging is inspired by ornaments of oriental carpets, which were commonly used as tablecloths during the 16th century. These precious predecessors were either knotted or woven. In the Upper-Rhenish region, this type of design was achieved by embroidering the textile. This hanging was presumably produced in 1539 in Strasbourg, which is evident in the date on the cartouche as well as the coats of arms of four Strasbourgian families. It was rediscovered in 1883 in the church of Schwarzenberg in the Ore Mountains. How the embroidered work got from Strasbourg to Schwarzenberg or why only two fragments of the hanging remain today is unknown.

13da07fe-8678-5b0a-9f85-cd3db783760a.name: Bird *Uşak* (fragment)
13da07fe-8678-5b0a-9f85-cd3db783760a.description: The Viennese bird *Uşak* is a fragment: the border of the bottom narrow side was sewn onto the shortened carpet field, whereby the original length of the carpet cannot be reconstructed. The eponymous rapport pattern unit of the white-grounded carpet field, four birds around a rosette, is repeated four times horizontally and seven times vertically. This special interpretation of the otherwise figureless *Uşak* carpets, is preferred again today, since an Ottoman source of the 17th century apostrophises the “crow pattern”. Moreover, it was established that numerous white-grounded carpets from the Ottoman region are located in the Habsburg inventories of the late 16th century that can possibly be indentified with bird *Uşak*s.

153bbb81-8ae2-506c-9a4e-b290f062e24d.name: Animal carpet
153bbb81-8ae2-506c-9a4e-b290f062e24d.description: The appeal of this small-format carpet is due to its unusual proportions. The borders take up far more space than the narrow, vertical central field, which is unassertively filled with geometrical hooked lozenges. The charm of this border is in its strong contrasts of colour. Stylised birds are arranged all around the inside of the delimited rectangles. They are enclosed and flanked by cream-coloured stylised vines. It is striking that the birds vary in colour and face alternately left and right, but are always shown vertically. This gives the carpet a distinct sense of direction. The vines are reminiscent of the stylised, vegetal border designs of early Spanish carpets. They are linked with the depiction of trees, which makes sense in combination with that of birds. A technical peculiarity is found in the symmetrical knots of the border. They are partly offset, presumably in order to achieve the desired incline of the diagonals. A further animal carpet (KGM 1885,984) in the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin displays this technique.

153bc1d1-5d6c-586c-8edb-2c0cf7039424.name: Double Niche Rug or Rosette Garland 'Transylvanian' Rug
153bc1d1-5d6c-586c-8edb-2c0cf7039424.description: A fashionable version of the 16th and 17th century Ottoman-Turkish prayer rugs was the "double niche" or *'mihrab* (prayer niche)' rug. The rhomboid medallion that fills the middle of the rug is created by mirroring the traditional *mihrab*, the niche in the mosque wall that traditionally had a single apex. These double *mihrab* Usak rugs were primarily popular in Transylvania. Their symmetric patterns were used as table, bed and catafalque covers, known in specialist literature as "Transylvanian" rugs. Additional characteristics of the Transylvanian rugs were the dominating red and blue colours and the line of Transylvanian medallions decorating the main band of the border. The pattern of the "Transylvanian" rugs was simplified from the middle of the 17th century the once complicated arabesque and floral ornaments of the central medallion were replaced by double garlands made of slightly schematic rosettes.

159db56e-edd6-577a-b51e-40b856217129.name: Prayer rug
159db56e-edd6-577a-b51e-40b856217129.description: The rich colour palette and the contrast between the undecorated *mihrab* field and the borders with intricate geometric motifs, the so-called *Crivelli güls*, convey a sense of vitality and unsophisticated beauty. The apex of the stepped *mihrab* echoes the crenellations on the narrow panel above. Identical motifs can be found on earlier carpets, which testify to the persistence of certain patterns over more than two centuries. These motifs, drawn from architecture, appear to have lost their original meaning, much like the columns turned into flower garlands on other 19th-century rugs. Two ewers featured in the spandrels on either side of the pointed top of the *mihrab* suggest, in all probability, the ritual ablution before prayer.

159e3b0b-362a-55fb-aa30-ee216a64766a.name: Prayer rug
159e3b0b-362a-55fb-aa30-ee216a64766a.description: Kula, a small town in western Anatolia, became a major site of rug production in the 18th century. A significant proportion of the rugs made there were prayer rugs, all variations on the same design featuring a pair of tall columns crowned with a simple triangular arch and a wide multi-striped border around the niche. The most distinctive feature of the Kula rugs are stylized floral motifs decorating the architectural elements: small flowers and leafy branches grow out of the columns, arches and spandrels, completely filling the borders and creating a symbiotic fusion of garden and architectural compositions unique to Kula rugs. All Kula rugs share a loose weave and a warm palette of yellow, blue, white and red.

1687a165-29f8-5b58-b99f-27a895254675.name: The Wagner Garden Carpet
1687a165-29f8-5b58-b99f-27a895254675.description:
Named after a previous early 20th century owner, the Wagner Garden Carpet is a 17th century Persian Kirman pile carpet with a formal garden layout on a dark blue background. It is dominated by two long parallel water channels that are linked by a central pool and two short branch channels, all together forming the shape ‘H’. The garden’s six rectangular sections are vertically symmetrical, with the right side of the carpet mirroring its left.  
  
Resembling a walled park, it is packed with a variety of trees, shrubs and flowering plants amongst which animals, birds, butterflies and moths live. The animals depicted include foxes, deer, onagers, goats, hares, wild boars, lions and leopards; storks, ducks, peacocks and smaller birds. Its waterways meet at a central pool, and are all teeming with fish and ducks.  
  
The layout of the flora and fauna gradually changes direction in the top half of the carpet, creating a panoramic view of the garden for the person sitting on it at the bottom half – a most unusual layout for this type of garden carpet. It almost invokes a heavenly walled menagerie that immerses the person sitting on it in its natural but well-ordered world. Reminding the viewer of its cultural roots, its design was inspired by both the pre-Islamic Persian Paradise and the descriptions of the Garden of Heaven in the Qur’an.

1719f15c-e08b-55ce-a654-6a3286d1c836.name: Medallion
1719f15c-e08b-55ce-a654-6a3286d1c836.short_description: This textile is unique. It is a tapestry, a technique that in the period was otherwise used primarily in Mongol China. The fact that the “gold thread” is animal in origin and spun around cotton, however, points in the direction of a western weaving center. The textile was probably made by or under the supervision of Chinese weavers in Ilkhanid Iran or Iraq.

172c1382-0e81-55ba-805f-8035e133cc1d.name: "Lotto" Carpet with Closed Kufesque Border
172c1382-0e81-55ba-805f-8035e133cc1d.short_description: A so-called "Lotto" carpet with stylized pseudo-*kufic* (Kufesque) inscription around the border. The red field has an allover pattern of arabesques in yellow with touches of white, blue, red, and brown. The arabesques form quatrefoiled and irregular compartments symmetrically arranged. The green border is decorated with an angular interlacing derived from *kufic* writing, in white with brown outlines. The guard bands have a ribbon design in red and brown on a blue ground (inner guard band) or in blue on a red ground (outer guard band).

177e0811-3e15-572b-95e1-041901bc5047.name: Carpet
177e0811-3e15-572b-95e1-041901bc5047.description:
Spanish carpet of the Holbein series, incomplete.  
Field: The field is divided into two columns with each containing five squares, one of which is incomplete. Each square houses a double-frame octagon, whose vertices are surrounded by radial geometric decorations. These converge on a central eight-pointed star that rotates counterclockwise.  
Each square is separated by a geometric valance, which is repeated successively, and whose motifs could be inspired by calligraphic stylisations.  
The background of the field is formed by reticulated polychrome motifs, leaving no part of the carpet without decoration.  
Border: Only part of border decoration is preserved on one of its narrower sides and consist of stylised plants and trees.  
The carpet utilises wool of blue, red, yellow and green. According to Campana (Campana, M, 1966: Tappeti d’́occidente, p. 38) this carpet is similar to oriental productions that are known as the Holbein series.  
A similar copy is also presented in the catalogue of the Washington Textile Museum, Plate XVI.  
In Spain, very few copies of this series are preserved and the best preserved specimens can be found in the convent of Santa Clara de Medina de Pomar, although it presents great differences in colour.

17c36009-e18b-5127-b723-8d7a283f5251.name: Grotesque Animal Carpet fragment
17c36009-e18b-5127-b723-8d7a283f5251.description:
A rare Safavid period Herati pile carpet-border fragment with dark blue and yellow-coloured backgrounds, showing animal heads growing amongst flowers, buds and leaves on meandering vegetal stems. The animals appearing on the symmetrically laid out arabesque design are lions, bulls, fish, foxes and horses. The delicate rendition of the animals has made use of a variety of colour shades to highlight the animals’ features. This can be seen especially on the horses’ foreheads and noses, where fine ivory knots are gradually mixed with the red knots to give a pink-shaded impression, accentuating the shape of the horses’ heads. The bellies of the fish have been rendered in a similar fashion, with paler cream threads used to shade the undersides.  
  
The term “grotesque animal design” is applied to this type of pattern, where animals’ heads spring out of stems. This type of pattern first appeared on Middle Eastern metal wares and on works on paper during the Seljuq and Ilkhanid periods (11th – 14th centuries), and subsequently on Safavid manuscripts and textiles. The Burrell fragment seems to belong to a unique carpet of its age and place of manufacture. And although very little is known about who owned it before Sir William Burrell acquired it, a small number of other fragments from the same carpet have survived. One border fragment was acquired by the Nationalmuseum in Stockholm, Sweden, in 1899 from the art collector Fredrik Robert Martin (1868 - 1933), a Swedish Islamic Art historian, orientalist, collector and diplomat; four fragments from the centre field of the carpet are in the Musee des Arts Decoratifs in Paris, France; another field fragment is in the Museum of Fine Art in Boston, Massachusetts, USA; and an eighth fragment is reputed to be in a collection in Hanover, Germany.
17c36009-e18b-5127-b723-8d7a283f5251.method_for_provenance: Stylistic analysis. Part of a large carpet with other known fragments in public collections

1834ffc3-67d6-503e-b212-298000fe04fb.name: Carpet
1834ffc3-67d6-503e-b212-298000fe04fb.short_description: Throughout a history of political instability, carpet design would potentially incorporate political realities and cultural conditions of the time as well as geo-politically sensitive landmarks. Knotted in the late 19th century in the city of Herat, known for large Turkmen workshops, hand-spun wool and natural dyes, this carpet depicts Sultan Ghiyath al Din Muhammad from the Ghurid Dynasty (1163 - 1202) riding his horse through the Afghan landscape. The landscape includes prominent landmarks such as the UNESCO-protected Minaret of Jam, the Buddha of Bamyian and other monuments of the local Islamic and Buddhist heritage. The carpet bears the signature of the craftsmen with the words, "the work of Wijdani." Textiles such as this fine example would offer one of the few decorative elements in Afghan homes as symbols of status.

18c89e89-802f-568c-9a64-e8df0931e34b.name: ‘Portuguese’ Carpet
18c89e89-802f-568c-9a64-e8df0931e34b.description:
In the past the origin of this type of carpet has been the object of many theories, however, when taking into consideration their technical characteristics, especially the use of Jufti knotting, it seems to be agreed that they were woven in Khorasan. The “Portuguese” carpet-type’s name derives from the figurative motifs present in the four corners of the field depicting European boats and sailors, and identified as Portuguese because of Portuguese presence in the Persian Gulf throughout the 16th century.  
Eventually the Portuguese diplomatic and religious missionaries, as well as traders would bring prints and drawings to the East, which would inspire painters and other local artists.  
Independently of their being Portuguese people or those of other European nationalities, these representations lend themselves to the exotic dimension, as well as to the marked impact of “the foreigner” in Persian art.  
As with the other known carpets (12 pieces, as well as some fragments), this example has the distinctive and prominent central-field design consisting of indented serrated, concentric flame-like bands. The middle of the central lozenge is decorated with a small rosette, itself flanked by four large palmettes, with nautical scenes in the corners. These are made up of single vessels manned by two figures in European dress and accompanied by sea monsters and figures swimming in the water.

19436bb0-e910-5297-bf56-dfae31040762.name: Polonaise carpet
19436bb0-e910-5297-bf56-dfae31040762.short_description: The MAK owns six sensational silk carpets from Central Iran, brocaded with silver and gold, which were produced during the reign of Shah Abbas I (r. 1587–1629). He is said to have shown a lively interest in carpets and to have established court workshops. The so-called Polonaise carpets were not manufactured in Poland, as examples with European emblems preserved there might assume, but rather, to some extent, made especially for export to Europe. Although Alois Riegl, the former textile curator of the Austrian Museum of Art and Industry (today, the MAK), pointed to this misleading name, coined in the 19th century, it nonetheless stuck. Polonaise, respectively Shah Abbas carpets of the late 16th century, are localised in the silk city of Kashan; in the 17th century, workshops of the new Safavid capital, Isfahan, possibly overtook production. They are distinguished by a voluminous patterning, the once lively, strong colours, whose effect is hardly imaginable today, and the silver and gold brocading.

194eae24-474f-5738-ae6d-da405e61b7f3.name: Wall hanging
194eae24-474f-5738-ae6d-da405e61b7f3.description: After an apprenticeship as a stage painter, Erwin Hahs (1887–1970) began to study at the Berlin School of Decorative Arts under Bruno Paul. Through his contact with Walter Gropius, he received a commission for a wall hanging for Gropius’ building at the Cologne Werkbund exhibition in 1913 (Work Federation of Architects and Builders). He was appointed to the School of Applied Arts Burg Giebichenstein after the First World War. There, he founded a new painting class in 1919 and was made professor in 1922. In addition to teaching, he continued his work as a designer, creating wall hangings for public spaces, stage curtains for theaters etc. This may have sparked his interest in the art of tapestry. In 1925, under the direction of Benita Koch-Otte, two tapestries were produced after designs by Erwin Hahs. The collection of Burg Giebichenstein features a photograph of one of the tapestries, whose remains are unknown. The other tapestry is this piece, which was formerly in the artist’s family estate.

19712bce-3702-52aa-a6e1-3f6ba2529789.name: ‘Transylvanian’ rug
19712bce-3702-52aa-a6e1-3f6ba2529789.description:
The term “Transylvanian” rug is related to small prayer rugs made in the villages of Anatolia but preserved mostly in the region of Transylvania. Commonly these are decorated with two prayer niches in mirror image and have a border filled with elongated, polygonal cartouches.  
The Kraków rug represents both these features. The red field of the double niche is ornamented with palmettes and cogwheels organised along the vertical axis, and two flowering branches flanking it. The indigo-colour spandrels are filled with an ornament of the “rosette and leaf”-type with large rosettes among lanceolate leaves. In the main border, flanked by two narrower borders, there are cartouches with lozenges, placed on the red ground.  
So-called Transylvanian carpets were very popular in Poland and many are preserved in Polish collections. We can also find such rugs depicted in Polish paintings. On the refectory ceiling in the former Piarist monastery in Rzeszów, a Transylvanian rug covers the table in a scene from “The meeting in Emaus”, painted at the end of 17th century by Łukasz Ziemecki. It looks very much like the rug in the Kraków collection. It is interesting that in the Brukenthal National Museum in Sibiu, Transylvania, a rug with almost the same design as the Kraków version is preserved. The only visible differences are colouristic. On the edge of the Sibiu rug is an inscription with the date 1675. Therefore, the Kraków rug was probably made in third quarter of 17th century.

1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.name: Prayer rug.
1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.description:
This rug belongs to the group of prayer rugs from Ghiordes, a village between Izmir and Ushak, where most of the Anatolian prayer rugs were manufactured in the AH 12th–13th / AD 18th–19th centuries. It shows in the central field a pointed niche with a half-niche on each side on a cream background. The motif of the three-arched niche derives from rug patterns of Ottoman courtly manufacturing during the AH 10th–11th / AD 16th–17th centuries. In contrast to these original designs, the columns of this rug are based on stylised carnations. Edged with trefoiled blossoms they support the main niche and separate it from the half-niches. The spandrels are filled with stylised carnations on a dark-blue background. A large bouquet of flowers hangs in the apex, reaching nearly to the bottom where a row of carnations is presented. The panel above the spandrels is filled with rosette blossoms and ornaments.  
The border is formed by two horizontal and two vertical stripes showing an endless pattern of stylised plants on a dark blue background. The wavy motif of a flower scroll alternately coloured in blue, red and tan is repeated on the inner and outer guard bands.
1a476191-4d4c-570a-ab3c-a49e3f98f66c.short_description: Prayer rug, probably from Ghiordes. In the central field the rug shows a pointed niche with a half-niche on each side. Stylised carnations and bouquets of flowers are the most important motifs of this rug. The central field is framed with a border.

1bcda966-0907-5cad-9985-11a269890212.name: Niche or prayer carpet
1bcda966-0907-5cad-9985-11a269890212.short_description: The carpet represents a crowning achievement of Ottoman court manufacturing in the second half of the 16th century. Besides Istanbul as the place of manufacture, where knotted carpet production at this time is verified, the silk city of Bursa remains an option for its origin. The so-called *saz* style – emanating from the court – shaped the period’s textile arts, book painting and ceramics, bringing them into full bloom. The niche or prayer carpet is an early example of the incorporation of architectonic motifs ‒ here, two flanking columns ‒ into carpet art. Nearly perfectly preserved, this Ottoman carpet shows an arch in the field, characteristic for the genre as a decoration or stylization of a prayer niche (*mihrab*) in a mosque. Technically, the Ottoman carpets are similar to those of the Mamluk and Safavid empires, since they feature asymmetrical knots allowing a nuanced design. However, the story of the 11 carpet makers summoned by Sultan Murad III from Cairo to Istanbul in 1585 shows that craftsmen could travel and work throughout the Ottoman Empire.

1bf69490-ca90-5412-8d8f-d71fe19527b9.name: Carpet
1bf69490-ca90-5412-8d8f-d71fe19527b9.description:
Incomplete carpet of Renaissance style, the decoration of which is articulated on the axis of symmetry that reproduces stylised scrollwork linked upon a hexagonal frame, depicting floral shapes resembling open tulips and lilies. Due to the carpet being incomplete, only two whole hexagons and part of another are visible.  
Field: The field contains a complete decorative motif and two alternating half motifs on the sides.  
Border: The border is separated from the field by a narrow line and is formed by Renaissance era motifs where opposing decorative floral mallets appear that house other forms of grotesques in an upright position.  
The motifs of the field and the frame are outlined in yellow.  
The carpet consists of a woollen warp and weft in its natural colour as well as the use of brown. The decoration is made of dark green, yellow, orange and red wool.  
This carpet was probably made in the workshops of Alcaraz due to similarities in colour and design with other pieces from these workshops rather than with those in the Cuenca area. However, this assumption does not definitively rule out that such a piece may have been made in the workshops of Cuenca.  
Although it does not fully fit other carpets from the Lotto series, this piece certainly draws inspiration from it. In the field, the green decoration stands out upon the orange-red field, the colours being reversed in the border. The border is incomplete and has suffered some damage. This carpet is published by Ferrandis Torres, J. 1933, Catalog of the Exhibition of Old Spanish Carpets. Madrid, nº 30, plate XXI, p. 111, and was displayed by the Count Welczeck. In addition, there is a similar piece in the same catalogue (no. 33, p. 112.)  
It is possible that it corresponds with carpet number 6 of the Weissberger collection, although the measurements differ slightly.

1bfea8bf-24e7-5c2a-971a-d0c258670c2c.name: Kilim, *Rašić's pattern*
1bfea8bf-24e7-5c2a-971a-d0c258670c2c.description: At the end of the 19th and in the first decades of the 20th century Pirot kilims were very popular in urban interiors in Serbia. The kilim of large size belongs to *batal* type which was used for floor covering. It was owned by Borislav Muškatirović, ironmonger from Belgrade and his wife Nada. The kilim was decorated with *Rašić's pattern* (*Rašićeva šara*) and the colours used are red, black, blue, green, orange, yellow and white. *Rašić's pattern* was named after divisional general Mihailo Rašić, who served as an orderly officer, adjutant and Court Marshal to King Milan and King Alexander of Serbia in the late 19th century. According to tradition, Rašić escorted king Milan on the journey to the East and brought back the kilim with the pattern which Pirot weavers used as a sample. The same patterns are found on Karabakh kilims from Caucasus and Sivas and Malatya kilims from Anatolia.

1c321ff2-f9fc-51f3-9f64-5dbfe87b3948.name: *Der Tag wird kommen (The Day will Come)*
1c321ff2-f9fc-51f3-9f64-5dbfe87b3948.description:
This bright, colourful tapestry is made from dyed wool. Four rectangular fields seem to be in front of a white background with a bright red sun. The upper right field shows five male figures with arms stretched towards the sky. They stand naked upon a field of skeletons and flowers symbolizing a graveyard. The living and the dead are separated by formal antagonisms in respect to orientation, flesh, eyes and hands. The shape of the people’s bodies and limbs, however, parallels the bone structure of the dead. The artwork’s title translates to “The Day will Come”, which might point to a resurrection of the dead accompanied by the downfall of earth, symbolized by the tilting flowery fields on the left side of the tapestry.  
In her use of colour, human shape and ornament, Margarita Pellegrin is influenced by the naïve art of the South American natives. During her time in Chile, she was at first assistant and later on lecturer at Chile University in Antofagasta, both were positions that presumably served to intensify Pellegrin’s artistic exchange with local artists. The power that this artwork assigns to life and death, taking place as a magic, yet integral part of nature, might reflect a perspective linked to the close-to-nature lifestyle of the indigenous South American people Pellegrin encountered when she was living in Chile in the 1960s.  
The artist studied at Dresden Hochschule für Bildende Künste, where she met her future husband Hernando Léon. In 1963, she moved to Chile with him. From 1964-69, she worked at Chile University in Antofagasta. After the military coup in 1973, she returned, together with her husband and their three children, to the German Democratic Republic. Since then, she had been living as a freelance artist in Dresden until her death in 2016.

1c83b59f-bba0-5630-b9da-a13188474ac4.name: Prayer rug
1c83b59f-bba0-5630-b9da-a13188474ac4.description: Outlined on the contrasting green of the central field, the red prayer niche has a stepped arch fringed with hooks along its inner edges. Inside the niche, a floral composition encircled by 12 tiny ewers recalls the mosque-lamp motif. A recurrent motif of prayer rug designs, ewers are traditionally associated with an *aide-mémoire* meant to remind the believer of the ritual ablution required before prayer. The present rug features a main border reminiscent of the so-called Gothic border of 16th- and 17th-century carpets, and, in the upper corners of the main field, stylised vegetal motifs, which show the Western influence on Turkish art. This rather unusual blending of two stylistic sources is illustrative of the two main “forces” with a strong impact on the decorative vocabulary of 19th-century Ottoman carpets: the Turkish tradition and the influence of European art. The bright colour scheme is quite remarkable and its sharp contrasts almost shocking compared mainly to the fine colouring of the Gördes and Kula carpets that reigned supreme on the European market of Oriental carpets at the turn of the century.

1d09ef00-f799-5214-9495-07ffcd396eb9.name: Hungarian Silk Rug
1d09ef00-f799-5214-9495-07ffcd396eb9.description: The designer of this rug was the painter and designer Pál Horti (1865-1907), one of the Hungarian pioneers in modern applied arts and a distinctive representative of the Art Nouveau style at the turn of the 20th century.                                                                                                                                                                                                               The central field is decorated with a peacock, blue-green rosette inset against a terracotta base. It is connected to the inner stripe of the border with four curved tendrils that end in leaves. The inner border is ornamented with cherry-red against a green base. The outer, wider border shows Art Nouveau wavy ornaments in cherry red, blue and yellow against a grey base. The wave turns terracotta at the corners.  The carpet was exhibited at the Turin Exhibition of 1902.

1d2768ad-2141-599f-8c1c-15909185df1d.name: Kilim, *Zorić’s pattern*
1d2768ad-2141-599f-8c1c-15909185df1d.description: Pirot kilims were presented in many exhibitions abroad among which was the World Fair (*Exposition Universelle*) in Paris in 1900. For this occasion, engineer Svetozar Zorić, a professor at the Belgrade Higher School (future University of Belgrade), designed a pattern which was named after him *Zorić’s pattern* (*Zorićeva šara*). Different Pirot kilim patterns designed for 1900 Paris World Fair were exhibited in *Ilija M. Kolarac Endowment* in Belgrade in 1899. The exhibited patterns expressed the search for the national style inherent to arts of that period. This kilim, decorated with *Zorić’s pattern*, belongs to *šestak* (a kilim of six square ells) type, which was used as a cover for bed or wall. The colours used are: red, green, yellow, white and black.

1d6c98e5-6c31-5edc-99b5-0d1528d23d86.name: *Arbeiterfestspiele (Workers' Festival)*
1d6c98e5-6c31-5edc-99b5-0d1528d23d86.description:
This tapestry was a commission of the FDGB on the occasion of the *Arbeiterfestspiele* (workers‘ festival) in 1974. Arbeiterfestspiele had been arranged in the German Democratic Republic (GDR) almost every year since 1959, it was a cultural festival of “Lebensfreude”, or joy of life, at which fine artists and folk artists from within the country and abroad would meet. Correspondingly, the tapestry shows a colourful and detailed narrative that illustrates every aspect of these meetings.  
The artwork shows eight horizontal rows of human figures. They are characterised by their silhouettes; ornamental seams delineate the bodies’ inner contours. The formally strict alignment of figures is given relief to with elements that overlap into neighbouring rows or that interact with objects or other people. This form resembles the *Trajan’s Column*, the key artwork of figural narrative that has been standing in Rome since c. AD 112, being a canonical artwork for European artists throughout the ages.  
Prominently positioned on the middle left is the emblem of the workers‘ festival. Noticeably smaller is the abbreviation of the commissioner, the FDGB. Public procurement in the GDR fostered a special kind of art production that was markedly infused with socialist ideology. The predominant colours in this tapestry – bright yellows and reds, accentuated with blueish green and purple in the darker bottom part – are the main colours associated with the red and golden flag of Soviet Russia which is manifold reflected in the political iconology of the GDR. The artist signed her name among floral elements on the lower right side.  
Ursula Jobst had managed different folk art circles since 1959 and committed herself to amateur art groups in the districts of Leipzig and Altenburg. In the 1970s, she initiated the revival of the historical Lindenau painting school at Lindenau-Museum Altenburg. She subsequently was managing and teaching at the Studio Bildende Kunst at Lindenau-Museum Altenburg until 1999.

1ea784c2-43a6-5b56-a630-cf0e65b51980.name: Carpet
1ea784c2-43a6-5b56-a630-cf0e65b51980.description:
In 1664 Jean-Baptiste Colbert, King Louis XIV’s minister in charge of buildings, began a campaign to transform the Louvre (the royal residence at the time) into the grandest and largest palace in Europe. Central to this project was the renovation of a 1,450-foot-long space known as the Grande Galerie. This amazing interior overlooked the Seine and connected the Louvre and Tuileries palaces.  
For this hall Colbert commissioned the Savonnerie carpet factory to produce ninety-three carpets. The commission’s scale was unprecedented in the history of French woven arts, and the carpets that were ultimately produced rank among the greatest artistic achievements of the 1600s.  
Production of the carpets, which were each some thirty feet in length and required the construction of new looms made from particularly long and stout tree trunks, began in 1668 and continued until 1688, by which time the king had lost interest in the project and moved the court to Versailles. In the following centuries the carpets were given away as diplomatic gifts or, on special occasions, brought out of storage for use at the royal residences and elsewhere.  
In 1788 the Museum’s carpet was sent for one day to the Paris church of Saint-Roch for the marriage of the Duke de Montmorency. And on June 18, 1919, when the treaty that ended World War I was signed at Versailles, twenty-four of the carpets adorned the Galerie des Glaces (Hall of Mirrors).  
Although each of the Savonnerie carpets is individual in design, they share certain distinct traits: a black background, a modified egg-and-leaf border, scrolling acanthus leaves in the corners, and cartouches at each end that contain either a landscape or allegorical scene. All display decorations replete with royal emblems. The design of the Museum’s carpet includes the crowned monogram of the king four times in the center and a crowned globe with the motto NEC PLURIBUS IMPAR (One Among Many) at each end.

1ea85cb9-0757-5c4b-8946-2a77eb3721c6.name: *Padishah* kilim
1ea85cb9-0757-5c4b-8946-2a77eb3721c6.description: This extremely fine silk tapestry weaving with metal thread was given its name on account of the word *Padishah* woven into four cartouches. This is the Persian word for emperor or prince. The overall design corresponds to that of a medallion carpet. In the centre of the inner field is a green-ground medallion with a battle between a dragon and a phoenix. The spandrels contain red-ground quarter-medallions filled with the mythical creatures called *qilin*. These motifs derive from East Asian cultures and have been known in Islamic art at least since the 13th century. In addition the inner field is filled with a number of blossoms and birds. In the borders are elongated cartouches alternating with quatrefoil medallions. The cartouches are filled with beasts of prey, the medallions with grotesque faces. Technically this tapestry weaving, unlike a knotted carpet, consists only of warp and weft threads. There are no knots forming a pile. The special character of the piece lies in its materials. The areas in the field and border which today appear grey were originally gleaming silver. The yellow and red surfaces were also adorned with metal threads. These fine metal threads, which were spun around a silk core filament, have by now become corroded, so that they no longer effectively reflect the light and the surrounding colour surfaces. One must also imagine the tapestry as highly and vividly colourful. Since silk is very delicate, the colours, particularly on the front, have become seriously faded on account of their exposure to light. The blurred impression given by the motifs is accounted for by the technique. Various coloured wefts have been interlocked, that is, alternately wound around a common warp. This produces a soft outline, but avoids the appearance of slits, which would have detracted from the stability of the textile.

1fe8c60c-8233-5366-8669-298db2abbead.name: War-Rug
1fe8c60c-8233-5366-8669-298db2abbead.short_description: Since the late 1970's, Afghanistan experienced a continuous state of civil war punctuated by foreign occupation. Afghan carpets were one of the country’s most famous folk arts as an important trade item. Carpets had a strong social meaning, and often comprised part of a bride’s dowry. Shortly after the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan the "war rug" appeared on the market, drawing great attention from consumers, collectors and museums. Adapting the Baluchi convention of depicting plants and animals on their carpets, refugees in Pakistan started to weave images of war. This particular rug represents the scars of the Soviet-Afghan war of 1979-89.

20307948-fcd2-5df5-81f3-34a9ced1ac3d.name: Knotted carpet (fragment)
20307948-fcd2-5df5-81f3-34a9ced1ac3d.description:
The oldest preserved knotted carpet fragments date back to the Islamic era and were produced in Egypt between the 8th and 10th centuries. However, only a few carpets produced before the 16th century have stood the test of time. Most of the preserved historical pieces found today stem from subsequent periods. These carpets are divided into two categories: those produced in urban or court weaving mills, and those hand-crafted in countryside homes. The former is closely linked to stylistic developments of contemporaneous art. To create their elaborate symmetrical patterns a template – provided by contemporary painters – was often used. The manner in which rugs were produced in the countryside differed: the pattern designs were long-lived and traditionally passed down from one generation to the next.  
The pattern template for this carpet has also been preserved. Arabesque and palmette tendrils, as well as cloud bands, cover the red middle field in horizontal and vertical mirroring patterns. They are framed with a broad dark-green border of spiral tendrils, palmettes, and birds. This type of design emerged in Herat and Kashan, beginning around the late 16th century, and later also Isfahan.

2150f414-c029-55db-bbc1-2009b71383c4.name: *Lotto* carpet
2150f414-c029-55db-bbc1-2009b71383c4.short_description:
In the central field, the carpet shows a network of yellow stylised arabesques arranged in crosses and octagons on a red ground. This decoration is characteristic of so-called Lotto carpets, named after the Renaissance painter Lorenzo Lotto (AD 1480-1556/57 / Hegira 885-963), who immortalised such a carpet on a famous altarpiece in 1542.  
  
‘Lotto’ carpets usually have a border in pseudo-kufi, which is sometimes interpreted as a combination of the letters lam and alif. Here, on the other hand, it is a simple leaf tendril on a medium blue ground, which perhaps goes back to Persian models.  
  
‘Lotto’ carpets were produced in commercial workshops in western Turkey from about 1516 to about 1700.
2150f414-c029-55db-bbc1-2009b71383c4.method_for_datation: By comparison with stylistically similar and approximately dated objects

materials: Wool (warp, weft and pile)

21ac3a7d-d4d0-5c9e-9017-11a7d6aa7b6c.name: Summer carpet
21ac3a7d-d4d0-5c9e-9017-11a7d6aa7b6c.description:
Wool carpets had little fashion in India during the heat of summer and damp of the monsoon season. Wool may smell or feel sodden underfoot in humid environments and a heavy pile may be unwanted in hot climates. At such times, summer carpets were preferred for furnishing domestic spaces. Usually made of cotton and silk threads, they varied in size and elaborateness depending on the means of the patron.  
This summer carpet features very fine, chain-stitched flora and fauna motifs in shades of pink, green and yellow floss silk on a pale pink cotton ground. A lobed rosette medallion at centre is repeated in quadrants at each corner. The arrangement calls to mind the layout of medallion carpets. Interspersed among the larger floral motifs are smaller floral motifs of great variety, size, and form. Secreted among the floral motifs are small animals such as rabbits, deer, and birds. They are repeated in the wide border.  
Much of the carpet’s charm derives from the embroiderers’ minute attention to detail. An intriguing variety of flowers, primarily sewn in pink threads, is offset by yellow threads differentiating petals and parts of the flowers. Green threads become leaves and stems which weave around the blossoms and form the medallions’ lobed borders. There is interest in naturalism, but it is offset by idealism. Every petal is in full bloom, a defiance of nature’s limitations. The carpet offers to the viewer’s imagination the most beautiful summer garden with prancing animals delighting in a display more perfect than nature.  
The textile is characteristic of Mochi embroidery of the 18th century from the Kutch region of Gujarat, India. Many beautiful examples are known to have been made during this period. A large one such as this may have been made at an urban or court workshop in the region. An inscription embroidered inside one border is now too degraded to read. To preserve the fragile carpet, netting has been gently tacked to the textile.

224ac8b1-6853-53b0-9795-ce4a3ebc91c3.name: *Der wunderbare Fischzug (The Miraculous Draught of Fish)*
224ac8b1-6853-53b0-9795-ce4a3ebc91c3.description: In 1515/16, on commission to Pope Leo X, Raphael produced ten large-format preparatory drawings for tapestries which were intended for the Sistine Chapel in the Vatican. These tapestries, which are among the most outstanding achievements of the High Renaissance in Rome, were woven in the manufactory operated by Pieter van Aelst in Brussels (they are now held in the Pinacoteca Vaticana, Città del Vaticano). Designed for use in celebratory masses, they depict scenes from the life of the two chief apostles, saints Peter and Paul. A few of Raphael's cartoons turned up in Genoa in 1623 and were purchased by the Prince of Wales, the later King Charles I. The designs were used again at the Mortlake Tapestry Works in England. The Mortlake works not only wove a series for Charles I but also produced the one that later came into the collection of Augustus the Strong in Dresden. Three of the six tapestries in Dresden are dedicated to Saint Peter, the other three to Saint Paul. The depiction of the Miraculous Draught of Fish (Luke 5, 1-11) begins the series devoted to Saint Peter: although Peter has been fishing all night without success, he follows Jesus’ instruction to put out into the Sea of Galilee and cast his net once again. This time the fishermen are so successful that their two boats return to the shore overloaded with fish. Peter and his companions James and John recognise the greatness of Jesus, fall at his feet and worship him. Jesus then summons them to become his disciples and follow him. The dynamic, monumental figures reveal a stylistic proximity to Michelangelo. The restoration of the entire series between 1991 and 1997 was made possible by a generous donation from the businessman Rudolf Augustus Oetker.

In 1728 Elector Friedrich Augustus I of Saxony (who was also King Augustus II of Poland) purchased it from him for his art collection.

225df813-478d-5038-a7f6-a57c1047907d.name: Carpet
225df813-478d-5038-a7f6-a57c1047907d.description:
Rectangular carpet from the Crown or Laurel series, derived from the Holbein series.  
Field: The field consists of crowns with an octagonal shape formed by foliage and shapes reminiscent of stylised cobs. Spread out cruciformly within the octagonal shapes are plant motifs that are curled into decorative scrollwork and ataurique motifs. The green coloured foliage stands out on the orange-red background.  
Border: The border consists of vegetal candlestick motifs.  
A two-strand Franciscan knot strip separates the field from the border. All the decorative motifs of the carpet are outlined in yellow.  
The warp is of naturally coloured linen and the weft is of naturally coloured wool. The decorative aspects are defined by woollen knots of green, yellow and orange red.  
This carpet is similar to one published by Ferrandis Torres, J. 1933, Catalog of the Exhibition of Ancient Spanish Carpets. Madrid, No. 36, Plate XXVIII, p. 112, presented by Count Welczeck. It is the carpet that appears in the Weissberger collection with the number 7.  
In the Holbein series the octagons were separated by registers, whilst in this one such a demarcation is only suggested in the intersection of the columns by a partial cruciform design.  
On the other hand, the decoration of the border and the field corresponds to the renovating models of the Renaissance period.

2292af80-5b22-5a47-a417-5ef4d3e112f5.name: Animal carpet
2292af80-5b22-5a47-a417-5ef4d3e112f5.description: The field design of this carpet is exceptional. Four double-headed creatures dominate the vertical centre of the field. They are embedded in cream-coloured star forms. The free spaces between the stars are filled with multicoloured octagons. The star points directed outwards and the animal heads each also pointing outwards lend a special dynamic to the carpet. This piece displays two technical peculiarities. On the one hand, the knots are partly offset, presumably in order to achieve the desired incline of the diagonals. A further animal carpet (KGM 1888,112) in the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin displays this technique. A special feature are the yellow wefts which are additionally inserted at regular intervals. It is assumed that they mark the day’s work of the weaver. These marks are also found in the so-called Dragon-Phoenix carpet (I.4) in the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin.
