2494bdbf-c4c0-5e69-9919-23f82e0ed33e.name: Carpet
2494bdbf-c4c0-5e69-9919-23f82e0ed33e.description:
Field: Carpet is formed by three cloths of a navy blue field in which the light blue floral decoration stands out, with eight rows of small branches in ascending and alternating positions.  
Border: The carpet consists of three sets of borders with the central one being the widest and consisting of light blue carnation vegetal motifs on a dark background. In the corners, a pomegranate is featured bisecting the angles between the two borders.  
The two narrow borders that frame the central border consist of dark blue geometric patterns on a light blue background. Wool is used in the two shades of blue.  
The production technique of looping is used to add some additional wefts, which go from selvedge to selvedge and are taken out in the form of rings to the surface with the aid of an auxiliary needle, whenever the design demands it.  
This technique was common to almost the entire peninsular territory and depending on the areas where it was carried out, it received different names: "garbancillo", "caracolillo" or "caramullo" as well as the "Alpujarras technique", a term referred to in historical texts linking it with the region in Andalusia. This reference however is not entirely appropriate as this technique would be found in other regions and the Andalusian reference only emerged at the end of the 19th century, despite the technique being significantly older.  
The same technique is visible in textile weavings of the Balearic Islands particularly for wall coverings as well as floor coverings of hemp and silk known as a *catalufa*.  
Most of the pieces of looped decorative patterns found in the museum, have been produced between the 18th and early 20th centuries. This decoration is possibly inspired by fabric ornamentations from the middle of the 18th century, particularly the corner motifs. The fine decorative solution used in the corners, suggests that it is inspired by cultured motifs, but the simplicity of chromatism indicates that it is a later production in time. In some areas, it produces a secondary decorative effect, since it uses two very contrasting colours.

24d526fe-7421-53a9-aca1-e36f943f39ee.name: Floral carpet
24d526fe-7421-53a9-aca1-e36f943f39ee.description:
A 17th century Mughal Indian pile carpet with an Arabesque floral design that consists of a wine red centre-field and a dark blue border. The centre-field is filled with a symmetrically laid out Arabesque network of multi-coloured palmettes intertwined with a more delicate pink network of vines with grapes and small leaves and flowers. This delicate pink network, imposed on the wine-red background, with no dark borderlines defining it and separating it from the wine-red colour of the field, is typical of Mughal Indian carpet designs.  
  
The border holds an ivory coloured winding vegetal scroll that meanders between large multi-coloured palmettes and rosettes. The bottom end of the border shows a well planned distribution of palmettes and scrolls, with the corner motifs worked out to transition smoothly from the horizontal to the vertical sides of the carpet. The top end of the carpet border seems to have been extended beyond the natural flow of the repeat patter of the border to accommodate the extension of the repeat design in the centre-field, causing the border patter to get disrupted in the corner areas, with palmettes merging to accommodate the transition from vertical to horizontal. This situation seems to have been caused by a mismatch between the over all design cartoon being used and the desired length to be achieved for the carpet. A not an uncommon situation found on many hand woven pile carpets.
24d526fe-7421-53a9-aca1-e36f943f39ee.obtention: Gifted by Sir William and Lady Burrell to the City of Glasgow, 1944
24d526fe-7421-53a9-aca1-e36f943f39ee.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: floral motifs; palmette; Iranian influence; vegetal arabesque; grape vine
materials: Cotton warp and weft; wool pile

254e7f7c-61c1-5991-8986-210fe384e734.name: Pile carpet fragment
254e7f7c-61c1-5991-8986-210fe384e734.description: This is the lower section of a border with a relatively legible *kufic* inscription which can be roughly translated: “*\[Blessing\] from God to the owner, what was made...*” The rich decoration is divided into two sections. One has a greenish-blue ground and the other a deep red. The first section is ornamented with two rows of lozenges with a cotton off-white contour, followed by two thin bands, one orange and the other greenish-blue, on which rest a mustard-yellow garland with triple-lobed leaves, surrounding the inscription as if to give it emphasis. The inscription is woven with undyed cotton on a deep red woollen ground. The vivid colours and dense, carefully worked weaving with additional wefts give this fragment its special quality.
254e7f7c-61c1-5991-8986-210fe384e734.method_for_datation: It belongs to a group of fragments attributed to Egypt and their dating between the 8th and the 11th century. In addition, the form of the *kufic* inscription belongs to this period
254e7f7c-61c1-5991-8986-210fe384e734.method_for_provenance: Factors that determine the provenance: 1. The use of linen, which is the basic Egyptian fibre, for both warps and wefts; 2. The left-twisting (S) spin of the materials is also an Egyptian feature. Linen warps S-spun, Z-plied are found in Coptic fabrics of the 9th-10th century. Right-twisted spinning (Z) is rarely found in Group A; 3. The technique of weaving with cut-pile loops which continues the long-standing Egyptian tradition of weaving with a pile made of loops; 4. The pattern, colouring and techniques of this group fragments bear a close resemblance to contemporaneous Coptic textiles. 5. The fragments display similarities to certain inscribed and non-inscribed fragments from Fustat.
254e7f7c-61c1-5991-8986-210fe384e734.bibliography: Published in Theologou, J., Ozoline, A., Sartzetakis, Y., "Fustat Carpet Fragments", *Hali*, 156 (summer 2008): 65-71.
254e7f7c-61c1-5991-8986-210fe384e734.author: Mina Moraitou
keywords: Fustat fragment; geometric; kufic script; inscription band; linen; wool; cotton

255f45d9-17b4-565e-8c90-1983dbce43f3.name: *Majlis* Carpet
255f45d9-17b4-565e-8c90-1983dbce43f3.short_description:
This large-scale textile is termed the *majlis* (council) carpet. Handcrafted in Hamdan from wool and camel hair utilizing the Seneh knot, it represents the spatiality of the Gulf-Arab "sitting place". The *majlis* unites notions of privacy and hospitality appearing to be incompatible in one entity.  
  
While the carpet would have stretched from one corner of the *majlis* to the other with design elements such as the paisley, damascene rose, diamond-shapes and symmetry characteristic of Persian carpets, the discrete sections of the textile embody the different spatial components of the room. The outer segments reflect sitting positions of the head of the household, the family, friends and guests. The centrepiece would offer room to dance, perform music, play board games or display food and coffee. It would have stretched from one corner of the *majlis* to the other.  
  
Due to the cost of these large pieces of art, merchants began cutting apart the separable sections and selling fragments to decorate hallways and corridors. Only few of such majlis carpets may still be reassembled into their original composition.

25615117-b95e-51bc-bba3-33731c28624f.name: Portrait of a young woman
25615117-b95e-51bc-bba3-33731c28624f.description: A young woman on the photograph poses in the interior, lying on the Pirot kilim. She is wearing an overcoat named *džube*, which belongs to traditional urban dress ensemble worn in Kosovo. For this occasion *džube* is turned into an evening dress and combined with modern accessories. The outfit was most probably worn at a costume ball, which was a popular practice at this time, related to the elements of traditional 19th century urban dress. The kilim on the photo is decorated with the *Crown Prince* (*prestolonaslednik*) ornament.

2633161b-f5f4-5b93-9f4f-f9cc6954257e.name: Star Ushak carpet
2633161b-f5f4-5b93-9f4f-f9cc6954257e.short_description:
The star-like motif, which is immediately recognisable, lends this carpet part of its name. The carpet is characterised by a clear arrangement of its motifs and by a distinct palette of the five colours, red, blue, yellow, green and white, as well as a few secondary colours such as purple or pink.  
  
The western Anatolian city of Ushak was a centre of carpet production from the second half of the 15th century. In addition to carpets dominated by the star-like motif, carpets with large medallions were also produced here. Many of these Ushak carpets ended up being exported to Europe where this particular design present here enjoyed particular popularity.

26a27bde-c75d-503b-b339-fc2c2f75b4c7.name: Tree Carpet
26a27bde-c75d-503b-b339-fc2c2f75b4c7.description:
This carpet is one of the best known and most highly respected examples of the classic era of Persian carpet weaving (the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries). The six column-like cypress trees in varied blue-green shades form a striking symmetrical arrangement.  
Originally, the carpet was almost forty feet long, twice as long as it now appears.

276c2c49-a8b4-526b-9394-194f30fc855a.name: Shadda
276c2c49-a8b4-526b-9394-194f30fc855a.description: Caucasian flatweaves in the so-called Soumak technique (wrapping of weft yarn around warp threads) with additional brocades (floating wefts; so-called Cicim technique) are referred to as Shadda; in older literature, they are also called Verneh. Various types of patterns are known. Mostly, pieces were made from two panels, like this example. This Shadda was for personal needs and used as a representative hanging or cover that stood for wealth and high social rank, most probably a part of a bride's dowry. It is dated H.1310 (AD 1892/93) and shows a large caravan of camels. Pieces of this caravan type are well documented in the literature. They are ascribed to the Southern Caucasus, whereby they often feature a static-looking pattern and generally appear somewhat rigid. This Shadda, however, is an excellent example of the caravan type. This fine and superbly done fabric shows a vibrant and skilful drawing of the caravan with its beautiful colours. It is remarkable how the highly stylized motives are diversified and make the piece appear strong and lively yet by no means rigid or crowded, even though lots of little secondary motives fill the field and the border. Along with seven other flatweaves from the holdings of the Museum für Völkerkunde Dresden, this piece was shown in 1986 in the exhibition "Oriental Kilims" in the Islamisches Museum der Staatlichen Museen Berlin (Islamic Museum of the Berlin State Museums, now the Museum für Islamische Kunst) and was published in the accompanying catalogue (Enderlein, V., Orientalische Kelims, Wesel: Uta Hülsey Verlag, 1986: 99, no.51).

277c2330-13d4-5a0a-b00f-b07533e627aa.name: Carpet.
277c2330-13d4-5a0a-b00f-b07533e627aa.description: A large rectangular carpet of the type known as a Medallion Uşak. On a red ground, a large blue primary medallion, in the shape of a slightly flattened oval with pendants, occupies the centre of the carpet and is reflected at either end. Four elaborate secondary medallions, which would have 16 lobes each if they were not interrupted by the border of the main field, occupy the quadrants above and below the central medallion. Each of the carpet's medallions contains arabesque patterns, and the red ground between them is filled as well with a continuous floral pattern which fills the space without appearing to go 'behind' any of the medallions. The carpet's triple border has repeating floral patterns on yellow, red, and blue backgrounds. The compelling abstract complexity of this carpet is testimony to the skill which Ottoman designers lavished on the creation of non-figurative patterns.
277c2330-13d4-5a0a-b00f-b07533e627aa.short_description: A large rectangular carpet of the type known as a Medallion Uşak. The design, which includes elaborate medallions on a ground of a continuous floral pattern, is quite complex and shows the skill with which the Ottomans created non-figurative designs.
277c2330-13d4-5a0a-b00f-b07533e627aa.method_for_datation: The quality of the pattern and the sophistication of its execution have led scholars to attribute this carpet to the late 10th / 16th century, a period of high artistic attainment in Turkey.
277c2330-13d4-5a0a-b00f-b07533e627aa.method_for_provenance: Carpets of this type have been associated with the town of Uşak for many years. Yet while Ottoman historical sources confirm that Uşak was an important center of carpet weaving, it is difficult to be certain that any given carpet was woven there.
277c2330-13d4-5a0a-b00f-b07533e627aa.provenance: Possibly Uşak, a town in west-central Anatolia (modern Turkey).

27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.name: Prayer rug.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.description:
This rug, dominated by the colours red, brown and white, is dedicated to prayer because of its niche motif in the central rectangular field. The niche is formed by a stepped, pointed arch and edged all around with carnations. A geometrical ornament is set against the light brown background of the area below the arch. A floral device replaces the lamp often to be seen in other prayer rugs. The spandrels are filled with five red flowering bushes. There are two transverse panels, one above the spandrels and one below the niche. Both show the same motif of a cloud-band in combination with rosette blossoms filling the spaces. The small central field is framed by a broad border consisting of an inner and an outer row of heavily stylised carnations and seven narrow stripes coloured alternately white and red.  
There were two places, Ghiordes (Gördes in Turkish) and Kula, manufacturing prayer rugs of similar patterns. This rug combines characteristic elements of both: for example, the seven narrow stripes are found in Kula prayer rugs and the niche with two transverse panels and a colour scheme dominated by red are typical of Ghiordes prayer rugs.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.short_description: Rug dedicated to prayer because of the niche motif in the central rectangular field. The floral device in the area below the arch replaces the lamp often to be seen in other prayer rugs. The central field is framed by a border of stylised carnations and seven narrow stripes.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.method_for_datation: In the 13th / 19th century, rugs from Ghiordes and Kula show a strong stylisation of the floral motifs similar to that of the rug described above.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.method_for_provenance: The rug cannot definitely be ascribed to Ghiordes or Kula. It shows characteristics of both manufacturing centres such as the two transverse panels, one at either end of the central field, typical of rugs from Ghiordes, and the seven narrow stripes which are to be found in rugs from Kula.
27f64d8c-b2e4-52c4-a51c-fbe641ebcaef.obtention: Bought for the collection of Wilhelmina von Hallwyl (1844–1930) in Saloniki in 1896. Count and Countess Walther and Wilhelmina von Hallwyl donated the collection and their home to the Swedish state in 1920.

28485e93-6aee-597e-b6d4-519ba9eeb8e4.name: Caucasian Rug
28485e93-6aee-597e-b6d4-519ba9eeb8e4.short_description:
Although the Ummayad and Abbasid caliphates overthrew the Iranian empires in the Caucasus and Azerbaijan, the cultural influence of Persia remains. This Caucasian carpet displays a blend of influences from Islam and pre-Islamic Persia.  
  
Primary colours from natural dyes typically brighten carpets from the Shirvan region with blue likely representing water as a life's source. The symmetry in these textiles creates harmony with repeated shapes such as the *kubpa* (hexagonal medallion) with tooth-like edges and diamonds to protect from the evil eye.  
  
Bright colours and geometric figures adorn this rug with abstracted religious symbols. The *mehrab* (arched prayer niche) denotes the direction toward toward which Muslims pray, Mecca. The upper end of the carpet displays the date, 1281 Hegira (1864 AD). Two chequered rectangles resemble a chess board, which suggests a possible alternative use for this carpet for entertainment during travels.

2862e8f6-d332-5544-a574-53dd68d204ec.name: *Partida de Emigrantes* – Gare Marítima da Rocha de Conde de Óbidos
2862e8f6-d332-5544-a574-53dd68d204ec.description:
Although Portugal never had a tradition of tapestry manufacture, a manufactory for fine hand-woven contemporary tapestries was created in Portalegre in 1948. Weaving by means of a totally manual procedure and on vertical looms from the base up and from the reverse, the manufactory specialised in translating the paintings of famous contemporary Portuguese and international artists into tapestries.  
One of its best examples is a set of three tapestries titled *Partida de Emigrantes* (‘Departure of Emigrants’), based on the murals by José de Almada Negreiros (1873‒1970), a multidisciplinary artist and one of the key-figures of the Portuguese modernist movement. Having foreseen the deterioration of the murals that decorated the departure lounge of the Rocha de Conde de Óbidos Harbour Station, built during the 1940s near the Tagus river in Lisbon, Almada Negreiros suggested that they should be remade into tapestries at Portalegre. Such would be a perfect way to trustingly preserve his artwork.  
With a strong modernist aesthetic and a chromatic richness, these works focus on the departure of emigrants, in a ship docked at Rocha de Conde de Óbidos. The moment of the farewell, and in particular the behaviour of the individuals involved (both the remaining and departing), is depicted vividly. The upper section of the first third of the tapestry shows the control deck with those on the quay saying good-bye below. In the central tapestry the accommodation ladder, already collected and suspended by a crane, is indicative of the moment of departure; at the ship’s bulwark one sees the sad and worried expressions on the faces of those departing. In the third tapestry, close to the prow, one can see wooden scaffolding from which a worker, carrying an object made of cement, looks on those who are departing.

28aa8b45-d054-5e14-b453-dac969602bb2.name: Rug
28aa8b45-d054-5e14-b453-dac969602bb2.description: This arabesque rug features a composition of spiralling stems bearing leaves and blossoms. Its precise drawing and fine weaving were produced by a trained artist and an experienced weaver. It was probably made in a workshop in Isfahan, and its exquisite style evokes the architectural tile decorations, miniature paintings and manuscript drawings from this period. Its minimalist palette of three colours is unusual for classical Persian rugs and is reminiscent of Cairene rugs of the late fifteenth to mid-sixteenth century.

28b0548c-f552-5757-958a-3d914767931a.name: Carpet
28b0548c-f552-5757-958a-3d914767931a.description: This carpet is a typical example of Egyptian carpet production after the fall of the last Mamluk dynasty. The MAK owns three carpets of this group. Nearly square Mamluk carpets like these were often produced for the European market, where they were popular as table carpets. Most were imported to Europe via Venice, which maintained trading bases in Egypt. Today it is assumed that Mamluk carpets were produced in Cairo until at least after the mid-16th century, and that carpets with patterns strongly influenced by the Ottoman style, such as the Cairene Ottoman (T 8344) carpet, up until the first quarter of the 17th century.

2bf9cea5-1c42-51eb-896f-5fb33a3aa734.name: Isfahan Carpet
2bf9cea5-1c42-51eb-896f-5fb33a3aa734.short_description:
This Persian wool carpet displays a central flower vase and a prayer niche (mihrab) at the top. This rug represents an example of textiles produced for the Qajar courts in Isfahan, one of the most prominent centres since the 17th century.  
  
Isfahani carpet manufacturers would employ the seneh knot, harmonious colours and Arabesque flowers such as the carnation and Damascene rose. The roses on the border embody the lively inhabitants of Isfahan.  
  
The top of the carpet reads the "The eternal reign of the Sultan, son of Sultan Mozafaradin Shah Qajar in the village celebrating the factory of Mullah Alimorad 1317 Hegira" (1899). A poem praising Isfahan and the Shah embellishes the carpet with the repetition of the word *zafar* (success, victory), also part of the Sultan's name.

2d16dd66-a963-5f6f-b65b-339f7f17148f.name: Carpet
2d16dd66-a963-5f6f-b65b-339f7f17148f.description:
Carpet composed of three cloths joined together with approximately the same width of red and green wool decoration.  
Field: The decorative motifs on the field are formed by a collection of rhombuses that contain palms with small pineapples with a red core lodged in their centre.  
Borders: It consists of five red borders separated by spans. The short sides are extended with green borders.  
The carpet is topped by a woollen fringe of the same colours as the field and borders, with slight wear on its narrow sides.  
The production technique used in this carpet was common throughout the Iberian Peninsula and was known by different names according to the geographical region in which it was utilised; "garbancillo", "caracolillo" or "caramullo". It is more commonly known as the "Alpujarras technique", a term referred to texts and treaties that geographically linked it with historic Andalusia in southern Spain. However, this reference is not wholly correct as this would only be one of several regions in which the technique was used. Furthermore, this association with the Alpujarras region would only occur at the end of the 19th century, despite the technique being considerably older.  
In the Balearic Islands, a similar technique was used for hemp and silk textiles that would adorn walls as well as floor coverings and are more commonly known as *catalufa*.  
Most of the pieces found in the museum, with their decoratively looped wefts, have been produced between the 18th and early 20th centuries. The technique used in this carpet consisted of adding extra wefts, which go from selvedge to selvedge, and are taken out in the form of rings to the surface through the use of an auxiliary needle, whenever the design demands it.  
The design of this carpet evokes the rural countryside and its decoration imitates the Renaissance period carpets known as “of Toledan brocade”. Another inspiration visible in the borders of this carpet is its aesthetic emulation of counted-thread embroidery, a technique common in older Spanish carpets. The calligraphy and style of the borders indicate that this carpet most likely could have been from the 18th century. Similar pieces are preserved in the museum, such as the carpet with inventory number CE00981.

2e37ae24-5c92-5eeb-bdae-5fa66679ca7b.name: Ladik prayer rug
2e37ae24-5c92-5eeb-bdae-5fa66679ca7b.description:
Ladik, in Anatolia, had been an important carpet-making centre since at least the 17th century. Two types of prayer rug can be assigned to Ladik, but both have one charming feature: a row of elongated tulips in a cross-panel. The first group, considered to be earlier, are triple-arch prayer rugs. These have a narrow cross-panel with tulips over a *mihrab*. Another group consists of mostly 18th- and 19th-century rugs. They have a much smaller central niche and a wide cross-panel with upside down tulips beneath the *mihrab*.  
The Kraków rug belongs to the second group. The small, red *mihrab* niche is closed with a stepped, pointed arch, decorated with hook motifs. It has three elongated blossoming shrubs inside the niche that resemble the columns of the first group of Ladik rugs. The spandrels are decorated with five rosettes, a pair of lanceolate leaves and three ewers. The *mihrab* niche and ewers are symbols connected with the everyday ritual prayers of Muslims. Beneath the *mihrab* there is a wide cross-panel with two rows of arcades, upside down tulips, roses and stems with flowers. Six borders surround the field of the carpet. The main border is filled with an ornament of bold, strongly geometrised carnations.  
It is interesting that a very similar Ladik rug was depicted in a painting dating to as early as the second quarter of the 17th century. In the votive picture of the priest Tarło in one of the Polish churches, the rug can be seen beneath the altar of the prayer scene.

2eb076be-b166-5091-8049-e6bf0adeed60.name: Carpet of the ‘animal combat’-type
2eb076be-b166-5091-8049-e6bf0adeed60.description:
The city of Kashan was famous for the trade and production of silk from the 16th century.  
European descriptions from that period mention the existence of beautiful knotted carpets with sophisticated designs sometimes made of silk, the most luxurious carpet material in Persia. Carpets of this quality were made to decorate royal palaces and to be offered as prestigious diplomatic gifts.  
Produced in royal or urban workshops, they are characterised by an extensive use of silk (both the foundations and the knotting), relatively small sizes, brilliant colours and masterful designs that drew influence from the Persian art of the book. With its sophisticated design, this carpet is an exceptional example of its type, being unique in its combination of the central-medallion format with animal combat scenes in both the medallion and in the field. It incorporates a four-lobed medallion in the centre, with phoenixes fighting dragons. In the field, are lions, tigers, panthers, antelopes and bulls fighting on a floral background. The border, with a moss-green ground, has a balanced design featuring pheasants, alternated with palmettes and flowers.  
This carpet was probably produced during the reign of Shah Tahmasp I (1524‒1576) who was a great patron of the arts.  
  
Click [here](https://youtu.be/e73lWeTVSfI) to **watch a video presentation** of this artefact.

2ee1b7b6-9886-531d-8c6d-ea0bad0ac390.name: Tekke
2ee1b7b6-9886-531d-8c6d-ea0bad0ac390.description: Most of the Turkmen pile weavings in the Dresden carpet collection are the work of the Tekke, the largest Turkmen tribe in the 19th century. Among them are three almost entirely preserved so-called main carpets (*khaly*) as well as further *khaly* fragments. These large-format pile carpets by the Tekke were initially very popular in Victorian England and soon after also on the European continent. With their distinguished, restrained red tones, they decorated libraries and smoking rooms. They were known as "Gentleman carpets" and "Bokhara carpets." This quite finely woven piece on a bright red ground shows a repetition of 4 x 10 Tekke main guls, both prominent and round, together with the Kurbage minor gul. The major border features the characteristic star-filled octagons, alternating with richly varied dividing panels. Parts of the main border and the minor outer border are missing. Flat-woven skirts (*elems*) at the top and bottom are not preserved. It is probably a work by the Achal-Tekke.

2f8a5281-9aad-56b2-94ab-cc71340502a0.name: Prayer rug
2f8a5281-9aad-56b2-94ab-cc71340502a0.description: Pirot kilims are woven very finely. Weave density can measure up to seven to nine grains per centimetre, like on the kilim with a *mihrab* and pots with flowers in the central field. At the top of the *mihrab* there is a lamp, and in the corners there are flower braches. Kilim has three borders and the one in the middle is narrower than the other two. Borders are decorated with vegetable ornaments, *almonds* (*bademčići*) and *octopuses* (*oktapod*). The colours used are: red, green, blue, yellow, brown and violet.

30241187-e18e-5731-96d9-ec8bc8d23e75.name: Tile picture of a Cuenca carpet
30241187-e18e-5731-96d9-ec8bc8d23e75.description:
An unusual “carpet,” this panel consists of 484 underglaze-painted tiles which together form the picture of a Cuenca carpet. The panel was probably intended as flooring, a kind of al fresco carpet which, when set into the ground, would add colour, pattern, and interest to an outdoor setting. Tiles would be decidedly more durable in inclement weather than a wool or silk carpet.  
In shades of blue, yellow, green and manganese on a white ground, the panel has a shield at centre bounded by the phrase "Ave Maria Gracia Plena Dominus Tecun." The shield is surrounded by a series of borders: the deepest interior border has mirrored, inverted, and repeated foliate scrolls; the outer borders feature patterned triangle, diamond, and oval motifs in a continuous repeat.  
Made about 1921, the tile panel’s design derives from a genuine Spanish carpet probably made in the 17th century. It is not known if the tile maker worked from the historic carpet itself or a photographic reproduction of it. An extant black and white image of the original carpet confirms the tile picture closely resembles the source. It is unclear, however, if the colours mimic it. A comparison between the two reveals that the tile maker opted to standardize colour usage across the tiles, whereas the carpet was woven with more variation.  
The tile picture was one of two that made its way to Florida, where it later came into the hands of Berberyan Galleries. Each shows a Cuenca carpet, although not the same carpet. Doris Duke purchased both panels for her home Shangri La, in Honolulu. Neither was used as flooring, but instead were wall mounted similar to hanging textiles. Later, Duke had one panel shipped to her home Rough Point in Newport, Rhode Island where it remains today. Ceramic may be an unusual vehicle for the display of the Cuenca aesthetic, but it was an aesthetic Duke adored. She purchased several Cuenca carpets for her collection, including a massive 17th century one for Shangri La’s Living Room.

3262ef55-4fbe-5fc0-9e94-2afa5079798b.name: The Kevorkian Hyderabad Carpet
3262ef55-4fbe-5fc0-9e94-2afa5079798b.description:
This carpet is known as the “Kervorkian Hyderabad Carpet” due to the fact that it was owned by Kervorkian, who was a famous Islamic art dealer and collector. This wool and cotton pile-woven carpet is nearly sixteen metres long and might have been created for the palaces of the Deccani sultans who ruled in Hyderabad during the 17th century.  
This carpet, which symbolizes the tradition of paradisical iconography in Islamic art, features a garden composition that includes geometric lozenges with a variety of vegetal motifs arranged in a mirrored composition. At the centre, a polylobed shape represents an abstracted fish pond decorated with multi-coloured fish. The rug presents a reach palette of colours (yellow, brown, blue and green) with a majority of vivid red, characteristic of that production.  
The border, which recalls manuscripts illuminations of the same period, is also highly decorated with repeated polychromic arabesque cartouches and foliated motifs.  
Carpet production in India during the Mughal period and the Deccan sultanate, especially during the 17th century, demonstrate the transfer of motifs and patterns from the cultural and commercial exchange with Iran, the Middle-East and Europe.

32f9c7a9-b359-535c-adc8-ea6b3f80b836.name: Baluch Tribal Grain Bag
32f9c7a9-b359-535c-adc8-ea6b3f80b836.description:
A 19th century Baluch grain bag with pile carpet weave on the front and plain flat weave on the back. Its design layout consists of a rectangular shape divided into a pale ivory coloured narrow centre field with wide dark blue borders. The centre field is dominated by a symmetrically designed tree, predominantly red with dark blue and brown, branching out to the left and right. Each of the tree’s stems bares a carnation-like flower motif. The dark border consists of rows of dark red and brown diamond-shaped patterns. The plain woven flat back is dark red. In total five colours have been used in this carpet: ivory, brown, dark blue, dark red and light red. Six black tassels are attached to the corners and the centres of the narrow sides of the bag; five of which are horse hair and the sixth is a wool replacement.  
  
Called a “Balisht” (grain bag), this type of weaving is a female craft, carried out by the women and girls in Baluch tribes. This Balisht would have been suspended on the interior side of a Baluch tent. Baluch tribes live in several regions in eastern Iran, southwestern Afghanistan and southeast Pakistan. This particular grain bag is thought to have been made by Baluch tribes living in the Khurasan region of north-eastern Iran and western Afghanistan. Baluch tribes are nomadic, and those who produce this type of grain bag tend to wander between Herat in Afghanistan and Sistan in Iran.

339ae7ee-bffe-50db-8587-b97adc8dcef0.name: Yomut Turkmen Tent Bag
339ae7ee-bffe-50db-8587-b97adc8dcef0.description:
A 19th century Turkmen Yomut tent bag with one side woven in pile knots (the front side) and one flat in weave (the back of the bag). With a deep red background, the pile-carpet side is divided into a centre field framed by a border. Nine large geometric rosette motifs, known as guls (with white, light red, yellow, green and blue segments) are lined up in three rows. Interspersed between them are smaller diamond-shaped vegetal motifs, coloured in light red, dark blue, green and yellow. The frame of the design has a white background and is filled with a chain of alternating red, blue and green arrow-like heads. On the flat woven back of this bag there is a hand written inscription in Farsi, which seems to give a lot number that translates “1/42 Ruh”.  
  
This shape and size of tent bag is called a “chuval”. It is a flat storage bag, the largest in a range of tent bags woven by tribal women of the Yomut Turkmen. Usually made in pairs and used as containers for cloths and other personal items, it would have been hung on the inside of the framework of a round tent.

33d56671-7bf3-5042-8973-1e88842c1245.name: Carpet
33d56671-7bf3-5042-8973-1e88842c1245.description:
Field: The field is of a reddish hue and depicts motifs of interwoven green ribbons that form elongated hexagons. Inside of these upright pineapples framed on serrated palms are housed.  
Border: The carpet consists of two borders: the interior consists of green and white motifs upon a dark background; The exterior features calligraphic elements and flowers upon a blue background.  
Naturally coloured wool is used for the warp and weft. The wool knots utilise blue, green, red, yellow and white hues.  
The carpet is of a Gothic-Moorish type in which Gothic motifs predominate in the field, while Mudejar styles persist in the valances. The outer border resembles the pseudo-*kufic* inscriptions of the Admiral series, but much more schematic.  
A similar carpet is reproduced in the painting 'The Annunciation' which is currently housed in the Prado museum and dated to around 1500 CE. The painting is composed by the unnamed artist 'Master of the Sisla'.  
The current dimensions do not reflect the original size of the carpet, since it is composed of numerous fragments due to several successive restorations. It is the first in a series that is inspired by contemporaneous fabrics.  
The carpet comes from the Weisberger Collection.

341215d6-e654-51ec-a66e-0dc193fca6c0.name: Carpet
341215d6-e654-51ec-a66e-0dc193fca6c0.description:
Even though the manufacture of Arraiolos carpets has been documented since the late 16th century, the earliest surviving examples are from the first third of the 17th century. In essence, these early pieces reveal a marked similarity to oriental carpets, especially those from Iran, but also from Turkey. Although there are no Turkish carpets in Portuguese collections, other documentary and iconographic sources confirm the presence of them in Portugal, especially during the first half of the 16th century. Just as with paintings, where representations of carpets of Turkish and Iranian origin have been recognised, some Arraiolos carpets bear testimony to the consumption habits of old, attesting to their presence in, and influence upon Portuguese artistic production. Such is the case with this example, whose composition recalls those of the “small-pattern Holbein”-type carpets, made in Anatolia.  
Despite that today it appears yellowish, the profusely decorated border was originally red and would have contrasted vividly with the blue field, where large palmettes form orthogonal lines, alternated with miniscule birds, which frame small rosettes.

3481e842-be03-549a-be65-9ec6969a8ba5.name: Marasali prayer rug
3481e842-be03-549a-be65-9ec6969a8ba5.description: A Caucasian Marasali prayer rug woven in 1253 Hijra (1838 AD) with the quintessentially Azeri flaming buta motif. The main, and very dark blue, field of this pile carpet is occupied by rows of multi-coloured pear-shaped leaf motifs with serrated edges.  These motifs are better known as flaming butas (also botehs or Paisley pattern motifs), and are here alternately coloured across the horizontal rows, creating uniformly coloured diagonal rows on the vertical axes from bottom right to top left. A geometrical arch is positioned at the top end of the centre filed creating the distinctive prayer-niche design of the prayer rug. To the left of the arch’s tip is discretely woven the date of manufacture using red knots. In Arabic letters and numbers it states “year 1253” in the Islamic calendar. The border shows a row of “bird motifs”, resembling bunches of red grapes, on an ivory background. These bird motifs are one of the key distinguishing features of Marasali carpets, and have evolved from clearly rendered abstracted birds bending to peck at the ground to the form you see on the border of this carpet, which looks more like a bunch of grapes with a leaf at its base.
3481e842-be03-549a-be65-9ec6969a8ba5.obtention: Gifted by Sir William and Lady Burrell to the City of Glasgow, 1944
3481e842-be03-549a-be65-9ec6969a8ba5.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: prayer niche; prayer rug; Paisley Pattern; boteh; buta; flaming buta; bird; inscrption; date
materials: Silk warp and weft; wool pile

34a076dd-a17c-5255-8e20-be760dc55f04.name: Kilim (fragment)
34a076dd-a17c-5255-8e20-be760dc55f04.description: The fragment shown here is the upper right corner of a two-panel, large format Central Anatolian kilim, of which only this part of one panel has survived. Such pieces were produced for personal use and were part of the dowry. They served primarily as a representative cover for bedding and containers and were stacked directly opposite the tent entrance, clearly visible to any guest entering the tent. The fragment of this white-ground Konya kilim, with its massive hook motif, features individual scattered motifs in brocaded technique, which indicate the weaving direction of this slit tapestry. It shows the subdued coloration typical of the Konya region in the early 19th century.
34a076dd-a17c-5255-8e20-be760dc55f04.holder: Museum für Völkerkunde Dresden (Ethnological Museum Dresden), Dresden State Art Collections
34a076dd-a17c-5255-8e20-be760dc55f04.obtention: Donated in 1979 by Dresden painter Wilhelm Müller (1928–99) from his private collection with intent to begin a museum collection. In the last decade before the Berlin Wall came down Müller collected oriental rugs, carpets and flat weaves for the Ethnographic Museum of Dresden in the Dresden-Leipzig-Berlin region to secure remaining rural and nomadic textiles from the 19th and beginning 20th century. Textiles were acquired from private households, private and state shops and even from demolition sites or waste containers.

3558a994-b678-5475-882b-7ed108686a25.name: Polonaise carpet
3558a994-b678-5475-882b-7ed108686a25.description: As of the 17th century, carpets in Iran were increasingly produced for export to Europe and Asia. Small-size Polonaise, respectively Shah Abbas carpets like these, were quite favoured in Europe; today there are still around 250 examples preserved in European and American collections, which tells of their earlier popularity. Unlike most of the carpets of this group, this piece features no metal brocading. Its pattern system is based on a vertically and horizontally mirrored quarter cartoon. This example has likewise lost much of its former colourfulness, which indicates the use of not overly high-quality dyes. The knot density of this carpet is nowhere near as high as that of the Vienna hunting carpet.

35acaf2f-4c57-5f70-8e92-0ba54bcab677.name: Carpet
35acaf2f-4c57-5f70-8e92-0ba54bcab677.description:
Renaissance carpet from the Brocade series, which contains small decorative elements with Mudejar roots, particularly the use of bird motifs. The use of this style is something that takes time to disappear in carpet productions within the Alcaraz area. Judging by the preserved copies, as well as by the frequency with which they appear in the inventories, this series must have been very large. Such carpets would have relied on templates from carved velvets and brocades. In the documentation these were also known as 'guadamecí work', due to their resemblance to golden and polychrome leathers that utilised these same motifs.  
Field: On a pink background containing vegetal nets that form rhombuses with a central axis of symmetry and ascending arrangement as well as two half motifs equal to these on both sides. Open pineapples or artichokes are housed in the openings which are also in an ascending position. In free spaces are located similar decorative motifs with a diagonal arrangement. All these decorative motifs appear in two shades of blue and are outlined in the lightest shade.  
Border: The carpet is made up of three blue toned borders, two of which were narrow and a wider central border. The central border is made up of eses or interlinking scrollwork and contain a stylised flower bouquet with small birds. These motifs are outlined by the same colour, but in a lighter shade. The narrower borders, on the short sides, are formed by a broken profile line containing a small serrated leaf and similar motifs that run on the long sides.  
The background of the border is dark blue, while the background of the field is in pinkish tones.  
In some segments of the carpet's border, different shades of blue can be seen which may be due to it being made with different tints or to its restoration.  
The warp and the weft are made of naturally coloured wool. The knots are made of naturally coloured wool along with three shades of blue and pink.
35acaf2f-4c57-5f70-8e92-0ba54bcab677.method_for_datation: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.
35acaf2f-4c57-5f70-8e92-0ba54bcab677.method_for_provenance: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.
35acaf2f-4c57-5f70-8e92-0ba54bcab677.bibliography: Ferrer, Sánchez, *Carpets antiguas de la provincia de Albacete*, Lámina LXXI: 423.
35acaf2f-4c57-5f70-8e92-0ba54bcab677.author: Mª Dolores Vila Tejero
keywords: Alcaraz
materials: Warp: Wool, Weft: Wool/Spanish knot [Colours: natural colour, three tones of blue, strong pink. Density: 2600 knots/dm2]

375624b2-b7da-5d9b-97be-c7702f618061.name: Joshagan Diamond Design Carpet
375624b2-b7da-5d9b-97be-c7702f618061.description:
An 18th century Joshagan diamond-lozenge design pile carpet. It’s predominantly wine-red centre-field design is placed on an ivory coloured background, and its equally red border design is placed on a dark blue background. The centre-field is dominated by a large diamond-shaped medallion filled with a multi-coloured vegetal Arabesque pattern. The surrounding field is filled with rows of small square compartments set on the diagonal, with each compartment holding a geometric floral form laid out symmetrically. These multi-coloured floral forms are predominantly wine-red and pink in colour with blue, yellow and green details. The dark-blue border holds a chain of geometric arabesque pattern formed of eight-pointed-stars, with each star holding a floral motif.  
  
Joshagan carpets are distinguished in their lozenge designs, where rows of small square lozenges are laid out on the diagonal exemplified by this carpet.
375624b2-b7da-5d9b-97be-c7702f618061.obtention: Gifted by Sir William and Lady Burrell to the City of Glasgow, 1944

keywords: diagonal grid; floral motifs; medallion; vegetal Arabesque; geometric arabesque
materials: Cotton warp and weft; wool pile

37ce1ee9-08e8-5287-adba-58e53c991fc0.name: "Admiral" Hedonic Carpet
37ce1ee9-08e8-5287-adba-58e53c991fc0.description:
Shortly after the Muslims of North Africa introduced the art of making twisted-pile carpets into Spain, the weaving of this armorial carpet was undertaken. It was probably made for the founder of the royal house of Castile, Fadrique Enríquez, who held the titles of Lord of Medina and Admiral of Castile and was the grandfather of King Ferdinand of Spain. His coat of arms—an upright lion beneath two triple-towered castles bordered by anchors and ropes—is repeated three times in the center field. A decorative pattern in the main border at each end, formed by designs that resemble Arabic script, indicates its Mudéjar workmanship. Related objects reside in both the Hispanic Society Museum & Library and the Vizcaya Museum.  
The Royal emblem on the Armorial Rug in The Hispanic Society Museum & Library is slightly different as it is attributed to Maria of Castile, wife of Alfonso V, the Magnanimous. The Admiral Carpet in The Vizcaya Museum is also attributed to Fadrique Enríquez and bears a simplified version of the emblem of the Philadelphia Museum of Art carpet along with two different emblems.

3816252d-1e7b-505e-aad8-6913c3069310.name: Kilim (2)
3816252d-1e7b-505e-aad8-6913c3069310.description: A pair of the Pirot kilims of the so-called *draper* type was used as a double-bed cover. The kilims were part of the dowry of Miroslava Živanović, the daughter of Dušan Živanović, a judge of the Court of Cassation in Pirot. In both kilims, the central field features a large medallion filled with the so called *devil’s knee* (*vraško koleno*) ornament, whereas the remaining space is filled with the ornament called *bibice*. The wide outer border (*ploča*), which frames the central field on three sides, is also filled with the *devil’s knee* ornament. The colours used are dark red, black and white. Although very old, the *devil’s knee* ornament has remained one of the favourite motifs in the Pirot kilim-making. Its name is derived from the folk round dance (*kolo*), in which dancers form a circle, due to which the ornament has an apotropaic function. It was believed that the more “circles” and “wreaths” there were in a home, the stronger the protection from all evil powers. The same ornament can also be found in Anatolian kilims woven in the provinces of Van, Aydın and Esme.

38743f76-29ea-526a-ba0a-b802cc9a0d73.name: Saddle cloth with polychrome foliate and floral scrolls
38743f76-29ea-526a-ba0a-b802cc9a0d73.short_description: Cloths like this were laid over the hindquarters of the richly adorned horse. Like many of the carpets, it was originally owned by the Austrian Imperial House. The centre of the saddle cloth forms a flower, surrounded by an oval band of interlacing. Around this centre there is a pattern of additional floral and scroll motifs. One floral scroll running across the entire width of the saddle cloth is surrounded by a further band of interlacing with red ground. The decoration structure is based on the bands of interlacing and seems to imitate the shape of a saddle.
38743f76-29ea-526a-ba0a-b802cc9a0d73.author: Martina Dax
keywords: Ottoman textile; Floral motifs; Saddle; decoration; geometric patterns
materials: Silk, gold and silver lamella, cotton; Tapestry

38bee4ad-cee4-5177-b8e7-dff8c1f903a8.name: Inscribed reed floor mat
38bee4ad-cee4-5177-b8e7-dff8c1f903a8.short_description: A fine floor mat, woven on the loom, with sparse decoration, self-patterned borders with interlocking lozenge pattern and pairs of brown brocaded bands. The inscriptions, written in a *kufic* script, have benedictory content with details about the work's creation, as naming *Tabariya* the place of production. Such floor coverings were made for domestic and religious interiors and were possibly used during prayers.
keywords: Floor mat; Kufic; Prayers; Tabby weave
materials: Tabby weave with brocaded decoration, hemp and bast fibre

391155e6-8f22-5ca7-b93f-8756a927d4fd.name: Khotan silk carpet
391155e6-8f22-5ca7-b93f-8756a927d4fd.description:
A 19th century East Turkistan silk-pile carpet with a large light-brown field and a dark blue border. The centre field is divided by a square grid of strait, light blue coloured vine-stem structure bearing dark blue flowers positioned at the middle of each section of stem. In the compartments between the vine-stems are positioned light coloured floral motifs with leaves of various shades of brown/cream and blue/green. In the dark blue border is a scroll of curly brackets in light brown and blue colours. In the centre of each pair of brackets is a composition of six small flowers; and between each pair of brackets and the next is a larger rosette with pale brown and pale blue petals.  
  
This silk carpet was made by Muslim Ughurs, a Turkic-speaking people indigenous to East Turkistan (today in the Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region of western China). The layout is inspired by Persian carpets, the border pattern is derived from Indian styles, and the centre field pattern is east Central Asian.

392875c0-7574-582d-b567-f145659f7e9b.name: Prayer rug
392875c0-7574-582d-b567-f145659f7e9b.description: The oldest carpets preserved till today that were produced in Asia Minor date from the 13th century, from the time of the Seljuqs. Turkish carpets were exported to Europe from the 14th century onwards and that is when we start to find them in the paintings of the Italian masters, especially the Siena and Florentine schools. The best examples of the carpet art of Asia Minor, boasting exceptionally imaginative designs, can be found in the prayer rugs. In the centre of Kula prayer rug is a dark blue *mihrab* or prayer niche. In the middle of this field there is a stylised star-like floral design in the shape of a pillar. The inside edge of the *mihrab* has smaller flowers while the surrounding area is covered with large geometric, flower motifs. There are eight borders, of which three are missing at the narrow ends of the rug. One of the narrow borders is repeated several times, with the same geometric motif, but in contrasting colour combinations. The other borders have a floral motif. The colours used are blue, brown, red and green.

39cb9cff-d1fa-57f2-b037-4ff3cc366db5.name: Wheel Rug
39cb9cff-d1fa-57f2-b037-4ff3cc366db5.description: This is the finest example in an American collection of the Turkish "wheel rugs," so named in European inventories of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries for their wheel-like pattern of octagons filled with interlaced geometric forms. This pattern can also be found in many Spanish rugs and European paintings of the period.

3aec02c1-1e7f-5fd5-9462-c560686fc934.name: Fantastical Mughal animal carpet fragment
3aec02c1-1e7f-5fd5-9462-c560686fc934.description:
A late 16th century fantastical Mughal Indian animal carpet fragment. It once formed part of an exceptionally large and predominantly deep red pile carpet. The piece shows wild animals from the Indian jungle pouncing out of each other’s mouths in a chain of fantastical compositions. The range of animals is extensive, including the heads of elephants, rhinoceros, camels, nilgai antelopes, blackbuck antelopes, tigers, lions, a leopard, black panthers, oxen, onagers, rabbits and hares, snakes, geese, black-necked storks, parrots, peacocks, fish, and crocodile-like beasts; whole figures of cheetahs, turtles, and hyena, dog and monkey-like quadrupeds; and two types of demonic masks – the only supernatural creatures on the carpet.  
  
This carpet fragment belongs to an early genre of Mughal Indian carpets known as ‘grotesque’ carpets. Studies on this fragment – and six others that belong to the same carpet – reveal that the original complete carpet must have been about 4 meters wide and at least 20 meters long! It is thought to have been made in the Farrashkhana, the royal weaving workshop of the Mughal Emperor Akbar (r.1566 – 1605), in either of his capitals Fatehpur-Sikri or Lahore sometime in the 1580s or 90s.  
  
Emperor Akbar is credited with introducing the craft of pile-carpet weaving into India with the aid of Iranian master weavers brought over to establish the royal workshops and train Indian artisans in this art. An additional seven fragments scattered around museums in Europe and the USA indicate that this carpet had a pair. The animals and plants were all generally drawn in a style closely matched by animals and plants painted in Akbar-period miniature paintings. However, this particular fantastical design was inspired by a combination of Timurid Persian and Hindu Indian depictions of such animals in paintings and on textiles and architecture.
3aec02c1-1e7f-5fd5-9462-c560686fc934.method_for_provenance: Stylistic analysis. Part of a large carpet with other known fragments in public collections
3aec02c1-1e7f-5fd5-9462-c560686fc934.obtention: Gifted by Sir William and Lady Burrell to the City of Glasgow, 1944

3aec02c1-1e7f-5fd5-9462-c560686fc934.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: animal decoration; Birds; fish; reptile; mammal; fragment; hunting; imaginary animal
materials: Cotton warp and weft; wool pile

3b5489ed-d098-56e9-994e-74de894d359b.name: Medallion *Uşak*
3b5489ed-d098-56e9-994e-74de894d359b.description: The centred medallion structure of the *Uşak* carpets, which replaced the repetitive rapport pattern, is probably based on East Asian models and developed at about the same time in both the Ottoman and Timurid empires. The region around Uşak produced carpets not only for export, but also for the large Ottoman market. Textile production constituted a substantial part of the Ottoman economy. European merchants maintained numerous branches along the coasts of the Ottoman Empire. Frequent depictions in portraits and imitations by European manufactories documented the popularity of this production.

3c2f75c0-8f03-55ba-9868-6dcd5d8d0617.name: Cartouche carpet
3c2f75c0-8f03-55ba-9868-6dcd5d8d0617.description: In addition to this Berlin carpet fragment, a second, somewhat larger one exists in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Both fragments are considered among the most outstanding examples of early Safavid carpet art. The two fragments together allow the design of a cartouche carpet to be clearly recognized. In staggered rows, tall rectangular cartouches alternate with slightly oval medallions. To even out the size difference of the two motifs, the medallions are adorned at top and bottom with shield-shaped additions. The two motifs touch at their vertical and horizontal central axis. Each of the areas between the two main motifs is filled with two semicircular lancet leaves. The special character of the carpet lies in the subtle drawing of its individual motifs, its variety of colour and its colour composition. Each colour area is separated from the next by a differently coloured outline. The carpet ground, which is normally in one colour, also changes its colour in each field. The interplay of twenty different colours and colour shades succeeds perfectly. The knotting technique and the very short pile allow the colour and the motif design to emerge precisely – some of the outlines are only one knot wide. There is frequent evidence of cartouche carpets in Timurid miniature painting, but no carpets from this period have been preserved. Because of the use of individual Jufti knots the province of Khorasan is presumed to be the area of production.
3c2f75c0-8f03-55ba-9868-6dcd5d8d0617.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
3c2f75c0-8f03-55ba-9868-6dcd5d8d0617.method_for_datation: The carpet has been dated on stylistic analysis of its pattern, due to its colours and knot-technique

3d802c09-002a-52b1-a0f5-eb87daa52e0b.name: Arraiolos rug
3d802c09-002a-52b1-a0f5-eb87daa52e0b.description:
Arraiolos rugs are one of the most typical forms of manufacture and those with the oldest tradition in the art of embroidery within Portugal. With its beginnings in the end of the 16th century, production reached its apogee in the 18th century, with its decline commencing in the 19th century, when the designs began to become broader and the size of the stitches, began to increase. The quantity of surviving examples allows us to recognise the recourse to various sources of inspiration in the conception of designs, which would themselves evolve throughout time.  
This rug, a piece of oriental influence which is thought to date to the 17th century, was most probably inspired by the so-called “wheel” carpets, a type associated with the “small-pattern Holbein”-type of Turkish carpets. It has a yellow field decorated with stylised flowers and the border is filled with flowers and birds of popular tradition, embroidered in faded pink (originally red), green, blue and yellow. Both the module constituting the base unit of the carpet’s design, as well as the alternated and bi-directional – horizontal and vertical ‒ manner in which it is repeated, forming a veritable grid, allowed it to be transposed into tile form. This is one reason why this type of carpet is also known as the “tile-pattern carpet”. Such is the proximity between the component parts of these forms of artistic creation.

3dd1f0fd-db2b-5a6a-ab0d-c44fbb0a337e.name: Caucasian Dragon Rug
3dd1f0fd-db2b-5a6a-ab0d-c44fbb0a337e.description: One of the museum’s early carpet acquisitions is a late 17th-century Caucasian dragon rug bought in 1894 from Boris Sparber. On the crimson brick red field are three ivory palmettes alternating with three ivory field "blazon" palmettes. The space between the palmettes in the lower row, above leaves and vines is filled with a stylized flaming lion, and in the upper row it is filled with dragons. The palmettes face upward in the lower two rows and downward in the top row. The irregular central field has a more rigidly formed "vine cup" border on a yellow field. There is a late 17th or early 18th century Karabagh or Shirvan carpet fragment with a similar border and field but with a more regularly formed and narrower central field held by the Washington Textile Museum.
3dd1f0fd-db2b-5a6a-ab0d-c44fbb0a337e.obtention: Purchased from Boris Sparber (1864‒1928), co-proprietor of the Budapest carpet business *Sparber & Schwalbe* in 1894.

3e399b3c-2b94-5510-956a-2f7247172045.name: Carpet
3e399b3c-2b94-5510-956a-2f7247172045.description:
Carpet from the Lotto series.  
Field: The field consists of a cruciform pattern separated into four columns, three rows and two halves.  
Border: The border is wider than usual than other carpets in this series and is of Renaissance era design. This is the only known specimen that contains this type of border and due to it being made up of several pieces there is some difficulty in interpreting the design. Diagonal brace motifs of scrollwork are linked with a plant stem. The blue used within the carpet is typical of Cuencan carpet productions of this period.  
The field and border are separated by a narrow blue line. The knots utilise wool of dark blue, turquoise blue, yellow and orange red.
3e399b3c-2b94-5510-956a-2f7247172045.method_for_datation: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.

3e773882-ba87-529a-be5c-6d45adeb4e00.name: Caucasian carpet
3e773882-ba87-529a-be5c-6d45adeb4e00.description:
In the Caucasus there is great variety of motifs due to artistic exchange among the ethnic groups. Different classifications of carpets are based on the weaver's ethnicity, geographic origin of the carpet or the carpet structure. No system of classification is based on design or motifs. Therefore, for this peculiar carpet, it is difficult to establish its origin.  
In the central field, on the dark blue background there are four medallions which resemble ovoid palmettes. Each medallion has a central polygonal motif surrounded with two white rectangular stripes decorated with stylized floral motifs. The white rectangular stripes and their decorations resemble the white stripes on Kasim Uşak. In the central axis there are three red secondary medallions. Numerous polygonal green, red, orange and blue motifs are field repeats. The central field is framed with three borders. The main border is the dragon border – double black and red S motifs alternating on the white background. The inner border is a variation of floral meandar border. The outer border is a crosshatch border. This type of border is used throughout the Caucasus and may be either a major or minor border.
3e773882-ba87-529a-be5c-6d45adeb4e00.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Caucasus
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

3ed39d69-ec98-5cf4-a1dd-bce572ba5e59.name: Tekke '*ensi*' rug
3ed39d69-ec98-5cf4-a1dd-bce572ba5e59.short_description: *Ensi* or *engsi* rugs are often treated by art historians as door hangings of a yurt, a traditional Turkmen nomadic tent. Covering the doorway of the tent *ensi* was supposedly destined to preserve the inside temperature from winter and summer extremes. There is also a different opinion that suggests treating *ensi* as a ritual rug used only for special social and cult occasions. *Ensi* is considered a complex kind of Turkmen rug in the aspects of design and iconography. Here in the middle of the carpet there is a cruciform composition of two broad stripes filled with small geometric elements. Small hooked motifs of various kinds also fill the four rectangular fields formed by the central "cross" and several stripes of border. Above the central field there is a stylized image of the tent or a *mihrab*. The design of the carpet is known as "*hatchli*" and is typical for Tekke, one of the major tribes of Turkmen. Ethnographic studies suggest the connection of a central cross-like pattern with the idea of rivers and canals, while a variety of smaller elements - with sheep and cattle, together with water make up the main resources of nomads' lives. The background of the carpet is dark ruby, other colours of the pattern include lighter shade of red, dark blue, brown and ivory white.

3f0f0780-c98f-5db2-b815-f80d5e985f50.name: Medallion carpet with hunting animals
3f0f0780-c98f-5db2-b815-f80d5e985f50.description:
This beautiful medallion carpet was woven in Iran, probably in the first half of the sixteenth century, during the reign of the Safavid dynasty. While it does not have any inscriptions linking it with a specific patron, place or date, the design holds many parallels with the arts of the book in early Safavid Iran.  
  
Despite its large scale, the carpet has a fine and complex design that rewards very close inspection. In its general layout, there are two lobed black medallions down the central axis, with four diagonal radiating oval pendants each, all set against a dark red main field. These medallions are then repeated by quarter-medallions in the four corners of the field, and by two half-medallions on either side. Each medallion is filled with a very refined radial design of yellow strapwork and large flowers, while each oval pendant is occupied by fluttering birds and Chinese-style cloudbands. Below this medallion superstructure, the red main field is a rich and varied garden landscape of trees filled with wildlife. There are trees with white blossoms, and others filled with ripe pomegranates. There are also leafy spiralling stems, with large lotus flowers. Among this greenery, the carpet is filled with animals and birds: there are resting pairs of spotted goats, lions and treetop birds. Predominantly though, the main field is full of hunting scenes: leopards killing horned goats, hawks killing long-legged water birds and lions killing stags. Down the central axis of the design, there are ornate Chinese style vases, formed of dragons, lions and peacocks, and lobed ponds full of fish.  
Beyond the main field, the main border features a reciprocal pattern, of an interlocking arcade in red versus black (or rather extremely dark blue indigo). On a slightly more condensed scale to the main field, this border also features hunting pairs: a snow leopard attacking a horned goat, and a lion pinning down a bull. A beautifully drawn pair of supernatural creatures confront each other in the dark blue arcading: a Chinese-style dragon opposite a long-tailed phoenix. Throughout the main and two minor borders, the design also features overlaid designs of leafy plant scrolls and Chinese cloudband motifs.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O85144/the-chelsea-carpet-carpet-unknown/)
3f0f0780-c98f-5db2-b815-f80d5e985f50.method_for_datation: This carpet’s design and structure connect it with other known examples of medallion and compartment carpets woven in wool on silk foundation, which have also been attributed to the sixteenth century. Nonetheless we can only hypothesize as to where exactly it was woven: Tabriz or possibly Qazvin, each of which served as the Safavid capital during the first half of the century.
3f0f0780-c98f-5db2-b815-f80d5e985f50.method_for_provenance: The carpet is attributed to Iran because of its design and technical structure, which fits with sixteenth-century production under the Safavids.
3f0f0780-c98f-5db2-b815-f80d5e985f50.obtention: Purchased from Alfred Cohen (Kings’s Road, Chelsea, London) in 1890. The carpet is nicknamed “the Chelsea Carpet” as a result of this provenance.

3fb86eda-1e8c-5fdf-9e0b-53b50204bf6c.name: Seljuq Rug
3fb86eda-1e8c-5fdf-9e0b-53b50204bf6c.description: A “Konya Group” rug found in the Konya Aladdin Mosque and acquired by the museum in 1911. The condition of this rug is poor, nevertheless it is possible to perceive the general decoration. The rug is in three pieces, the remaining parts of a large carpet. The main border is wide and light red in colour. Stylized *kufic*letters in dark red are contoured with brown and placed side by side. The main border is separated from the basic ground by a yellow band framed with a narrow brown line. The dark blue ground is a diamond pattern with hooked ends. There are small heart shapes in their middle of these diamond shapes. Seljuq rugs were commonly woven in large sizes. They were decorated in plain geometric patterns, generally with a small number of colours in various shades contrasted with a wide *kufic* border.

40618ecc-b658-5395-a1e3-3a6178bd928f.name: Uşak Rug with bird
40618ecc-b658-5395-a1e3-3a6178bd928f.description: Bird rugs are named for the S‒shaped stylised bird motifs arranged in vertical and horizontal rows in the centre field. This is a subgroup of rugs called white ground Ottoman rugs. The other types of white ground rugs are scorpion and *çintamani* rugs. The most popular ones are the bird rugs. Generally, the origin of this type is Uşak, however, research has found that many of these rugs were produced in Selendi in Manisa city. The rugs first appear in Western paintings in the 16th century and were probably not woven after the 18th century.
40618ecc-b658-5395-a1e3-3a6178bd928f.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

40bc55d4-fab4-578d-91a1-4762408dc1a2.name: Animal combat carpet
40bc55d4-fab4-578d-91a1-4762408dc1a2.description: Herat, already an important centre of court art during the Timurid dynasty in the 15th century, is repeatedly mentioned as a major carpet production site. However, it has not been clarified whether the MAK Collection’s exemplars attributed to this actually originate from there; a more plausible place of production seems to be southern Iran. Stylistically, these high-quality pieces are closely oriented to the art of the Timurid period. The carpet seen here, the most famous of this production, has a counterpart located today in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York. The motifs of the immensely fine design are mirrored four times on a red ground around the horizontal and vertical axes; fantasy blossoms alternate with animal depictions and Chinese-inspired cloudbands. Moreover, the contrasting green-grounded border exhibits three delicate tendril systems laid on top of each other. In the accompanying border, a poem by the 12th-century poet Zahir Faryabi, written in *nasta \`liq* script, praises love, nature and the king of the world, for whom the pair of carpets was made.

41b30023-ded2-5dd2-ae27-67f95b77df76.name: Small-pattern Holbein carpet
41b30023-ded2-5dd2-ae27-67f95b77df76.description: This fragment is the earliest example of a so-called small-pattern Holbein carpet in the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin. Hans Holbein the Younger very frequently painted a number of examples of this type, thus giving his name to this distinctive group of carpets. The two motifs arranged in offset rows are characteristic. One is an octagon formed from a braided band, which is filled with white in this carpet. The second motif is a lozenge which is formed from several stylised leaf forms. The unusual variegation of the leafy vines and their over- and underlapping are signs of an early design. This is also indicated by the wide, heavily braided border. Its design is based on the script known as *kufic* and is referred to as pseudo-*kufic*. The leaf forms at the tips of the strokes, the endless knot and the over- and underlapping of the basic line are evidence of the highest complexity and craftsmanship. This early form of the border is already to be found in 15th-century paintings, for example those of Domenico Ghirlandaio (1449-1494).
41b30023-ded2-5dd2-ae27-67f95b77df76.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
41b30023-ded2-5dd2-ae27-67f95b77df76.method_for_datation: The carpet has been dated on comparison with carpets in paintings as well as on stylistic analysis of its pattern, due to its colours and knot-technique
41b30023-ded2-5dd2-ae27-67f95b77df76.obtention: 1940 in exchange with the Museum for Applied Arts, Duesseldorf
41b30023-ded2-5dd2-ae27-67f95b77df76.bibliography: Beselin, Anna, *Geknüpfte Kunst. Teppiche des Museums für Islamische Kunst*, Berlin: Minerva, 2011.
41b30023-ded2-5dd2-ae27-67f95b77df76.author: Anna Beselin
keywords: Hans Holbein; Domenico Ghirlandaio; painting; Pseudo-Kufic; Rosette; Fragment
materials: Wool; knotted pile carpet, symmetrical knot

4205c7c4-c568-5ae6-a6bf-a01b9201a6e6.name: Fragment of a Mughal Court Carpet with Design of Lattice and Blossom Pattern
4205c7c4-c568-5ae6-a6bf-a01b9201a6e6.short_description: A rectangular fragment of a Mughal court carpet, with the claret-red field having a trellis framework of leaves forming lozenges. Floral scrolls are interlaced with the trellis and bear leaves, buds, and large composite palmettes filling the center of each lozenge.
4205c7c4-c568-5ae6-a6bf-a01b9201a6e6.dates: Hegira Probably mid 11th century / AD probably mid 17th century
4205c7c4-c568-5ae6-a6bf-a01b9201a6e6.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
4205c7c4-c568-5ae6-a6bf-a01b9201a6e6.method_for_provenance: The early Mughals brought Persian weavers to India where they created court factories at Lahore, Agra, and Fatehpur-Sikri. Initially, designs were freely borrowed from Persia, but by the 17th century Indian weavers were replacing the Persian naturalistic motifs with specifically Indian plants and flowers, animals, and human figures.

43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.name: The Pearl Carpet
43a8c5d9-b3aa-529b-a3f9-5e64b5b32a48.short_description: The foundation of silk and fine deer hide is densely embroidered overall with a design worked in strings of natural ‘Basra’ pearls, measuring approximately 1-3 mm, and English coloured glass beads. There are on average 78 pearls and beads per vertical dm. (10 cm), and 68 per horizontal dm., equaling a density of c.4,990 pearls and beads per dm2. The total area of the carpet is c. 45,670 cm2. The 32 smaller rosettes cover an area of c. 400 cm2 with smaller gems, and the total area embroidered with pearls and is beads is approximately 44,500 cm2. Therefore, over 2.2 million pearls and beads have been used to decorate the field. In our estimation, the number of pearls employed in the design is therefor at least 1.2-1.5 million.
keywords: Pearls; gems; silk; rosettes
materials: Pearls, silk, deer hide, beads, gems

43f2e562-6eda-5dde-81a4-a1b3639f9c94.name: 'Transylvanian' Double Niche Rug
43f2e562-6eda-5dde-81a4-a1b3639f9c94.description:
A characteristic type of Ottoman rugs is the 'Transylvanian' double niche rug. Several variants of the type fashionable for over two centuries are known. Its common feature is the hexagonal medallion filling the central field. This is created by mirroring the original *mihrab* (prayer niche) of the traditional prayer rug across the central axis. This rug of symmetrical design was particularly popular in Transylvania where it was used as table or bed cover and wall hanging. The name "Transylvanian" refers to the place of frequent occurrence and not to the place of origin.  
  
This exquisite specimen is from the first double niche rug period and is characterized by arabesque tendrils (First Period "Transylvanian" Double Niche Rug). The dark blue field is filled with subtly designed tendrils, with flowers and leaves arranged symmetrically to both axes. This design is complemented by two mosque lamps hanging from the apexes of the *mihrabs* (prayer niches). Ochre fields above the niches with blue arabesque tendrils can be traced to Persian design prototypes. The main strip of the 'Transylvanian' border pattern contains elongated polygonal cartouches alternated with eight-pointed stars, a pattern typical of this carpet type. A similar design with an ochre central field is kept in the collection of the “Black Church” in Brassó (now Braşov, Romania).

4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.name: Prayer rug.
4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.description:
This carpet demonstrates through its design that it belongs to the group of prayer rugs. The inner area is adorned with a red-coloured arch-shaped *mihrab* (prayer niche). Placed in front of the niche is a basin, seen from above, from which emerges a small tree with green leaves, rendered in a semi-abstract design with fine lines. A small yellow jug with a handle and short spout has been incorporated into the centre of the tree. This jug may relate to Sura 5 verse 8 of the Qur’an, which mentions obligation of ablutions to be undertaken before prayer. Green-coloured, eight-pointed plaited stars can be seen in the corners of the *mihrab* arch. Above the *mihrab* is a rectangular space filled with palms and cypresses. Two borders frame the inner area. The thinner border is filled by a decorative cloud-motif band. This cloud-motif band is a common feature of Ottoman art since the AH 9th and 10th / AD 15th and 16th century, and it originated in China. On this rug, the yellow cloud-motif bands are displayed over a red background, and are positioned very close to one another. The rug’s wider border consists of a continuous tendril-like interlacing band involving plant motifs, over a light-green background.  
The rug’s symbolism derives from the connection between the *mihrab* motif and that of the garden of Paradise, which is perhaps what is being illustrated on the rug through the pool of water and the tree. Paradise, described as a wonderful garden, is promised at different points throughout the Qur’an to those who believe in the Islamic faith. Followers of Islam will one day arrive and stay in this garden full of lovely streams, wonderful plants and beautiful young virgins (*Huri*s).  
Prayer rugs from Cairo are frequently mentioned in the sources, but this particular rug is the only surviving Mamluk prayer rug. It is particularly noteworthy for its incorporation of Mamluk motifs with those derived from Ottoman art, hence the reason for dating it to around AH 900 / AD 1500 or a little later.  
Mamluk rugs can be seen in Italian paintings from the 15th and 16th century and moreover are mentioned in a great number of sources. During this period there was also a flourishing trade between Mamluk Cairo and Italy.
4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.short_description: This is the only prayer rug to have survived from the Mamluk period. It was probably made in Cairo around 1500. Its design shows a mixture of Mamluk and Ottoman features. Carpet manufacture flourished in Egypt under the Mamluk sultans and rugs were also exported to Europe.

However, as all that remains is this single Mamluk prayer carpet, it is difficult to give an exact date.
4477e256-7ea2-5cbe-bda1-f87ba36cdb04.method_for_provenance: The whole host of its unique motifs, colours and characteristic asymmetric or Persian knots all collude to suggest that this carpet was made in Cairo in a Mamluk carpet workshop.

44e70b80-28df-5f9b-8d20-02c6d7b7b1db.name: Carpet
44e70b80-28df-5f9b-8d20-02c6d7b7b1db.description: Small-pattern Holbein carpets take their name from a carpet depicted in Hans Holbein the Younger's 1532 portrait of the Hanseatic merchant Georg Gisze of Danzig. This style of carpets was woven in large numbers in the Ottoman Empire from the late 14th century to the early 17th century and was enormously popular in Europe. Their actual production locale in western Anatolia, and what they were called locally, remains uncertain. But their powerful influence in the development of rug patterns elsewhere is quite evident. Based on its fine and delicate drawing and rich colours, this carpet is possibly an older example of this type, and probably dates to early 16th century. The design of the carpet is based on geometric interlaced strapwork elements, often termed girih. The interlaced strapwork creates the medallions that infinitely repeat on the dark blue surface of the carpet. Alternating red and white ground of the medallions gives movement to an otherwise repetitive design. The secondary motif is a quatrefoil, defined by eight split-leaf forms that constitute its outer contours.
