44ff5030-1782-52cb-a816-7b58f2d32a22.name: The *Mass of Saint Gregory*
44ff5030-1782-52cb-a816-7b58f2d32a22.description:
References in Portuguese inventories to the carpets of “Castile” and the “Levant” became progressively more frequent in the first half of the 16th century and coincided with the period when representation of knotted carpets, in the form of Iberian and Turkish carpets, reached its peak in Portuguese painting.  
This fact is owed to the Muslim presence in the Iberian Peninsula. Pre-existing contact with Arab culture, as well as the production of knotted carpets, preceded the arrival of oriental counterparts and restricted their demand in the market. Facing an already-established network of Iberian, Turkish and North African manufacturers, carpet manufactories had to respond to the demands of a society well used to the consumption of exotic luxury goods.  
The *Mass of Saint Gregory* originally constituted one of the panels from the *predella* of an altarpiece in the church of the Convent of São Francisco. The *predella* comprised 16 paintings depicting scenes from the Eucharist. The painting seen here represents a story made popular in the Golden Legend of the moment when Christ reveals himself on the altar to Pope Gregory; Christ responds to Pope Gregory’s prayer for a sign to convince a deacon, who had earlier confronted him with doubts about the doctrine of transubstantiation. In the painting, St. Gregory kneels before the altar on a carpet of Spanish origin. The carpet’s field is filled with octagonal medallions in which stars and quatrefoils are alternately inserted; the border is filled with a pseudo-*kufic* design interwoven with stylised floral motifs.

451583b8-a3a8-528a-b5bb-8db3d1096e78.name: Ladik Prayer Carpet (*seccade*) on Red Ground
451583b8-a3a8-528a-b5bb-8db3d1096e78.short_description: A prayer carpet in which the lower part of the field has an arched prayer niche in red. Small trefoils project into the field from each side of the niche. The blue spandrels are decorated with lanceolate leaves, rosettes, triangles, ewers, and hooks in various colors. The panel above the spandrel is separated from the latter by a band with a wavy floral scroll. The panel in red encloses the characteristic Ladik pattern of five lily stalks and *vandykes* with triangles and hook motifs. The field is framed by a narrow blue stripe containing S-motifs. The border has a repeat pattern of lilies and rosettes separated by varicolored narrow bands on a blue ground. The guard bands in yellow or orange contain wavy floral scrolls. Small S-motifs form the design of the guard stripes.

45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.name: Coupled-Column Prayer Rug
45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.description: A version of 17th century Ottoman Turkish prayer rugs very popular in Hungary was the "column" rug, in which the *mihrab* (prayer niche) is divided into three fields by three, four or eight columns. The most common is the six-column version, considered by many to have the most beautiful design of 17th century Turkish rugs. Their general characteristic is a *mihrab* (prayer niche) whose background colour is red or ochre (rarely ivory or blue), divided into three parts by slender columns in a 1+2+2+1 distribution. The rug’s ochre *mihrab* (prayer niche) is supported by six narrow columns, dividing it into three fields. The spandrels have a blue and red arabesque decoration on an ochre field, and the crenellated frieze above has straight-stem flowers growing out of it. The design of the peak field and the frieze are not sharply delineated. Rounded cartouches of alternating colour run along the border; the outer border has a row of leaves of alternating orientation and the inner border is decorated by leaves and flowers strung along an undulating stem. In May H. Beattie’s classification, the rug is an early, type I Coupled-Column Prayer Rug.
45181682-9ce4-506e-a0dd-e86b8fb972d9.dates: First half or middle (?) of 17th century

It was exhibited in the 1914 'Transylvanian' Turkish Exhibition in the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts by the Bihar County Museum of Nagyvárad (Oradea, Romania). The rug entered into the inventory of the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts in 1962 as 'Item in store, of unknown origin'.

45ee6a65-f56e-5a10-958f-eb5e8f23eac7.name: Carpet
45ee6a65-f56e-5a10-958f-eb5e8f23eac7.description:
By the middle of the sixteenth century, Iran was an important producer of luxury textiles that gained renown abroad for their beauty and craftsmanship. Safavid carpets first came to the attention of Europeans in the early seventeenth century, and from the beginning were valued more highly than Turkish carpets. These classical carpets, produced in commercial workshops for high-end clients, are defined by the shared main feature of their design: a central, deeply indented star medallion with pendant cartouches and finials overlaid on top of finely-drawn leaf and floral scrolls.  
  
In spite of its unusually small size, this carpet is considered one of the best examples of classical Persian carpets with the open lotus blossom medallion design. Many Oriental carpets, including most Persian carpets, share a design format that contains a rectangular central field surrounded by borders. In the central field of this carpet, there are several patterns which seem to overlay one another. The underlying pattern is a scrolling vine repeated with vertical and horizontal reflection. Utilizing the same symmetries is a stylized leafy arabesque. The combination of high-quality and well-drawn design and careful juxtaposition of colour on this carpet suggest the possibility of court-inspired production.

46a42ac6-bb32-5dfe-9c49-34ee32742fe1.name: Coronation Carpet
46a42ac6-bb32-5dfe-9c49-34ee32742fe1.short_description:
LACMA’s Coronation carpet received its name because it was used at the 1902 coronation of the United Kingdom’s Edward VII, son of Queen Victoria. Set before the king’s throne in Westminster Abbey, the carpet was also prominently featured in Edwin Austin Abbey’s painting of the event. The carpet was selected for the coronation ceremonies by the Duveen brothers, art dealers who were commissioned to provide tapestries and rugs for the event, which they borrowed from prominent collections. Shortly after the coronation, the carpet was acquired by American collector and self-made millionaire Marsden J. Perry. It subsequently belonged to two other American tycoons: Clarence Mackay, followed by J. Paul Getty, who donated it to LACMA in 1949.  
As is typical of the design structure of such sixteenth-century Persian carpets, each quarter repeats exactly. The carpet is generically classified as a medallion carpet with flora and fauna, although its decoration more specifically suggests a paradisiacal garden with an abundance of trees and animals. Flowing water is indicated by the smaller blue medallions, which are reminiscent of linked pools. What clearly makes this an unearthly setting are the dragons, phoenixes, and qilins (creatures borrowed from Chinese mythology), and especially the winged celestial beings, or houris, in each of the quarter medallions.  
Like the Ardabil Carpet, the Coronation carpet was given to LACMA by Getty. It also shares other features with that more famous carpet: although it is undated, it was likely made in the second quarter of the sixteenth century, and it too had a mate, of which a small fragment survives in the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin.
46a42ac6-bb32-5dfe-9c49-34ee32742fe1.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
46a42ac6-bb32-5dfe-9c49-34ee32742fe1.method_for_datation: There is no firm basis for dating such early Safavid carpets, especially since very few survive. The dating of this carpet is based on comparison with other early Safavid art.
46a42ac6-bb32-5dfe-9c49-34ee32742fe1.method_for_provenance: The high quality of the carpet suggests it may have been produced in Tabriz, the seat of the Safavid court until 1555.

46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.name: Panel of *azulejos* with a carpet composition
46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.description:
Like many other examples, these *azulejos* testify to the affinity between textiles and *azulejos* in Portugal during the 17th century. Such was the case with the embroidered Arraiolos rugs made in the Alentejo region where the same sort of patterns and even palette can be recognised.  
This pattern was relatively common in the *azulejos* used in Portugal during the first half of the 17th century. Because this is a 2 x 2 composition, four *azulejos* are required to make a pattern that can be repeated to infinity. Use of this sort of *azulejos* was mainly in the lower areas of architecture to allow viewers to approach the decoration more directly. In it, we can perceive a cross-like composition that is achieved by a much-intertwined element with a dense blue background, at the centre of which is an acanthus leaf motif. This rope-like cross composition is placed against a yellow background; here, a distinctive eight-point motif, which has its origins in leather- or metalwork, can be traced by the presence of nail marks left in all four of its extremities. The beautiful frame that can be seen in one of its borders is known in Portuguese as *rendas* or lacework, inspired by actual works.  
Some studies have shown that prints of these lace motifs could be made by the immersion of real lace in the pigments, which were then juxtaposed in the *azulejos*, or that these were painted using similar gestures as those used to make the real lace. This has not been the case for the motifs that decorate these *azulejos*, but nevertheless the elegance of this decoration gives a new and more regal understanding to this pattern type.
46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: 17th-century production of *azulejos* in Lisbon can easily be identified by the intense blue and yellow of the palette.
46cbec75-25a9-5fc1-8bab-1ae4fe10c861.method_for_provenance: The National Tile Museum holds a large number of *azulejos* of unknown origin, many gathered during the period of the destruction of the convents and palaces in the late 19th century, in the aftermath of the abolition of the religious orders in 1834.

46e3e6fd-d34a-5dd6-b24a-24b19a30320a.name: Qajar Double-sided Carpet
46e3e6fd-d34a-5dd6-b24a-24b19a30320a.short_description:
Persian carpets have long stood out by including socio-political elements from local history within the thread as a story-telling motif woven into their fabric. This distinctive trait has become the Iranian carpet-making “cultural birth-certificate” still enduring today.  
  
While the style of this pictorial carpet characterizes the Qajar dynasty, this unique example was manufactured using a rare technique mastered in the town of Kerman, Iran. Like the flip sides of a coin, the carpet portrays two opposing scenarios: paradise and the universe, using floral and geometric patterns, Qur’anic verses, and poetry in Persian and Arabic. While one side depicts a lush garden with floral motifs, doves and peacocks, the other illustrates a central medallion with peonies, lilies and lotus flowers.
46e3e6fd-d34a-5dd6-b24a-24b19a30320a.owner: Sheikh Faisal Bin Qassim Al Thani
46e3e6fd-d34a-5dd6-b24a-24b19a30320a.method_for_datation: The date and commissioner are reflected on the carpet.

472961a4-b441-5a30-8117-15f1a9623203.name: Ardabil Carpet
472961a4-b441-5a30-8117-15f1a9623203.short_description: This spectacular carpet was made as one of a matched pair, and its mate survives in the Victoria and Albert Museum, London. According to their identical signatures, the carpets were the work of Maqsud of Kashan, probably the one who prepared the designs and oversaw the project. They were royal carpets, perhaps commissioned for Shah Tahmasp (r. 1524–76), presumably for his ancestral shrine at Ardabil. Inscribed just above the dated signature of each carpet is a Persian couplet by the renowned fourteenth-century poet Hafiz: "I have no refuge in this world other than thy threshold / My head has no resting place other than this doorway."
472961a4-b441-5a30-8117-15f1a9623203.holder: Los Angeles County Museum of Art (LACMA)
472961a4-b441-5a30-8117-15f1a9623203.method_for_datation: An inscription on the carpet dates it to Hegira 946 / AD 1539-40.
472961a4-b441-5a30-8117-15f1a9623203.method_for_provenance: The inscription that dates the carpet indicates it was made early in the reign of Shah Tahmasp (1514-1576). The carpet and its mate were likely a royal commission, given the quality and size of the carpets, and the inscription’s reference to Maqsud of Kashan as a servant of the court. They therefore might have been made at a royal workshop in Tabriz, which was the seat of the Safavid court until 1555.

473c085f-9830-5584-affd-3362c3aff805.name: Coupled-column Prayer Rug
473c085f-9830-5584-affd-3362c3aff805.short_description: A prayer rug where the creamy-white field is decorated with a triple arch on double columns in yellow, red, blue, and green. Between each pair of columns is a row of lozenges in yellow and red. The spandrel is decorated with a diaper of geometrical scrolls in white, reserving in the ground double arrow motifs in yellow and red. Across the top of the field is a panel with stalks of lilies alternating with other plants (probably tulips) in yellow, red, light and dark blue, and green on a creamy-yellow ground. The arches or so-called *vandykes* along the bottom of the panel are in blue and yellow and enclose arabesques in white, red, blue, and green. In the border is a row of compartments in blue, yellow, or green with floral devices in yellow, red, blue, and green. The guard bands contain a repeat pattern of a flower and leaf motif in white and red on a yellow ground (inner guard band) or in yellow (or green) and red on a white ground (outer guard band).

47ac58d0-5993-5a08-9fd3-789f0c8a452b.name: Confronted animal rug
47ac58d0-5993-5a08-9fd3-789f0c8a452b.short_description: When this rug was discovered, its unusual design of confronted animals with smaller animals within was otherwise known only in a rug depicted in a Sienese painting of about 1410, *The Marriage of the Virgin*, in the collection of the National Gallery, London. The pattern of the rug in the painting, partially obscured by standing figures, was not comprehensible without this example. The purchase, hailed in carpet-collecting circles, brought one of the best preserved, earliest Turkish carpets in the world to the Museum. The field design probably derives from medieval textiles patterned with single or paired animals in compartments.

47fe8af0-32fe-5514-b757-89268ef87eee.name: Lattice design carpet fragment
47fe8af0-32fe-5514-b757-89268ef87eee.description:
A 17th century Safavid Kirman pile carpet fragment. Uncommonly long and narrow, it is decorated with a single-plane lattice design on a dark blue background. The carpet's lattice structure is made up of long red serrated leaves linked together by round yellow-coloured flowers. The lattice’s compartments each holds a one of a variety of flowering plants, including irises, carnations, narcissi, lotuses and roses; all of which are organised in a directional fashion, giving the carpet design a top and a bottom.  
  
Even though this carpet is a fragment, upon close technical examination of its foundation’s structure, its width was found to be complete, indicating that the carpet was purposefully woven with no left and right borders. However, its top and bottom ends are now missing. The shape of this carpet fragment, especially its narrowness, suggests that it may have been made to cover a specific floor space that required it not to have any conventional borders.

keywords: leaf lattice; floral motifs; fragment; iris; carnation; narcissus; lotus; Kerman

48a971b4-cbfc-56cb-a20b-430077a3b1cf.name: Carpet
48a971b4-cbfc-56cb-a20b-430077a3b1cf.description:
Carpet with a continuous field decoration, Lotto series.  
Field: It has two complete rectangular motifs and two unequal fragments due to the displacement of the symmetrical axis of the central motifs.  
Border: It is composed of three borders with predominantly geometric patterns and separated by fine lines. The two narrowest are composed of a zigzag that combines schematic floral elements, which contain a wider one composed of a sinuous line, where opposing plant elements are presented.  
The warp is of a plain linen in its colour and weft is comprised of orange and white wool. The knots consist of blue, green, yellow and white wool. The decoration of this carpet is typical of Near Eastern carpets from the period. It has a decoration similar to No. 51, sheet. XXXVI, Exp. Count of Welcreck and the valance belongs to the type of No. 47, sheet. XXXVIII, owned by the Marquise de Bermejillo del Rey, both from the mid-17th century. It comes from the Monastery of the Barefoot Carmelites located in Segovia, Spain.

48af1635-ab16-56ac-b150-046ce304c2cc.description: Mamluk carpets are characterized by a central, dominant octagonal medallion surrounded by a great variety of smaller, geometric motifs. 491b4b4e-6024-574f-8938-d8c2d64f3343.name: "Bird" Rug
491b4b4e-6024-574f-8938-d8c2d64f3343.description: Small Bird Rugs such as this one have been found frequently in Protestant churches in Transylvania. The background of this piece is completely ivory white, with very limited coloring. It lacks any blue or green and relies on brown red and yellow ornamentation. The carpet features large clouds motifs spanning its fame, while its field is decorated with red and yellow, abstracted bird motifs. The corners of this carpet are cropped. This could be for architectural reasons or because of wear and tear.

49544dd7-3631-5322-bd3a-4eeabe7bf31a.name: Garden carpet / ‘Figdor’ carpet
49544dd7-3631-5322-bd3a-4eeabe7bf31a.description: Although small in format, this garden carpet is among the most famous and earliest preserved of its type. Owing to its technical peculiarities, it is the only carpet of the Kirman group that features gold and silver brocade, making it one of a kind. The field depicts a garden, consisting of six parts, carried into the plain, an extended *chahār-bāgh*\-style garden form of the time is present: water channels and basins, once brocaded in silver, structure the field. Fish and ducks scrimmage in the watercourses; the individual compartments are vegetated and populated with animals. An exemplar closely related in terms of the motif is located today in the collection of the Maharajah of Jaipur.

496c91ec-0db6-55e6-a0ec-27b0d984738e.name: Carpet
496c91ec-0db6-55e6-a0ec-27b0d984738e.description:
Field: Rectangular carpet, with a central field formed by three rectangles with floral motifs linked to designs of the era of Carlos IV (r.1788-1808)  
Border: The border that frames the field is composed of alternating squares and rectangles which are arranged so as to suit the size and field of carpet. These contain smaller rectangles with vegetal motifs and squares with simplified flowers.  
The carpet also has an external border that occupies its entire perimeter and consists of a faux marble and jasper design.  
This carpet was made in 1822 by Stuyck at the Royal Tapestry Factory in Madrid, a provenance which is attested to by the inscription on the outer border. These decorations, which have survived the test of time, are still being made today in the Royal Factory and derive from neoclassical templates (associated with art under King Carlos IV), due to the great acceptance of this typology in bourgeois society. Unsurprisingly, other manufactures have also imitated such neoclassical carpet designs, albeit with an inferior quality.

4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.name: Prayer rug.
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.description: In the AH 12th and 13th /AD 18th and 19th centuries, the small town of Milas in the southwest of Turkey was a centre for the manufacture of prayer rugs. A characteristic feature of later Milas prayer rugs is the dark red angular prayer niche. The inner side of the niche is edged all around with small flower-like ornaments. In the lower part of the niche is an octagon connected with four rosettes. The ornamentation within the arch is badly worn. Four green and red peonies with a rhomb between on a white background fill the area of the spandrels. The central rectangular field containing the prayer niche is framed several times by stripes of different geometrical patterns. The next border shows on a yellow background a design consisting of red octagons, alternating with large stylised blossoms in red, white and dark and light blue. From each of these blossoms emerge four heavily stylised carnations. The outer band shows a row of multicoloured small octagons on a white background.
4a4a3490-2975-5ac7-9ff7-8346fbdc5189.short_description: Prayer rug from Melas. Its characteristic feature is the dark red angular prayer niche surrounded by several stripes of geometrical pattern. Different kinds of flowers are spread over the whole area of the rug.

4c4757fd-8356-5ee9-841b-cb1cab47f528.name: Pair of shaped carpets
4c4757fd-8356-5ee9-841b-cb1cab47f528.short_description:
A pair of shaped carpets, each of arched trapezoidal form, lie together to form a large, rectangular carpet with a hexagon cut-out at centre. The carpets terminate in mirrored tips such that a narrow opening is formed when the carpets are paired. The purpose of the opening and the function of the carpets generally has been the subject of debate. Could they have been tent or palace furnishings? Might they have surrounded a throne or a fountain? Or was there some other purpose?  
Each carpet’s deep red field is replete with discrete floral sprays arranged in rows and oriented to the left, upper, and right edges. The polychrome floral sprays are rendered with enough detail to enable identification of chrysanthemums, poppies, tulips, and irises among other flowers. Works of art produced during the reign of the Mughal dynasty are famous for their delicate floral motifs. During the first half of the 17th century in particular, the Mughal emperors showed great interest in carefully observed forms found in nature, which court artists translated into a variety of materials, the best known of which is the stone inlay on the Taj Mahal. Intricately woven flower carpets are known to have been made for the Mughal court of pashmina wool and silk, at least one of which has a staggering 1,085 knots per square inch.  
These shaped carpets are more modest in production. With a cotton warp and weft and a pile of sheep’s wool, they show a weave of approximately 156 knots per square inch. They are part of a well-known group associated with the Jaipur royal house of India. They may once have been furnishings at Amber Palace, but were later moved to Jaipur where most of the group is still sealed in storage at the City Palace. Many of those carpets still have their original inventory labels which indicate the group was purchased around 1650 in Lahore (Pakistan). However, it is not certain if they were woven there, or in Kashmir, or perhaps elsewhere in Northern India.

4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.name: Prayer rug with multiple prayer niches (fragment).
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.description:
This carpet fragment is the preserved part of a considerably larger prayer rug featuring multiple prayer niches. The carpet features a row of six red niches of various widths that are closed at the top by dark-blue arches. The sixth niche on the left-hand side is only a half-niche as the carpet was cut at this point and the border repaired. The niches are separated using fine green lines that run down to the bottom and which could be interpreted as substitute columns. The carpet’s narrow border consists of a double-edged, reciprocal pattern of alternating light-blue and yellow crenellations. The wider, less complete, border has a single row of crenellations, yellow alternating with blue.  
The particular clarity of the carpet’s design and its use of colour demonstrate the Ottoman understanding of the decorative arts and their practice. Unlike most of the other known multiple prayer-niche carpets, this one is very simple, in that nowhere is it overly decorated; however even in its simplicity, it still follows a systematic composition of ordered patterns covering the surface, as can be seen repeatedly within Ottoman art from as early as the AH 9th / AD 15th century. Its simplicity, vibrant colours and the combined overall impact it creates would definitely have appealed to middle European tastes. Followers of the Islamic faith would have prayed on multiple prayer-niche carpets placed parallel to the *qibla* wall in the mosque. Admittedly, the rows of niches on this carpet merely refer to its function or use, because, essentially, each clean surface acts as a pad on which to pray. The narrowness of each niche on the carpet hints that a believer would have required more space in which to pray than that afforded by the narrow niches on the carpet.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.short_description: This carpet with its pattern of multiple niches is part of a once much larger rug. It was probably made for use in a mosque. It is unique because the design does not include the usual complicated patterns but instead makes a strong impact through its plain vibrant colours.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.method_for_datation: The carpet has been dated on the grounds of its pattern, colours and knot-technique to be from the 11th / 17th century.
4cff674a-5737-5495-a700-496faacc7750.method_for_provenance: The carpet belongs to a group of Ottoman carpets that are referred to as the Ushak Group.

4eb58eb4-04ef-58af-ab87-11a2314bc748.name: Mamluk Rug
4eb58eb4-04ef-58af-ab87-11a2314bc748.description: Woven in Cairo, Egypt in the late fifteenth century, this Mamluk rug is an exceptional model of its kind. Predominantly red, with traditional accent colors of light green and blue, the rug also introduces a light touch of yellow. The center of the rug showcases two interwoven octagons, each of which is in-turn comprised of miniature triangles, squares, and stars. Above and below the octagons are panels of fleur-de-lis. The cross panels contain figures such as blue cypress trees and green plants. The blue borders are off-set with green and red octofoils and cartouches containing lotus flowers. This Mamluk rug, while in many ways representative of its type with its use of colors and imagery, is distinguishable in its usage of mandala-like roundels in the center motif. The roundels are reminiscent of similar motifs in east Asian art and the prominence of the lotus blossoms cements this association. Additionally, the compression of the center motif makes this carpet unique in a style which focuses on elongated centerpieces. Similar rugs can be found at the St. Louis Art Museum and the Brooklyn Museum.

4ee7fe82-e416-5820-a768-7626a3306e3b.name: Daghestan prayer rug
4ee7fe82-e416-5820-a768-7626a3306e3b.description:
With a few notable exceptions, Daghestan rug motifs are field repeats. Many of the field repeats are used under *mihrab*s in prayer rugs. White-field prayer rugs of this same design were woven with little obvious change for over a century.  
In the prayer niche, as the field repeat motif, there are “floral lattice” motifs on the white background. The bird-like figures are palmettes. In the *mihrab* arch there are small florets, half of the stepped medallion and two small square motifs. The arch is a field with a red meander on a light green background. The central field is framed with three borders. The main floral border is decorated with polychrome floral motifs. Minor borders are “floral meander” on light blue ground in the inner border and floral meander on a dark blue background in the outer border. Floral meander is a very common major and minor border in Caucasian rugs.
4ee7fe82-e416-5820-a768-7626a3306e3b.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Prayer rug; Caucasus
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

4f9d11b2-a662-5fcc-ad96-aa981c116e77.description: Decorated with stylised geometric ornaments; against the background of the central red field are arranged medallions in contrasting colours of green and yellow. In the remaining area cross-shaped elements  develop. The border consists of three stripes; the wide central border has a white background bordered with red, green and dark red.

505bdab1-a532-5c33-a25d-9582f4309467.name: Carpet
505bdab1-a532-5c33-a25d-9582f4309467.description:
Initially, the production of Arraiolos carpets was characterised by a rigid and faithful adoption of Eastern carpet patterns, with their palmettes, lotus flowers, “vine scrolls”, arabesque motifs and other elements. This faithfulness to characteristic design elements allows recognition of the main sources of inspiration in this production, such as carpets from the Iberian Peninsula, Persia and Turkey, the “Holbein” and “Lotto” versions among them.  
This carpet is of great interest, since it is a rare extant example of an Arraiolos carpet based on the standard “Lotto” pattern, the influence of which in carpets currently extant in Portugal is residual. “Lotto”-design carpets were popular in Europe during the 16th century, as evidenced by interiors represented in many contemporary paintings of the period, such as in *Presentation of the Head of Saint John the Baptist*, attributed to Gregório Lopes (c. 1539‒1541).  
The carpet’s field features the characteristic geometric design of palmettes and stylised arabesques. In a contrasting colour, rosettes with angular forms fill the border. Originally, the background colour of the field was red; and traces of the pigment can still be seen in between the wool embroidery.

50b6f8e1-16d0-5432-9b45-cc0512192157.name: Double niche ‘Transylvanian’ carpet
50b6f8e1-16d0-5432-9b45-cc0512192157.description: The term “Transylvanian” rug refers to 17th- and 18th-century rugs preserved in large numbers in Transylvanian Saxon churches, and once considered to have been made in Transylvania, whereas in fact they were produced in western Anatolia. Certain Transylvanian rugs have a *mihrab* design, typical of prayer rugs; others, such as the present one, feature two opposing arches. The shape of this double niche and its undecorated beige ground are characteristic of later “Transylvanian” rugs, while the border of alternating polygonal cartouches and octagons can also be found in earlier examples. Several technical imperfections such as the inaccurate rendering of space, which accounts for the incomplete motifs in the main border, and the lack of left–right symmetry though indicative of a modest workshop, retain a certain appealing charm.

51d86b78-1536-574b-bf4e-c0258d547857.name: Carpet
51d86b78-1536-574b-bf4e-c0258d547857.description:
Field: The field is divided into four columns and four rows in which rectangular spaces house elongated octagons that contain a classic cruciform design. Other smaller cruciform elements appear between the columns. Upon the green triangular leaves, three small birds are housed. The field is framed by geometric floral schemes.  
Border: The border is composed of two smaller zigzagging borders that are separated by yellow lines and which enclose a larger border which is contrastingly decorated with facing esses linked by clamps. This motif is inspired by Chinese oriental carpets and their depiction of cloud designs.  
The warp is made of wool and the weft of naturally coloured linen. The woollen knots rely on several shades of blue, orange, yellow and green.  
The carpets knot density allows it to be classified as one of a low-medium quality in regards to its fineness.  
The design inspired by Ushak carpets, an Anatolian Turkish carpet design that was abundant since the first half of the 16th century. However, the design schemes used in the production centres of Cuenca differ from that of Anatolia, especially in regards to its colour.  
The Spanish variant, such as this one, consists of borders with Chinese clouds and opposing S or zigzag patterns. There are two examples of such a variant within the Museum.  
This carpet can be provenanced from the Monastery of the Barefoot Carmelites located in present day Segovia.

529e4353-d9fb-5895-a243-1a19e6cb982c.name: Kula prayer rug
529e4353-d9fb-5895-a243-1a19e6cb982c.description:
The rug-weaving areas of Anatolia are conventionally divided into western, central and eastern regions. Western Anatolian centres such as Uşak, Ghiordes, Kula and their vicinity have a long tradition of carpet and rug production. Carpets from these centres were very popular in Europe. The town of Kula lies southeast of Ghiordes. The most notable of its varied weaves is a type of prayer rug formerly considered as among the most successful Anatolian town and village weaves. Characteristic of Kula rugs are mellow and subdued colours of yellow and brown, and more solemn shades of red, blue and green. The cross panel is usually found only above the arch.  
In the central field there is a *mihrab* (prayer niche) with field repeat motifs organized in three rows. An interesting fact is that all motifs are faced in the opposite direction from the *mihrab* arch. Motifs in the central row resemble motifs on the so-called cemetery carpets. This motif has its origin in pictorial landscapes of the Turkish Baroque period beginning in the second half of the 18th century. The other two rows have vase with stylized flower motifs. Such a large repeating hanging floral ornaments are typical for mid-nineteenth century Kula carpets. Above the spandrel there is oblong field with a dragon and phoenix motif. The central field is framed with six rows of *sobokli* border and two minor borders with a dragon motif. The *sobokli* border is common in prayer rugs. It is made up of narrow stripes, usually seven, which symbolize seven steps of paradise.
529e4353-d9fb-5895-a243-1a19e6cb982c.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: prayer rug; Kula; Anatolia; Ghiordes
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

530ca1c3-4a81-5d51-9ca6-66560c02aee0.name: Batári-Crivelli Carpet Fragment
530ca1c3-4a81-5d51-9ca6-66560c02aee0.description: Dating from the first half of the 14th century a new type of carpet with Anatolian animal figures appeared in European, mostly Italian paintings. These floor rugs utilized squares or octagons, each shape containing animal or bird figures. This design was popular until the last third of the 15th century and was subsequently replaced by carpets of only geometric design. Literature classifies the early 15th–16th century Ottoman Turkish rugs by the name of the European painters who depicted them. The dating of these carpets relies on the dates of the paintings as clues. In two paintings by the Venetian artist Carlo Crivelli (c. 1435–c. 1495), the right wing of the *Annunciation Triptych* (1482, Frankfurt am Main, Städel Museum and the altarpiece *The Annunciation with St Emidius of 1486* (London, National Gallery), an as-yet unknown carpet type appears. Two star-shaped medallions filled with birds and geometric forms appear in a yellow background. This design element, the only known specimen of the carpet type in Crivelli’s picture with naturalistic bird representations, became a part of the collection of the Museum of Applied Arts in 1917, likely acquired from Transylvania. Its world fame owes to Ferenc Batári (1934–2005), a prominent expert of Ottoman Turkish carpets who published this design under the name “Crivelli Rug” in his study of 1984. The Museum re-named it “Batári–Crivelli Rug Fragment” in honour of Ferenc Batári on the second anniversary of his death.
530ca1c3-4a81-5d51-9ca6-66560c02aee0.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis; comparison with similar carpets depicted by Carlo Crivelli

53a8079b-66d0-5e3d-b237-95276f9697b6.name: Small Pattern Holbein Rug
53a8079b-66d0-5e3d-b237-95276f9697b6.description: Early Ottoman Carpets with endless geometric designs of the kind found on paintings by the German painter Hans Holbein Jr. (1497/8–1543) are called "Holbein Rugs". The small pattern version of the Holbein Rug is more common.  Belonging to the group having the more traditional blue-green field, it has a lower knot density and higher pile than the Museum's other small pattern Holbein Rug (MAA inv. nr. 8546), and its broad kilim weave tapering towards the ends puts it into to the less refined group of Holbein Rugs. The execution of the rug – the colouring of the Holbein guls and arabesque crosses, the irregularly alternating red-ivory and red-ochre colour pairs, the departure from tradition in the border and other characteristics already mentioned – is suggestive of village carpets. What makes this rug so valuable is that at the kilim-woven top edge, an approximately 40 cm section of the end finish, has remained in its original condition. The edge was folded over and stitched down a width of 2–3cm.

53fb542e-7715-5b8d-b6ac-6fba66ddeae6.name: Pictorial carpet with landscape and a pair of birds
53fb542e-7715-5b8d-b6ac-6fba66ddeae6.short_description: Lahore, one of the new capitals of the Mughal Empire after the Emperor Akbar had abandoned the imperial complex of Fatehpur Sikri, was a major centre of carpet production on the Indian subcontinent. Stylistically, the carpet’s design fits very well into the late Akbar / early Jahangir period respectively. The idealised garden scene with identifiable pairs of birds (peacocks, cranes, fowls, etc.) and plants is designed naturalistically and delicately so that one can assume its model originated from the court studio. Its alignment suggests that it was likely used as a wall hanging. In the border, the carpet features grotesque masks typical of Mughal India, as well as a *ton sur ton* colour scheme and the omission of sharp contouring. For a carpet with wool flora, it has a very high knot density, which underscores its extraordinary quality.

559aa521-7185-5807-b191-e79fc16098c9.name: Tree of Life Carpet
559aa521-7185-5807-b191-e79fc16098c9.short_description:
Vegetal and animal motifs decorate this Iranian carpet with the central Tree of Life motif. Originating from Kerman in the Qajar dynasty, the pile is only cut once the knotting process is complete and the textile is taken off its loom.  
  
People of different faiths and geographic contexts have embraced the tree of life as a symbol of the essence and interconnectedness of all living things. As such, the motif becomes a thread binding people in their shared ideas of the evergreen tree from Bhutan to Germany, the Mayan Empire and the Iroquois People.  
  
Qajar depictions of the tree of life stem from pre-Islamic Zoroastrianism, considered to be the ancestor of all humans, animals and plants. In Islam, the life tree is called *sidra* or *tuba* and grows in paradise. The fruits known as *haoma* (also *homa*) feed those who enter heaven after death. The carpet displays fruits including grapes, pears, figs and pomegranate. The woven peacock, phoenix and eagle are protectors of the tree according to Persian mythology.  
  
A poem by Sufi poet Saadi frames the carpet within its border. The poetry mirrors the garden imagery, as one of Saadi's central themes and symbols of Persian cultural continuity.

5606ef72-d7ce-5f38-b3cf-6741f5dab43a.name: Uşak Lotto
5606ef72-d7ce-5f38-b3cf-6741f5dab43a.description:
Anatolian rug-weaving areas are conventionally divided into western, central and eastern regions. Western Anatolian centres such as Ushak, Gördes, Kula and their vicinity have a long tradition of carpet and rug production. Carpets from these centres were very popular in Europe. Ushak has been a centre of carpet manufacturing since the 15th century and possibly long before. Larger carpets woven in the vicinity of Ushak were probably reaching European markets by the 15th century and many western Anatolian rug designs appear in Italian Renaissance paintings.  
The co-called “Lotto” carpet was named after the Venetian painter Lorenzo Lotto (1480–1556) who depicted it at least twice, in *The Alms of Saint Anthony* (1542, Ss Giovanni e Paolo, Venice) and *Family Group* (1547, National Gallery, London). These carpets are characterized by a repeating pattern of arabesques in different tones of yellow, usually on a red background.  
In the central field, on the red background, there is a yellow symmetrical arabesque pattern – two parallel rows of octagons and quatrefoils with numerous tendrils and hooks. The main border has a cartouche pattern with medallions in alternating colours – yellow and light blue medallions on dark blue background. The secondary border is decorated with red and blue meander motif on a white background. On its narrow sides the carpet has kilim finishes.

568aa288-3d05-5bf2-9461-11f5d3c78666.name: *Portrait of Charles of Bourbon*
568aa288-3d05-5bf2-9461-11f5d3c78666.description:
The Portrait of Charles of Bourbon (Charles III of Spain), one of a pair together with a portrait depicting Queen Maria Amalia of Saxony, now lost, is one of the first creations of the Royal Tapestry Factory in Naples.  
Founded by the young King in 1737, soon after his arrival in Naples, the tapestry factory, together with a factory for the carving of semiprecious stones, was one of the first established by order of Charles of Bourbon. This decision must have been influenced by the young Charles’ interest in the Medici factories that were still operating in Florence. This interest developed when the future King stayed in the city in 1732, as the future successor to Gian Gastone de’ Medici.  
In fact, a small group of Florentine weavers and carvers of precious stones was responsible for giving life to the first two royal Bourbon factories in Naples, located near the church of San Carlo alle Mortelle. The factory, which was also composed of a local workforce, with the aim of promoting the development of new artistic techniques in the Kingdom of Naples, was under the direction of the Florentine Domenico del Rosso. And it was to the Florentine weaver that Charles entrusted his portrait and that of his consort; as with other items produced during the initial phase of the factories, these works were intended to celebrate the King and their patron. Production of the tapestry was completed in 1741, as indicated by the presence of the signature and date on the bottom right-hand edge of the tapestry: “DOM.CO D. L. ROSSO 1741”. The artist who provided the preparatory study for the tapestry is unknown; however, there is speculation that it may have been Giovan Battista delle Piane, who was a court portrait painter during these years; or Francesco Solimena, based on the tapestry’s extraordinary expressiveness and the intensity of the light and the colours in its original state.

56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.name: Prayer carpet '*sajada*'
56bb796e-7473-5c75-af83-c44e76fe7578.short_description: A highlight of the Khanenko Museum's Islamic collection is an Ottoman carpet dating to AD late 17th–first half of the 18th century. The carpet belongs to the traditional type of "*sajada*", or prayer, carpets, with composition based on a stylized picture of *mihrab* - a prayer niche in a mosque indicating the direction where Muslims turn during the prayer. The composition and motifs of the carpet, particularly the central niche coloured in plain dark blue and crowned with arch of an acute stepped shape as well as a peculiar geometrized carnation pattern above and below the niche, suggest that the item was manufactured in workshops of Giordes or Kula, two leading centres of Turkish carpet-making in the 17th–18th centuries. Numerous narrow ornamental borders that fringe the central arch add a specific elegance to the piece of art.

5759d9cd-8272-5ef6-8d47-591a7af392bc.name: *Allegory of Autumn*
5759d9cd-8272-5ef6-8d47-591a7af392bc.description:
The figures for Autumn are in an open landscape in the foreground grouped together off the central axis. The allegory of Autumn is characterised by the seated woman in the middle flanked by winged female genii symbolising the two months of September and October, which hold the Zodiac symbols of Libra and Scorpio. November balances the group, shown as a winged female genius riding on a Centaur holding the sign of Sagittarius. On the ground in front of the figures area still-life groups composed of autumn fruits. To one side, in the background, is an open porch within which people are busy harvesting grapes; on the other side, in an open landscape partly closed by hills and mountains, four other figures are busy in autumnal labours.  
*The* *Allegory of Autumn* tapestry belongs within the *Four Seasons* series, of which the Museum also owns *Winter*; of the *Four Elements* series, the Museum holds *Air and Water*. It is likely the tapestries' designs are after cartoons by Ludwig van Schoor and are representative of Brussels tapestry production of the period showing a strong Rubens tradition and French influence, especially the painter Le Brun. Weaving took place in Pieter den Hecke's workshop in Brussels. He inherited cartoons from the workshop of his father, Jan Frans, using them repeatedly in tapestry series that were popular on the European market between 1690 and 1720.  
The original border on the Museum's tapestry *Autumn* was cut-off lengthwise and the signature – usually found on the border –probably removed as a result.  
*The Allegory of Autumn* belongs to a series of tapestries depicting Seasons and Elements made after van Schoor's cartoons, kept in the Royal Museum of Arts and History in Brussels, in Würzburg Palace and in a private collection.  
*Allegory of Autumn* and two other tapestries acquired at the end of the 19th century were probably part of the refurbishment of Pribislavac Manor carried out by the heirs of Count Festetić.
5759d9cd-8272-5ef6-8d47-591a7af392bc.short_description:
*Allegory of Autumn* belongs to the tapestry series *The Four Seasons* made in Pieter van der Hecke's workshop probably after cartoons by Ludwig van Schoor. Pieter van der Hecke took over the workshop of his father, Jan Frans, repeatedly using cartoons he had inherited from his father's workshop in a series of tapestries. Today, other tapestries in the series are in the Royal Museum of Arts and History in Brussels, Würzburg Palace and a private collection.  
*Allegory of Autumn* and two other tapestries acquired at the end of the 19th century were probably part of the refurbishment of Pribislavac Manor carried out by the heirs of Count Festetić.

576b29fe-1757-5d8f-b8d8-aa0a86493db6.name: Carpet
576b29fe-1757-5d8f-b8d8-aa0a86493db6.description:
Carpet of rectangular format with a continuous field decoration.  
Field: On a dark blue background, two zigzagging white parallel ribbons, depicting alternating spaces, which contain stars separated by rhombuses. The different colours of these elements show diagonal bands, producing a false transverse decoration effect.  
Border: Composed of multiple borders. The long sides alternate four narrow and wide borders with motifs similar to the field as well as the decoration of other carpets of this same series. The short sides contain a very wide border, with pseudo-*kufic* writing of a purely aesthetic nature, including similar motifs. The perimeter is topped by a single border with a double zigzag motif in the same colours as the field.  
The knots consist of wool in navy blue, yellow, red, white and brown.  
The border is composed of multiple borders, something characteristic of a series identified as "carpets of a honeycomb field and multiple borders", as Sánchez Ferrer calls them. This series is named by some scholars as a heraldic series or "of the Admirals", since in some of the preserved specimens there are heraldic motifs of various aristocratic families inserted in the field.  
The decoration of this carpet is in the Mudejar style.  
Whilst the carpet does not retain its original size, decoratively speaking, it has been very well reconstructed.

57fdd991-8257-544b-a045-69da20f95d9c.name: Arabesque carpet with medallion
57fdd991-8257-544b-a045-69da20f95d9c.description:
A 17th century Safavid Persian pile carpet with an Arabesque design dominating its large yellow centre-field, which is adorned with a pink medallion. The centre-field is framed with quarter medallions in its four corners, and surrounded by a narrow dark blue border.  
  
The Arabesque design consists of two intertwined networks of meandering vegetal stems and tendrils with foliates and rosettes. One stem network is in dark blue and pink leaf scrolls, and the other is a lighter blue network of large leaf scrolls and coloured flowers. Multi-coloured palmettes are positioned at the junctions where the two networks overlap or criss-cross. The superimposed pink medallion in the centre of the field is decorated with an arabesque motif too. Dark blue foliates on lighter blue vegetal stems form the medallion’s pattern. The four quarter medallions in the four corners of the filed are formed of arabesque motifs of salmon-pink coloured stems and foliates adorned with dark blue palmettes on an ivory background. The carpet’s border pattern consists of two networks of foliate scrolls that intertwine, one in blue and one in light brown / ochre colour.  
  
The best of its type, this early carpet’s quintessentially Islamic Arabesque design shows how effectively such patterns can be employed to create a visually pleasing floor covering.

58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.name: Floor Spread (*sofra*) with Design of Tulips and Pomegranates
58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.short_description: A circular floor spread (*sofra*) with design of tulips and pomegranates. Around the outer edge is a narrow border of floral motifs. Within this comes a wide ring containing large tulips and artichoke or pomegranate motifs which have tulips within them set alternately. In the center is a double circle containing floral motifs like those in the border. The textile is mounted on a red velvet background. The design features red, blue, green, white, and yellow embroidered elements on a natural plain cloth background. There are slight repairs and many stains. The textile is pieced down the middle.
58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.dates: Hegira 11th century to early 12th century / AD 17th century
58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
58571b94-fb2a-50e6-8245-cbdd1f785d50.method_for_provenance: This circular shaped *sofra* is filled with tulip motifs characteristic of Ottoman embroidery. Tulips were originally a wild flower growing in Central Asia, and by the late seventeenth century Ottoman artists had perfected representations of the tulip form.

58fd0ec7-5172-5bbf-bac4-88e40da41359.name: Alpujarra Rug or Bedcover
58fd0ec7-5172-5bbf-bac4-88e40da41359.description:
The Alpujarra rugs (or bedcovers) with pile in loops were produced in the Alpujarra region south of Granada between the 15th-16th and the 19th centuries. Alpujarra rugs or covers are classified as European folk art and were influenced by Eastern rugs.  
The cover was woven in three parts on a narrow beam loom, then stitched together. The weaver used only three colours of mercerized cotton (ivory, abrashed saffron yellow and light green) and metal thread. The yellow ground field is adorned with a diagonal lattice with green and ivory rosettes in the rhombuses. A two-headed eagle with a crown is in the centre. On the lower edge of the field in the inscription “DOÑA ROSALIA BTAVO” (BRAVO?). The border is green and has a crowned lion in each of the four corners. Between the lions is an alternating pattern of rosettes and pairs of doves atop bowls. The outer border contains stylised lilies alternating with star rosettes.  
Alfréd Hoffman, owner of *Eggenberger*, one of the oldest book companies in Pest (founded in 1768), donated the bedcover in 1894 to the Museum of Applied Arts in accordance with the will of friend, János Kovachich-Molnár (1838-1894), who had been his business partner since 1863.

5ae10050-97a5-5615-99f1-15adf017d907.name: Carpet
5ae10050-97a5-5615-99f1-15adf017d907.short_description: This carpet is remarkable both for its beauty and age, with the distinction of being the oldest silk-pile carpet still extant. Dated to the early AH 9th century / AD 15th century, it has been attributed to either Central Asia or Iran, or to the Deccan region of India, areas that were linked by political and commercial ties. This carpet stands out for its bright colours and the unique motif of a gaming board. The chess board was found only on carpets of the AH 9th and 10th centuries / AD 15th century.

5b14fcda-5a67-5716-a58e-6c03e43b9e8f.name: Ushak carpet
5b14fcda-5a67-5716-a58e-6c03e43b9e8f.description: Woven for the wealthy Ottoman home market, Uşak carpets were also used as diplomatic gifts and appeared in European paintings during the 16th century by artists such as Velasquez, Zurbaran and Vermeer. The principal design of this Uşak carpet consists of elaborately complex pattern which was believed to be influenced by stylistic developments in illuminated manuscripts during the rule of Mehmet II Fatih (1432-1481). The most magnificent early examples of these carpets shared border features with each other, and also an elegance of drawing of the main field, which make it clear why the design was so prevalent.

5b20368a-3b46-5473-bfd6-eef5207b3b2f.name: Kashan carpet
5b20368a-3b46-5473-bfd6-eef5207b3b2f.description:
At the end of the 15th century, Kashan was considered (along with Tabriz, Isfahan, Mashhad and Kerman) to be among the finest weaving centres in the East. Its reputation lasted throughout the 17th century, not only due to the quantity, but also to the technical and aesthetic superiority of its products. Kashan carpets are among the most beautiful, expensive and finest of all Persian carpets, thanks to the extremely high silk knot-count (approx. 10,000 knots per square decimetre), which allows for highly detailed and minute decoration. Currently there is knowledge of 16 small carpets (1.65-metre loom) of which this carpet is one. It has a rectangular field with a red background filled in with fine branches, small flowers and a wide, quadrilobed, green central medallion. It is framed by a yellow, sinuous, phytomorphic band, with two palmettes suspended at its upper and lower edges. The corners of the field, with blue quarter-medallions, contain arabesques in tones of yellow and beige.  
With a dark-green background, the main border is ornamented with delicate red tendrils, which alternate together with flowers, palmettes and Chinese cloud scrolls (*tchi*) of different sizes.

5c46dc00-745f-5333-a2a8-b677f0639b27.name: Camel flank decoration *asmalyk*
5c46dc00-745f-5333-a2a8-b677f0639b27.description: Turkmen weavers produced special pentagonal rugs (*asmalyk*) to decorate the camel that carried the bride during the wedding ceremony. The rugs were fastened together with bands of braids, and a tent for the bride, made of embroidered textiles, was placed between them on the camel’s hump. When weaving such a rug, the task of making the point of the pentagon, using a combination of plain and pile weaving, required special skill and experience on the part of the weaver. This *asmalyk* is remarkably even in its shape and perfect in its weaving; unfortunately, it is missing a fringe, an important part of the embellishment of traditional Turkmen animal decorations.

5c8ba1d5-36db-53e5-9a66-80b59acef816.name: Medallion and Çintamani Ottoman Rug
5c8ba1d5-36db-53e5-9a66-80b59acef816.description:
New styles incorporating chiefly Iranian, but also Mamluk elements, appeared in Turkish Court art as the Ottoman Empire expanded after the capture of Tabriz (1514) and Cairo (1517). The court style developed by the artists, painters, illuminators and calligraphers working in the Court, which started with manuscripts and miniatures, came to dominate every branch of art – jewellery, tiles, fabrics and carpets. The term "court carpets" designates those rugs produced to a very high standard with patterns designed by the court artists. Some of these are products of the court luxury manufactories in Istanbul and others come from workshops supervised by the court (Cairo, Uşak). In the Mamluk carpet weaving manufactory in Cairo, which came under Turkish control in 1517, the hitherto dominant geometric pattern gave way to the court floral style favoured by the Ottomans. It was only the pattern which changed on the Cairene Ottoman carpets; the technical features, asymmetric knots and the use of silk warp and weft threads, stayed the same.  
  
The carpet’s red background is occupied by a central ragged-leaf mandorla with arabesque or *rumi* (arabesque, based on floral, foliate or biomorphic design) lilies framed by *saz* (reed, bullrush) leaves and lotus flowers in the centre. The four corners of the background are cut off by quarter-star medallions of intricate design and *rumi* decorations. The remaining area is occupied by small *çintamani* (Ottoman court motifs of triangular arrangement of three balls above two cloud bands of waves, or a cloud band with one ball) arranged in horizontal rows, offset row by row. The main border is the typical 16th century floral Court style adornment, Chinese lotus flowers and rosettes arranged along an undulating stem, and the outer and inner borders contain alternating red and yellow rosettes strung along an undulating stem. This kind of rug is regarded as a “mass produced” item which the Court workshops made for sale, this evidenced by four known nearly identical rugs (London:Victoria and Albert Museum; Berlin: Museum für Islamische Kunst; Paris: Musée Jacquemart-André; New York: Metropolitan Museum). According to Atıl Esin, four of the five rugs – all except the New York piece – come from the Palazzo Corsi in Florence.

5c9448f2-2078-5ba5-bdf7-7a4281eb8172.name: Çanakkale Rug
5c9448f2-2078-5ba5-bdf7-7a4281eb8172.description: The rugs of the Çanakkale region are famous for their wool. Pure wool, obtained from sheep owned by the weaver, was used to weave the rugs. All of the steps required for the production of the wool yarn was done within the weavers family. This included shearing the sheep and colouring the fleece with natural dyes. This is a rare and important example of the geometric design typical of Çanakkale rugs. A distinctive pattern of eight arm stars is woven with geometrical border decorations. The field is called a “box” or *sandik* motif. It is a traditional rectangle shape resembling a box containing the bride's trousseau, likely a reference to marriage. The ground of the rug is decorated with flower motifs locally called “apple blossoms”, *elma çiçeği*. The border is decorated with palm tree leaves.

5ce189d9-6756-515c-a640-1fb05875a7b5.name: Carpet
5ce189d9-6756-515c-a640-1fb05875a7b5.description:
The style of this carpet ties it to Mughal court arts; in particular, the red ground floral carpets associated with the palace at Jaipur in northern India. The dark red field is covered with a diaper lattice composed of stylized leaves; inside of each cell is a different spray of flowers. The flowers all grow in the same direction, giving the carpet design a directional orientation; there is only one way to view it so that the flowers are right-side up.  
  
Characteristic of the Mughal floral style is the greater use of botanical details and more complex compositions than in the arts of the neighboring Islamic empires to the West. This is largely because of European herbals, which were major source of inspiration for the Mughal artists. On the other hand, the Mughal artists brought the floral representations to a more idealized state. Mughal flowers are more symmetrically composed and a greater degree of orderliness in the individual details of the plant can be seen compared to their European originals, which arises from naturalistic representations through direct observations.  
  
The way flowers are represented in art depends upon the artist’s medium. Carpet weaving has technical constraints and challenges, and each carpet weaver must confront them by altering and adjusting as they weave. This is especially true for floral designs. It is the pile that carries the designs in carpets. Thus, a carpet design is created knot by knot, row by row. Only a highly skilled weaver can transfer sophisticated curvilinear floral designs such as the ones seen on this carpet to this medium. The materials used for the weaving also need to be very fine so that the weaver can pack as many knots as possible into each square inch to create the curvilinear lines of flowers in a medium which favors 90° angles. In summary, the thickness of yarns used for warp, weft, and pile, the type of knot, the construction of the loom, the skill of the weaver, the complexity of design, and the weaving tradition are all factors that affect the final carpet design.

5d4e9859-0856-5412-b38f-7901f60473ea.name: *Afshari* carpet
5d4e9859-0856-5412-b38f-7901f60473ea.description:
Little is known about the rural rugs of Kirman so authors often describe them as *afshari* only for convenience and not as a precise label. The Afshari appear to be a minority population, although they may be the most important. They are a Turkic tribe with groups in the Caucasus, Turkey and Iran south of Kirman.  
Afshari products are seldom larger than about 170 x 200cm and they tend to be slightly more square-shaped. Some pieces have a striped kilim band at the ends. There are great variations in design, and many motifs found elsewhere are given a fresh approach, such as *boteh*, lozenge-shaped panels, medallion designs with flowers and a stylized vase.  
The central field is divided into nine fields in a form of rhombus. Each field has a horizontal vase motif surrounded with *boteh* and floret motifs. *Boteh* is a universal oriental rug design element. *Boteh* is Persian for “bush” and *buta* is Hindi for “flower”. It is thought to have originated in Kashmir in its curvilinear form. The form and content of botehs are often distinctive for particular areas and may be valuable clues to the origin of a weaving. The central field is framed with four borders. The main border has floral hexagons on narrow sides and on wider sides there is the Y motif between floral hexagons. Two minor borders have zig-zag motifs. On its narrow sides the carpet has kilim finishes.
5d4e9859-0856-5412-b38f-7901f60473ea.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Persia; Afshari; Kerman
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

5d615bba-7bb8-5344-bdfe-e5a68d229f03.name: South Persian carpet, Khamseh (?)
5d615bba-7bb8-5344-bdfe-e5a68d229f03.description:
The province of Fars lies south of Isfahan and west of Kirman, bordering the Persian Gulf to the south. At one time, Fars was the centre of the Persian Empire. It is an area inhabited by people of diverse origins. There are two major tribal divisions in Fars: Qashqa’i and the Khamseh Federation. It is difficult to define the areas inhabited by each group but basically the Qashqa’i occupy the area west of Shiraz and the Khamseh area to the east of Shiraz.  
The Khamseh Federation arose as a political entity during the 19th century as a counterpoint to the Qashqa’i. It consists of five tribes: Ainalu, Baharlu, Baseri, Nafar and Arab. *Khamseh* is Arabic for “group of five”. The Arab tribe is the largest and most important. They were for decades the most prolific rug weavers in Fars. Many of the 19th-century Arab rug designs show stylized bird figures, often with a series of a small, lozenge-shaped medallions along the vertical axis. Khamseh bird rugs appear in a dozen of different formats, and they are obviously made by an assortment of tribal groups.  
Southeast Persian carpets from the province of Fars can possibly be attributed to one of the tribes from Khamseh confederacy. In the central field on the red background there are two inscribed double hexagonal medallions. As a field repeat motif the herati pattern can be observed – curving leaves and a lattice. The central field is framed with five borders. The central border is decorated with florets and *kochak* (ram's horns) motifs on a dark blue background. Inner borders are variations of a floral meander. The outer border is decorated with diagonal white, blue and red stripes.
5d615bba-7bb8-5344-bdfe-e5a68d229f03.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Persia; medallion carpet; Khamseh
materials: Wool;knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

5dfe61da-e979-574a-b7b8-1d7d4aaa5094.name: Safavid *Herat* Spiral Vine and Palmette Rug
5dfe61da-e979-574a-b7b8-1d7d4aaa5094.description: The 16th/17th century *Herat* Safavid carpet belonged to the museum’s first director, Dr György Ráth (1828–1905). A lawyer and art collector, Ráth furnished his villa at 2 Városligeti Avenue, in Budapest, with more than 1,000 art works, including some oriental carpets. Archive photographs show that the carpet was hung on the wall of the ‘Gems Room’ in the villa. We have no information on the provenance of Ráth’s carpets, but he probably acquired them via art dealers. The scarlet field of the *Herat* carpet has a pattern of scrolling vines with palmettes and blossoms and an unusual border of cartouches of different colours and shapes on a dark blue field, a design type that is more often attributed to 17th-century central Persia. Despite its fragmentary condition, the design gives the impression of being complete.

5e3bd511-e913-550c-a38c-80f8d87cf0e9.name: *Capture of Francis I, King of France*
5e3bd511-e913-550c-a38c-80f8d87cf0e9.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014).  
The central episode represented in the tapestry is the capture of Francis I. After having passed through the copse, depicted high up on the left, and after having fought bravely on the muddy terrain, unfavourable to the heavy French cavalry, the King is captured following a shot from an arquebus that wounds his horse.  
Francis I is depicted in the foreground while three cavaliers from the enemy formation, La Motte de Noyers, the German Nicolas von Salm and the Count of Montmartin – as indicated by the abbreviated text that tends to be included on the horses’ tack and armour – help him to get to his feet. On the left is depicted the Viceroy of Naples, Charles de Lannoy, identified by the letters “VISSEROV” on the blade of his sword, while he dismounts from his horse to accept the surrender of the King.  
Behind him a horseman raises the imperial standard, on which one can distinguish the double-headed eagle and Hercules’ pillars with the motto “PLUS OVLTRE”. In the centre of the tapestry, the man on a horse, who is wearing a dark outfit, on which stands out the white cross that indicates that he is on the side of the French, is Henry II, King of Navarre, captured in battle; in the distance, on the right, among the horsemen who have just come out of the copse, appears Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, identified by the word “BOURBON” on the reins, as well as by the presence of French *fleurs-de-lis* on the horse’s peytral.  
In the foreground, on the ground, there is the arquebus with which Francis I’s horse was hit. This is also a symbol of the new way of fighting in battle and the end of the cavalry: the use of firearms, striking from a distance, allowed the less courageous to prevail.

5e6943fd-7101-58f0-8df8-80cc6f82f37e.name: *Advance of the imperial troops and attack of the French gendarmerie led by Francis I*
5e6943fd-7101-58f0-8df8-80cc6f82f37e.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries of the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections with the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Through the decorative cycle of tapestries, the intention was to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, commanded by Francis I, which took place on 24 February 1525, and was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia. Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014).  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels and to adorn a large room in the Royal Palace to mark the occasion of the Assembly of the Estates-General of Brussels in March 1531, the cycle arrived in Spain in the 1550s with Mary of Hungary, who later gave it to her young nephew Don Carlos. It is Don Carlos who links the history of the tapestries to the d’Avalos family, bequeathing them to Francesco Ferdinando d’Avalos (Buchanan 2002), Marquis of Pescara, and direct descendant of Fernando Francesco d’Avalos, the hero of Pavia depicted in the tapestry *Defeat of the French cavalry* and identified thanks to the writing on the neck of his horse.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris), a renowned painter, and designer of tapestries and stained-glass windows. The preparatory cartoons for the weaver were derived from these designs, or *modelletti*, with scenes reversed, given that, at the time in Brussels, tapestries were woven on “low-warp” looms. The presence of the weaver’s mark on the border of two of the tapestries provides a reference point for when the series was produced, because a decree of 1528 required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and this has allowed the workshop in which they were made to be identified as that of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen).  
The initial stages of the battle are represented in the tapestry. In the background, the infantry and cavalry of the imperial army are advancing, led by Charles III, Duke of Bourbon, Constable of France (recognisable from the writing on his horse’s peytral), ready to attack the French troops. On the right, in the middle distance, King Francis I is depicted in the act of killing the Marquis of Civita Santangelo, commander of the enemy troops, an event that marks one of the first French successes. In the extreme foreground, on the right, several imperial arquebusiers can be seen preparing their weapons: across their shoulders, they wear a strap from which hang pouches containing gunpowder charges that have already been measured out; at their waists they have horn-shaped powder magazines. The legs of the arquebusier seen from behind, which are cut off at the knee, were originally hidden by a section of the wall of Visconti Park, as is also shown by the preparatory drawing for the tapestry, now in the Louvre. This section of wall could have been removed together with the border of the tapestry, no earlier than the second half of the 18th century. In fact, according to a description from the 1770s, the lower border, still intact, displayed decorative motifs with tritons and sea horses, similar to those that appear in the *Hunts of Maximilian*, another series of tapestries produced for Charles V from designs by van Orley, and today in the Louvre (Buchanan 2002).  
In the foreground, the King is depicted again, with his sallet visor lowered, as he heads with his elite guard towards a copse, where a fatal trap will be set for him.

5e9b4b02-68df-5a5e-b287-ce07332661a1.name: Block printed cotton hanging
5e9b4b02-68df-5a5e-b287-ce07332661a1.short_description: Typical products of the Qajar dynastic period, the Persian term *qalamkar* (literally, “pen-work“) refers to printed or/and painted cotton fabrics decorated with animals, depictions of Persian heroic fables, floral and tendril patterns or cypresses growing out of vases. Depending on the motif, *qalamkars* were employed as fabric for clothing, wall hangings or table cloths. The most famous member of this dynasty, Naser ad-Din Shah, visited the Vienna World’s Fair in 1873.

5ef10542-ba11-5392-a54d-cdb92c9a5449.name: Mughal floral carpet fragment
5ef10542-ba11-5392-a54d-cdb92c9a5449.description:
A 17th century Mughal Indian carpet fragment with a wine-red background and a design that consists of a variety of multi-coloured floral shrubs lined in staggered rows, with a wide border of more compact floral shrubs on two of its sides. On closer inspection, this fragment appears to be made up of several fragments, large and small, from the same carpet. These fragments have been stitched together to create a tidy piece. For this reason, some pieces do not match in floral design with adjacent parts of the carpet.  
  
Woven of fine wool on a cotton and silk foundation, the floral shrubs have been naturalistically depicted, as is typical of this type of Mughal carpets. These flowers include irises, roses, carnations and tulips. But even though the floral shrubs in the centre field are similar to ones that appear in other Mughal carpets of this genre, the border design is believed to be unprecedented. In manufacture, this carpet belongs to Lahore, and may have been woven for the Amber Palace in Jaipur. The only other known fragment to have survived from this particular carpet is believed to be in a German private collection.
5ef10542-ba11-5392-a54d-cdb92c9a5449.provenance: India, Jaipur, possibly from the Amber Palace

keywords: floral motifs; floral decoration; fragment
materials: Cotton warp; silk weft; wool pile

606e0f77-a91d-5886-be20-1823ea36ebff.description: Milas, in Muğla Province was an important rug producing centre of Anatolia. Typical Milas rugs began to appear in the 16th  and 17th centuries. The continuous motif, locally called “cattle water” is the most distinctive decorative element of Milas rugs. In this example, it appears  as five stripes on the main ground. Flower rosettes complete the outer border.

60db83b0-e090-5ad3-b467-090f3263e0b9.name: Single Niche 'Transylvanian' Prayer Rug
60db83b0-e090-5ad3-b467-090f3263e0b9.description: A characteristic type of Ottoman rugs is the "Transylvanian" double niche rug. Several variants of the type fashionable for over two centuries are known. Its common feature is the hexagonal medallion filling the central field created by mirroring the original *mihrab* (prayer niche) of the traditional prayer rug across the central axis. The carpet is a fine example of the rare single niche version of "Transylvanian" rugs. Its red *mihrab* (prayer niche) is filled with a floral-foliate scroll symmetric about the long axis, and a mosque lamp hangs from the peak of the *mihrab*. The spandrels are decorated by a large rosette and serrated leaves on a dark blue field. In the border, "Transylvanian" cartouches alternate with eight-pointed stars.

612351f2-75a6-5485-beb3-2f66e1312be5.name: Ceramic floor
612351f2-75a6-5485-beb3-2f66e1312be5.description:
The Palatine Chapel, founded by King Dinis (1261‒1325, crowned 1279) in the early 14th century, contains one of the oldest ceramic floors in Portugal. This rare floor of the main altar probably dates from the 15th century, contemporary with the reign of King Afonso V (1432‒81, crowned 1438).  
The Chapel, a Christian religious space dedicated to the Holy Spirit, is characterised by the Mudéjar style, Hispano-Muslim ceiling decoration in *alfarge* carved wood and by the *alicatado* floor, formed from ceramic pieces of many colours and shapes. Both the mosaic floor and the wooden ceiling are among the oldest examples of Mudéjar craftsmanship in Portugal.  
The configuration and decorative composition used in the ceramic floor remind one of the Mudéjar-style carpets, decorated with a network of interlacement motifs containing geometric patterns, commissioned to embellish palaces and churches.  
Up until the second half of the 15th century, the term “*alicatado*” (Spanish for cut-tiles, derived from the Arabic verb qata’a, “to cut”) was given to the ceramic mosaics made in this technique. It requires piecing together monochromatic enamelled *tesserae* (small glazed ceramic pieces of various geometric shapes and colours that had been glazed and cut beforehand) to create decorative compositions with geometric patterns, a delicate, painstaking and expensive task, used mostly for paving floors, but also for wall surfaces.  
This ceramic floor might date from the same period as that of the room where King Afonso VI was imprisoned, one of the Royal Palace’s oldest rooms.
612351f2-75a6-5485-beb3-2f66e1312be5.method_for_datation: Other art historians have dated the Palatine Chapel ceramic floor to the 15th century, probably contemporary with King Afonso V (1432‒81; r.1438‒81). This monarch was born and died at the Royal Palace of Sintra and resided there frequently, as demonstrated by the countless documents signed by him here. Like King Duarte (1391‒38; r. 1433‒38), his father, King Afonso V seems to have held a special affection for the Palace at Sintra and carried out various improvements. He undertook the expansion and embellishment of the Palatine Chapel, probably from the mid-15th century (possibly between 1448 and 1476).
