61963b6b-6f90-512a-b6cc-db9799eb953a.name: Ersari, so-called *Beshir*
61963b6b-6f90-512a-b6cc-db9799eb953a.description: Measuring 4 metres long and 1.70 metres wide, this piece is representative of the large-format carpets from the middle Amu-Darya region, probably made in oasis cities. In older literature, it is also referred to as Beshir or Ersari-Beshir. The pattern and ornamental repertoire of such carpets are predominantly of non-Turkmen origin and often go back to Ikat motifs. Furthermore, variants of the Minah Khani pattern, boteh forms, or large rhombus patterns are characteristic. This piece shows a rhombus cross pattern, which can already be found on a colour plate of the first monograph of Turkmen carpets, published in 1908/1909 in St. Petersburg. The pattern's design concept in the publication of the Russian general A. A. Bogolyuvov also corresponds to that of the Dresden carpet. Despite some sections with a more pronounced pile, this knotting is characterized by its lustrous wool and a wonderful play of colours. The field and border ornaments seem to hover over the base, alternately designed in shades of blue and green. The rich reddish-brown colour, combined with the accentuated use of yellow, appears somewhat restrained, which further enhances the composition's overall effect.
61963b6b-6f90-512a-b6cc-db9799eb953a.holder: Museum für Völkerkunde Dresden (Ethnological Museum Dresden), Dresden State Art Collections
61963b6b-6f90-512a-b6cc-db9799eb953a.obtention: Purchased in 1989 from a Dresden Collector, Friedrich Uhlemann, who afore acquired the piece from a private household in Reichenbach, Vogtland. The owners offered the piece in response to a newspaper announcement searching for old carpets. Uhlemann was very much engaged in helping Dresden painter Wilhelm Müller (1928–99) to secure oriental rugs, carpets and flat weaves of rural and nomadic tradition that were still on the territory of GDR with building up a collection for the Ethnographic Museum of Dresden, mainly between 1979 and 1986.

61f8f6ec-92d5-556e-b7d6-2e874ba81191.name: Hanging
61f8f6ec-92d5-556e-b7d6-2e874ba81191.short_description: This prayer rug is woven with a triple arcade, hanging lamps, vases with bunches of flowers and large flower scrolls. The pastel pinkish colours and the band woven with a flower scroll are typical of Chian silks. A famous one dated 1742 is kept in the monastery of Nea Mone on Chios. The export of Chian silks is recorded from the 15th century when the island was under Genoese rule and continued when the island passed into Ottoman hands in 1566.

6291cb5f-19ca-54c3-bfec-a8fe553b43e2.name: Pashmina carpet
6291cb5f-19ca-54c3-bfec-a8fe553b43e2.description:
Although this piece was purchased, and came to Portugal in the 20th century, Indian carpets began arriving in Portugal as the consequence of trade in Asia from the 16th century onwards. This influx occurred within a similar time frame, although on a smaller scale, as that of Persian carpets. This large fragment was produced in Kashmir or Lahore in the middle of the 17th century, during the reign of Shah Jahan (1592‒1666); a period that itself is associated with the use of floral designs. This emperor, like Akbar and Jahangir, stood out due to his having supported artistic development through the workshops of the royal court: a similar sort of workshop production was probably responsible for this piece, and the material used and the high quality of the design both attest to this. The use of pashmina-pile knots made from the fleece of the Himalayan mountain goat (*Capra hircus laniger*) onto a silk foundation allowed for a high knot-count and consequently a very detailed design.  
Although the earliest Mughal carpets from the 16th century reveal the direct influence of Persian archetypes, by the 17th century, Mughal carpet designs would be composed of a greater number of Indian motifs (local elements, such as exotic flora and fauna). The designs had also become more naturalistic due to the impact of European botanical albums, introduced to the court through missionaries and merchants. Such is the case with this piece, which represents the sub-category of North Indian knotted-pile carpets with all-over flower and lattice pattern. This style of carpet, with its rows of flowers framed by geometrical lattices, themselves displayed in bright lac-red fields, would reach its peak during the reign of Shah Jahan, he who ordered the construction of the Taj Mahal mausoleum.

62a91891-033f-5f20-ba88-1767990a9e1f.name: Kilim
62a91891-033f-5f20-ba88-1767990a9e1f.description: On the preserved Pirot kilims of earlier date mild and calm nuances of dark blue, red and green prevail. Besides, on this kilim also appear yellow and white colours. In the middle of the central field there is a rhomboid medallion filled with *čenđeli* ornament. Inside four smaller rhombi, placed in the corners, there are interesting stylisations of a human figure surrounded by the branches with *pomegranates* (*narovi*). The rest of the central field is filled with *bibice* ornament, while the wide border (*ploča*) is decorated with the *tree of life* motif. According to Milena Vitković Žikić, a similar kilim is preserved at the Osman Pazvantoglu mosque in Vidin.

62e26164-3e84-51be-af2d-1435ccc48245.name: Rug
62e26164-3e84-51be-af2d-1435ccc48245.description: Flat woven rugs from Gafsa are characterized by their brightly coloured, bold geometric patterns (triangles, squares, crosses and rhombs) arranged in panels, and executed in a weaving technique known as dovetailing. Though many motifs are repeated throughout the piece, they are never used in exactly the same colours or combination more than once. Rows of marching camels in the centre of this rug are a signature of the Gafsa style. In this rug bright blues, oranges and greens were achieved with chemical dyes that have been used in North Africa since the late 19th century. In more remote areas, chemical dyes would be often combined with natural dyestuff.

63d6fb13-9493-5237-89ca-6de88f9706ee.name: Kilim
63d6fb13-9493-5237-89ca-6de88f9706ee.description: The Pirot kilims are characterised by variety of motifs (zoomorphic, anthropomorphic and motifs of surrounding objects and phenomena) that derive their names from associations to objects and living beings found in immediate surroundings. A small kilim, with a place and year of making woven in Cyrillic letters in the upper part – *PIROT 1941 g.*, is conceived as an embroidery sampler and decorated with a large, almost encyclopaedic span of ornaments. The ornaments are arranged into friezes, boxes and within the border. The colours used are: red, blue, green, white, orange, black, yellow and brown. Among the ornaments and patterns represented on the kilim there are: *bombs* (*bombe*) and *bibice*, *wreath* (*venac*) and *devil’s knees* (*vraško koleno*), *Crown Prince* (*prestolonaslednik*), *tables* (*sofrice*), *chair* (*stolica*), *bird* (*tiče*), *pomegranates* (*narovi*), *flames* (*plamenovi*), *turtle* (*kornjača*) etc.

64f8833e-9443-5af8-a2d9-546e35bd469a.name: Arraiolos rug
64f8833e-9443-5af8-a2d9-546e35bd469a.description:
Despite carpet production beginning in Portugal in the 14th century, carpet production centred in the town of Arraiolos had later origins, with its first references dating to the end of the 16th century, and first known examples dating from the beginning of the 17th century. Created in a domestic setting, these carpets have the particularity of being entirely wool-embroidered through a thread-counting process. This was done on a linen or hemp canvas. Its characteristic stitch is that of Arraiolos, a cross-stitch known as Greek stitch or as Slavic cross-stitch (also known as *ponto de Arraiolos*). This said, the earliest examples also present motifs outlined in “stem-stitch”, as in this case.  
This rug represents the “flower pattern” decoration sub-category of carpets, which is thought to date back to the 17th century and is characterised by vegetal inspired ornaments. In opposition to a field balanced and organised in accordance to a central longitudinal axis of symmetry, a border formed by eight well-designed, alternated, elongated lobes and winding vegetal motifs is continuously embroidered in such a manner that it does not respect the edges of the rug. The recourse to flower-like lobed medallions, alternated with quatrefoils, filling up the field, as well as the colour scheme and the tri-dimensional effect suggested by the layout, lead this type of carpet to be called “tile-pattern” carpets. This is due to their similarity to the patterned tile (*azulejos*) panels produced in Portugal during the same period.

65011066-4ed5-5528-a635-0088b486989b.name: Portrait of Cardinal Sembratowicz
65011066-4ed5-5528-a635-0088b486989b.description:
Sylwester Sembratowicz (1836–98) had been metropolitan Archbishop of Lviv (in Polish Lwów or Lvov), of the Greek-Catholic denomination, since 1885. In 1895, he became Cardinal. He was also a professor and Dean of the Theological Faculty at the Jan Kazimierz University in Lviv.  
Cardinal Sembratowicz is depicted sitting on a highly decorated armchair in the sacral interior, behind him is a lectern covered with embroidered drapery. Beneath his feet, we see a precious carpet, probably a Persian carpet of the Tabriz type. On the carpet’s softly painted surface it is possible to recognise an ornament of elaborately woven palmettes, with many colourful details that are joined with wavy tendrils, on a red ground. The border is dark-blue, filled with a row of palmettes. Persian carpets were very popular among wealthy inhabitants of Lviv in the 19th and 20th centuries. A very similar carpet, dating to the 19th century, is preserved in the collections of the National Museum in Kraków (inv. no. MNK XIX-12064). In spite of this carpet’s generous dimensions, the Janelli family took it with them into exile when forced to leave Lviv by the Soviet authorities in 1946.

66b33fdf-e0ea-56b4-b735-839f6aaca1fe.name: Rug.
66b33fdf-e0ea-56b4-b735-839f6aaca1fe.description:
The rectangular rug belongs to the group of so-called 'bird' rugs. These rugs are distinguished by their cream white ground and by their use of mainly warm, earthy hues – yellow, red and brown – contrasted with small areas of blue and greenish-blue. The design of the rug is divided into a central field and a border. The significant motif of the design, which gives it its name, is a shape resembling a stylised double-headed bird, always with four birds arranged around a large blossom forming the repetitive design of the central field. The areas between them are filled with a standardised motif composed of a central rosette and four blossoms on stems. Additional small rosettes and whirling motifs are set between the large blossoms and the birds of the horizontal lines. The framed border has cloud-bands, which are connected to each other by arabesques.  
This rug, however, shows a peculiarity which distinguishes it from the usual style of bird rugs. In the middle of the rug is a nearly square field showing a coat of arms and a mitre. The inscription underneath names the person for whom the rug was probably made, Archbishop Johannes Andreas Próchnicki. Próchnicki was Latin archbishop of Lemberg from 1614 until his death in 1633. It is assumed that the Armenians of Lemberg who had close connections with Istanbul helped Próchnicki to obtain this rug. That it was an order is evident from some illegible letters within the inscription. It is also interesting to know that some of the preserved Persian carpets commissioned by an Armenian of Lemberg on behalf of the Polish King Sigismund III in 1601/02 in Kashan also show a middle square including the king's coat of arms.  
In 1704 the Swedish King Charles XII (1682–1718) conquered Lemberg. We can assume that the rug was part of the booty of this war. Afterwards, the rug is supposed to have been the property of a noble Swedish family for about 200 years before it was sold to the collectors Axel and Nora Lundgren in 1937.
66b33fdf-e0ea-56b4-b735-839f6aaca1fe.short_description: Rectangular rug from the group of so-called ‘bird’ rugs. The significant motif is a shape resembling a stylised double-headed bird. The unusual field in the middle of this rug contains a coat of arms and a mitre. This rug was probably made for J. A. Próchnicki, archbishop of Lemberg 1614–33.

The predecessor of Johannes Andreas Próchnicki had bought 20 rugs in Constantinople to embellish the cathedral of Lemberg.

673ed749-0097-5438-a8aa-12b5086fcbb8.name: Holbein Rug
673ed749-0097-5438-a8aa-12b5086fcbb8.description: The characteristic delicate, lacy pattern of this rug is named for the Netherlandish painter Hans Holbein the Younger, who reproduced it in paintings between 1527 and 1543. Though still in common use today, the term “Holbein” rug is misleading because it was not used by Turkish weavers and this type of carpet was first depicted by European painters long before Holbein was born.

67b5627a-c276-578c-922b-18b7916f64a5.name: The Ardabil Carpet
67b5627a-c276-578c-922b-18b7916f64a5.description:
The Ardabil Carpet is one of the world’s most celebrated carpets, woven in 1539-40 for the Safavid dynasty in Iran. It is a magnificent example of courtly design, as well as weaving technology, and has a remarkable significance for Safavid dynastic kingship. Together with its twin (today in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art), the carpet was produced for the ancestral shrine of the Safavid shahs, the pious foundation built around the tomb of Shaykh Safi al-Din (d.1334), in Ardabil, north western Iran. At the time when these two carpets were commissioned, Safavid shah Tahmasp (r.1524-1577) was completing a significant expansion to the shrine complex, with new buildings allowing for greater emphasis on his dynasty’s right to kingship. Cementing the Safavid s’ very recent conquest of Iran (led by Tahmasp’s father Isma\`il), this kingship was also claimed as a moral entitlement, thanks to direct descent from their saintly ancestor, Shaykh Safi. Under Tahmasp, the Safavid s further claimed their family bloodline went back to the Shi\`a Imams and ultimately to the Prophet himself. This sacred lineage made the shrine of Ardabil very important as a basis of Safavid royal entitlement, which explains why Tahmasp expanded the complex with such splendour. Based in the capital of Tabriz, Safavid court culture also emphasised the dynasty’s magnificence through the visual arts, with an extraordinarily beautiful and complex design tradition produced for the arts of the book and other media. The specific design of the Ardabil Carpet therefore, in its complex design, iconography and site-specific format, confirm a Safavid message of kingly magnificence, pious charity, and divine grace.  
The Ardabil Carpet has a medallion design: the main field has a bold central medallion (also called a *shamsa*) radiating oval pendants. Quarter versions of this medallion are repeated in the four corners of the main field. Along the central axis of the carpet, two hanging lamps are depicted: representing divine light, these lamps refer to the Safavid dynasty’s claim to direct descent from the Prophet, whose holy nature is often described in terms of light (or *Nur-Muhammadi*). The backdrop of the main field is an extraordinary performance of Safavid court design: there are two independent systems of spiralling leafy plant scrolls, laid one above the other, one with dark red stems, the other with thinner cream stems, all against a dark blue ground. The main border is a series of lobed cartouches, each containing designs of cloudbands and lotus flowers.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O54307/the-ardabil-carpet-carpet-unknown/)
67b5627a-c276-578c-922b-18b7916f64a5.type: Carpet; medallion carpet with hanging lamps and dated inscription.
67b5627a-c276-578c-922b-18b7916f64a5.method_for_datation: Woven at the top end of the carpet is a text panel, which quotes two lines from the Persian poet Hafez, and then the statement “`amal-e bande-ye dargah Maqsud Kashani” (work of the slave of the court Maqsud Kashani), followed by the date 946H. This date corresponds to the years 1539-40, as the given date for the carpet’s production.
67b5627a-c276-578c-922b-18b7916f64a5.method_for_provenance: The carpet is attributed to Safavid Iran because of its woven date, design, technical structure, and direct association (together with its twin carpet) with the Ardabil shrine. As noted above, the Ardabil Carpet at the V&A is one of a pair, the other of which is now in a museum in Los Angeles. It is important to think of the Ardabil Carpets as a twin commission, designed for the Safavid shrine estate. Measuring approximately 10m each in length and 5m in width, the two carpets were designed to lie side by side, perfectly occupying a square space under the dome of the Jannat-sara, one of the new buildings completed by Shah Tahmasp at the shrine. This grand chamber would certainly have been used by Tahmasp in 1544 as a royal reception hall, when he invited the exiled Mughal emperor Humayun to visit the royal shrine. Both of these men loved the arts. As is well documented, Humayun was deeply taken by the court arts of Iran, and he would return to India with a number of Safavid court artists in his entourage. The impact of Humayun’s visit to Ardabil, when he sat upon the carpets, may have contributed to that lasting impression.
67b5627a-c276-578c-922b-18b7916f64a5.obtention: In 1893, the South Kensington Museum (today the V&A) paid £1,750 for the Ardabil Carpet, to the London-based art-import firm Vincent J. Robinson & Co. Ltd. Robinson's in turn had purchased the carpet from Ziegler's of Manchester, a trading firm with offices in both Tabriz and Sultanabad (modern Arak) in Iran: Ziegler's (directly or indirectly) bought the carpet around 1888 from the shrine of Shaykh Safi in Ardabil, repairing it heavily. In 1889-90, the shrine authorities completed new restoration works on the earthquake damaged buildings of the complex: arguably, the carpet was originally sold in order to fund this renovation. It was not in perfect condition: before its sale to the V&A, the carpet was heavily restored, using fragments removed from its twin, the second Ardabil carpet (today in Los Angeles).

67ead56d-5ad0-56ee-b69c-34454186890b.name: Caucasian carpet
67ead56d-5ad0-56ee-b69c-34454186890b.description:
In the Caucasus, there is a great variety of motifs due to artistic exchange between the ethnic groups. Different classifications of carpets are based on weaver's ethnicity, geographic origin of the carpet or the carpet structure. No system of classification is based on design or motifs. Therefore, it is difficult to establish the origin of this peculiar carpet.  
The central field is filled with 21 octagonal small fields. They are alternately filled with a star in octagon medallions and four radially placed C motifs. In each small octagonal field there are numerous triangle motifs. The main border is the S border, common through the Caucasus.

67ead56d-5ad0-56ee-b69c-34454186890b.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Caucasus; fields composition
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

67ff552b-5358-5aae-8559-fd654b60cc10.name: Large Fragmentary Ushak "Quatrefoil" Carpet
67ff552b-5358-5aae-8559-fd654b60cc10.short_description: A full-pile wool carpet of so-called "Star Ushak" design. The brilliant red field is decorated with a quatrefoil medallion, two half-medallions, and a small portion of another medallion, all in deep blue. In the center and the lobes of the medallions are compartments formed by arabesque devices filled with palmettes and leaves. The rest of the field has an intricate floral pattern of scrolls bearing leaves and palmettes. Within the border, arabesques interlace with palmette scrolls. The guard bands enclose intermittent floral scrolls. The carpet is asymmetrical in that it has been shortened at the bottom. Its top and bottom borders have been reconfigured from the original borders.
67ff552b-5358-5aae-8559-fd654b60cc10.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
67ff552b-5358-5aae-8559-fd654b60cc10.method_for_provenance: Although this Star Ushak is unique for its motif of a repeated blue star and diamond combined, it is characteristically Ushak in the coloring of blue medallions on a brilliant red field. Star Ushak carpets typically consist of large star-shaped medallions which alternate with smaller diamond-shaped units. Curving arabesque forms and floral elements fill the remaining spaces.

6952044c-cc8b-5648-b20d-435ae6281ac3.name: Niche or prayer carpet
6952044c-cc8b-5648-b20d-435ae6281ac3.description: This is the first carpet purchased by the MAK after its founding. Together with numerous embroideries, it was bought in 1868 from the Mechitarist congregation based in Vienna and formed the start of the MAK’s internationally notable carpet collection. It supposedly came via Iran to Vienna. If one compares it with the pictorial carpets containing landscapes and pairs of birds, one clearly recognises the further development of the Mughal style: away from the naturalistic depictions towards the detailed *mille-fleur* design of the centre field and the integration of vegetal elements into the architecture, such as the flanking cypresses. The carpet displays a flora made of fine Pashmina wool, which allowed especially detailed lines.

69a554fe-128c-59b5-a563-4ccb1cd627fe.name: Anatolian prayer rug
69a554fe-128c-59b5-a563-4ccb1cd627fe.description:
Anatolian prayer rugs with two columns in the central field can be found in the west (Ghiordes and Kula rugs) and central (Ladik rugs) parts of the region. The spread of common design features makes it at times difficult to determine just which pieces are from which part of the region. It is very difficult, e.g. to determine the exact origin of this particular rug. The two column *mihrab* (prayer niche) resembles, with its geometrical decorated columns, some 19th century Kula prayer rugs. Palmettes in the border resemble some Caucasian palmette designs. The colours of the carpet are vibrant shades of red and blue that can be seen on Ladik rugs. The *mihrab* arch consists of a series of step-like progressions towards the top, which is also a characteristic of Ladik rugs.  
This Anatolian prayer rug was a gift to Izidor Kršnjavi, former director of the Museum of Arts and Crafts, from Ćiro Truhelka, former director of the National Museum of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. In the central field, on red background, there are two columns of geometric blue and white motifs. The border is decorated with rosettes, palmettes and octagons on the blue background. In the upper left corner there are two medallions with an inscription. In the upper medallion there is the Hegira 1190 /AD 1776. In the lower medallion there is the name of the weaver: Insuf.
69a554fe-128c-59b5-a563-4ccb1cd627fe.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and inscripted year
69a554fe-128c-59b5-a563-4ccb1cd627fe.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: prayer rug; Anatolia, inscription band; Ghiordes
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

6a0c973e-5200-5907-8a65-03d76ead030f.name: Carpet
6a0c973e-5200-5907-8a65-03d76ead030f.description:
Field: The field contains an allover design, divided into quadrangular registers organised upon a symmetrical axis.  
Border: There is a single border, with decorations of scrollworks, *fleur de lis* and clamps bounded by two jagged borders.  
The carpet has remains of its fringe on the smaller sides.  
The woollen warp is naturally coloured and the wefts are blue. The wool decoration is in russet, yellow and green.  
Manufactured in Fundación Generalísimo (1941-1990), Industrias Artísticas Agrupadas, Madrid. It copies a design from the Lotto series of Cuenca.  
The border shows the typical decoration of scrollwork inspired by those of Renaissance carpets.  
The techniques of the colours are applied to mimic the dyeing effects of Cuenca carpets.
6a0c973e-5200-5907-8a65-03d76ead030f.method_for_datation: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.
6a0c973e-5200-5907-8a65-03d76ead030f.author: Mª Dolores Vila Tejero
keywords: 20th Century; Lotto series
materials: Warp: Wool, Weft: Wool, Spanish knot

6b5eaee2-e833-55b1-a701-b1fe1fcc8ef0.name: Vine scroll carpet (fragment)
6b5eaee2-e833-55b1-a701-b1fe1fcc8ef0.description: Vine scroll carpets of this type were very successfully produced and exported during the 17th century, as depictions in contemporary European paintings and the many exemplars that have been preserved in European collections prove. The density of their knotting is less than that of the proceeding examples; the fact that their design no longer features animals is a characteristic of the Safavid carpets of the 17th century. This exemplar is among the finest and earliest of its type; the warp and weft are still of silk and wool and not – as later – in cotton. Two delicate tendril systems lying on top of each other, one white and one green, sustain the expressive fantasy blossoms of the middle field. Cartouches of various colours and shapes clearly subdivide the border.
6b5eaee2-e833-55b1-a701-b1fe1fcc8ef0.holder: MAK – Austrian Museum of Applied Arts / Contemporary Art

6b677ac0-2063-5c3a-9411-8a0d1eef448f.name: Caucasus *soumak*
6b677ac0-2063-5c3a-9411-8a0d1eef448f.description:
*Soumak* weaving is a form of weft-wrapping. The weft thread goes forward in front of a group of warp threads and then backwards behind a smaller group. The weft forms a colourful pattern.  
*Soumak*s include large pieces intended for floor use as well as small saddlebags and animal trappings. Most Caucasian *soumak*s were made in the northern Caucasus. Red-field *soumak*s in a relatively narrow range of designs, with two, three, or four medallions, were woven in the Kuba district.  
In the central field on a red background there are three large blue polygonal medallions. Between them there are smaller star-like medallions. Each of the large medallions has a central octagon with a *lesghi* star. This motif is used throughout the Caucasus. The twelve points of the *lesghi* star, the radiating arrows and the star within a star distinguish it from other stepped stars motifs. Despite the name of the star, the Lesghians (several tribes inhabiting the northeast Transcaucasus) are not specifically associated with it. The central field is framed with four borders. The main border is leaf and calyx on blue ground. Two inner borders are decorated with hexagons with S motif and hooked squares in between on white ground. The outer border is the “running dog” border. The waveform of this motif has various frequencies and amplitudes; the Vitruvian scroll described it as “running dog” and it was often used in ancient Roman architecture.
6b677ac0-2063-5c3a-9411-8a0d1eef448f.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: soumak; medallion soumak; Caucasus
materials: Wool; soumak weaving

6bb34fe7-eaef-56c1-b556-3d1d89dfb069.name: Marriage tent
6bb34fe7-eaef-56c1-b556-3d1d89dfb069.short_description: A complete early 20th century Egyptian tent adorned with colourful textile panels in interior part. *Khayamiyya* or Egyptian art of tent-making is created using a hand-applique technique in which fabric pieces are cut, folded and skillfully hand-sewn to canvas, producing impressive tents and wall hangings. These vibrant textiles are widely used in ceremonial contexts such as weddings, funerals, street parties and religious events. This tent was used for the wedding of a daughter of the last Khedive of Egypt in 1903. It can be erected with the decoration reversed should it be thought more appropriate.

6bba06d5-c173-5556-b5da-1c1423de2bf1.name: Isfahani Carpet
6bba06d5-c173-5556-b5da-1c1423de2bf1.description:
This monumental carpet was probably woven in Isfahan during the seventeenth century, either for export or for the domestic market. The design is a densely packed trellis formation of dramatic large flowers (lotus, prunus and more) and feathery leaves, on scrolling black stems. These busy scrolling stems nonetheless follow a symmetrical organisation, folding across a central vertical axis. Placed at intervals, ring-like clasps hold the scrollwork within this ordered layout. The flowers and leaves are in different blues, pinks, oranges and creams, set against a dark wine-red field. The black outlines and stems have receded, as the iron in the black dye has corroded back the woollen pile, creating an (unintended) relief effect, and revealing the foundation threads behind. Hidden within the design are small birds, which is unusual for this carpet group.  
Also nicknamed “Shah Abbas” and “Isfahani”, many examples of this carpet group survive today, and they are also largely in evidence in European painting, particularly that of the Dutch Golden Age, throughout the seventeenth century. Isfahan was then the capital of Safavid Iran, when the city attracted international merchants for the raw silk trade.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O472056/carpet-unknown/)
6bba06d5-c173-5556-b5da-1c1423de2bf1.method_for_datation: The carpet design fits with dateable architecture in Safavid Isfahan, during the seventeenth century.
6bba06d5-c173-5556-b5da-1c1423de2bf1.method_for_provenance: The group have previously been attributed to Herat, and have been nicknamed “Herati”, “Indo-Isfahan” and “Afghan” as a result. Today they are more firmly attributed to Isfahan, Iran.

6bcf4975-1310-52ec-9b3e-e5e3a2352047.name: Safavid Carpet with animals and spiral strings
6bcf4975-1310-52ec-9b3e-e5e3a2352047.short_description:
This Safavid carpet is decorated with floral ornamentation and hunting scenes. Parts of the central section and border are missing. Various flowers, buds, and leaves interweave to make a decorative pattern on a dark red background, and the middle of the carpet is bisected by a line of palmetto flowers. Different animals can be identified among the floral pattern: a lion leaping towards a spotted bull, a tiger hunting an ibex, three single panthers, the mythical creature Qilin and, in the centre of the rug, a pair of leaping deer chased by tigers.  
Bands of clouds, originating from Chinese mythology, fill the space between the animals and floral ornaments. The complete pattern is symmetrical, the row of palmette flowers forming the axis of the mirrored halves. The dark green outer border is also decorated with flowers.  
The motifs of this carpet resemble Safavid book design and are reminiscent of paradise gardens.

6bfda02c-c63c-5abb-8ec9-834074af723f.name: Para-Mamluk carpet
6bfda02c-c63c-5abb-8ec9-834074af723f.description:
A 16th century pile carpet of the type termed “Para-Mamluk”, and sometimes “Chessboard”, having been made in the early period of Ottoman rule, in either Damascus or Anatolia. This predominantly red and blue compartment layout carpet has a red field on which nine compartments are formed and distributed in rows, three vertical by three horizontal. Each compartment is formed of four light blue corner triangles creating a hexagonal space between them. In the centre of this hexagonal space is positioned a light blue sixteen-pointed star, which is surrounded by eight pairs of light blue cypress trees that radiate from the star and towards the boundaries of the space. The dark blue carpet border is made of a row of alternating light blue diamond shaped cartouches with red coloured rectangular ones.  
  
Produced during a short era, the Para-Mamluk type was developed during the early period of the Ottoman conquest of Egypt and Syria from 1517 AD, where transitional designs from Mamluk to Ottoman styles bridged the two cultures. The term "chessboard" is also applied to this type of carpet in reference to the layout of its main field.

6d2b1226-8d1a-55f3-87af-210f0136a472.name: *Die Himmelfahrt Christi (Ascension of Jesus Christ)*
6d2b1226-8d1a-55f3-87af-210f0136a472.description: The extremely elaborate series of tapestries known as the "Old Passion" was purchased for the Dresden court during the reign of Duke George the Bearded (1471-1539). The tapestries held in the collection at the Palace in Dresden, which numbered around 230 items in 1565, not only constituted a valuable financial asset but also functioned as a symbol of state power. In addition to the four tapestries preserved in the Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister, which were woven in Brussels between 1524 and 1528, the series probably also included six further scenes from the Passion, which were presumably destroyed during a fire in the Palace in 1701. The tapestry depicting the Ascension of Christ, which was produced in the Brussels workshop of Peter van Edingen van Aalst shows the Son of God being transported upwards on a phenomenon consisting of light and clouds carried by angels. He raises his arms in a gesture of blessing over his disciples, who are left behind on the Mount of Olives. The exaltation of Christ symbolises the end of his earthly existence as he takes his seat at the right hand of God. It is presumed that the designer of this composition was Bernard van Orley, who was clearly influenced by the graphic works of Dürer and Raphael. Although this tapestry is still in keeping with the traditional style of 15th century painting, the monumentality of the figures and the realistic depiction of the landscape already reveal the influence of the Renaissance.
6d2b1226-8d1a-55f3-87af-210f0136a472.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections
6d2b1226-8d1a-55f3-87af-210f0136a472.obtention: The first mention of Flemish tapestry in Dresden dates from an entry in the 1565 inventory of the "Tapetzerey Gewelbe" in the Palace. As part of the series known as the Old Passion, which originally included ten tapestries, this work probably came to the Saxon court during the reign of Duke George the Bearded (1471–1539).

6d98ea50-5803-5087-8c76-c692fcff4093.name: Carpet with flowering tree motif.
6d98ea50-5803-5087-8c76-c692fcff4093.description:
Acquired by Wilhelm von Bode, this fragmented carpet is thought to have first come from a church in Tyrol before finding its way into the hands of Munich art dealers. Its shape is long and narrow, and its patterns are clearly divided. Along its red centre lies a thin tree trunk, whose evenly spaced branches stretch out at a right angle, holding up large blossoms. A yellow border frames the carpet’s central area, and features an Arabic word in *kufic* script, which is repeated throughout the border. Along the top edge, the word is shortened to just two letters that are joined together. This stylistic depiction of the Arabic script could be an incorrect representation of the Islamic confession of faith. Small rosettes are used as partitions. A second border runs along the outside edge, patterned with a row of repeated double pearls. Both borders are additionally framed by thin blue stripes.  
Friedrich Sarre was the first to suspect that this carpet came from a Spanish synagogue, and that the repetitive blossom-like geometric pattern represented a stylised depiction of a Torah shrine. Similar representations of a Torah shrine can be found in mosaics on the floors of synagogues in Palestine built in Late Antiquity. This conjecture over the carpet’s origin has not yet been supported by examples from Spain. The six-pointed star (known as the Seal of Solomon) also features frequently within Islamic ornamentation, but this motif cannot conclusively be interpreted as signifying the Star of David.  
As depictions in paintings frequently testify, Arabic inscriptions written in *kufic* were commonly employed in the Medieval Christian realms in architecture and on carpets and textiles. Even though there are as yet no known carpets that can be compared to this one, it is believed that it could still represent the oldest known example of a Spanish carpet.
6d98ea50-5803-5087-8c76-c692fcff4093.short_description: This unique and earliest known Spanish carpet has a design of a central tree with branches bursting into large flowers. These have been interpreted as depictions of a Torah shrine, giving the carpet the name Synagogue carpet. Of special interest is the stylised repetitive Arabic inscription.
6d98ea50-5803-5087-8c76-c692fcff4093.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
6d98ea50-5803-5087-8c76-c692fcff4093.owner: Arts and Crafts Museum, Berlin, Germany.
6d98ea50-5803-5087-8c76-c692fcff4093.method_for_datation: In the absence of carpets that have been dated, it is thought that this carpet is earlier than the group of carpets featuring coats of arms that have been attributed to the 15th century. The reason for this lies in its different ornamentation and in the archaic calligraphy of its inscription, executed over a monochrome background. These differences justify the hypothesis that this carpet could have been woven in the 14th century.
6d98ea50-5803-5087-8c76-c692fcff4093.method_for_provenance: The technical peculiarity of the use of Spanish knots for the knotted weave, as well as the inscription and the ornamental details, point to the carpet having a Spanish origin.

6da483f8-19ce-5f70-9bd8-3d093b8b1250.name: Carpet
6da483f8-19ce-5f70-9bd8-3d093b8b1250.description: The field of this knotted-wool carpet is decorated with a prayer niche (*mihrab*) whose centre features a willow flanked by two pear trees upon which birds are perched. Snakes coil themselves around the branches, while two lions lie at the foot of the trees. Deer on fields of red adorn the upper corners. The cartouches on the side-borders show birds in pear trees, while those on the horizontal borders depict doves or rabbits. The warp and weft yarns are in cotton. The three-millimetre-high wool knots – the rug has 4,030 of them per square decimetre – are asymmetrical. The motifs are in a wide array of colours: pink, red, yellow, green, orange, blue and brown.

6ef65cc3-4c33-56d6-9397-2ea841e48bc8.name: Carpet
6ef65cc3-4c33-56d6-9397-2ea841e48bc8.description: Carpets had a number of functions in Central Asia, dictated by the specific way of life in this part of the world. The nomadic tribes wove smaller carpets, while the population in large settlements mostly used larger carpets. These carpets retained a great number of traditional patterns since they were less exposed to foreign influences. A strictly geometric pattern is always used in composing the design and flowers are skillfully stylised into geometric shapes. In prayer rugs, the top of *mihrab* or prayer niche is slightly emphasised. The central field is most often filled with geometric shapes – octagons, rhombi or stars. The rhombi are sometimes graduated and sometimes filled with hook motifs. Motifs taken from nature most often take on an octagonal shape. We also encounter dogs and camels, faithful companions of the nomads. Carpets belonging to this group are always distinguished by a central field and borders, usually three borders of which the middle border is most accentuated. The so-called *ensi* rugs have a central field within a frame or cross, which are filled with decorative patterns. The colours are mainly dark, mostly different shades of red, from brown to purple. The borders and central field are always the same colour, which may vary in tone. The individual patterns are blue, green, yellow and white. The warp is traditionally wool, and the weft and pile material fine sheep’s or goat’s wool, sometimes even camel hair. The carpets are usually made by knotting and the asymmetrical knot is almost always used. The central field of this carpet is divided into patterned strips with four mini-fields and at the centre of each of them is the *tree of life*. The main field has six borders of which two narrow ones are repeated, while the other four are different. The third border from the edge is the widest and is filled with geometric shapes in the form of squares. The overriding colours are dark red, blue, white and brown.

6ef65cc3-4c33-56d6-9397-2ea841e48bc8.obtention: Obtained through the restitution after the Second World War

714698bd-511a-567d-a25e-31f2836df495.name: Portuguese carpet
714698bd-511a-567d-a25e-31f2836df495.description: The so-called Portuguese carpet of the MAK Collection can be regarded as the best preserved of the group of nine extant carpets and three fragments. “Scenes” depict people in the four corners of the main fields: boats with passengers in European attire sail on a heavy sea; a swimmer, fish, and a sea monster are in the water. Unusual for carpets, this depiction has led to various interpretations and notions about its genesis. Thus, one thought is of the legend from the Book of Jonah as a purely formal model, another is of the death of Bahadur Shah the Sultan of Gujarat, who drowned in 1537. European prints, converted to meet the more exotic tastes of an Iranian clientele, supposedly served as the template for the corner solution. The term “Portuguese carpets” developed out of the assumption that they had been produced in Iran for Portugal or Portuguese settlements in India, known as the Estado da India. Today, based on technical arguments, the Khorasan province in northeast Iran is generally accepted as the place of origin.

71d27a74-72e5-584a-a669-aeffec6787d6.name: Prayer rug (fragment)
71d27a74-72e5-584a-a669-aeffec6787d6.description: Although less than half the size of the original rug, the fragment is still one of the most remarkable textiles of the Islamic art collection in the Museum. Following the latest research, the original rug was reconstructed based on several well-preserved details (see the virtual reconstruction of the original design, ill. 1a). The *mihrab*, an essential element of the mosque architecture represented on prayer rugs, has been replaced here with a triple arch reminiscent rather of a gateway or the cross section through a mosque; the dome over the centre arch in the original design supports this hypothesis. The coupled-column motif could be traced back to the architecture of Muslim Spain, and was apparently disseminated by Sephardic Jews. Similar columns, whose bases are rendered in linear perspective, feature on 16th-century Ottoman prayer rugs some of which were imperial court commissions produced in Istanbul; others, as is the case here, were made in Cairo, where the tradition of Mamluk workshops continued long after the Ottoman conquest (1517). The asymmetrical knot is characteristic of Mamluk carpets, whereas the decorative repertoire is typical of Ottoman art. The original rug may have served as a prototype for “Transylvanian” coupled-column carpets dating back to the 17th and 18th centuries, which only comes to highlight the historical significance of this fragment.

72ba3bfe-0cc8-514d-9707-7a480f54966b.name: Prayer rug
72ba3bfe-0cc8-514d-9707-7a480f54966b.short_description:
This is one of approximately 90 prayer or niche rugs often known as a ‘Salting’ group which are now generally accepted as having been woven in Iran sometime in the 16th or 17th century. Many are believed to have come from the Topkapi Palace Museum (which still holds some 35 examples), sold off during the economic crisis resulting from the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–8. It is very likely that they were a diplomatic gift and that they entered the Topkapi Palace sometime before 1680, as a treasury ledger of that year mentions Persian prayer rugs with embroidered inscriptions in metal thread. It has been suggested that they may have remained unused in the Palace stores due to the presence of inscriptions integral to Shi‘i daily prayers on some of them, which may account for the bright colours and often remarkable condition of many examples, including this one.  
  
The inscriptions on this carpet consist of the *Ayat al-Kursi* (‘Throne verse’), *sura* *al-Baqara*, (II), verse 255, in the outer border and *sura* *al-Ahzab* (XXXIII), verse 56, in the inner one. The corner medallions enclise the phrase, ‘Glory to my most high Lord, and to His praise’. A pair to this carpet, previously known as the ‘Perez’ prayer rug, is in a private collection in Italy.

73436f09-e1ab-55c5-bea1-c885fb7a2df8.name: Fragment of a rug
73436f09-e1ab-55c5-bea1-c885fb7a2df8.description:
Uşak, western Anatolia, was one of the most important carpet-making centres in the Ottoman Empire. The carpets made there are of a very high standard of workmanship, with well-balanced compositions, and a harmonious use of colour. The Iranian influences are visible in the precise and very detailed treatment of motifs. The most beautiful Uşak carpets were made during the 16th and 17th centuries (we can trace them also in paintings). It is now believed that carpets from the “Uşak” group were also made in Anatolian towns.  
Uşak rugs can be divided into five groups concerning their pattern and colour. The “white rug” group, with grounds of un-dyed wool, ivory or pale beige, with a pattern of *cintamani* motifs, so-called “birds”, or “scorpions”, were probably made in Selendi. According to the sources, “bird rugs” were known in Poland from at least the 16th century. We know that the Polish king Stephen Báthory, the former Transylvanian prince, in 1585, commissioned carpets described as “white with red paint, as in Turkey they commonly make, with birds”. At the beginning of 17th century, the Archbishop of Lviv, Jan Andrzej Próchnicki ordered a “bird rug” with his coat of arms – it is now preserved in Medelhavsmuseet, Stockholm. Representations of white-ground rugs were also painted on the walls of Tarnow burghers’ houses at the end of 16th century.  
The Kraków rug can be assigned to the “white rug” group, but its ornament is very specific. While it most closely resembles a “bird rug”-type, “bird-like” forms are substituted with “dragon-like” motifs. In the preserved fragment, we can see four rows of star-like rosettes. Each of these is flanked by “dragons”. Delicate cloudbands and palmettes, connected with geometricised scrolls, decorate the border. It is worthy of note that both the pattern and the colour of the rug are very sophisticated and that the ornaments are delicate and detailed. As for the use of colour, the Kraków rug differentiates itself against the others in the “white rug” group for its ornaments, woven in nicely chosen shades of blue, red, pink, orange and emerald-green.
73436f09-e1ab-55c5-bea1-c885fb7a2df8.method_for_datation: The rug resembles the “bird-rug”-type carpets of the Selendi group, even if the shape of the ornaments differ from the “bird-like” forms characteristic of this group

73f9091d-afae-5193-8338-ac3476f58f18.name: Khamseh Confederacy carpet
73f9091d-afae-5193-8338-ac3476f58f18.description:
The province of Fars lies south of Isfahan and west of Kirman, bordering the Persian Gulf to the south. At one time, Fars was the center of the Persian Empire. It is an area inhabited by people of diverse origins. There are two major tribal divisions in Fars: the Qashqa’i and the Khamseh Federation. It is difficult to define the areas inhabited by each group but basically the Qashqa’i occupy the area west of Shiraz and the Khamseh the area to the east of Shiraz.  
The Khamseh Federation arose as a political entity during the 19th century as a counterpoise to the Qashqa’i. It consists of five tribes: Ainalu, Baharlu, Baseri, Nafar and Arab. *Khamseh* is Arabic for “group of five”. The Arab tribe is the largest and most important. They were for decades the most prolific rug weavers in Fars. Many of the 19th century Arab rug designs show stylized bird figures, often with a series of small, lozenge-shaped medallions along the vertical axis.  
This South Persian carpet from the province of Fars can be attributed to one of the tribes from the Khamseh confederacy. In the central field there are three interrelated hexagonal medallions, the so-called *murgi* medallion. In the medallions, on a white background, there are motifs of chickens and florets as field repeats. The *murgi* medallion is on a blue octagonal field also filled with chickens and floret motifs. Corners of the central field are filled with florets and stylized animal motifs on a white background. The central field is framed with four borders. The main border is the *boteh* border – two *boteh*s are oppositely placed and between them there is a cypress motif. This border is taken from the rugs from Qainat. *Boteh* is a universal oriental rug design element. *Boteh* is Persian for “bush” and *buta* is Hindi for “flower”. It is thought to have originated in Kashmir in its curvilinear form. The form and content of *botehs* are often distinctive for particular attributions and may be valuable clues to the origin of a weaving. The inner border is a simplified version of the Arab border. The outer border has a polychrome nested *mihrab* motif.
73f9091d-afae-5193-8338-ac3476f58f18.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Khamseh; Persia; medallion carpet
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

74348eb1-1326-5002-8493-0ebbebd23a4b.name: Bergama Rug
74348eb1-1326-5002-8493-0ebbebd23a4b.description: Bergama a town in Izmir Province was one of the most important rug producing areas of Anatolia. Many decorative style rugs were produced in Bergama including large pattern, small pattern, double *mihrab*, single *mihrab* and geometric. This is a rare example of a Bergama rug with a geometric design. The main theme is composed of four geometric motifs arranged in squares, locally called *elibelinde* or hands on hips. This is a very popular motif in West Anatolia and was widely used on various woven textiles.

74d909b3-d5bf-58e9-8fd5-7f17c21f3c2b.name: Carpet fragment
74d909b3-d5bf-58e9-8fd5-7f17c21f3c2b.description: The lower corner of this fragment of a high-pile carpet is decorated with a quarter of a lobed medallion. The field is made up of two half-medallions and a mosaic of acanthus leaves, crescents, palmettes, foliated scrolls and flowers. The dark-blue main border is adorned with a series of palmettes surrounded by sickle-shaped leaves. Although it has been restored, the border retains its original design. As the pile of the field has largely been repaired, it is possible that some of the motifs there have been reworked. Therefore, the half-medallion in the upper part of the fragment was originally a half-palmette. The quarter-lobed medallion was patched and painted, and its relation to the initial design remains to be determined. The warp and weft yarns are in cotton. The five-millimetre-high wool knots – the rug has 1,920 of them per square decimetre – are asymmetrical.

74ea15a9-ac23-5535-b370-ed2de11dd563.name: Carpet.
74ea15a9-ac23-5535-b370-ed2de11dd563.description:
A woollen carpet that belongs to the Ottoman genre of so-called ‘Lotto carpets’, distinguished by a wide central field and a broad border. In this particular example, the central field, its ornamental elements rendered in a mustard brown with blue detailing, is set against a deep-red ground. In the centre, three octagons formed from abstract arabesque, split-palmette, leaf and geometric elements are superposed; the upper one curtailed, the lower one halved by the border. On either side two interconnected star motifs, composed of the same elements as the octagons, embellish the remainder of the central field. The border has a succession of cusped medallions enclosed by a narrow blue line and containing abstract motifs in either dark-blue or light-purple and green, on a red ground. The background is composed of halved, stylised floral motifs that fill-in the spaces in between the medallions. A narrow outer border in red, with a simplified floral scroll within it, encloses the entire composition.  
Carpets such as this example occur in varying sizes and can be up to six meters long. They were popular from the early AH 10th–late 11th / AD 16th–late 17th centuries. It is not yet clearly understood how the distinctive design of these carpets evolved, but perhaps they were inspired by octagonal and star motif tile compositions used in Seljuq wall revetments.
74ea15a9-ac23-5535-b370-ed2de11dd563.short_description: This type of Ottoman carpet is called a ‘Lotto’ carpet after the Italian painter Lorenzo Lotto, who depicted them in the AH early 10th / AD early 16th century. ‘Lotto’ carpets were made in Western Anatolia from the early 10th / early 16th century to the late 11th / 17th century.
74ea15a9-ac23-5535-b370-ed2de11dd563.method_for_datation: This type of carpet occurred in western Anatolia during the early 10th–late 11th / early 16th–late 17th centuries. They were manufactured in local urban workshops situated in Ushak and elsewhere. This type, known as ‘Lotto carpets’ was so named after the Italian painter Lorenzo Lotto, who depicted these particular carpets in his paintings in the early 16th century. Later they occur in other European paintings until the end of the 17th century.
74ea15a9-ac23-5535-b370-ed2de11dd563.method_for_provenance: This type of carpet occurred in western Anatolia from the early 10th–late 11th / early 16th–late 17th centuries. They were manufactured in local urban workshops situated in Ushak and elsewhere.

7544bf88-1c99-5fae-86d6-41a4b6204b0c.name: Carpet decorated with shrubs
7544bf88-1c99-5fae-86d6-41a4b6204b0c.description: A fragment of the identical pair of carpets decorated with shrubs that was part of the MAK Collection, obtained from the Austrian imperial household, was sold between the First and Second World Wars and is located today in the Rijksmuseum in Amsterdam. Eponymous are the plant forms in the field. Unlike the differentiated field design, the border comes across as somewhat schematic. Border and field patterns were varied and combined in terms of both colour and motif. The influence of the Indian Mughal Empire (1526‒1707) forms, which is noticeable in the near-realistic design and the arrangement of the motifs, can be ascribed to the active cultural and economic exchange between both empires.

77bb79c8-0e18-5f85-a486-475e3b24e773.name: 'Scorpion' rug
77bb79c8-0e18-5f85-a486-475e3b24e773.description: Standing in distinct contrast to the typically red and blue colours of Ottoman Turkish carpets are the 'white' rugs, whose fields are created using undyed wool, which is an ivory or light beige colour. They have a maximum of 5–8 colours (usually white, red, blue, yellow and brown), but also can include manganese violet, green and pink, with low knot density, between 621 and 837. They are subdivided by pattern as "ball" or "çintamani", "bird" and "scorpion" white rugs. Referred to in Hungarian historical sources as *fejér* (white) carpets, they were popular in 16–17th century Hungary, and particularly in Transylvania (now part of Romania). The rarest version of white rugs has a motif reminiscent of a stylised scorpion, seen by some as a crab. They are known as "scorpion" rugs. Four scorpion rugs are known of Transylvanian origin. Apart from the Budapest rug, there are two in Transylvania (in the collections of the Black Church in Braşov and of the St Margaret Church in Mediaş), and one in the Keir Collection in London. The main field of the rug is divided into two rectangles by narrow columns of arrowhead rods linked to round rosettes in the centre and the two edges. Palmettes reminiscent of a stylised scorpion or crab arranged in varying orientations and colours in a vertical column alternate with each other in the rectangles.

77c9a164-87ca-547f-8060-581825027030.name: *Dragon* carpet
77c9a164-87ca-547f-8060-581825027030.short_description:
The large central field of the carpet is dominated by two interlocked lattice structures (white and blue) set onto a red ground with stylised palmettes placed to mark their points of intersection. The carpet design's name derives from the inclusion of a sinuous dragon which fills half of the recessed diamond-shaped fields. In this example, the other half of the fields are filled with motifs that can be understood as representing palmettes. A narrow border of Z-shaped motifs encloses the central field.  
  
Whilst the Chinese dragon found its way into the art of the Islamic world as early as the 13th century, dragon carpets of this kind were made in the southern Caucasus from around the 17th century onwards. The structural parallels to Persian vase carpets of that time is also noteworthy. The strong stylisation of this carpet, which in some cases extends to the point where the motifs are unrecognisable, suggests that the carpet dates from the later 18th century.

78dc7240-0279-5897-8e09-8c53ec24d765.name: Tibetan 'Three Medallion' Rug
78dc7240-0279-5897-8e09-8c53ec24d765.description: 19th-century Tibetan rugs serve a variety of functions and come in many sizes. Their decorations consist mainly of Buddhist symbols. The Tibetan rug in the collection of the Museum of Applied Arts is a small and rectangular *khaden* (sleeping) rug called a "three-coin" or "three-medallion" rug because of its design. The four corners of the field contain light blue and light green swastikas in a pale-yellow spandrel with stepped edges. The brick red central field is adorned with three medallions surrounded by cloud motifs along the central axis. In the main border, lemon yellow and ochre strips meander. The minor border has a dark brown ground adorned with a row of pearls. The rug is framed by a 3-8 cm, knotted fringe of yak hair.
78dc7240-0279-5897-8e09-8c53ec24d765.obtention: Purchased from Ervin Baktay (Gottesmann) (1890-1963) painter, art historian, orientalist, writer and translater, who visited Western Tibet in 1928.

79ec3799-6c99-5734-a810-73dca9b04725.name: *Bildnis der ältesten drei Kinder Karls I. von England (Portrait of the eldest three children of King Charles I of England)*
79ec3799-6c99-5734-a810-73dca9b04725.description: This painting depicts the three eldest children of King Charles I of England and his wife Henrietta Maria. The five-year-old Crown Prince Charles (Prince of Wales and later King Charles II) is on the left leaning against a pillar, imitating the pose of a court dignitary. Beside him, grasping his hand is his younger brother James (Duke of York and later King James II of Scotland). On the right stands the upright, demure figure of the four-year-old Princess Mary, the future wife of William of Orange. Van Dyck masterfully depicts the opulent costumes of the children posing, as befits a courtly portrait, in front of a pillar and a sumptuous curtain, standing on a valuable oriental carpet and framed by two dogs at their feet.

7a7a05cc-36a8-5c0e-8472-83ba70b38b5d.name: *Alaska*
7a7a05cc-36a8-5c0e-8472-83ba70b38b5d.description:
“I imagine Alaska being white and all colours in between white and black \[…\] cramped between the ice”, says artist Carola Helbing-Erben. This image of Alaska as a cold, foreign place is reflected in the techniques (weaving, knotting) and the alteration of seemingly graphic and three-dimensional zones. Plush, protruding wool in knotted areas represent the pack whereas coloured, woven parts appear graphic and stand for the rocky ground, nature and life breaking through. While tapestries (or rugs) usually signify warmth, this association is contorted here by the motif.  
Helbing-Erben’s design was realised by Christine Bargenda, who then worked at VEB Haweba Halle (Halle Weaving Mill). The department for textile art at Hochschule für Industrielle Formgestaltung Halle (HIF) goes back to Willi Sitte, who was later on chairperson of the VBK DDR (Union of Fine Artists of the German Democratic Republic \[GDR\]) and is considered, together with Werner Tübke, Wolfgang Mattheuer and Bernhard Heisig, one of the most important artists of the GDR.  
In 1953, Sitte was appointed head of the field of textile design, which he continuously expanded. In 1966, the department merged with VEB Haweba. The Haweba engaged in mass production as well as the manufacturing of design tapestries. In seeing artists and artisans united, its concept resembled those idealized by the Bauhaus or Jugendstil movement. Exhibitions of Halle textile works like those in the Wiener Künstlerhaus in 1984 or Deutsches Textilmuseum Krefeld are proof of the high regard GDR Textile Art was held in. VEB Haweba survived the political and economic reorganisation after the German reunification and, after severe financial crises, had been taken over by Burg Halle in 2012.  
Carola Helbing-Erben (\*1952 in Ostrau near Halle) is a German artist who studied at HIF Halle, specializing in tapestry design under Prof. Inge Götze. She has been a freelance artist since 1982, exhibiting in Germany and Switzerland. She now lives in Bremen.

7ad14588-eea1-5356-a391-b6b7351cca18.name: Genje Runner Rug or Genje Runner
7ad14588-eea1-5356-a391-b6b7351cca18.description: The long and narrow, pile carpet style (runner), the lively yellow, light blue, green and red colouring, and the geometric patterns are characteristic of early, classical carpets from Ganja (Genje). The yellow-base make-up area is ornamented with a net of octagons, filled with stars whose colours (red, green, dark blue, and blue) shift diagonally. In the ivory-coloured main stripe of its border, colourful rosettes and quadruple leaf motifs alternate. In the outer and inner side borders, rows of black reciprocal lilies run against a green and blue base, respectively. Of special importance is the fact that the carpet is dated and the name of its Armenian owner (Voskan) is known. This item was purchased by the Museum of Applied Arts from Mrs Sándor Barcsay in 1986. According to the seller's family traditions, it had once ornamented the proscenium before the altar in Bishop Ottokár Prohászka's (1858-1927) private chapel in Székesfehérvár. This might explain its uneven fraying.
7ad14588-eea1-5356-a391-b6b7351cca18.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis. On one of the narrower ends of the carpet, black-on-yellow knotted Armenian inscription and Arabic date: "OSKANIN 1821 ASIN" (for Voskan in the year 1821) [Tigran Sayadyan's reading]

7b08d044-2db4-5143-bf2f-b25e72ac1a12.name: A massive Safavid Isfahan gallery carpet
7b08d044-2db4-5143-bf2f-b25e72ac1a12.description: Nicknamed “Shah Abbas” and “Isfahani”, this monumental carpet was probably woven in Isfahan during the golden age of Safavid weaving either for export or for the domestic market. The design is a densely packed trellis formation of dramatic large flowers (lotus, prunus and more) and feathery leaves, on scrolling black stems. These busy scrolling stems nonetheless follow a symmetrical organisation, folding across a central vertical axis. Placed at intervals, ring-like clasps hold the scrollwork within this ordered layout. The flowers and leaves are in different blues, pinks, oranges and creams, set against a dark wine-red field. The black outlines and stems have receded, as the iron in the black dye has corroded back the woollen pile, creating an unintended relief effect, and revealing the foundation threads behind. Hidden within the design are small birds, which is unusual for this carpet group.

7bcd6db4-d987-50e0-981f-a7795e9365a4.name: Star *Uşak*
7bcd6db4-d987-50e0-981f-a7795e9365a4.description: In all probability, the rapport pattern of the star *Uşak* carpets originated earlier than that of the medallion *Uşak* carpets. The earliest illustrations of carpets in miniature paintings consistently show rapport patterns in connection with depictions of carpets. Surely, due to the high demand as well, the characteristic and very popular patterns were produced over a long period in variations. Here, the original principle of the rapport pattern is particularly distinctly to be seen in the field. The large-scale main pattern of this exemplar consists of eight-pointed stars and rhomboids placed in offset rows. Furthermore, the field is overlapped by the border in such a manner that two stars and two rhomboids lie in the middle, thus centring the field.

7cc8e498-9f8e-5bf0-86e3-fa80f50e98a5.name: Carpet with vases (fragment)
7cc8e498-9f8e-5bf0-86e3-fa80f50e98a5.description: The often-published, white-grounded fragment consists of one part each of the border and field, and is a part of the once very large vase carpet. It was purchased at the end of the 19th century for the Orientalisches Museum, which was founded with the goal of promoting the international trade of the Habsburg Empire. When this museum was partially taken over, the fragment then came into the MAK’s Collection. Technical criteria are crucial for the establishment of this specific Kirman group of carpets, which were produced from the end of the 16th century to the post-Safavid period. The preserved field displays the characteristic pattern of two tendril systems overlapping in a rhomboid shape. Paradisiacal associations were evoked by the fantastically combined floral décor. One sees the eponymous vase, filled with a bouquet of pink-blooming branches, in the lower half.

7d6738d8-b16b-541c-9f7f-2661b681821c.name: Carpet
7d6738d8-b16b-541c-9f7f-2661b681821c.description:
Carpets of late 15th century Egypt, are among the finest ever produced anywhere. Red, green, and blue create intricate patterns in lustrous wool pile, reflecting a superlative play in the manipulation of colour and form. Green and red are complementary colours directly opposite each other on a colour wheel, so the human eye perceives these two colours as extremely high in contrast. Egyptian weavers under the Mamluk sultanate exploited this optical principle to produce visually complex patterns using only a limited range of colours. By juxtaposing jewel-like tones of sharply contrasting green and red, Mamluk weavers created a dynamic interplay between ground and foreground.  
  
The quality of materials and excellent craftsmanship is indicated by the equal number of knots per linear unit of measurement in both vertical and horizontal directions. This supreme control of the relationship among warp, weft, and pile enabled the execution of squares and circles without elongation. Focused on three colours, the art of the Mamluk carpet is a mathematician's art that plays with the ambiguities inherent in pattern making.

7d6738d8-b16b-541c-9f7f-2661b681821c.method_for_datation: Stylistic analyses, comparative materials, and historical documentary evidence
7d6738d8-b16b-541c-9f7f-2661b681821c.method_for_provenance: Its motifs, colouring, materials, and structural characteristics all join together to suggest that this carpet is made in Cairo carpet workshop during the Mamluk Sultanate.

7f15595e-0560-5d45-8f3b-204ab651fd8d.name: Yomut Turkmen Kepse Göl Main Rug
7f15595e-0560-5d45-8f3b-204ab651fd8d.description: Hungarian collectors began to show interest in Turkmen carpets in the early decades of the 20th century. There were ten Central Asian carpets in the 1924 *Early Oriental Carpet Exhibition of the Hungarian Carpet Collectors* in Budapest, nine from private collections and this one from the very small number held by the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts at that time. It has an offset pattern of ivory, blue and red kepse güls on a wine-red ground. The white border, with its severely geometric vine and simple, reciprocal "boats", the running dog guards and the *elems* (end panels) decorated with stylised floral shapes are ornaments characteristic of Yomut carpets. The upper and lower ends are incomplete, the sides are missing and conserved.

7fd7cbfd-ce60-550a-91a1-62fabf75edad.name: Rosette carpet
7fd7cbfd-ce60-550a-91a1-62fabf75edad.description: The only counterpart to this unusual carpet is in the painting of the so-called *Darmstädter Madonna* by Hans Holbein the Younger of 1526/28. As early as 1877 Julius Lessing cited this painting in dating the carpet. Large red rosettes in a braided band are arranged in offset rows on a brilliant yellow ground. The motif-forming outline surrounds an inner field with changing colours. At the outer edges of the field the rosettes are cut precisely in the middle, so that the field shows a section of an endless repetition of the motif. The strong white ground of the border implies white heart-shaped forms, but in fact it is leaf forms, pointing inwards and outwards in a staggered formation, with pointed blossoms in red and aubergine on a white ground, that decorate the border. This border type is recorded as early as 1500 in a painting by the Master of St Giles in the National Gallery, London.

80275793-c91b-5334-93ac-d4126f4e645c.name: Prayer rug
80275793-c91b-5334-93ac-d4126f4e645c.description: Gördes prayer rugs of the 18th and 19th centuries were much appreciated in Western Europe as well as in Romania, where they have been preserved in large numbers. Here, the stepped arch of the niche is featured on a white ground; the floral and geometric motifs of the *mihrab* field are reminiscent of a mosque lamp. A tiny brown mosque lamp appears as such in the centre of the composition, hardly discernible amid stylised flowers and stars. The elaborate decoration, with a wealth of floral motifs on the inner edges of the niche, is a recurrent feature of 19th-century Ottoman carpets at a time when architectural motifs derived from courtly art were gradually losing their original shape and meaning. The cross panels featured above and below the niche are decorated with Chinese cloudbands. The main border is made up of seven narrow bands on white and red ground, sometimes associated with the seven heavens, while the secondary borders contain flowers connected by wave scrolls.

8028a66a-6f38-592c-b57a-6daaa241314b.name: Rug.
8028a66a-6f38-592c-b57a-6daaa241314b.description: In the AH 12th and 13th / AD 18th and 19th centuries, the small town of Milas in the southwest of Turkey was a centre for the manufacture of prayer rugs. This rectangular rug belongs to a group of Anatolian Milas rugs characterised by geometrical stylised, angular scrolls. There are the same white wavy scrolls against a background of dark hues dominating the visual impression of this rug. Its design is composed of sections of borders in two zones and a small rectangular field in the middle. All parts are separated from each other by narrow stripes embellished with a geometrical pattern. The blue field in the middle shows three vessels with stylised flowers. Small white and yellow rosette blossoms are randomly spread over the ground. The motifs of the inner border also occur in the outer one, although against different backgrounds of red and dark brown colour. The areas under the curves of the scroll are filled with big blue and red flowers on stems; the areas above it contain stylised trees.

80da057a-50e4-5b41-a93e-f12cf060df80.name: *Invasion of the French camp and the taking of the Castle of Mirabello. Flight of the ladies and civilians following Francis I*
80da057a-50e4-5b41-a93e-f12cf060df80.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014). According to this perspective, the tapestry examined here precedes *Flight of the imperial troops from Pavia*, where the Lombard city is portrayed. In fact, juxtaposing the two tapestries, the landscape bordered in the foreground by the walls of Visconti Park can be re-created; furthermore, both in the foreground and in the distance, the defensive system that marks the edge of the French encampment, composed of a series of gabions, field fortifications comprising large baskets of entwined branches filled with earth, can be linked together.  
According to the chronology of events, the tapestry represents one of the early moments of the final phase of the battle: at dawn on 24 February, the imperial troops burst into the French encampment. The French had pitched camp within the Old Park, occupying the Mirabello Castle, a fortified hunting lodge, depicted in the background on the left. In the centre, several infantrymen are trying to save themselves by crossing the Vernavola river, using their pikes. Beyond the flames, which are caused by the explosion of casks of gunpowder, one can glimpse Francis I’s tent, decorated with the French *fleurs-de-lis*. In the foreground, through a breach in the wall, one can see the flight of soldiers and civilians who were with the French army that was camped there, among them ornately dressed women. In the distance, on the right, one can see tranquil scenes of camp life, with people busy preparing food and overseeing meals.

818b39ce-ad1e-5f82-b688-1af67ea40373.name: Tekke
818b39ce-ad1e-5f82-b688-1af67ea40373.description: A Tekke-Khaly, a so-called main rug with 4 x 9 Tekke guls and Chemche minor guls on a purple-red base. The major border features star-filled octagons with a small radiating wreath as well as motifs of trees, diamonds and Kotshanak motifs. At the top and bottom of the carpet, the border is much simpler than on the sides, where richly varied fields of different sizes join octagons and cross shapes. The densely filled border, decorated with intricate ornaments, makes the piece appear somewhat stocky overall. It is less finely woven and of a slightly smaller format, more like a square. Parts of the characteristic flat-woven ends (*elems*) have been preserved at the top and bottom – a red kilim with narrow blue horizontal stripes. Among the pile-woven works of the Tekke, some pieces stand out from the vast majority with lighter, less bluish-red – sometimes referred to by specialists and collectors as the "purple group" – mainly because of a fond red with a high blue component. The carpet can be attributed to this category.

824d176c-062b-5951-a4d5-6072ca939d81.name: Caucasian Dragon Rug
824d176c-062b-5951-a4d5-6072ca939d81.description:
Caucasian carpets dominate the carpet auction of the Ernst Museum, and the most remarkable of  
these are the Armenian carpets. Armenian rug number 31, for example, could be the pride of any  
museum. Its bold ornamentation and distinctive colouring make it a true masterpiece. Its surface is  
adorned by dragons surrounded by large leaves, large palmettes, birds and lions struggling with  
chamois. It has been dated to the late 16th or early 17th century.  
  
We do not know who was selling the carpet at that time or who bought it, but six years later, in 1924, it appeared in the unillustrated descriptive list of the Museum of Applied Arts’ *Early Oriental Carpets* exhibition, marked as the property of a very sophisticated art collector, Zoltán Mauthner (1880‒1936), the co-proprietor of the leather company Gebrüder Mauthner und Co. He probably purchased the carpet at the 1918 Ernst auction. He exhibited it in 1924 and sold it together with other items in his collection either at an auction or via an art dealer around 1930. That may have been when Mrs. Endler acquired it.
824d176c-062b-5951-a4d5-6072ca939d81.obtention: Exchanged with Mrs Jenő Endler in 1940

825dc341-7c3b-5904-b96f-01b166afdff8.name: Rug
825dc341-7c3b-5904-b96f-01b166afdff8.description: The rug was most probably commissioned and woven in a city workshop for a special occasion. It is woven in knotted pile technique with woollen pile and cotton warp and weft. It features a medallion composition with a large blue medallion of a complex shape on the white ground surrounded by the borders containing inscriptions with Persian poetry. External borders feature stylised floral blue-and- red designs. A white cartouche in the external border contains the date 1250 in Hegira that corresponds to 1834 AD.

828023f8-679b-506f-ac98-b27b93a5b797.name: Carpet
828023f8-679b-506f-ac98-b27b93a5b797.description:
Field: The field shows two symmetrically facing vegetable motifs separated by the inscription "Santa Ana".  
Border: The border consists of an S shaped valance that is joined by clamps from which there are sprouting motifs of the *fleur de lis*. Small birds and quadrupeds are sandwiched between the scrollwork.  
The warp of the carpet utilises brown wool and the weft is made of blue wool. The decorative motifs consist of blue, brown, peeled, yellow and white wool. This carpet is inspired by the designs of the Lotto series, although the geometric rhythms are different. The central flowers and foliage have their parallels in Anatolian carpets, although interpreted through a western lens, while the border is typical of Spanish Renaissance productions that include interlacing scrollwork, clamps, *fleur de lis* and small birds. Furthermore, the colour is also different from that included in Lotto carpets.  
Although the carpet shows horticultural designs, both in the field and in its border, we find small representations of figurative birds and quadrupeds interspersed throughout. This is largely reminiscent of older antique carpets that remained popular in Spanish productions until the 20th century.  
Due to the size and the inscription, this is most likely a votive carpet for a chapel dedicated to the worship of Santa Ana.  
Within its chronology, the knot density indicates an average quality. This carpet comes from the old Weissberger collection.
828023f8-679b-506f-ac98-b27b93a5b797.method_for_datation: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.

82850beb-2fc7-5463-8d56-45c22b84b71b.name: Carpet with triple-arch design
82850beb-2fc7-5463-8d56-45c22b84b71b.short_description: This carefully drawn, subtly coloured carpet is among the finest of all Ottoman weavings. One of the earliest carpets to include a triple-arched gateway, its design probably originated in the Ottoman imperial workshop. The hanging lamp in the centre arch recalls verses from the Qur’an that liken God to the light of a lamp placed within a niche. The combination of this carpet’s imagery, high quality, and relatively small size suggest that it was used as a prayer rug by a member of the Ottoman courtly elite.
