82d02e71-067a-5cf6-827f-c856db5a69f1.name: Chahar-Bagh carpet fragment
82d02e71-067a-5cf6-827f-c856db5a69f1.description:
A large 17th century north-west Iranian pile carpet fragment designed in the Chahar-Bagh (four-gardens) style, a bird’s-eye view of a garden that consists of a symmetrical layout of flowerbeds and waterways.  
  
On this fragment, the main waterway runs longitudinally along the centre of the carpet and branches out into two shorter waterways to the left and the right of it. The water in them is illustrated by red and cream zig-zag lines, and within it swims blue and white fish. At the junction between the main and branch waterways sits a green-coloured hexagon, decorated with a multi-coloured vegetal arabesque motif, forming an island. Out of each corner of this island grows a tree that radiates out between the waterways and into square flowerbeds. The square flowerbeds are arranged either side of the main waterway and between its branches; their background colour range include green, red and ivory. The vegetation in these flowerbeds is represented by arabesque layouts of rosettes and palmettes, and bordered by rows of small flowering plants on a dark blue background. The carpet has a wide dark blue border holding a row of alternating green and red cypress trees, floral shrubs and pairs of birds.  
  
Believed to be of Kurdish manufacture in north-west Iran, its Chahar-Bagh layout is a visualisation of both the ancient Paradise garden of Persian Art, and the description of the Garden of Heaven in the Qur’an, a layout that has inspired many gardens across the Islamic World, from Spain to India.  
  
Before it entered The Burrell Collection, this fragment was once owned by a renowned art critic, Sir Sidney Colvin (1845-1927), who was a Slade Professor of Fine Art at the University of Cambridge and the director of the Fitzwilliam Museum.

8309ae92-56ae-57a5-a8f5-e185e5452550.name: Tent bag *chuval*
8309ae92-56ae-57a5-a8f5-e185e5452550.description: Nomads of Central Asia stored household goods, clothing and food in textile bags of various sizes and shapes. *Chuval*, a large flat bag that hung on the wooden tent construction, served as a wardrobe. Often *chuval*s were woven in pairs to be used as soft containers attached to either side of the camel on migration. They were woven in knotted pile, plain weave or in mixed techniques.This bag was made by a Tekke Turkmen weaver who were the most prolific rug weavers of Central Asia. In contrast with other Turkic-speaking people of Central Asia, who used only Turkish (symmetrical) pile knot, the Turkmen also wove with Persian or asymmetrical pile knot and the density of pile knots was high. The arrangement and nature of geometric patterns on the central field and in the borders of the bag are typical for Tekke bags of the mid – late 19th century.
8309ae92-56ae-57a5-a8f5-e185e5452550.bibliography: Reswick, Imtraud, “Traditional Textiles of Tunisia”, *African Arts*, 14.3 (May 1981): 58-65.

keywords: Central Asia; Wool

837d4ab7-afdf-58fe-9c68-49a12741d257.name: Court carpet (fragment)
837d4ab7-afdf-58fe-9c68-49a12741d257.description: Although the carpet appears homogenous at first glance, it constitutes a fragment assembled from numerous pieces—especially in the lower part and the upper edge. Further pieces of this once-spectacular large-sized carpet – or even pair of carpets – that were originally produced and used in a courtly context, are located in eight European and American collections. The field shows a rapport pattern, dominated by dark cartouches on a dark-red base; the main border is only preserved on the right and left. One recognises the *saz* leaves characteristic for the period and the white, Chinese-inspired cloud designs knotted in cotton. The outer side-borders and their accompanying stripes are missing. Moreover, the characteristic silk base with the flora knotted in wool and cotton identify the carpet as a product of Ottoman imperial manufacturing.

847012ff-11f1-5a0c-b2dd-0128cd68ab78.name: Textile fragment
847012ff-11f1-5a0c-b2dd-0128cd68ab78.description: This piece of cloth comes from a silk lampas fabric of which other fragments are in the collections of the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, and Dallas Museum of Art (Keir Collection of Islamic Art), among other institutions. The fabric is decorated with the figures of turbaned hunters, some of them holding a bird in each hand, while others carry a gazelle in their arms. Woven in light-yellow and orange thread, the hunters stand out clearly against the black silk. Hunters wearing turbans are typical of the Safawid period (1501–1722/36) and also adorn contemporary miniatures.

8488ba1a-a07a-593d-9692-714fd62bc5ad.name: Pile carpet fragment
8488ba1a-a07a-593d-9692-714fd62bc5ad.description: It is made up of three pieces and the original size was probably about 43cm square: more than half the lower section of the carpet survives, including the selvedges, and as the width is known, the height can be calculated on the basis of the pattern. It is possible, though less likely, that it had a repeating pattern and was intended for use as a runner. The lozenges of the single border (width 6-7cm) gain in vividness from the interplay of successive dark and light colours. The central square is dominated by a cruciform decoration with a dark contour, which probably contains stylised animals or birds, woven with white cotton. Similar decoration is often found on contemporaneous Coptic textiles. The abrashed deep red colour of the field and the rich details in cotton give the carpet its special quality. Although the pile has relatively few loops, it appears thick and well-preserved. The carpet probably passed through a fuller’s workshop for finishing.
8488ba1a-a07a-593d-9692-714fd62bc5ad.method_for_datation: It belongs to a group of fragments attributed to Egypt and their dating between the 8th and the 11th century
8488ba1a-a07a-593d-9692-714fd62bc5ad.method_for_provenance: Factors that determine the provenance: 1. The use of linen, which is the basic Egyptian fibre, for both warps and wefts; 2. The left-twisting (S) spin of the materials is also an Egyptian feature. Linen warps S-spun, Z-plied are found in Coptic fabrics of the 9th-10th century. Right-twisted spinning (Z) is rarely found in Group A; 3. The technique of weaving with cut-pile loops which continues the long-standing Egyptian tradition of weaving with a pile made of loops; 4. The pattern, colouring and techniques of this group fragments bear a close resemblance to contemporaneous Coptic textiles. 5. The fragments display similarities to certain inscribed and non-inscribed fragments from Fustat.
8488ba1a-a07a-593d-9692-714fd62bc5ad.bibliography: Published in Theologou, J., Ozoline, A., Sartzetakis, Y., "Fustat Carpet Fragments", *Hali*, 156 (summer 2008): 65-71.
8488ba1a-a07a-593d-9692-714fd62bc5ad.author: Mina Moraitou
keywords: Fustat fragment; abstract decoration; geometric; linen; wool; cotton

84f78d34-dc25-5f33-ad22-e9dd02d56228.name: The Ardabil Carpet Fragment
84f78d34-dc25-5f33-ad22-e9dd02d56228.description:
A small border fragment from the famous pair of Persian Ardabil Carpets, one being at the Victoria and Albert Museum in London and one at the Los Angeles County Museum of Art in the USA. This pile carpet border fragment shows a two thirds section of a lobed roundel that would have sat in the main border field between oblong cartouches. The lobed roundel’s design consists of a radiating vegetal Arabesque pattern with a maroon coloured network of stems on a light green background. Intertwined with this maroon network of stems is a fine ivory-coloured network of stems holding multi-coloured palmettes and maroon rosettes.  
  
The Burrell fragment’s missing part – a third of the lobed roundel – has been inserted into the V&A Ardabil Carpet’s lower left corner of the border to complete a similar lobed roundel with a green-background.  
  
This pair of Ardabil carpets have the maker's signature, Maqsud of Kashan, and the date A.H. 946 (1539-40 AD). The pair were made for the great prayer hall of Shrine of Safi al-Din Ardabili, an early 14th century Sufi saint and the ancestor of the Safavid Dynasty that ruled Iran between 1501 and 1736. Both originally measured 5.35m x 10.44m, but the Los Angeles carpet was cut down to repair and complete the V&A carpet. Some twenty surplus fragments resulted from this alteration exercise, one of which is this Burrell Collection fragment.

85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.name: Horizontal ground loom
85597a71-d670-530e-8302-7a8eb8d08410.description: This useful tool has been used since the Neolithic age. A horizontal ground loom is a simple arrangement of four pegs tied in place. The warp (vertical) threads are wound onto the sticks and tied in place. The loom has a heddle, batten, jacks, a warp beam and a shed rod. The weaver works the weft (horizontal) threads, by hand, through the stretched out warp. A shuttle is used to pass the wool.

856ab43b-74e0-516c-a676-63e57ceac57a.name: Arraiolos carpet
856ab43b-74e0-516c-a676-63e57ceac57a.description:
The Arraiolos carpets, inspired by oriental carpets, are one of the most characteristic types of this manufacture, produced in the Alentejo region, in the south of Portugal. These Portuguese carpets are embroidered in wool in oblique or Slavic cross-stitch (known as *ponto de Arraiolos*), which makes the transposition of decorative patterns more difficult than in knotted-pile carpets; for instance, the more curvilinear motifs like those seen in this carpet. However, the skill of the embroiderers is evident when we compare some of the items produced in Arraiolos with Oriental carpets.  
Inspired by the “vine scroll”-type of decorative scheme, this piece is embroidered in a small stitch, with vegetal and floral motifs in a decorative design of quarter-plan layout, and big motifs of Persian *herati* design, dominated by undulating bands and large palmettes.  
The border, with a brown background, features a repetitive and interlocking system of stylised and tinted flowers, these turning alternately inwards and outwards, and corners marked by wide palmettes, each with a different design, yet with identical colouring.  
The predominant tones are brown, yellow, green, blue and ivory. In some burnt-yellow and brown surfaces, the original tone of the dye would have been red, but nowadays that is totally faded.

85ff813c-0cdf-5dee-aca9-ba1ade396dcd.name: Kilim, *Serbian crown*
85ff813c-0cdf-5dee-aca9-ba1ade396dcd.description: A wall kilim (*zidnjak*) is decorated with *Serbian crown* (*Srpska kruna*) motif. In the centre of the kilim is the coat of arms of the Kingdom of Serbia. The surface around the coat of arms is filled with ornament called *bibice*, and the corners with *devil’s knee* (*vraško koleno*) ornament. Along the upper border is woven the year 1899, when the kilim was made. The colours used are: red, white, black, blue and green. The *Serbian crown* motif appeared in Pirot kilim production together with the proclamation of the Kingdom of Serbia in 1882. The motif transformed together with the state and forms of government so after 1918 there were also Pirot kilims with the motif of *Yugoslav crown* and after 1945 with the coat of arms of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia. In the contemporary era logos of different institutions and companies also found their place on Pirot kilims and doilies.
85ff813c-0cdf-5dee-aca9-ba1ade396dcd.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material and technique; the year of making is woven on the item

88071a72-b42c-5d63-9d3b-4a84261620cc.name: Carpet
88071a72-b42c-5d63-9d3b-4a84261620cc.description:
From the second half of the 16th century, textiles were among the most frequently traded and most profitable goods introduced into Portugal through the Carreira da India, the route that from 1498 directly connected Europe to Asia. Despite Indian cloth having first constituted the majority of imported textiles, Persian textiles also arrived in Portugal during the first half of the 16th century in smaller quantities. Among these, knotted-pile carpets were in high demand within the upper classes of cosmopolitan Portuguese society, as elements of luxury and status that since the mid-16th century successfully displaced previous Spanish and Turkish imports.  
This small carpet, from the Santa Clara convent in Évora, embodies the Golden Age of importation, when the colourful and vivid Persian imaginary was proudly displayed in both sacred and profane European interiors. In its multicoloured decoration, we can see an elaborate ornamental network of “vine scrolls” interlaced with palmettes outlining the decorative geometry of the field. In addition, there are S-shaped cloud scrolls (*tchi*), rosettes and lotus flowers, arranged on a bright-red background, which contrasts with the dark-blue colour of the border, itself filled with palmettes and lotus flowers.
88071a72-b42c-5d63-9d3b-4a84261620cc.method_for_datation: Jessica Hallet and Steven Cohen have attributed the carpet to Persia based on stylistic analysis as well as thematic and pictorial parallels with other carpets
88071a72-b42c-5d63-9d3b-4a84261620cc.obtention: Transferred from the Convent of Santa Clara, Évora, Portugal, to the National Museum of Ancient Art in 1903
88071a72-b42c-5d63-9d3b-4a84261620cc.bibliography: Hallett, Jessica and Pereira, Teresa Pacheco (eds), *The Oriental Carpet in Portugal: Carpets and paintings, 15th‒18th centuries*, Lisbon: MNAA, 2007.

keywords: Carpet; Iran; 17th century; Portugal
materials: Cotton and wool; knotted; knot, 2Z; asymmetric knot, open to the left

88a1a2c9-da3a-59b6-88ec-2a538e5b82e2.name: *Flügelaltar (Winged Altar)*
88a1a2c9-da3a-59b6-88ec-2a538e5b82e2.description: The creator of this triptych, which was intended as a small travel altar for private prayer, was Jan van Eyck, the most important representative of Old Netherlandish painting. Characteristic features of his new artistic style are the miniature-like, extremely realistic rendering of details and the use of brilliant colours. Enthroned in the centre of the Basilica is the Madonna with her son, the infant Christ. Stretched out at her feet is a precious woven carpet. It has a rhombic pattern featuring eight-pointed stars set in circles. Its intense colours contrast with the muted hues of the ingeniously patterned floor tiles.
88a1a2c9-da3a-59b6-88ec-2a538e5b82e2.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections

88fdffe1-bb72-50c9-8158-0c092180c361.name: *Lotto* carpet
88fdffe1-bb72-50c9-8158-0c092180c361.short_description:
This small-sized carpet is dominated by a cross-shaped motif that normally forms a part of a more extensive pattern made of crosses and diamonds. However, it is thanks to this motif that this carpet can be identified as of the so-called Lotto type, named after the Renaissance artist Lorenzo Lotto (Hegira 885-963 / AD 1480-1556-57), who immortalised such a carpet on an altarpiece depicting the charity of Saint Anthony.  
  
The border is quite untypical, pointing to a probable date of the late 17th century for this particular carpet.

890603fe-bd5e-5732-81cf-6842de790a60.name: *Der heilige Sebastian (Saint Sebastian)*
890603fe-bd5e-5732-81cf-6842de790a60.description: Antonello da Messina set the martyrdom of Saint Sebastian in Venice, as is evident from the waterways in the background or from the typical chimneys. As one of the largest European trading cities, Venice was a key hub for the exchange of exotic luxury goods. The two carpets depicted here would also have come to the lagoon city via trading routes. According to information provided by Stefano Carboni (2015), these were carpets from the Ottoman Empire. They were highly sought after as decorative items throughout Europe. Antonello da Messina painted this picture for the first altar of the Brotherhood of Saint Roch in the Church of San Giuliano in Venice. With its extremely steep perspective, the lifelike rendering of the flesh and the three-dimensional modelling of the nude figure, this work is a tour de force of early Renaissance painting.

893a4a5f-de0f-59f6-8769-67314920dd45.name: *Concerto Grosso*
893a4a5f-de0f-59f6-8769-67314920dd45.description:
Following the widespread international acceptance and recognition of the Portalegre Tapestry Manufacture in 1952, their tapestries began to be internationalized, attracting many foreign artists. One of the aims of the manufacturer has been to translate famous contemporary paintings into tapestries. The piece in question is a wool, handwoven wall tapestry after a painting (of the same name) by English practitioner Tom Phillips (1937), himself a multidisciplinary artist whose creative activities include writing, photography and music (both as a musician and composer).  
Several of Philips’ music-themed paintings have been transposed into tapestries. *Concerto Grosso* is one such example, a representation of the dialogue between a set of soloists (*concertino*), usually two violins and a cello, and the remainder of the orchestra.  
The complexity of its formal language is owed to the multiplicity and accuracy of the draughtsmanship, as well as to the infinity of nuances present in its rich chromatic composition, itself enhanced by the Portalegre technique. The wider colour palette (with over 7,000 tones available) allows for high definition of small details and for the creation of very precise forms. *Concerto Grosso* was part of Tom Phillips’ solo exhibition *Tom Phillips – Woven Music*, held at the Galeria Tapeçarias de Portalegre, in Lisbon, in 2002.

89b49f74-0b20-58b1-a4a0-9699eb76d737.name: Caucasian prayer rug
89b49f74-0b20-58b1-a4a0-9699eb76d737.description:
In Caucasus there is a great variety of motifs due to artistic exchange among ethnic groups. Different classifications of carpets are based on the weaver's ethnicity and the geographic origin of the carpet or the carpet structure. No system of classification is based on design or motifs. Therefore it is difficult to establish the origins of this peculiar rug.  
In the prayer niche there is a diagonally placed polychrome (white, yellow, blue and green) of small hooked medallions on a red background. These medallions resemble an *aina kochak* motif. In the upper part of the *mihrab* (prayer niche) there are two larger medallions which resemble hooked diamond medallions. The central field is framed with three borders. The main border is a “floral vine” border in red, blue and green blossoms (possibly carnation) on a white background. This type of border can be found in Kuba, Seishour and other rugs of the Caucasus. It may be used as either the main or a minor border. Two minor borders are *laleh abbasi* (abbasi tulip).
89b49f74-0b20-58b1-a4a0-9699eb76d737.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: prayer rug; Caucasus; medahil
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

8a565cb4-5f00-5edf-8fb8-497e1fbd6e0d.description: This carpet remains one of the finest examples of its type, despite numerous reweavings and fading. The complex pattern of floral motifs and arabesques, with two types of medallions in rows, testifies to the skill of the weavers.

8a7b4508-e3fd-5303-a123-f294b1fd40d5.name: Silk Mamluk carpet
8a7b4508-e3fd-5303-a123-f294b1fd40d5.short_description: Extant documents verify that knotted-pile carpets were produced and traded in Cairo between the second quarter of the 14th century and the first quarter of the 17th century. Apparently, silk pieces were also found among them. Nonetheless, this is the only preserved Mamluk silk carpet worldwide and one of the MAK Collection’s most famous exhibits. As its impressive size, materials, and design quality suggest, the carpet is a product of an accomplished court workshop and likely dates from the late period of the last Mamluk dynasty. The quantity of the colours used speaks for an earlier dating around 1500; the delicate vegetal border with leaf tendrils and the characteristic umbrella leaves rather points to a later dating. In 1517, the Ottomans conquered the Mamluk Empire, but Cairo’s carpet workshops still produced pieces until the mid-16th century in a post-Mamluk style.

materials: Silk warp; asymmetrical knot; wool weft; knotted

8b89a466-d3b6-5240-867c-7b39739d1576.name: Animal Carpet
8b89a466-d3b6-5240-867c-7b39739d1576.description:
A 17th century Mughal Indian Lahore pile carpet showing an imaginary jungle scene with wild animals running about. The wine-red centre-field is framed by a dark blue border. Satisfyingly complete, though well worn, its scrolling vine and animal design is composed of a network of curving and intertwining vine branches and stems that cover the whole plane of the design, carrying a variety of flowers and palmettes - the large multi-layered palm-leaf shaped leaves. Several wild animals and birds are imposed on this network of scrolling vines. They include leaping tigers and rabbits; running cows, onagers and deer; lions in combat with bears, cheetahs catching gazelles, winged lions attacking antelopes; and cockerels and parrots. The designers of this carpet cleverly used their asymmetrical pattern to evoke a real wilderness in which these wild animals live. Wild as it may seem, the animal composition consists of a three fold repeat pattern. This pattern starts with a salmon-colour tiger in the bottom left corner of the carpet and ends with the lion in combat with a bear on the same side. This pattern is repeated a second time in the middle part of the carpet; and then lifted and flipped right to left, and repeated a third time, but this time the salmon-coloured tiger appears on the right side of the top third of the carpet. By doing so, the designers of the carpet cleverly create a more convincingly wild scene by avoiding symmetry in pattern, whether between right and left or top and bottom of the centre-field.  
  
While most of the animals are illustrated in a Mughal Indian style of figurative depictions, the border of this carpet and its large multi-coloured palmettes, as well as the scrolling vine system in the field, are in the Safavid Persian style. Not an untypical composition, as the art of pile-carpet-weaving was introduced by Iranian master weavers under the patronage of the Mughal court, which sought to emulate its rival the Safavid court of Iran.
8b89a466-d3b6-5240-867c-7b39739d1576.obtention: Gifted by Sir William and Lady Burrell to the City of Glasgow, 1944
8b89a466-d3b6-5240-867c-7b39739d1576.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: animal decoration; wild animal; bird; hunting; jungle; Iranian influence; palmette
materials: Cotton warp and weft; wool pile

8b9039c3-f010-523c-9cec-4f3c5d591596.name: Shahar Khanum's Trees Carpet
8b9039c3-f010-523c-9cec-4f3c5d591596.description:
An 18th century west-Iranian pile carpet with multi-coloured weeping willows, blossoming trees and cypresses symmetrically lined up to fill the ivory coloured centre-field. The carpet’s border is red in background with a chain of alternating dark blue palmettes and pale blue serrated leaves. The name of its female weaver, Shahar Khanum, is discretely woven amongst the light green leaves of a large dark-blue tree with symmetrically extended branches. This dark-blue tree stands on the right side of the carpet close to its border, with its top edge, where the inscription is woven, is aligned to the centre line of the carpet. The three word inscription (‘Amal Shahar Khanum) state that it was made by Shahar whose honorific title is Khanum, indicating social seniority within her community.  
  
The overall design of the centre field is known as a Bid Majnun design, and is found in Kurdish carpets from Bijar and in Heris / Heriz carpets from Azerbaijan province amongst other westerly locations.

keywords: tree motifs; cypress; weeping willow; Bid Majnun design;  inscription; maker; maker's name
materials: Cotton warp and weft; wool pile

8bd5335a-9a4a-53d2-8954-6a840f501d11.name: Pictorial Rug
8bd5335a-9a4a-53d2-8954-6a840f501d11.description: This carpet is decorated with chinoiserie scenes against a white background; a garden appears in the bottom third of it with a group of three figures holding a parasol situated among coloured flowers, leaved trees and exotic animals. Beside the garden is a building with a tower. In the middle, on the left, and in the upper third on the right are green islands with leaved trees and flowers; the left one shows a couple talking, while the right one depicts a building with small towers, flags, and a man smoking a pipe. The background is decorated with insects and flying birds that hold boughs with berries in their beaks. The dark brown border is filled with colourful flowery foliage and various kinds of birds. Opinions differ as to the place of manufacture. It was considered a French carpet in the literature up to 1980. Sándor Csermelyi was the first to mention in 1915 that, "this kind of carpet served as a basis for French carpet making, with the works of Savonnerie as the model." Ferenc Batári, on the other hand, denies the French origin, and, based on motifs identical with tapestries and embroideries made in England in the late 17th-early 18th century, he supposes the carpet was made in England. Features of the Polish knotted carpets from the second half of the 17th century on— strict geometrical ornaments, a background of natural colour, sudden, striped shading and black outlines of the motifs — in many ways agree with this piece. However at this stage of our knowledge, the place of manufacture is still in question.
8bd5335a-9a4a-53d2-8954-6a840f501d11.obtention: Purchased from the becquest of Henrik Egger in 1915

8c4c25d1-c138-5454-9937-8a71723f3492.name: Prayer rug
8c4c25d1-c138-5454-9937-8a71723f3492.description: The singular shape of the *mihrab* on Milas prayer rugs with its two side indentations can be traced back to 17th- and 18th-century Ottoman carpets. Here, a triangular indentation has been added at the bottom of the niche. The red ground of the *mihrab* is decorated with parallel rows of small red or white floral motifs. The inner side of the niche is edged all around with tiny blossoms. Different coloured stylised flowers identical in shape cover the white area of the spandrels. The rather unusual decoration of the wide border includes eight-pointed stars separated by red octagons. The warm colour scheme dominated by a strong red is typical of 19th-century Milas carpets.

8d25f83f-18fd-5325-94b2-f08b80f825b7.name: Pictorial Tapestry 'Woman in front of a Landscape'
8d25f83f-18fd-5325-94b2-f08b80f825b7.description:
Johanna Schütz-Wolff (1896–1965) wove the pictorial tapestry “Woman in front of a Landscape” in 1954, creating it by assembling five separately woven pieces. The background is made of black-dyed thread and for the woman’s figure and the landscape she used untreated white and brown wool. The yellow hat and pink vase in the right corner of the motif give it a colorful accent. Otherwise, the piece is dominated by dark-light contrasts. In her early days, the artist worked as a graphic designer. She first began pictorial weaving in 1920. The influence of graphic design is evident in the composition of the figure into single, overlapping sections.  
Schütz-Wolff pushed artistic boundaries with the woven artwork she created. She made pictorial textiles directly at the weaving loom without using colour templates or the traditional Gobelin technique, which only utilised the coloured weft thread to create the motif. Instead, she also integrated the warp thread into the process of creating a motif. She created fine gradient shading in her pieces by combining different ways of weaving the textile. Schütz-Wolff's pictorial tapestries first received public attention and acclaim in the late 1920s, yet in 1933 her promising career came to an abrupt halt. During the Third Reich, her art was deemed “unsuitable” and she was forbidden to exhibit it publicly or participate in art competitions. In 1938 she was forced to destroy most of her work to evade persecution by the Nazis. It was not until the end of the war, that she was able to resume her artistic career. In the 1950s she began exhibiting her work and competing in art contests. This wall hanging was awarded the gold medal at the 1954 Triennale in Milan.

8db210d7-0a0f-5187-a7b8-59e88115b5c5.name: 'Ghirlandaio' carpet
8db210d7-0a0f-5187-a7b8-59e88115b5c5.description: This carpet design in all its complexity has survived worldwide exclusively through this example. But the most important motif is also known from other, mostly smaller carpets. The motif is a diamond, formed from overlapping leaf forms. In this carpet, the red-ground field is filled exclusively with densely arranged, offset diamonds. The centre of the diamond is covered by a rectangle, also with a red ground. The rectangle is filled with a yellow star, in whose centre is an octagon. In contrast to most carpets of this type, the motif is here arranged in an endless repeat. The depiction of a carpet with this motif by the painter Domenico Ghirlandaio (1449–1494) has induced carpet researchers to name this carpet type after him.

8de9b633-bd8a-5dc3-8bc1-cea21fc40ec5.name: Seljuq Rug
8de9b633-bd8a-5dc3-8bc1-cea21fc40ec5.description: This is an outstanding example of the “Konya Group”. It is considered one of the earliest Turkish rugs found in the Konya Aladdin Mosque in Anatolia. The main border bears large stylized green *kufic* letters which are contoured with white on a dark blue background. This design gives a monumental image to the rug. Such monumental *kufic*script borders are characteristic of Seljuq rugs. The thin border framing the main border inside and out has eight‒cornered dark blue crosses. The stylized double diamond infinity motifs are a dark red on a light red background. One end of the double diamond motif is open and looks like tongs. The motifs have blue dots in the middle.

8eb182c4-306d-58fb-8c86-4ae38f3e70d0.name: Medallion carpet
8eb182c4-306d-58fb-8c86-4ae38f3e70d0.short_description:
Whilst the composition seems to follow the classical Persian medallion carpet there are, however, some special features which stand out: Primarily, this is because the carpet is comparatively large and exceeds the usual format for a main carpet in Persia during the 19th century. Such carpets were placed in the middle of the room and flanked by two narrow runners with another medium-sized head rug at the upper end of the room.  
  
Furthermore, in addition to traditional motifs, foreign elements such as tree branches, oak leaves and acorns catch the eye, as they decorate the inner medium blue field. Another unusual stylistic choice are the red cloud bands curling around the medallion and the black-brown split leaf scrolls in the four corner compartments. Although these are classical motifs, they have a slightly “rococoish” effect on the European observer.  
  
The carpet is dated to the Persian New Year of 1313, i.e. 20 or 21 March 1896. It was made, as can be read in a cartouche, “by order of Shabestari”. It is therefore reasonable to assume that it was a New Year's gift.
8eb182c4-306d-58fb-8c86-4ae38f3e70d0.method_for_datation: Carpet is dated and carries name of customer who ordered it
8eb182c4-306d-58fb-8c86-4ae38f3e70d0.author: Axel Langer
materials: Wool (warp, weft and pile)

8ed9a07e-c99d-5258-9787-4c342eb9d4c2.name: Uşak Rug (Lotto type)
8ed9a07e-c99d-5258-9787-4c342eb9d4c2.description: This type of Uşak carpet, is known as a “Lotto carpet” because it appears in the paintings of the Italian artist Lorenzo Lotto. The main base is red and it is divided into squares, five along the width and eleven along the length. The inside of the squares are filled with stylized octagonal motifs in yellow. Characteristic of Lotto carpets, the composition is based on the notion of infinity from a cross at the connection of squares. The carpet has three borders. The main border is a blue ground, filled with yellow swastikas and stylized dragon motifs. The inner border is a thin band with wavy plant motifs on a blue base. The outer border is a line of plant motifs on a yellow base.

8f36e403-6097-58ff-8669-eab997217fe7.name: Spanish carpet.
8f36e403-6097-58ff-8669-eab997217fe7.description:
This large fragmented carpet belongs to a group of Spanish carpets from the AH 9th / AD 15th century that feature the coats of arms of the Enriquez family. The motifs used in the carpet, as well as its colours and entire appearance, indicate that it belongs to this group. They were probably made in the Spanish town of Letur in the second half of the AH 9th / AD 15th century. The Spanish knots in the weave are a typical characteristic of Spanish carpets, including this one.  
It was thought that carpets of this kind, known as Mudéjar carpets, were made by Oriental craftsmen for Spanish patrons. However, no further direct link can be made, as these Spanish carpets show big changes to the structural principles of carpet patterns in Islamic countries.  
The pattern within the central area is composed of consecutive rows of a single motif: a six-pointed star within a blue hexagon, repeated continuously. Birds and rosettes alternately occupy the diamond-shaped spaces in between. Four borders of different widths frame the central area. Starting from the inner border and moving outwards, the borders are composed of zigzags, interlinked plaited stars, rows of blossoms and, finally, an outer border of motifs recalling *kufic* script on a blue background. Long letters, embellished with hooks, alternate with pointed triangles. Animal motifs in a heraldic style (peacocks, ducks, lions. etc.) and geometrical motifs, such as diamonds decorated with hooks, fill the spaces in between.  
In Islamic countries, coats of arms knotted into carpets indicate that the carpet was commissioned. The coat of arms belonging to a bishop can be seen in an Ottoman carpet that was preserved in Sweden; other Ottoman carpets show the coats of arms of Genoese families. They are an important testimony to the widespread extent of Mediterranean trade.
8f36e403-6097-58ff-8669-eab997217fe7.short_description: This carpet was once over five metres long. Its inner field has a small star pattern. The outer border, reminiscent of *kufic* inscriptions, is filled with animal motifs including lions and ducks, and is therefore a considerable contrast to Mamluk or Ottoman carpets.

8f36e403-6097-58ff-8669-eab997217fe7.owner: Museum of Arts and Crafts, Berlin.

8f36e403-6097-58ff-8669-eab997217fe7.method_for_provenance: The literature mentions the Spanish town of Letur, in the province of Murcia, as a possible place of manufacture of this group of carpets. The Spanish knot supports the hypothesis.

8ff19610-7179-5f91-98b9-6a0065997c52.name: *Brieflesendes Mädchen am offenen Fenster (Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window)*
8ff19610-7179-5f91-98b9-6a0065997c52.description: This painting was the first in a series of quiet interior scenes incorporating only a few figures, which became characteristic of Vermeer's art from the late 1650s onwards. In particular, the theme of a woman writing or reading a letter is to be found in a number of his works; probably as a consequence of the vogue for letter-writing which had spread in Holland since the middle of the century. At the front of the scene is a carpet, decoratively crumpled so as to form a kind of barrier in front of the viewer. Similar Oriental carpets are to be found in many other paintings by Vermeer, suggesting that the Delft artist may have owned one himself.

8ff19610-7179-5f91-98b9-6a0065997c52.obtention: This painting was originally part of the Carignan collection in Paris, from which it was purchased for Dresden by De Brais in 1742.

90f24fd2-747c-586e-b28c-441b69be0537.name: Textile fragment
90f24fd2-747c-586e-b28c-441b69be0537.description: This fragment of silk velvet came from the tent of Süleyman the Magnificent (1520–1566). The tent would have been seized by the sultan’s troops during one of the campaigns the Ottomans conducted in Persia from 1534 to 1554. Like the other fragments of the tent that have survived, it shows the refinement of the Persian textile arts in the 16th century, as well as their close links with miniatures. The execution of the figurative and floral motifs is highly accomplished. The design derives from the famous story of Khusraw and Shirin told in the poet Nizami’s *Khamsa* and illustrated in a great many miniatures. In that scene, Khusraw, who does not appear here, is usually shown with his finger to his lips in a gesture calling for silence. Another fragment of the tent is in the Keir Collection at the Dallas Museum of Art. The Montreal Museum of Fine Art’s fragment shows Shirin bathing, her clothing hung on the branches of a tree and her saddled horse nearby. Unlike the other surviving fragments, the inscription “amal Ghiyāth Al-Dīn Djāmī” on the saddle enables the piece to be attributed to the celebrated Safavid weaver Ghiyāth Al-Dīn Djāmī. According to Ackerman, Djāmī was not only a virtuoso weaver, but also one of the masters of the royal library. Eight other pieces attest to the fact that the weaver was active during the second half of the 16th century.

9162fc12-a74b-5bea-9466-0cb933b226e4.name: Asmalyk
9162fc12-a74b-5bea-9466-0cb933b226e4.description:
Turkmen organized in tribal groups, living nomadic and semi-nomadic lives in Central Asia. Their textiles, woven to be functional as well as decorative and ceremonial, were their most treasured possessions. Considering they travelled throughout the year with their herds, they used lightweight textiles for protection and transportation. A majority of their textiles were made by women on portable ground looms and were for their family’s consumption.  
  
Among the Turkmen, it was customary for a girl of marriageable age to have woven or made all of the ceremonial items required for the wedding and her new home. These included the textiles used to decorate the camel on which she would ride from her family’s tents to that of the groom. The decorations included a pair of large weavings used to cover the flanks of the camel, one on each side. During the ride, the bride was concealed within a covered litter (palanquin) carried by a camel decorated with her work. The palanquin was roofed over with curved wooden rods and covered with a white curtain decorated with tassels. The decorations outside included a pair of large weavings used to cover the flanks of the camel, one on each side. This camel trapping not only advertised the bride’s dexterity and ability as a textile artist, which was considered a crucial asset in marriage negotiations, but also symbolized the transition to a new life as a wife.

91ab6224-2ce2-5787-a444-869b675ead5e.name: Camel cover
91ab6224-2ce2-5787-a444-869b675ead5e.description: Because of their comparatively low weight, their durability, multifunctionality and their versatility in design, flatweaves and pile weavings were of great importance for a nomadic or semi-nomadic lifestyle. Large tent bags, throws, or hangings were prominently displayed, especially on treks. This kilim belongs to a group of pieces that were used as camel covers. When thrown over a loaded animal, the large-patterned sections hang down on either side, while the solid red centre section envelops the humps and back. The surface design, coloration and patterning of the piece are characteristic of southwestern Anatolia and refer to the Fethiye region. A full description of how such pieces were used and their design was illustrated in detail by Harald Böhmer in 2004 (English edition 2008). The Dresden piece is in excellent condition. It shows a clear, skilful pattern and colour design and appealing, well-balanced details, such as the bright, lateral line pattern separating the zigzag of the red background and blue border.

95668e33-c2a0-511f-8651-023745cf8bff.name: Armorial carpet
95668e33-c2a0-511f-8651-023745cf8bff.description:
Inspired by Ottoman Anatolian carpets, this 17th century Spanish armorial pile carpet has a typical Oriental carpet’s layout with a large centre field and a wide arabesque border, both symmetrically laid out. The centre is dominated by a Spanish coat of arms (quarterly, first and fourth: Gules, fleur-d-lys Or; second and third: Or lion rampant Argent impaled with Gules three castles Or) crowned by a feathered helmet. Two pairs of blue lizard-like creatures with large eyes and yellow spots are positioned on the yellow field, a pair above and a pair below the coat of arms. In the four corners of the centre-field are quarter arabesque medallions. A large red carnation is positioned at each end of the centre-field and between the quarter medallions. These carnations are rendered in the Ottoman fashion for illustrating carnations on textiles. The boarder is filled with a series of yellow and red Chinese clouds alternating with white rosettes.  
  
At least two carpet-history sources name the place of manufacture for this type of Spanish carpet as being the city of Cuenca in east-central Spain. This city was well known for its Moorish carpet weavers. The ones holding coats of arms were usually made to mark the marriages of the nobility. Further research is needed to determine the identity of the coat of arms on this armorial carpet. Some have suggested that it is the coat of arms of Castile and Leon, but this has not been proven.

958f2e19-cf88-5446-b5c3-619ff5ee8038.name: Rug.
958f2e19-cf88-5446-b5c3-619ff5ee8038.description:
This is an outstanding example of a 'Konya rug', considered one of the earliest Turkish rug groups in Anatolia. Both warp and weft are wool. The weaving technique used is the 'Turkish double knot', known as the Gördes knot. The colours are red, dark-blue, blue, and beige. The main field of the rug has a geometric pattern with hooked red motifs on a light-red background. Triangles, octagons, hands-on-hip, and hook motifs form a repetitive geometric composition characteristic of Seljuq rugs. The decorative composition is dominated by the principle of 'infinity', as is typical with Turkish rugs. The design is repeated continuously. Between the repeating motifs are blue dots, which provide a strong contrast to the red background.  
  
The field of the rug is surrounded by a narrow border of eight-pointed, dark-blue star motifs separated from each other by yellow-beige lines. The most striking feature of the rug is the wide border decorated with pseudo-*kufic* script. Bold, stylised, *kufic* letters in light-blue follow one another on a dark-blue background. The letters are divided by red bands outlined in beige. Such monumental *kufic*\-script borders are characteristic of Seljuq rugs.  
  
The decorative composition of the rug is completed by a narrow outer border decorated with red eight-pointed star motifs on a blue background. The rug is quite worn; much of the pile is gone. Areas of the outer border are missing, and there is a large tear in the middle.  
  
Seljuq rugs commonly were woven in large dimensions and decorated with plain geometric compositions consisting of a small number of colours in various shades contrasting with a wide *kufic* border.  
  
Found in the Alaaddin ('Ala' al-Din) Mosque in Konya, this is one of eight Seljuq rugs brought to the Museum and registered in the inventory on 30 Rabi' al-Awwal 1329 / 31 March 1911.
958f2e19-cf88-5446-b5c3-619ff5ee8038.short_description: This is the oldest known example of a 'Konya rug'. The rugs of this period are characterised by contrasting light and dark shades, repetetive geometric motifs in the ground representing the principle of infinity and a wide border with stylised *kufic* script, and were woven in Turkish (Gördes) double-knot technique.
958f2e19-cf88-5446-b5c3-619ff5ee8038.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
958f2e19-cf88-5446-b5c3-619ff5ee8038.method_for_datation: The Seljuq sultans had many mosques built and it is known that they endowed Qur'ans, candlesticks, Qur'an-stands and rugs to furnish them. This rug is believed to have been woven specially for the Alaaddin Mosque by order of the Seljuq Sultan Alaaddin (Ala' al-Din) Keykubad I (r. 616–35 / 1220–37), who had the mosque enlarged in 618 / 1221. Stylistic analysis also dates the rug to the 7th / 13th century.
958f2e19-cf88-5446-b5c3-619ff5ee8038.method_for_provenance: Most high-quality rugs produced under the Anatolian Seljuqs come from Konya; the colours used in this rug are predominant in Konya rugs.
958f2e19-cf88-5446-b5c3-619ff5ee8038.obtention: Eight rugs were spotted by the scholar, Marin in the Alaaddin ('Ala' al-Din) Mosque in Konya in 1322 / 1905 and the information was brought to the attention of Loydved, the German Consulate. The rugs were first published in 1325 / 1908 and were registered in the Museum in 1329 / 1911.

960d37b6-f360-5606-98af-30bf823e004f.name: Fragment of a pile “Seljuq carpet”
960d37b6-f360-5606-98af-30bf823e004f.short_description:
This fragment has traditionally been linked with a number of carpets found in Konya and dated to the 13th century. Nearly all of them have a *Kufi*\-like border and simple, geometric main field. This is the youngest in the group, confirmed by carbon-14 dating.  
Anatolian carpets were praised by travellers such as Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta in the late 13th and 14th century.
keywords: Carpet; Fragment; Kufic; Wool; Geometric patterns
materials: Wool

9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.name: Carpet
9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.description:
The rug’s red-background, three-part prayer niche (*mihrab*) is supported by slender columns set on footings and arranged in a 1+2+2+1 formation. A carnation representing a lamp hangs from the peak of the central, higher arch and from each of the two outer, three-peak arches. The blue spandrels above the arches are decorated on each side by two arabesque-like curved leaves leaning towards each other and one serrated rosette; in the middle, the palmette growing out of the peak of the *mihrab* is surrounded by serrated leaves. The horizontal band, the frieze above the arch is filled with arabesque-like motives alternating with each other on a red ground.  
The main border contains undyed and red serrated rosettes sting along an undulating stem on ochre ground. The inner secondary border consists of small flowers of alternating orientation and colours. The outer secondary border is a succession of rosettes alternating with tree-of-life on a red ground.  
  
The provenance of the rugs is still uncertain, and so they are found referred to under a variety of names in the literature. Ernst Kühlbrandt, and later Emil Schmutzler mentioned this group of rugs as Säulenteppich (Kühlbrandt 1911, Schmutzler 1933), but later scholars, identifying their place of manufacture as the town of Ladik, designated them Ladik prayer rugs. In a 1968 publication, May H. Beattie called the Ladik origin into doubt and traced the six column type to 16th century Ottoman Court rugs, naming them, after the double column supporting the three-span vault, coupled column prayer rugs (Beattie 1968). Beattie classifies six column prayer rugs by the decoration in the spandrels above the arches. Ferenc Batári also considered there were insufficient grounds for asserting that the rugs came from the town of Ladik, he used the title ‘Ladik type prayer rugs’ (Batári 1994). Stefano Ionescu adopts the Beattie classification and maintains that the technical execution of the rugs is close to the other types found in Transylvania. He classifies column rugs by the number of columns, i.e. two, three, four, five and six column “Transylvanian” rugs (Ionescu 2007, p. 67–68). (Pásztor 2007, 137.).
9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.owner: Eszterháza Kulturális, Kutató- és Fesztiválközpont, Fertőd-Eszterháza

9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.method_for_datation: The six-column prayer rug, a version of Ottoman Turkish prayer rugs was very popular during the 17th century. Their general characteristic is a prayer niche (*mihrab*) whose background colour is red or ochre (and rarely ivory or blue), divided into three parts by slender columns in a 1+2+2+1 distribution.
9689a417-7d8e-5c3e-bb23-afdd8da1ff34.method_for_provenance: The carpet was exhibited at the 1914 Turkish Carpets from Transylvania exhibition in the Museum of Applied Arts in Budapest, it appeared under catalogue number 284. (Csányi 1914, 81). The carpet was published by Végh 1925, 24. Since then until xxxxxx the carpet's whereabouts were unknown. This carpet was the prototype of many  copies or forgeries made at  the Tuduc worshop in Rumania between 1925-1940. (Ionescu 2012, 94.)

9743f6aa-d6a5-5e28-9a16-365784151d17.name: Rug *l'ahmal n'ibouli*
9743f6aa-d6a5-5e28-9a16-365784151d17.description: Traditionally, Ait Ouaouzguite Berber rugs were flat-woven in natural white and brown wool with twining applied in the horizontal bands. In this rug, borders and horizontal bands are woven in knotted-pile technique in a palette of orange, red and yellow that is a result of the weavers’ exposure to urban weavings, Rabat carpets in particular. The tribe’s location on the trans-Atlas and trans-Saharan trade routes – through which goods moved from the Atlantic coast to Timbuktu (Mali) – made this cultural influence possible. These mixed knotted pile and flatwoven rugs were made long and narrow to conform to the room sizes typical of village architecture.
9743f6aa-d6a5-5e28-9a16-365784151d17.provenance: Morocco, High Atlas Mountains, the Berber, Ait Ouaouzguite tribe

97d4beaa-5849-5058-abb5-afc6bdc006cd.name: Tapestry ‘after the Indian Manner’
97d4beaa-5849-5058-abb5-afc6bdc006cd.description: A tapestry with a number of colourful scenes and figure groups arranged on small islands decorated with exotic birds and flowering plants on a dark brown ground. These include a couple standing under a canopy holding by servants in the centre, two girls standing in front of a zig-zag fence with a parrot at the upper left, a small pagoda and a group of a sitting and a standing man in the upper right, two musicians, one with a drum and the other with beaters (the musical instrument is missing) in the lower foreground, and a monkey sitting on a palm tree at the lower right corner. The borders are composed of garlands of flowers and fruit arranged in Chinese pots in the lower border, linked with bunches of a silk ribbon in the upper border, decorated with candlesticks (?) in the right and the left sides and parrots and herons at the corners.
97d4beaa-5849-5058-abb5-afc6bdc006cd.owner: Eszterháza Kulturális, Kutató- és Fesztiválközpont, Fertőd-Eszterháza
97d4beaa-5849-5058-abb5-afc6bdc006cd.method_for_datation: John Vanderbank worked as the head of the Great Wardrobe workshop in London from 1689 to 1717. The cheaper versions of tapestries 'after Indian manner', made for commercial sale were woven in the later period of the Vanderbank's workshop.
97d4beaa-5849-5058-abb5-afc6bdc006cd.method_for_provenance: John Vanderbank as the head of the Great Wardrobe workshop in London from 1689 to 1717, provided tapestries woven with ‘chinoiserie’ designs inspired by Chinese and Indian sources, lacquer panels, printed textiles etc. for Queen Mary’s apartments at Kensington Palace in 1690. Later he produced a second series with similar designs, but less elaborate figures, as cheaper versions for commercial sale. Numerous examples of Vanderbank's less elaborate series are known from the early 1700s – including, within the National Trust's collection, a small panel at Nunnington Hall in Yorkshire (no. 980694). – which is very close to this tapestry. Another, more similar item from the L. V. Hart collection was sold at Christie’s, November 12, 1964, no. 162, and November 29, 1979, no. 107. (Standen 1980, 126, fig. 10.), which depicts the same arrangement of the island panels, the couple under a canopy, the musicians, the ladies standing in front of a zig-zag fence, the pagoda, a monkey sitting on a palm tree and is framed by the same border-design.

9894288e-e20a-599a-a609-d59380647196.name: Floor mosaic
9894288e-e20a-599a-a609-d59380647196.description: During refurbishment of the villa in the late 18th-century, commissioned by Marco Antonio IV Borghese, the architect Antonio Asprucci decided to entirely relay the floor of the “Room of the Hermaphrodite” with ancient mosaics, a popular custom at the time, and whose decorative impact was powerfully suggestive. In fact, for visitors, the interior of a room with its authentic “mosaic carpet” covering the floor, became both an integral part of the modern refurbishment and a museum object. For the assemblage, which took place in 1781, Asprucci used mosaics from the excavation of a large Roman thermal complex situated in Castellarcione, a property of the Borghese family, located on Via Tiburtina at Bagni di Tivoli, not far from the famous Villa Adriana. The most ancient part of the mosaic, “little stars” on a white background (constructed from four black tiles juxtaposed in a form similar to a star), is surrounded by a frame, reproducing a polychrome meander. At the centre of the room, a panel, produced later, depicts a fishing scene, surrounded by multiple frames of braid motifs with acanthus leaves in the corners. A second panel, from the same period and depicting another fishing scene, is placed on the step in the window recess. The fashion for using authentic mosaic tiles to recall Antiquity is characteristic of the last decades of the 18th century. This is demonstrated in various buildings of the era, such as the Pontifical Galleries (for example the famous Sala Rotonda of the Pio-Clementino Museum with mosaics of the 3rd century BC) and in aristocratic residences, such as in the noble Cabinet of Palazzo Altieri in Rome.
9894288e-e20a-599a-a609-d59380647196.method_for_datation: Based on stylistic analysis, the part of the mosaic with “little stars” on a white background framed by a multicolour meander is from the 1st century BC; the “emblemata” with fishing scenes is from BC 200‒AD 300. The assemblage was made in 1781.
9894288e-e20a-599a-a609-d59380647196.method_for_provenance: The provenance is documented in the description of the Villa of 1796 (see Lamberti and Visconti, 1796).
9894288e-e20a-599a-a609-d59380647196.provenance: Excavations at Castellarcione near Bagni di Tivoli (Rome)
9894288e-e20a-599a-a609-d59380647196.obtention: The two panels with fishing scenes come from excavations carried out in the 18th century in Castellarcione near Tivoli, a property belonging to the Borghese family.

995266f4-4a66-52c0-aca4-1b45c8cbf765.name: Prayer rug *dhurrie*
995266f4-4a66-52c0-aca4-1b45c8cbf765.description:
In the late 19th and early 20th century, cotton prayer rugs (*dhurrie*) were woven throughout India in rural communities and in town and jail workshops. Cotton was the preferable material as the hot and humid climate of the subcontinent discouraged the use of woollen rugs. Prayer rugs were used for prayer and featured architectural details associated with the mosque - arches, columns and niches that have powerful symbolic meaning, creating a sacred space to concentrate in prayer.  
This multi-arched rug (*saph*) features five architectural niches (*mihrab*) boldly outlined in white on the indigo and navy-blue background.

995abd79-4a58-5ec8-b765-a1346e8414b0.name: Marby Rug.
995abd79-4a58-5ec8-b765-a1346e8414b0.description:
One of the few examples surviving in Sweden from a tradition of carpet–making in the early Ottoman period in Anatolia. In 1925, the so-called 'Marby rug', Sweden's oldest preserved oriental carpet, was found, cut in two pieces, at the abandoned church of Marby, a village in the province of Jämtland. Belonging to the group of animal carpets, it shows red, stylised birds standing symmetrically on either side of a tree set within octagons on an ivory ground. The birds and tree motif has been long known and very common in Central Asia.  
To judge from their presentations in Italian paintings of the 14th century, animal carpets with a tree flanked by two birds already seem to have been popular at this time. However, they reached the peak of their production and circulation during the first half of the AH 9th / AD 15th century. The provenance of this rug from a village in Jämtland in Sweden is important as it shows that the export was not restricted to Italy, but also reached the Baltic region. Animal carpets disappeared towards the end of the AH 9th / AD 15th century.  
Apart from the Marby rug, some fragments with the motif of birds flanking a tree from Fustat in Egypt are known and there are two completely preserved examples. The first was found in a church in Italy and is now in the Museum of Islamic Art in Berlin, Germany, and a second was acquired by the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York in 1990.
995abd79-4a58-5ec8-b765-a1346e8414b0.short_description: Rug, called ‘Marby rug’ after the village where it was found. Its pattern shows stylised red birds standing symmetrically on either side of a tree. This motif was long known and very common in Central Asia.
995abd79-4a58-5ec8-b765-a1346e8414b0.method_for_datation: The rug was dated by radiocarbon (Carbon-14).
995abd79-4a58-5ec8-b765-a1346e8414b0.method_for_provenance: The patterns of the border and the guard strips are characteristically Anatolian; the guard strips also appear in another group of early Ottoman carpets discovered in the 'Ala al-Din Mosque at Konya, Turkey.
995abd79-4a58-5ec8-b765-a1346e8414b0.obtention: Bought by the Museum of National Antiquities in 1925.

998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.name: Prayer rug.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.description: A rug produced by peasant weavers in Ghiordes, Anatolia, famous for their tightly woven work with a short, silky wool pile. Ghiordes was one of the major carpet-making centres during the AH 13th / AD 19th century and both the design and colour scheme of this rug, a deep-blue niche framed with elaborate spandrels and borders, is typical of Ghiordes rugs. The niche confirms that this is a prayer rug, used to provide a ritually clean place for the five daily prayers. The niche reflects the *mihrab* or prayer niche in an Islamic mosque, indicating the direction to Mecca, towards which Muslims turn in prayer. It may also symbolise the gateway to Paradise. The ornament suspended in its apex may have a spiritual meaning.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.short_description: Every household in Ghiordes, Anatolia, had a handloom for the womenfolk and girls to weave small carpets and prayer rugs on. This prayer rug is decorated with an elaborate central niche reminiscent of the architectural prayer niche found in Anatolian mosques.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.holder: St. Mungo Museum for Religious Life and Art, Glasgow Museums.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.method_for_datation: Artistic analysis: both the layout and weave of this rug resemble several other 13th- / 19th-century prayer rugs of this type, attributed to Ghiordes in Anatolian Turkey in particular.
998a912b-36fb-51e9-9d23-92392129a07c.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

materials: Wool (warp and weft and pile) with cotton in parts; woven on a handloom.

9a5f6ab0-8a7b-5628-869a-8623164a2cfe.name: *Invasion of the French camp. The Swiss refuse to advance despite the interventions of their leaders*
9a5f6ab0-8a7b-5628-869a-8623164a2cfe.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the border of two tapestries in the series. Furthermore, the presence of the mark has allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: that is, after 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and by the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014).  
This tapestry depicts one of the decisive moments of the Battle of Pavia: the civilians are escaping from the French encampment, which is being attacked by the imperial troops, in the vicinity of the Vernavola river, through the breaches made in the wall of Visconti Park during the siege. The episode provides an opportunity to show everyday narratives: a soldier in the foreground runs away, carrying off with him a couple of chickens, while he looks towards the viewer, involving us in the scene; a woman in the distance carries a basket with two geese; a friar, frightened, is running. In the foreground, the Swiss infantry (recognisable by the flag with a white cross) who had fought with the French, proving their courage and valour, all hope of victory lost and surrounded on all sides, yield to the imperial cavalry, throwing their pikes to the ground, deaf to the cries of their officers, and try to seek safety in flight or surrender. In the foreground, amongst the soldiers one can make out a drummer, a piper and a standard bearer with a longsword, figures who often recur in military iconography. The figure in the centre of the tapestry has been identified as the Swiss captain Jean de Diesbach, who offers himself up to the sword of the enemy cavalier so he can die with honour (Casali 1993).

9a65414e-f0c8-5205-b98f-8298259490d3.name: Small-Pattern "Holbein" Carpet with Closed Kufesque Border
9a65414e-f0c8-5205-b98f-8298259490d3.short_description: A so-called "Holbein" rug with a heavily stylized pseudo-*kufic* inscription around the border. The red field has a pattern of nine rows of small medallions alternately white and blue. Knotted bands in pink, red, and violet define the white medallions which enclose various rosettes in octagons in the above colors. The blue medallions are formed by arabesques in blue and green with cross motifs, in the above colors, within lozenges. The rug is bordered by interlaced angular bands, derived from *kufic* writing, in white, red, blue, and green on a violet or red ground. The inner and outer guard bands contain a ribbon design in red, blue, green, and violet on a yellow, and partly on a red ground.

9a80618f-fbfd-5d5e-b4ee-f9684139776e.name: Kirman carpet
9a80618f-fbfd-5d5e-b4ee-f9684139776e.description:
The name of Persia (modern Iran) is so intimately associated with oriental rugs that they are often referred to generically as “Persian”. The golden age of carpet weaving had been during the Safavid rule of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. The dynasty collapsed in 1722/3 and the country remained in turmoil for decades. It is likely that with the fall of Safavids most urban based weaving diminished greatly or ceased. All that remained was local production on a much reduced scale. The revival of the Persian carpet trade dates from the 1860s and was mainly due to enterprising merchants of the north-western city of Tabriz.  
Kirman has long been one of the major carpet-producing areas of Persia. Development of the carpet industry is poorly documented in Kirman, although there is clear evidence that weaving occurred during the Safavid times. Some of the best wool in the country is grown around Kirman. Weaving was well-developed during much of the 19th century. The rugs of Kirman always display a brilliant variety of colours and the number of shades is enormous. The dyes are varied and imaginative. Insect dyes have traditionally been used for reds and indigo was used for blues, providing a variety of shades. Colours can range from ivory, blue magenta to more golden and saffron cast.  
Persian workshops in the towns of Kirman, Tabriz and Kashan were the main producers of pictorial carpets. They portray humans and/or animals and illustrate historical and mythological stories. Sometimes the composition makes one or more characters that show famous people or events from the past.  
This pictorial carpet was a gift to the Museum of Arts and Crafts from Kemal Nanić and his family. The figural compositions depict the scenes from the famous Persian tragic romance *Khusraw and Shirin* written by the poet and writer Nizami Ganjavi (1141–1209). The poem describes the romance of the Persian king Khusraw II Perviz (590–628) and his wife Shirin, an Armenian Christian. The novel includes Khusraw's courtship of Shirin, their marriage and her romance with the architect Farhad. After a series of heroic romantic episodes, Shirin agrees to marry Khusraw who later built her a palace called Qasr-e-Shirin (the remains are visible even today). For the construction of palace architect Farhad was hired. Shirin then fell in love with Farhad, but their romance ended tragically.  
The central field of the carpet is divided into four horizontal rows. Each row has a mirror image of a group of human figures. They illustrate scenes from the poem *Khusraw and Shirin*, including a famous scene when Khusraw glimpses Shirin bathing. The central field is framed with four equally wide borders. The inner border is the *laleh abbasi* (abbasi tulip) border. The other three borders are a variation of the floral meander border.
9a80618f-fbfd-5d5e-b4ee-f9684139776e.dates: Second half 19th century / beginning of the 20th century

materials: Cotton; wool; knotted carpet; asymmetrical knots

9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.name: *Antependium with the Tribute of Continents and Imperial Countries to the Holy Family*
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.description: This colourful embroidery was executed as a “needle painting” and is set within an original gilded frame. An eventful scene opens out with a central motif of columned architecture with staircases and balustrades, and adoring female figures. At the bottom left, four girls kneel, with the coats of arms of the imperial Electors of the clergy who facilitated the foundation of the Franciscan Convent of St. Joseph in Brno. The Archbishops of Treves, Cologne and Mainz are represented by the coats of arms of Karel Kaspar von der Leyen (1652–1676), Maximilian Heinrich von Bayern (1650–1688) and Johann Philipp von Schönborn (1647–1673). Opposite, four girls kneel with the coats of arms of the imperial countries: Bavaria, Saxony, Brandenburg and Pfalz. In the centre are four female personifications of the continents, Asia, America, Africa and Europe, in precious attire. The women and a host of lay people of both sexes pay tribute to the Holy Family. The Virgin Mary is supervising the education of Jesus, while St. Joseph hands to the Pope – a personification of the Church – a sheet with the text *Ecclesiae Petenti Satisfiat*. The scene is crowned with the dove of the Holy Spirit. At the sides are monumental summerhouses with decorative vases and cartouches with the inscription *Ite ad Joseph* (Go to Joseph), while the Old Testament quotation (Gen 41:55) relates to the figure of St. Joseph of Nazareth. In combination with the text on the donated sheet, it elucidates the subject of the embroidered antependium emphasising the role of St. Joseph, patron saint of the Franciscan Convent of St. Joseph in Brno, as a righteous protector of the church and promoter of Divine will. Towards the horizon, various landscapes alternate on the antependium, valleys and hills dotted with dominant castles. The intricate layout of the embroidery may refer to a major event in the history of the Franciscan convent or it could commemorate the establishment and construction of the Convent Church of St. Joseph in 1651–1653.
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.short_description: The subject of the technically and artistically remarkable antependium is derived from the legends of St. Joseph, a popular saint of the Baroque period. It is one of only a few examples of the use of figurative embroidery in sacred art during the first half of the 18th century, and a specimen of monastery art.

9b8e8571-d3d9-56e2-967b-03113caec98e.name: Doily, *Parisian pattern*
9b8e8571-d3d9-56e2-967b-03113caec98e.description: A Pirot doily (*šustikla*) with the *Parisian pattern* (*Pariska šara*) was used as a chair seat cover. The central field is filled with larger ornaments called *bombs* (*bombe*) and smaller ornaments called *bibice*, arranged alternately in rows or columns. The wide outer border (*ploča*) is decorated with the *Queens’s sleeve* (*kraljičin rukav*) ornament. The colours used are: red, green, blue, pink, black and white. According to tradition, the *Queens’s sleeve* ornament was created upon request of Queen Natalija of Serbia, modelled on the pattern found on the sleeve of her Wallachian folk shirt. Most probably, the ornament represents a stylized vine.
9b8e8571-d3d9-56e2-967b-03113caec98e.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material and technique

9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.name: Panel of *azulejos* with a carpet composition
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.description:
The widespread use of *azulejos* ‒ that were initially produced in Seville during the first half of the 16th century ‒ in Portugal, allowed those involved in the placement of them in architectural settings many ways to experiment with a new decorative expression, giving an early original use to something that was previously foreign to Portuguese culture. In the 16th century, Spanish *azulejos*, like large tapestries with respect to the pattern, were used to create large walls expanses filled with the same motif.  
In the beginning, the Portuguese used the *azulejos* from Spain in the same way, but as time went on they started to become less concerned about the patterns in the *azulejos* and more interested in creating compositions. These compositions could be more architecturally related, like imitations of stained-glass windows, doors and *mihrab*s, or with the intention to re-create carpets, not by the repetition of the pattern, but by juxtaposing different decorations and thus creating something new, like this panel. This early and original understanding of the potential of *azulejo* became the basis for a tradition that has remained in Portugal to this day. This panel uses 16th-century *azulejos* in a composition that can be seen in the architecture of the church of Sé Velha in Coimbra.
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: in the 16th century, the *azulejos* in the techniques of *arista* or cuerda seca were imported to Portugal, because at that time there was no production of this type in Portuguese workshops.
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.method_for_provenance: The National Tile Museum holds a large number of *azulejos* of unknown origin, many collected during the period of the destruction of the convents and palaces in the late 19th century, in the aftermath of the abolition of the religious orders in 1834.
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.obtention: Probably salvaged during demolition of an unknown building where they had once been applied
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.bibliography: Meco, José, *O Azulejo em Portugal*, Lisbon: Publicações Alfa, 1989.
9bd67ea8-6822-56f9-b47d-e269735e0352.author: Alexandre Pais
keywords: *azulejos*; pattern; 16th century; Spain
materials: Ceramic

9c62737c-6dfe-513f-9b6e-e4b3b16cd00f.name: Carpet
9c62737c-6dfe-513f-9b6e-e4b3b16cd00f.description: Carpets, with designs of yellow geometric split-leaf (*rumi*) lattice on a red ground, are among the most popular classical Anatolian carpets. Carpets with this design are called “Lotto” or “Lotto-style” carpets from their appearance in a well-known altarpiece by the 16th century northern Italian painter Lorenzo Lotto. The earliest examples of Lotto-style carpets use what is called the “calligraphic” kufesque border with clearly denoted “letter finials” recalling *kufic* script. Later examples such as this one, probably from the late 16thor early 17th century, show a wide variety of borders based on repeating multi-lobed cartouches or elongated medallions. Most of the early Lotto-style carpets were woven in large sizes such as this exceptionally well preserved example.
9c62737c-6dfe-513f-9b6e-e4b3b16cd00f.holder: The George Washington University Museum and The Textile Museum
9c62737c-6dfe-513f-9b6e-e4b3b16cd00f.method_for_datation: This style of carpets appears in European paintings and is dated in approximation to the dates of these paintings.
9c62737c-6dfe-513f-9b6e-e4b3b16cd00f.method_for_provenance: Design analyses and comparison with carpets sharing similar design and structural characteristics.

9db8337d-de5f-5f6f-a8e2-71d2e87cca1b.name: Tent pole bag *igsalik*
9db8337d-de5f-5f6f-a8e2-71d2e87cca1b.description: In Turkmenistan, textile bags were the main containers for food, clothing and household goods, both at seasonal camps and on migration. A pair of special bags (*igsalik*) was made for packing and carrying tent poles on the camel back when on migration to seasonal pastures. Felted or woven, and richly embellished with long tassels, they had a conical shape and cupped both ends of the bunch of tent poles tightly tight with braided bands. This bag is one of the pair of *igsalik*s made by a Yomud Turkmen weaver. In order to create a proper shape, she wove one of its ends in alternating pile and plain woven sections. Unstitched, it has a square shape, but if stitched properly, the plain woven sections would be hidden inside and only the pile sections would show, creating a desired conical shape. The bag features red, blue, brown and white, typical colours of Turkmen rugs.

keywords: Central Asia; Wool
materials: Wool; knotted pile, plain woven

9e869f84-6a4f-54c1-8712-e043b8b2ce6c.name: Fachralo Kazak
9e869f84-6a4f-54c1-8712-e043b8b2ce6c.description:
Kazak rugs were made in the south central Caucasus, between Tbilisi in Georgia and Erivan in Armenia. The area is bordered by the Ganja area to the northeast and Karabakh area to the southeast.  
Fachralo or Fekhraly is a town 40km southwest of Tbilisi. This decagon medallion is one of the most common Kazak motifs and it is often found in the prayer rug format.  
The colours on this rug are clear, bright and contrasting. The central red field has a green prayer niche. In the niche there is a red and white *fachralo* medallion. The prayer niche is decorated with medallions and framed by a border decorated with polychrome rectangular motifs on the white background. Three rectangular fields have the inscription of the year (Hegira 1317/AD 1898) and probably the master weaver. The central field is framed with three borders. The main border is a polychrome rhomboid motif on a white background. Minor borders are decorated with *laleh abbasi* (abbasi tulip) motif. The inner minor *laleh abbasi* border is in red and blue, and the outer is red and green.
9e869f84-6a4f-54c1-8712-e043b8b2ce6c.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and inscripted year

9f376d69-2fed-50cf-81a4-5a918f774cdf.name: Carpet
9f376d69-2fed-50cf-81a4-5a918f774cdf.description:
Carpet of the Brocade series.  
Field: The field consists of a symmetrical axis that is composed of large leaf-palms in a specular array and interspersed with smaller flowers of the same height, which arise from a central stem that chains them longitudinally.  
These chains highlight depictions of small animals, birds and quadrupeds, which are presented between the chains on the blue background and frame stylised plant formations. The arrangement of all these elements is organised in a diamond pattern.  
Border: The border consists of a central valance of long stylised S shaped chains that is wedged between two narrow zigzagging bands against the blue background.  
The carpet relies on the Spanish knot technique with wool of varying blue, yellow, white and green shades.  
This carpet is part of a series that is inspired by Renaissance era brocaded carpets made in the Spanish city of Toledo within the 16th century.  
Only two carpets belonging to this particular series have such large dimensions. Aside from this one currently preserved in the National Museum of Decorative Arts, another was placed in the presbytery of the historic Cathedral of Cuenca and is currently in the Diocesan Museum of Cuenca.  
Such Renaissance era carpet designs continued during the 17th and well into the 18th century albeit with certain adjustments in production techniques, particularly the use of the Turkish knot as a replacement for the Spanish knot.  
A similar carpet can be found in: FERRANDIS TORRES, José: Catalog Exhibition of Spanish Carpets (Madrid, 1933) page 117. nº 65 (lam. XLIV). Exhibition by the Ilmo Mr. Bishop of Cuenca in the exhibition of Spanish Ancient Carpets.
9f376d69-2fed-50cf-81a4-5a918f774cdf.dimensions: Length: 680cm, Width: 345cm; Spanish knot?, Density: 700 knots/dm2
9f376d69-2fed-50cf-81a4-5a918f774cdf.method_for_datation: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.

9f376d69-2fed-50cf-81a4-5a918f774cdf.author: Mª Dolores Vila Tejero
keywords: Cuenca
materials: Weft: Wool, Warp: Hemp/Spanish knot, Taffeta [Ligament]

9f627bca-ad6b-52e9-92bd-a5b9836c7242.name: 'The Little Tree' Hammersmith Rug
9f627bca-ad6b-52e9-92bd-a5b9836c7242.description:
Pieces known as "Hammersmith" carpets were made in W. Morris's workshop near his home in Hammersmith, and from 1881 at Merton Abbey Works (London) for the Morris & Co. "The Little Flower" and the "Small Barr" patterns were variants of "The Little Tree"; William Morris used the motifs and colours of Persian and Indian rugs with all three. A drawing about the pattern of the carpet is published by A. Vallance.  
  
The border is surrounded by a green frame and decorated with alternating tulips and green pomegranates among flowery foliage, on a red ground. The dark blue base of the surface is filled with symmetrical plant motifs; beige and blue sunflower rosettes connected with curved, leafy tendrils, and small trees and foliage springing from blue rosettes on the two sides. There is knotted fringe at each end. A variation of the rug made around 1890 with identical decorations but a red central field and blue borders can be found in the collection of the Huntington Library, Art Museum, and Botanical Gardens.
9f627bca-ad6b-52e9-92bd-a5b9836c7242.obtention: Purchased from the Morris and Co, probably in 1895
