a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.name: *Presentation of the Child in the Temple*
a0292759-10a9-5092-8afb-5b3e2db3b197.description:
The production of knotted carpets in Portugal has been documented since the 14th century, mostly in association with the Moorish community. With the expulsion of the Muslims and Jews in 1496 by King Manuel I (1469‒1521; r.1495‒1521), the Portuguese carpet workshops were inevitably abandoned and the manufacturing tradition was lost. Aside from local production, Portuguese consumers imported high-quality items as well. This ensured the supply of luxury goods to the wealthier clientele. Despite that Spanish carpets were esteemed throughout the 15th century, according to representations in paintings, by the second quarter of the 16th century, they were replaced by Ottoman carpets produced in the regions of Anatolia and Uşak.  
Although, surprisingly, there are no surviving examples of this type of carpet in Portugal, its presence in paintings, as well as in other documentary sources such as in inventories, confirms their presence in Portuguese interiors, thus enabling us to identify the patterns and original colours of the imported carpets. This is the case with this painting, where a Turkish carpet, placed on the floor near the altar, displays most probably a “small-pattern Holbein” design: it comprises a repeated pattern of alternating quatrefoils and octagonal medallions, with *kufic* script motifs represented in detail on the red border.

a06054cf-1305-5f2c-b722-f5e5f3586c49.name: Sivas Prayer Rug
a06054cf-1305-5f2c-b722-f5e5f3586c49.description: Less well known than other regions, Sivas was an important centre for rug production. Sivas rugs are famous for their detail, an intricate design is created with a high number of knots per inch. This prayer rug is a beautiful example of a Sivas rug. Niche corners are decorated with stylized clove motifs and the *mihrab* niche is framed with four borders, from inside to outside. Very detailed plant motifs, including leaves and flowers are used to decorate the four borders.

a0ee7365-128d-5c65-8456-878c2ef46398.name: *Fireworks After A Really Big Event*
a0ee7365-128d-5c65-8456-878c2ef46398.description:
It is only on closer inspection that one realises this artwork is not a woodcut or a thickly layered painting. It is indeed a piece of red carpet into which the artist milled, cut and burned a graphic pattern that is typical of fireworks in the sky. The three-dimensional carpet and the white of the relatively thin underlying plastic material create a sculptural surface oscillating between image and object.  
Buth often uses red carpet as material for her artworks. As a prop inextricably linked to entertainment industry and political life, it has become a symbol for success, visibility, power and approval. *Fireworks After A Really Big Event* artistically deals with variants of power display used in many realms, including the art world itself. The object was acquired as a purchase made in support of artists by the Kulturstiftung des Freistaates Sachsen (Cultural Trust of the Free State of Saxony) for the Kunstfonds in 2007.  
Peggy Buth (\*1971 in Berlin) studied at Hochschule für Grafik und Buchkunst (HGB) Leipzig and at the Fine Art Department of Saint Martin’s College, London. She lives in Berlin. As of 2016/2017, she holds a professorship for Media Art at HGB Leipzig. Her works have been on display in Europe and North America.

a115a071-a444-5017-9250-8a310369de51.name: Vase design carpet
a115a071-a444-5017-9250-8a310369de51.description:
An early 17th century Safavid Kirman pile carpet with a large wine-red centre-field and a narrow dark blue border. The centre-field is decorated with a symmetrically laid out arabesque lattice consisting of four layers of stem networks, three main baring a variety of multi-coloured palmettes, and one minor baring small rosettes and leaves. A dark blue pear-shaped vase is positioned in the centre at one end of the carpet. Out of this vase spreads one of the three main stem networks and the minor one. The dark blue narrow border contains a row of alternating multi-coloured palmettes, rosettes and multi-bud stems.  
  
A very busy carpet, that may seem confused to many a viewer. However, an analysis of the design structure shows a deliberate plan to overlay, almost too many, networks of stems and floral compositions. The designers / weavers then decided to keep the a symmetrical layout of the shapes that form the design but not their colours, so that the left and right sides of the carpet mirror each other in design but not in the colour combinations of the many large and small palmettes, rosettes, buds and leaves. Nevertheless, the non-symmetrical distribution of the colours is still balanced enough to give the carpet great visual charm. By contrast the carpet’s narrow border is simple and uniform in its repeat design with good symmetry between the left and right sides of the carpet, both in shapes and colours, and in the well planned and executed floral configurations of its four corners.

keywords: vegetal Arabesque; floral decoration; floral motifs; vase; palmette; Kerman

a121479e-8919-5e90-a0d8-1b27de5172e5.name: Prayer rug
a121479e-8919-5e90-a0d8-1b27de5172e5.description: This rug belongs to a distinctive group of Caucasian rugs that come from the northeast Azerbaijan and are known as Kuba-Shirvan rugs. They are named after the historic rug centres and regions of Azerbaijan where they were produced. These rugs are products of the cottage industry developed by the settled population of the area, woven in homes and small town workshops by women trained in rug weaving by their families and working within local rug weaving traditions. They are woven with the Turkish (symmetrical) pile knot and show angular, geometric and stylized floral patterns executed in vivid colours. The key-shaped *mihrab* niche of the rug is one of the oldest types known in Middle Eastern prayer rugs; it became popular in the Caucasus in the 19th century and was widely used in Kuba-Shirvan rugs. The rectangular motif within the arch is probably a Kerbala tablet. Both the design and colour compositions are typical for this area.

a208cebc-edec-52c5-8d53-248017055f09.name: Memling Rug Fragments
a208cebc-edec-52c5-8d53-248017055f09.description:
From the second half of the 15th century when Sunnite aniconism rejected naturalistic representation, carpet design changed and the *gul* (flower, rose) motifs, strongly geometrized symbols of the Central Asian nomadic Turkmen tribes, spread. Anatolian carpets with animal figures were replaced by carpets depicting strictly geometric patterns composed of squares adorned with simple or more intricate geometric designs. Early Ottoman carpets in the 15th–16th century were named after the painters whose pictures typically included variants of these designs. Hans Memling (c. 1430–1494) often painted throne carpets in his Madonna pictures containing rhomboids of hook shaped or stepped edges (Memling guls) placed into octagons.  
One of the earliest known specimens of such carpets with Memling guls is represented by these two fragments bought by the Museum of Applied Arts from the carpet collection of Emil Sigerus (1854–1947), a historian and ethnographer of Nagyszeben in 1917. The dominant pattern consists of Memling guls; stepped and hooked lozenges in an endless arrangement of white-grounded octagons. The centre of the lozenges contains eight-pointed stars and the triangular fields between the octagons are decorated by dark brown hooks on a red background. The main border is a chain of "S" motifs on a field of red flanked by similar chains on a field of ochre. Memling depicted such a rug in his *Donne Triptych* around 1485 (London, National Gallery) and on the back of his *Portrait of a Young Man at Prayer*, in *The Flower Still Life* of around 1485–1490 (Madrid, Museo Thyssen-Bornemisza).

a223ba4c-72e4-5125-8f67-82e5f04a5794.name: Beiriz rug
a223ba4c-72e4-5125-8f67-82e5f04a5794.description:
Founded in Beiriz (near Oporto) in 1919, the Artisanal Carpet Factory of Beiriz is one of only a few factories in Portugal keeping alive the tradition of artisanal (handcrafted) carpets. The carpets are produced in pure wool using wooden handlooms that are entirely reliant on arm- and foot strength, as opposed to the mechanical shuttle. The knots used are the “star”, “Beiriz” and the “zagal”.  
Throughout its history, the factory has produced both conservative designs and those that follow contemporary artistic tendencies. With reference to the carpet seen here, the pattern takes inspiration from the drip-painting techniques developed by the American painter Jackson Pollock (1912‒56), a major figure of Abstract Expressionism. The main effort in this carpet has been to combine the utility of the soft-feeling texture of this 1.6 pile-high rug ‒ that is, the human experience of the object ‒ with the design. Thus while it translates visually the free movement and an informal way of painting, also it expresses emotion and the psychological experience of the object.  
The resulting impression of fading brushstrokes or drips was achieved by using several shades of each colour in a gradient effect. Since overlapping colours is not possible in rugwork, 38 colours were used to achieve this visual effect. One square metre of this type and quality of carpet would take 68 hours to produce.

a254f7c2-b126-5a1f-a57d-efb180d91b9e.name: Vienna hunting carpet
a254f7c2-b126-5a1f-a57d-efb180d91b9e.short_description: Due to its fineness, motifs, and size, the famous silk Vienna hunting carpet ranks among the world’s most exceptional carpets having been repeatedly publicised since the 19th century. Originating from the court of Shah Tahmasp I (r. 1524–76), the carpet’s design supposedly lay in the hands of the court painters working for the art-minded ruler. Comparable hunting scenes are found in miniature paintings, but also on fabrics of Safavid production. The middle of the balanced pattern forms a medallion with dragons and phoenixes – symbols of power brought over from China, found in the Iranian formal repertoire since the Ilkhanid period. The corners are marked by quarters of the main medallion. Safavid horsemen and prey in the surrounding fields form into one of the famous imperial hunts. *Peris* (angel-like beings) are depicted in front of dainty tendrils in the surrounding borders. How the Vienna hunting carpet entered into the possession of the Austrian Imperial Court is still not exactly ascertainable. Its extraordinary quality suggests it was a diplomatic gift.

a33cdc01-fc3e-5d40-b2cd-2e6102071211.name: ‘Lotto’ carpet
a33cdc01-fc3e-5d40-b2cd-2e6102071211.description: Anatolia, with Uşak as the textile centre, was one of the most productive carpet regions, as travellers of different origins reported. It is proven that exemplars of various qualities and sizes were knotted there in the late 15th century. Many of them were exported to Europe, where they have been preserved up to today in numerous historical collections. Their depiction in contemporary Italian paintings as of the second decade of the 16th century facilitates their dating. However, the earliest illustration of a so-called “Lotto” carpet is not to be found in a painting of the eponymous Italian painter Lorenzo Lotto (1480–1557), but in a portrait by Sebastiano del Piombo (1485–1547) from the year 1516. The pattern of the carpet field, an endless rapport, consists of two rows of geometric, yellow tendrils and is structurally reminiscent of the patterns of silk fabric. The dimensions of the pattern units is constant in all Lotto carpets, even if the size of the examples changes.

a45839e2-37d8-5fb0-8ec9-90569c5bc248.name: Floor mat
a45839e2-37d8-5fb0-8ec9-90569c5bc248.description: An almost complete mat has perimetrical bands with lozenge designs and triangular motifs. It combines brocaded decoration with self-patterned elements such as the beaded medallions in the centre. Two parallel lines of inscriptions are included in the composition and repeat the same word *baraka* (blessing) in a poorly executed *kufic* script. Geniza records describe how such reed mats were used to cover the floor surface and how detailed descriptions might be given to weavers in order to fill every available space. Based on this information, this small mat could be part of a larger commission, used to fill specific recesses or the entrance of a room.
a45839e2-37d8-5fb0-8ec9-90569c5bc248.method_for_datation: The form of the repetitive word in the *kufic* script places it to this period

a4a5eb77-13a0-5a5c-9e6a-16dc9862a0fb.name: ‘Transylvanian’ rug
a4a5eb77-13a0-5a5c-9e6a-16dc9862a0fb.description:
The term “Transylvanian” rug does not relate to the area of production but to the geographical region where many such rugs were preserved, that is, Transylvania. Rugs belonging to this group could be found mainly in Transylvanian churches. They were made in the villages of Anatolia during the 17th and 18th centuries.  
Size wise, Transylvanian rugs are rather small. Their most distinctive feature is a border filled with elongated, polygonal cartouches; however, sometimes, these are substituted by a row of simplified rosettes. The majority of so-called Transylvanian rugs are decorated with the double prayer niche, created from two *mihrab* niches in mirror image. They are mainly red, but some white-ground examples are known. “Transylvanian” rugs were very popular in Poland and many of them form part of Polish collections.  
The Kraków rug was probably made in Uşak. On the red field of the double niche, an indigo-blue cartouche of Uşak type joins with the pointed tops of the niches with flowering stems. The presence of such a medallion also suggests the place of origin of the rug. The lozenge-shape cartouche is decorated with a four-lobed motif inscribed within a double diamond, two palmettes situated on the vertical axis, and motifs of carnations and tulips as well. Placed along the edges of the cartouche are rows of graceful, small white flowers. The spandrels are decorated with lanceolate leaves and roses. The main border is filled with a row of rosettes and the outside borders with trefoil motifs.
a4a5eb77-13a0-5a5c-9e6a-16dc9862a0fb.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis of the rather geometrised ornament suggests this rug dates to the end of the 17th century
a4a5eb77-13a0-5a5c-9e6a-16dc9862a0fb.method_for_provenance: The “Uşak-style” central medallion allows us to presume that the prayer rug was made in Uşak, Anatolia

a4cc2ed5-ef19-5a77-af21-2099f0b17875.name: ‘Molla Narsaddin’
a4cc2ed5-ef19-5a77-af21-2099f0b17875.description: The central area of the carpet is taken up with a part of the plot from a “Molla Nasreddin” story , hence the name of this carpet. Designed to be read from right to left, there is a house on a white background, and representations of birds, donkeys and peasant motifs, all woven around “Molla Nasreddin”. Stylised flowers decorate the edges. Above Nasreddin’s head, “Molla Nasreddin” is written, and on each of the four sides of the central area within the white border the Arabic alphabet is written in black thread.

a6414cb5-5350-5e05-b2b9-dd437603d22a.name: Kilim, *shuttles*
a6414cb5-5350-5e05-b2b9-dd437603d22a.description: One of the Pirot kilims’ ornaments is named *shuttle* (*soveljka*) after a tool used in the weaving process. The kilim shows a typical disposition of a *shuttle* motif: a larger *shuttle* in the middle of the central field, and four smaller in the corners. The central field is also filled with the motif of *amajlike*. Inner border is filled with *almonds* (*bademčići*), while the wide border (*ploča*) is decorated with a hooked ornament named *čendjeli*. The colours used are: blue, red, green, yellow, white, brown and black.
a6414cb5-5350-5e05-b2b9-dd437603d22a.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis, material and technique

a668e314-0656-59ea-9a3c-9d85d601356f.name: Carpet
a668e314-0656-59ea-9a3c-9d85d601356f.description:
Fragment of a carpet that preserves part of the decoration of the field and the border.  
Field: The field contains thistle bundle motifs that are alternately distributed and form a series of rhombuses. In the openings, geometric motifs surround two small birds that face each other with surrounding six-petalled flowers, which in turn make a false cruciform division.  
Border: A single blue line separates the field and the border, of which only one valance is preserved. This depicts continuous waves that support two types of palmetto stems.  
Some motifs that show different profiles appear, some in blue and others in sandy yellow hues.  
The warp and weft are of a dark brown wool and woollen knot consists of yellow, orange, green, turquoise, ultramarine and mauve shades.  
This fragment is valuable in that it indicates a carpet belonging to the so-called Thistle series, of which very few specimens have been preserved. The reference copy of this type is preserved in the Valencian Institute of Don Juan.  
The motifs of the field and the disposition of the decorative motifs of the border, evoke textile designs from the beginning of the 17th century. It could be said that this specimen is coarser than the one preserved in the Valencia Institute of Don Juan. The piece has suffered some degradation of its fibres.
a668e314-0656-59ea-9a3c-9d85d601356f.method_for_datation: Through the stylistic and technical analysis of the piece.

keywords: Cardos; Alcaraz
materials: Warp: Wool, Weft: Wool, Spanish knot [Warp: 4 knots/cm Weft: 4 knots/cm. Two weft threads past each half]

a6aab42c-ba5f-5be5-a713-8a411fbb8fd8.name: Circular Mamluk-style carpet
a6aab42c-ba5f-5be5-a713-8a411fbb8fd8.description:
There exists a unique group of carpets made throughout the late 15th and early 16th centuries of the Mamluk period in Egypt, the colours and overlapping geometrical patterns of which are often likened to those seen through a kaleidoscope. These carpets were made in workshops in Cairo for the royal court, and additionally as export items to Europe, in particular Venice. Despite the overthrow of the Mamluk Sultanate by the Ottomans in 1517, production of these carpets continued and those made from this period on can be referred to as 'Mamluk-style' carpets.  
MIA’s carpet is thought to have made during the second quarter of the 16th century in Cairo, and thus can be classified as ‘Mamluk-style’. Earlier carpets generally included a palette of five to seven different colours, while later versions have a lesser range such as this example bearing red, blue, green and yellow. This carpet is in good condition and contains a centralized arrangement of a circle set within an octagonal star, which in turn is framed by a wide circular border. Stylised vegetal motifs in addition to circular and polygonal patterns cover the field of the carpet, while the border consists of alternating cartouches and circles alongside further vegetal and geometric designs.
a6aab42c-ba5f-5be5-a713-8a411fbb8fd8.method_for_datation: This carpet has been dated based on stylistic comparisons with other known Mamluk and Mamluk-style carpets from Cairo
a6aab42c-ba5f-5be5-a713-8a411fbb8fd8.method_for_provenance: This carpet has been stylistically attributed to Cairo based on comparisons with further extant examples

a70edf46-1e11-58a2-b84b-c323d16e494e.name: Carpet (fragment)
a70edf46-1e11-58a2-b84b-c323d16e494e.description: The Museum of Applied Arts ‒ MAK ‒ owns a unique collection of Mamluk carpets from the 15th and 16th centuries. This carpet – consisting of five larger and seven smaller fragments, of which the outer border is missing – is the oldest one in the entire inventory. Its dating to the late 15th century, the late heyday of Mamluk art under Sultan Qaytbay (1416/18–1496), can be explained, among other things, by the use of five colours, as well as by the absence of umbrella and lancet-shaped leaves regarded as typically post-Mamluk. Despite considerable gaps in the lower third portion, the overall design can be reconstructed. The carpet belongs to the group of Mamluk carpets with three octagons that define the field. It remains unclear why the carpet was cut up in this manner, but that the remnants were preserved.

a7c9b5ba-4e98-57ae-ae0f-0118a136e091.name: Garden carpet
a7c9b5ba-4e98-57ae-ae0f-0118a136e091.description:
Earthly gardens in the culture of Islamic countries represent an image of paradise as promised by God. These gardens were rectangular and divided into four parts by water channels representing heavenly rivers of water, honey, wine and milk. At the intersection of the water channels, a square or polygonal pool was situated, often together with a pavilion. Walking along the paths one would smell a strong fragrance from the flowers and blooming trees. Such a garden was called *chahār-bāgh* – four gardens.  
Representations of gardens are also found on Persian carpets. Usually they reflect the layout of *chahār-bāgh* from a bird’s-eye view. The oldest and the most beautiful example is a garden carpet in the Jaipur Albert Hall collections (1622‒32). The Kraków carpet is not as sophisticated, but we can recognise on it all the elements of a classical Persian garden harmoniously arranged. In the centre, there is a square pool with an island on which there is a pavilion. Four channels divide the “garden” into four parts, each with four flowerbeds: in two of these there are octagons with flowering shrubs, in one there is a bird sitting on a leafy branch and in another there is a small stream and flowers. Along the big channels are rows of cypresses, pairs of birds sitting atop shrubs and small vases with flowers on a dark-blue ground. The rippled surface of the water is represented by a turquoise and emerald-green pattern of wavy stripes. In the water-channels are pairs of fishes, and in the pool, ducks. The border is decorated with the *medachyl* pattern.  
Stylistically, the Kraków garden carpet closely resembles the carpet from the al-Sabah Collection, Kuwait, and it has similarities to a carpet in the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.

a878caed-2598-567c-80a3-7ec37561865b.name: Seljuq Rug
a878caed-2598-567c-80a3-7ec37561865b.description: Carpets from the 13th century Aladdin Mosque in Konya are known as the “Konya Group”. They were identified in 1906 as the first finds from this period. These carpets are of key importance in the history of World Carpet Art. This example was specially woven to be used in a mosque. It is decorated with religious motifs and*kufic*writing. A light blue eight‒pointed star design on a dark blue background covers the entire central field. The main border is divided into square sections with stylised*kufic* characters arranged back‒to‒back in light red on a dark red ground. On the small borders, bird motifs are stylized to form leaves on branches.

a8e1aee3-51aa-5dd1-bf6b-39ba4456b248.name: Carpet Fragment with Hunting Animals
a8e1aee3-51aa-5dd1-bf6b-39ba4456b248.description:
Despite the frail condition of this sixteenth-century carpet fragment, the very fine design may still be read and enjoyed. The section comes from the one side of the original carpet, with the dark green border on the right, and the main field in dark red. The central design is filled with hunting animals, stalking or pouncing upon their prey: lions, tigers, leopards, lynxes, foxes and wolves, all of them hunting after deer. These creatures are not depicted in a natural landscape though, but placed within two spiralling systems of flowering plant scrolls, against a vibrant red background. The largest flowers are lotus blossoms, drafted with bright colours and complex forms, and sometimes outlined against a large lotus leaf. The dark green borders are also filled with spiralling plant scrolls, with long-tailed birds perched on the curving stems.  
  
Even fragments of historic carpets were widely traded in late nineteenth-century Europe, among artists, designers, scholars and private collectors unable to afford the huge market prices reached by whole carpets from sixteenth or seventeenth century Iran. Deeply admired, such fragments could reveal just enough of the design and structure to be of value to a specialist. Two known fragments of this carpet are in design museums (this example in the V&A, and another in Paris at Musee des Arts Decoratifs). The V&A fragment was bought in Italy, from the estate sale of one William Wentworth Buller, in 1884. Buller researched textile history, and collaborated briefly with the British designer William Morris. He had built up a significant study collection of both European and Middle Eastern textiles (including carpets). He bought this beautiful fragment just before his death in 1883, from the auctioned estate of the painter Attilio Simonetti in Rome. Unable to pay for his carpet fragment straightaway, Buller had deposited it with the art-dealer Castellani: he died before he could take possession of it. Simonetti in turn had used his carpet fragment as a prop in at least one of his paintings: it is depicted in a scene (“The Musical Interlude”) laid out as a table carpet. Noticeably Simonetti has depicted the fragment, perhaps with wishful artistic licence, as a whole carpet.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O67199/carpet-fragment-unknown/)

None of this group is dated, however.
a8e1aee3-51aa-5dd1-bf6b-39ba4456b248.method_for_provenance: The carpet is attributed to Iran because of its design and technical structure, which fits with sixteenth-century production.

a99de48f-5471-5f11-b9a5-a352553d63e9.name: Spiral vine carpet
a99de48f-5471-5f11-b9a5-a352553d63e9.description: This fragment, at first glance unimpressive, must have been part of a very large carpet. Measuring almost two metres, it shows a short section of the right border, a small area of the white-ground field and a part of a brown medallion, presumably a corner medallion, truncated by the border. The preserved motifs suffice to assign the carpet to the early Safavid period. Thus, for example, the brown medallion lies on top of the red vines of the field, meaning that both pattern levels are perceived separately from each other – a perception that is later lost. The apricot-coloured forked leaves in the field are arranged in parallel with their vertical edges. They lie on the red vines and give rhythm to the field design. This ornamentation is frequently found in the 15th and early 16th century in Timurid book art (1370–1507). The geometric-looking design of the large forked leaf in the brown medallion speaks in favour of an early dating. The filigree design of the border is also traditional in the carpet depictions of the Timurids. But since no Timurid carpets have been preserved, it would be only with caution that this can be ascribed to the artistic work of the Timurids.

aa65e43b-2697-5ab6-8268-8bf7323bae3c.name: Qashqa´i kilim
aa65e43b-2697-5ab6-8268-8bf7323bae3c.description: In the 11th century, the Turkic peoples immigrated from Central Asia to Persia and probably lived first in northwestern Persia. It is unknown when the Qashqa´i moved to the southwest, but certainly at the latest when Turkmen conquered the Fars region in the middle of the 15th century. Many ethnic groups in southern and southwestern Persia, including several non-Turkmen, produced pile weavings and flatweaves. We have mainly come across works dating from the end of the 19th century to the first third of the 20th century. Due to confederations, pattern transfers and other considerations, it is not always possible to make a clear tribal attribution, especially with flatweaves. Some pieces are called "Qashqa´i" to indicate the outstanding quality of the work. The colour canon, pattern and shape, as well as material and fineness of this piece, suggest that it is a work of the Darashuri (sub-tribe of the Qashqa´i). The infinite repetition of colour-changing diamonds in free succession, often filled with diamonds and smaller cross shapes, appears both cheerful and unconstrained as well as powerfully determined. With its free, lively design, this flatweave is a characteristic example of a slit tapestry by southwestern Persia nomads.

aac59dc1-2358-5b8f-bfbe-7471da6800c9.name: Floral Rug
aac59dc1-2358-5b8f-bfbe-7471da6800c9.description: One of the very few Mughal carpets the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts owns dates from the late 17th century and was probably made in Lahore. The museum bought it from an unknown person for 15,000 crowns between 1915 and 1924 and showed it at the 1924 exhibition together with two other Indian carpets. The central field features the small scrolling vine-and-blossom pattern common on *Herat* carpets, while the ornamentation and colouring bears the traits of Mughal carpets; sickle-shaped wisteria among flowers and palmettes and *ton-sur-ton* colouring (areas lighter than the ground without contours). The main border consists of red, undyed and ochre round and oblong cartouches with little floral decorations on a dark blue ground. There is an analogue of the irregular cartouches on a late 16th-century or early 17th-century Lahore carpet from the collection of Vojtech Blau, Inc., New York City, formerly in the von Pannwitz Collection, Heemstede. The Lahore carpet is the same size and with similar ornamentation, but earlier, from the second quarter of the 17th century. It was formerly held in the collection of the Corcoran Gallery of Art, Washington, D.C., William A. Clark Collection (26.297). The carpet was auctioned in 2013.

aad32718-fb08-549a-94e5-925277ba5ba9.name: Pile carpet fragment
aad32718-fb08-549a-94e5-925277ba5ba9.description: This long, narrow fragment appears to comprise approximately one-eighth of a small carpet-cushion, whose original dimensions were approximately 42cm square, as indicated by the two surviving outer selvedges which establish its width. The few small patterns found in the narrow main border (width 7.5 cm.) – bands, lozenges, and white cotton dots – are the standard form of decoration on small carpet-cushions. There was originally a perimetric *tiraz*, as evidenced by the word *Allah* which is woven in undyed cotton, as in Benaki 16151. The thickness of the pile is 4-5 mm and microscopic examination shows it to have been roughly handled, as with Benaki 16148. A possible explanation is that the carpets underwent a scraping in a fuller’s workshop.
aad32718-fb08-549a-94e5-925277ba5ba9.method_for_datation: It belongs to a group of fragments attributed to Egypt and their dating between the 8th and the 11th century. In addition, the form of the *kufic* inscription belongs to this period
aad32718-fb08-549a-94e5-925277ba5ba9.method_for_provenance: Factors that determine the provenance: 1. The use of linen, which is the basic Egyptian fibre, for both warps and wefts; 2. The left-twisting (S) spin of the materials is also an Egyptian feature. Linen warps S-spun, Z-plied are found in Coptic fabrics of the 9th-10th century. Right-twisted spinning (Z) is rarely found in Group A; 3. The technique of weaving with cut-pile loops which continues the long-standing Egyptian tradition of weaving with a pile made of loops; 4. The pattern, colouring and techniques of this group fragments bear a close resemblance to contemporaneous Coptic textiles. 5. The fragments display similarities to certain inscribed and non-inscribed fragments from Fustat.
aad32718-fb08-549a-94e5-925277ba5ba9.bibliography: Published in Theologou, J., Ozoline, A., Sartzetakis, Y., "Fustat Carpet Fragments", *Hali*, 156 (summer 2008): 65-71.
aad32718-fb08-549a-94e5-925277ba5ba9.author: Mina Moraitou
keywords: Fustat fragment; geometric; kufic script; inscription band; linen; wool

aaed4a61-bb16-58f5-a602-11699296667c.name: The Dietrichstein Carpet
aaed4a61-bb16-58f5-a602-11699296667c.description:
An 18th century, or possibly 19th century, Iranian pile carpet with a large lobbed pink medallion dominating the centre of a dark blue field, framed by a yellow ground border. The central medallion is decorated with an ivory arabesque scroll amongst which are multi-coloured flowers joined by a network of blue stems. The centre-field is crammed with rows of large palmettes, some of which have sharply cerates edges so much so that they look like flames. Between the palmettes are pairs of elongated and wavy Chinese cloud bands in various colours. The border is decorated with three different sizes of multi-coloured palmettes spread in a repeat pattern on a scrolling network of vegetal stems.  
  
The Dietrichstein carpet came from a princely castle that belonged to the Bohemian and Austrian Dietrichstein family, whose seat was in the city of Nikolsburg in southern Moravia and near the Austrian border (known today as Mikulov in the Czech Republic). A descendent of the Dietrichsteins, and the man who sold it in 1929, claimed that the carpet had lain in the throne room of Nikolsburg Castle up to then. The Dietrichsteins were an important noble family during the 17th and 18th centuries, with connections and positions in the Austrian court. When the carpet was sold in 1929 by the then incumbent Prince Alexander Dietrichstein (1899 – 1964), he claimed that the carpet had been a gift to one of his ancestors by the Empress Maria Theresa (r. 1748 – 1780), who had in turn received it as a gift from the Shah of Persia. This story is now thought to be most probably fanciful family lore.
aaed4a61-bb16-58f5-a602-11699296667c.obtention: Gifted by Sir William and Lady Burrell to the City of Glasgow, 1944
aaed4a61-bb16-58f5-a602-11699296667c.author: Noorah Al-Gailani
keywords: medallion; vegetal arabesque; cloud pattern; palmette; diplomatic gift
materials: Cotton warp and weft; wool pile

ab2ad44c-568d-5824-b3c4-9961e9edec7a.name: Ceramic Floor
ab2ad44c-568d-5824-b3c4-9961e9edec7a.description:
One of the oldest and rarest ceramic floors in Portugal, possibly dating from the building campaign promoted by King Afonso V (r.1438‒81), in the mid-15th century.  
Tradition has it that King Afonso VI (r.1656‒83) wore down the floor as he walked back and forth from his bed to the window overlooking the Sintra mountains. The truth, however, is that this floor was already more than two centuries old when he was imprisoned here, between 1674 and 1683, by order of his brother, King Pedro II (r.1683‒1706).  
The rare and valuable floor in this room presents a composition that combines various types of ceramic techniques and decorative styles, imbuing the tile set with dynamism, colour and originality.  
This is one of the oldest rooms in the palace and the only compartment of the palace that has an iron-barred window. The Palatine Chapel’s ceramic floor may date from the same period as this one.
ab2ad44c-568d-5824-b3c4-9961e9edec7a.method_for_datation:
Other art historians have dated the Palatine Chapel ceramic floor to the 15th century, probably contemporary with King Afonso V (1432‒81; r. 1438‒81). This monarch was born and died at the Royal Palace of Sintra and resided there frequently, as demonstrated by the countless documents signed by him here. Like King Duarte (1391‒38; r. 1433‒38), his father, King Afonso V seems to have held a special affection for the Palace at Sintra and carried out various improvements. He undertook the expansion and embellishment of the Palatine Chapel, probably from the mid-15th century (possibly between 1448 and 1476).  
The absence of cobalt blue in the ceramic floor reinforces the theory about its age.
ab2ad44c-568d-5824-b3c4-9961e9edec7a.obtention: In situ, commissioned by the king

ab4e426c-8d5c-55f7-aabf-1a580562cf9b.name: Prayer hanging
ab4e426c-8d5c-55f7-aabf-1a580562cf9b.short_description: Pieced together from numerous embroidered fabric scraps, this cotton hanging is suggestive of a mihrab, or prayer niche. The arched "niche" form at center is formed by juxtaposing light fabrics against dark reds. In the Qur'an, God (Allah) is likened to the presence of a lustrous lamp in a niche. Hence, lamps are often placed in niches in mosques and, similarly, they are depicted in niches on tile panels and textiles. In this textile, two stylized lamps extend outward from the top of the arch.

ac82d495-0ecf-5ced-bc7a-791a0ede9ca4.name: Milas Prayer Rug
ac82d495-0ecf-5ced-bc7a-791a0ede9ca4.description: This prayer rug was woven in the Milas region, one of the most important rug producing centres of Anatolia. It differs from typical Milas prayer rugs because it is without a *mihrab*. Rather, the design uses a central rectangle in place of the *mihrab*. The rug borders are decorated with rosettes, dragons and stylized clove strings arranged from outside to inside. The same motifs are repeated in the main ground.
ac82d495-0ecf-5ced-bc7a-791a0ede9ca4.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

acea7b6c-81a3-5243-a0e8-bd0919e565b5.name: Compartment Rug
acea7b6c-81a3-5243-a0e8-bd0919e565b5.description: Although faded, this rug is beautiful and ornate. Inspired by older Egyptian Mamluk rugs it contains floral, star, and geometric motifs. The field of this carpet is divided into six compartments by its inner most frame. In each compartment is a hexagon filled with symmetrical decoration, centering around a star. This carpet was cut in half and was resewn together. The design on the Weld of this carpet—hexagons placed in a continuous grid of rectangular compartments—as well as the border design, is thought to be inspired by the older Mamluk rugs of Egypt.

ae562d58-2b83-5553-b963-06580bd6fc01.name: Tree & Shrub Cartouche Carpet
ae562d58-2b83-5553-b963-06580bd6fc01.description:
An 18th century north-west Iranian “tree-and-shrub-cartouche” pile carpet, with a multi-coloured centre-field containing more than fifteen small gardens, one in each of its cartouches. Each of the centre-field’s geometrical cartouches has a different coloured background including red, green, yellow, turquoise and dark blue gardens. The slightly distorted cartouches would have been originally eight-pointed star compartments. Each compartment holds a miniature garden with a variety of flowering shrubs and trees and a small pond or a stream at the foot of the main tree. The carpet is framed by a narrow ivory and dark blue border that contains a repeat arabesque motif.  
  
The multi-garden design of this carpet is inspired by earlier carpets of the “Wagner Garden” carpet type, which is also owned by the Burrell Collection. See carpet no. 9.2.

ae7c4ab2-69d3-5454-816e-13b25357dc86.name: Multiple-niche prayer kilim (*saf*)
ae7c4ab2-69d3-5454-816e-13b25357dc86.description: The multiple-niche prayer carpets, called *saf* (from the Arabic word for “row”), are sometimes improperly referred to as “family” prayer rugs. They were used in mosques, their particular design allowing several people to pray one next to the other. Here, the uneven colour areas in the *mihrab* field, the somewhat irregular shape of the arches, and the stylised vegetal motifs are indicative of its tribal, probably Kurdish, provenance. Unlike most large Anatolian kilims, made of two narrow bands, this one is made of only one piece. The Arabic inscriptions and the fact that the carpet was dated make it all the more valuable.

aeca6cc5-9faf-56c7-b2d1-f951f8663c0e.name: Kilim, *Smyrna pattern*
aeca6cc5-9faf-56c7-b2d1-f951f8663c0e.description: *Smyrna pattern* (*smirjanska šara*) is a very popular Pirot kilim pattern. The horizontal division of kilim surface through the use of rectangular boxes (*kuveri*) is characteristic for this pattern. The boxes contain rows of rhomboid ornaments, with *bibice* ornaments inside the shape and hooks on the outer borders. The borders of the boxes are decorated with *octopus* (*oktapod*) ornament, flanked with feathers. Between the boxes runs a frieze composed of *glasses* (*očila*) motif. A wide border (*ploča*) contains alternately *turtle* (*kornjača*) and *čurlinjak* ornaments. The colours used are: red, white, blue, green, brown and orange.

aecdf245-c267-5f1f-8bd4-3d182a56e623.name: Loom weight
aecdf245-c267-5f1f-8bd4-3d182a56e623.description: Early loom weights found in the ancient city of Assoss, today known as Behramkale, a small historically rich town in the Ayvacık district of the Çanakkale Province, Turkey. These provide evidence the textile industry existed in the region since the Chalcolithic Period and the Bronze Age. Loom weights prevented tangling by weighting to give tension on individual yarns to enable weaving.

aed82efb-32d2-5811-bb33-9c50bdadf8ac.name: Textile fragment
aed82efb-32d2-5811-bb33-9c50bdadf8ac.description: This fragment is an exceptional example of Buyid dynasty (945–1055) textiles from both a historical and an aesthetic viewpoint. The frieze is adorned with two-headed eagles carrying a winged creature and with stylized trees. The light-brown motifs are embellished with epigraphs that are particularly noticeable on the tops of the trees and on the band bordering the textile’s upper edge. The fragment’s style and iconography are similar to those of a group of four textiles discovered in the ancient necropolis of Nakhara Khanah, near Rayy. It remains to be determined whether this textile was designed to serve as a shroud or was selected from the belongings of the deceased.

af528e34-709f-5115-84f5-d579ab9b2848.name: *Tekke* Turkmen Main Carpet with Nine Rows of Four Major Tribal *Guls* in Repeat
af528e34-709f-5115-84f5-d579ab9b2848.short_description:
A large rectangular knotted pile carpet of a type known as "main carpets," the primary floor covering used in Turkmen tents. It is decorated with nine rows of four major tribal *guls* in repeat, with 36 *guls* in the main field and a traditional palette, with a range of reds, cream, black, and dark blue. This carpet can be attributed to the *Tekke* subgroup of the Turkmen nomads based on the specific form of the *gul* motifs, which are unique to each tribal unit.  
The red field of the carpet has a repeat pattern of lobed, elongated medallions arranged in four vertical rows. Blue lines, running through the centers of the medallions, divide the field into rectangular compartments. Each medallion with an orange-red or a white section encloses a star motif in red and green, or red and blue, with a smaller star-shaped form in red and white. Stylized floral forms in red and brown issue from the star motifs. Between the medallions are cross-shaped designs in white, blue, orange, and red. The border contains a row of octagonal medallions alternately in white, red, blue, or green. Each octagon encloses rosettes or star motifs in red and blue or green. The medallions are separated by bands with various geometrical designs. The guard bands, running only on three sides, are divided into narrow stripes in white, yellow, red, blue, and green. The guard stripes have a chequered pattern.
af528e34-709f-5115-84f5-d579ab9b2848.dates: Hegira Early 12th to early 13th century / AD 19th century
af528e34-709f-5115-84f5-d579ab9b2848.method_for_datation: Scholarly review and/or comparison to similar objects from the period.
af528e34-709f-5115-84f5-d579ab9b2848.method_for_provenance: This carpet can be attributed to the Tekke subgroup of the Turkmen nomads based on the specific form of the *gul* motifs, which are unique to each tribal unit.

b0443bbb-eb01-54f9-8118-65a65bdd2b41.name: Carpet
b0443bbb-eb01-54f9-8118-65a65bdd2b41.description:
Besides imports, carpets were produced locally in Portugal for domestic consumption. Persian carpets, specifically, greatly influenced the embroidered carpets in the workshops in Arraiolos, in the Alentejo region of Portugal, from the late 16th century onwards. This testifies to the esteem to which these carpets were held and to the high demand for them by various strata in Portuguese society, especially during the 17th century. In the Arraiolos wool-embroidered versions, which incorporated the Arraiolos-stitch or *ponto de Arraiolos*, knotted-pile carpets underwent a real metamorphosis.  
This carpet derives from the “vine scroll” carpets, the largest group of Iranian knotted-pile examples in the National Museum of Ancient Art’s collection. It is an excellent example of the creative process of the transposition of Oriental carpet pattern-design, through embroidery, which characterised the manufacture at Arraiolos during the early 17th century. Its decorative composition closely follows that of contemporary Iranian sources with its distinctive palmettes, lotus flowers and S-shaped cloud scrolls (*tchi*) on a green background. Simultaneously, new motifs were introduced, such as small birds, a heart-shape with three keys and three initials at the centre of the field, and four deer in the corners of the field.

b049bda5-eeb5-5e1b-97c2-cbcd748804fc.name: Arraiolos carpet
b049bda5-eeb5-5e1b-97c2-cbcd748804fc.description:
The existence of this and of other Arraiolos carpets in the collections of Portuguese museums mainly results from the transfer of assets and portable heritage into the public domain after the abolition of the religious orders and convents in Portugal (1834). Such a reality helps better to understand the contexts of use correspondent to these carpets: apart from the private domestic domain, to which their origin is associated, the Arraiolos carpets had the same function as other imported carpets and served as ornamentation in sacred spaces as well.  
This example, embroidered in a very small stitch, shows vegetal and floral decoration inspired by the classic motifs of oriental carpets, namely the Persian *herati* design, with a field dominated by a central medallion and border. Complementing the medallion, which stands out due to its dimensions, with a diameter of 114 cm, and colouring, the remaining field shows palmettes, cloudbands, lotus flowers and giant open flowers, interconnected by geometrising ramifications. The border stands out due to the notability of its curvilinear design, winding into a volute – interrupted, at each of its corners, by wide, palmette motifs – which appears in opposition to the more simple designs that tend to be characteristic of these elements in Arraiolos carpets.  
The predominant tones are brown, yellow, green, blue, red (almost entirely faded) and ivory.

b0ceeddd-b46f-5341-8b89-7b905eabd03a.name: Bordjalou Kazak
b0ceeddd-b46f-5341-8b89-7b905eabd03a.description:
Kazak rugs were made in the south central Caucasus, between Tbilisi in Georgia and Erivan in Armenia. The area is bordered by the Ganja area to the northeast and Karabakh area to the southeast.  
Kazak rugs from the Bordjalou district south of Tbilisi have a characteristic double-hooked, zig-zag border. In some rugs, the zig-zag line is doubled or tripled. Medium blue and red are typical colours.  
Rectangular central field is decorated with 5 by 3 rows of polychrome *kochak* (ram's horns) medallions on red ground. A distinctive feature is a wide frame of double hooked zig zag border.
b0ceeddd-b46f-5341-8b89-7b905eabd03a.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Caucasus; Bordjalou; Kazak
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

b2648886-b553-5399-8946-93cb4e8f1c49.name: ‘Transylvanian’ prayer rug
b2648886-b553-5399-8946-93cb4e8f1c49.description: The term “Transylvanian” rug is used to designate 17th- and 18th-century rugs preserved in large numbers in the Saxon churches of Transylvania, whose provenance, considered once to be Transylvanian, is, in fact, western Anatolian. Some of these rugs feature the *mihrab* design, typical of prayer rugs; in most cases though, the prayer niche becomes a purely decorative element devoid of its original meaning, a fashionable motif popular with carpet buyers outside the Islamic world. Here, the plain red field of the *mihrab* contrasts with the main border richly decorated with alternating rosettes and palmettes encircled by lancet-shaped leaves – a simplified version of the classical court rug border. The flower on the pointed top of the *mihrab* symmetrically divides the composition with highly stylised carnations and serrated leaves represented in the yellow and blue spandrels; as such, different coloured spandrels are rather unusual.

b38891de-f49d-5dd2-b4f0-dec5aad2f1bf.name: Carpet-Qajar Portrait
b38891de-f49d-5dd2-b4f0-dec5aad2f1bf.short_description:
This wool rug depicts fifty-one prominent personalities across history in an assemblage portrait. Like many Iranian carpets in the 19th century, this textile reflects the emergence during the Qajar dynasty of pictorial carpets displaying religious, historical or literary scenes.  
Among prophets like Moses, Solomon, and Jesus, are men known throughout Asian history such as Genghis Khan and Confucius. In addition, Socrates, Christopher Columbus and Napoleon Bonaparte contribute to this group portrait.  
  
The border, an essential element in Persian carpets, frames the scene of famous people with floral patterns and a legend with the names of individuals. Interestingly, the numbers appear mirrored, suggesting that the carpet maker was illiterate or unfamiliar with Arabic numbers, leaving his mark within the thread.

b3ac404d-9f7e-54b9-a43e-8f0f1e36045d.name: Kuba carpet
b3ac404d-9f7e-54b9-a43e-8f0f1e36045d.description:
The town of Kuba and its surrounding area have a long tradition of carpet-weaving. In the late 19th century, Kuba was a district town on the Kudial River northwest of Baku. Rugs from this town and surrounding villages were very finely woven with short pile and complex designs.  
The central field is framed with four borders. The main border is the compound border. Although it has been described as a stylized eagle's head or beak, it may very well derive from the split leaf border. Two minor borders are “running dog” on red and blue backgrounds. The waveform of the this motif has various frequencies and amplitudes; the Vitruvian scroll described it as “running dog” and it was often used in ancient Roman architecture. The outer border is the S border. The central field is decorated with derivate *afshan* motifs (“scattered” in Persian) The *afshan* motif consists of right-angle flower calyxes, palmettes and rosettes. Calyx in this field repeat is more geometricized and given a sawtooth edge. Palmettes are converted to stepped polygons. There are also zoomorphic and dragon motifs as field repeats.
b3ac404d-9f7e-54b9-a43e-8f0f1e36045d.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Kuba; Caucasus; leaf elements
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

b3d75056-35c3-5258-acbf-bbe88d25a45b.name: Panel of *azulejos* with a carpet composition
b3d75056-35c3-5258-acbf-bbe88d25a45b.description:
Although many people believe the word *azulejo* derives from the Portuguese word *azul* (blue), this is a misconception. The use of this colour in *azulejos* can be limited to a very narrow timeline of approximately 60 years (c. 1690‒1750) in a larger history of more than 500 years of uninterrupted use in Portugal.  
Nevertheless, there are some exceptions for the single use of blue in Portuguese *azulejos* outside this chronology, one of which can be seen in this panel. In this complex pattern of 6 x 6 *azulejos*, 36 pieces are required to obtain a single motif that can be reproduced to infinity, whereby its intertwined double four-lobe design has a lighter dimension on account of the monochromatic use of blue. Although complex, the blue gives a subtlety to the design of this motif, and in this way focuses the attention rather than tiring the senses.  
By contrast, the frame uses a different kind of composition. Instead of the motif in blue over the white background, it opens the decoration in white over a dense blue using a decoration that can be compared to woodcarving or some jewellery of this period. By this, the contrast between a very dense frame and the motif is lightened by a less compact pattern, creating equilibrium between elements, which provides the viewer a harmonious sense of beauty.

b3fd9abb-aa85-59f0-a82c-3e714538514a.description: Lorenzo Lotto was a Northern Italian painter (1480-1557) who included richly woven carpets in his paintings. Carpets corresponding to these designs are popularly known as Lotto Carpets.  These carpets are defined by their wine-red background and golden and black ornamentation.

b461bebe-c5d3-55da-8d06-a7c6d2700115.name: Rug: Boucherouite (Rag rug)
b461bebe-c5d3-55da-8d06-a7c6d2700115.short_description: In the central High Atlas of Morocco, Berber carpets are hardly woven any more in the traditional manner. Discarded synthetic fibres from second-hand fabrics and artificial materials have replaced sheep's wool and goat hair. The young weavers have forgotten how to spin a uniform thread. After the spinning work is done, the warp threads are no longer ritually "cut off" from the weaving stool. More recently, the weavers have also been employing recyclable and non-tear able plastic bags of polypropylene, in which they embroider their patterns. Small-format rugs and saddlecloths are produced, at first for their own use. Later they appear out of thin air in the carpet bazaar in Marrakesh, where they are given the label *Boucherouite* ("rags"). By now, they are offered for sale in Europe and the United States in the relevant art and textile galleries for a great deal of money.
b461bebe-c5d3-55da-8d06-a7c6d2700115.obtention: Purchased 2010 in Marrakesh by Dr Axel Steinmann, curator at the Museum für Völkerkunde, during his fieldwork in Morocco.

b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.name: Pashmina Niche Rug
b4e72974-c00c-5720-9454-206dc84e1405.description:
The new carpet style in the time of Mughal ruler Shah Jahan (1628-1647) was the flower style, featuring the naturalistic depiction of flowering plants. The refined elegance of the decorations, the use of expensive silk and pashmina and the high knot count are characteristic of the luxury carpets of this period. The silk warp was frequently dyed in bands. The flower style lived on in the works of the post-Shah Jahan workshops.  
  
In the field, the ivory-coloured *mihrab* (prayer niche) with lobed arch is adorned on both sides by a crimson half cypress growing from a finely delineated column base. From the apex of the *mihrab* hangs a trapezoidal lamp; in the centre below, a three-branched floral bush grows from the bottom of the *mihrab*. Faint glimmers of the colourful bands (ivory, yellow, crimson, blue and green) can be seen in the plain ivory surface. The crimson spandrel is adorned on both sides with symmetrical floral patterns – vines, leaves and poppy blossoms. As is typical of flower style rugs, the major border of the rug contains lotus flowers against a dark blue ground and is enclosed in ivory field minor borders.

b5d98077-c404-5849-b74b-cc9708d159d7.name: Kilim
b5d98077-c404-5849-b74b-cc9708d159d7.description:
This superbly preserved kilim, considered to be one of the finest surviving flatwoven rugs from Iran, still retains its vibrant colours, metallic sheen and wonderfully animated imagery that visually communicates the classic design favoured by the opulent Safavid court under the patronage of Shah Abbas I (1588–1629).  
  
The design arrangement of a central medallion with quarter medallions in the corners framed by a border of alternating cartouches and small lobed-medallions was developed in the *kitābkhāne* (royal design atelier), initially for book bindings and illuminated manuscript pages, and then adapted for use in architectural decorations and the decorative arts, which included textiles.  
  
Ornamental motifs of the kilim consist of floral elements, birds, and quadrupeds popular in the decorative arts of the time. Several of these elements, such as the dragon and phoenix in the centre and qilin with flaming shoulders and haunches in the corners, are Chinese in origin, but had been absorbed in the Persian ornamental vocabulary. The dragon and phoenix as visual symbols, however, assumed new meanings in the art of Iran and were adapted to conform to the age-old animal combat iconography of the Middle East.  
  
The craftsmanship apparent in planning, drawing, and execution of this kilim is quite extraordinary. The precisely laid-out design was executed using the finest materials available at that time. Silk tapestry weave is an exacting textile-making technique. The craftsmen who produced this textile were highly skilled and respected masters in their chosen craft, possibly the best craftsmen in Iran. Their training and apprenticeship would have taken decades before they reached a sufficiently high level of mastery to be selected to work on a project like this. Someone at the court of Shah Abbas I, or Shah Abbas I himself with his great human and financial resources, could have commissioned a kilim with such high quality as this one.

b79db95f-a5f3-5cd7-a129-ce4e759fa1fe.name: Polonaise Carpet
b79db95f-a5f3-5cd7-a129-ce4e759fa1fe.short_description:
This silk-knotted rug depicts voluminous floral and leaf-vine patterns in pastel green, pink, and blue adorned with gold and silver thread. This textile falls under the rare “Polonaise Carpets”. Contrary to the name, these rugs originate from Iran during the 16th and 17th centuries, when Shah Abbas I introduced lively patterns and soft colours. The Safavid capital Isfahan and the silk city of Kashan soon become celebrated production centres for the carpets, desired by the Persian elite.  
  
While attempting to please the European palate, royals of Poland would commission numerous Polonaise carpets, contributing to the ambiguous origin behind their name. The shimmering designs and pastel hues still influence contemporary carpet-making.

b7f46ff9-52a1-5495-80f5-c075d3bfc0da.name: *Defeat of the French cavalry. The imperial infantry seize the enemy’s artillery*
b7f46ff9-52a1-5495-80f5-c075d3bfc0da.description:
The famous series of seven Flemish tapestries depicting the Battle of Pavia, which are displayed in a large room in the Museum of Capodimonte, entered the public collections as part of the 1862 bequest of Alfonso d’Avalos, who donated his family’s collection to the National Museum of Naples.  
Produced to be given to Emperor Charles V by the Estates-General of Brussels, on the occasion of the latter’s meeting in Brussels in 1531, the decorative series of tapestries was designed to celebrate the victory of the imperial troops over those of the French, under the command of Francis I. This victory, which occurred on 24 February 1525, was fought in the environs of the Visconti Park, at the gates of Pavia.  
Woven in Brussels, the tapestries were produced using designs by Bernard van Orley (now in the Louvre in Paris) in the workshop of William Dermoyen (or Van der Moyen), identified thanks to the presence of a weaver’s mark on the right-hand border of the fabric; this mark can also be observed on another tapestry in the series. The presence of the weaver’s mark has also allowed the years in which the series was produced to be established: between 1528, the year in which a decree required tapestry workers to “sign” their products, and the start of 1531, given that the tapestries would be presented to the Emperor in the March of that year.  
Recently, an interpretation of the entire cycle has been proposed that aims to recreate sequentially the landscape depicted in the seven tapestries as a single, panoramic, overview (Paredes 2014). According to this perspective, the tapestry examined here should be read in close continuity with the subject represented in *Advance of the imperial troops*. In fact, by juxtaposing the two tapestries one can reconstruct, as C. Paredes suggests, the landscape and the troop movements on the battlefield. In particular, in the foreground one can recognise the group of imperial arquebusiers, led by their commander, Fernando Francesco d’Avalos, who is identified by the letters “MAR. DE PES” (an abbreviation of “Marquis of Pescara”) on the neck of his horse. In the centre, further writing, “MARQ.IS DU VASTE”, indicates the presence on the battlefield of Alfonso d’Avalos, Marquis of Vasto. On the right is depicted the ferocious battle between the imperial landsknechts, led by Georg von Frundsberg, distinguished by their white and red sashes, and the mercenary troops of the “Banda Nera”, in the service of the French. Noting the detail of the capture of the French artillery in the panoramic overview extending into the preceding tapestry, as mentioned above, it is possible to discern that the French canons have stopped firing to avoid striking the back of their King, who, breaking through the ranks, throws himself at the enemy, just as sources describe.  
This tapestry, along with three others in the series, still has its original border, with decorative motifs in which flowers, fruit, birds and animals are depicted. However, according to a description from the 1770s, the lower borders originally introduced decorative motifs with tritons and sea horses, similar to those that appear in the *Hunts of Maximilian*, another series of tapestries produced for Charles V by the same workshop from designs by van Orley, and today in the Louvre. Hence, the entire lower strip, detached some time after the 1770s and subsequently reassembled, appears to have been re-sewn using parts of the borders of other tapestries, which now are missing them, and which were originally intended to adorn the vertical edge of the fabric (Buchanan 2002).

b8862166-9876-528c-ab02-49ee6cc50168.name: Kilim
b8862166-9876-528c-ab02-49ee6cc50168.description: Delicate colouring and fine weave account for the widespread popularity of the kilims produced in Senneh (Sanandaj), the capital of the Kurdistan province in northwestern Iran. Those dating from the second half of the 19th century were probably made in urban workshops, and were destined to cater to a demanding clientele. Their predominantly floral patterns recall the ornamental repertoire of knotted carpets produced in the same area, but are also reminiscent of the Qajar embroideries. The design usually involves a central medallion surrounded by tiny floral motifs; other Senneh kilims, such as the present one, feature a central field decorated with *herati*\-type patterns – rosettes inscribed in lozenges encircled by lancet-shaped leaves.

b8c5288f-fd29-51c6-b180-287defa99c74.name: Small Pattern Holbein Rug
b8c5288f-fd29-51c6-b180-287defa99c74.description:
Early Ottoman carpets with endless geometric designs of the kind found on paintings by the German painter Hans Holbein Jr. (1497/8–1543) are called "Holbein" Rugs. The small pattern version of the Holbein Rug is more common. This rug is one of the Museum’s earliest 19th century acquisitions. The rug is one of those few small pattern Holbein Rugs which have survived almost completely intact.  
A special feature of the Holbein Rug is the red central field, used instead of the usual blue or green. The field contains star-centred Holbein guls on an ivory field strung along two axes in the longitudinal direction. The area between the guls is occupied by blue and green arabesque medallions forming crosses and arranged into an almost continuous lattice. A closed *kufic* band, ivory on a dark red ground, forms the main border with a narrow secondary border of "S" motifs on each side. Its well-balanced pattern and harmonious colour pairing, the red of the field in the bright frame complementing the green of the arabesque lattice, results in a tranquil, balanced effect.

b90b0508-6a6c-59c8-8ed1-50f4877c3f38.name: Carpet
b90b0508-6a6c-59c8-8ed1-50f4877c3f38.description:
This superbly preserved carpet is a type known as “animal carpet” variant. It probably dates to somewhere between the late 16th and the first half 17th century. So-called animal carpets comprise a well-known Persian carpet group dating to the 16th century with patterns of flowers/palmettes, cloud bands, and animals including mythical beasts on a background of spiraling tendrils/vines. The place of manufacturing of animal carpets and their variants are not clear, but Herat, Isfahan, and Kashan were given in literature as possible manufacturing centres. The most famous carpets in this group is the pair which once belonged to the Hapsburg Emperors The carpets are called “emperor carpets”; now one is in New York Metropolitan Museum of Art and the other is held by the Vienna Museum Fur Angewandte Kunst.  
  
Fashion for compositions filled with both real and imaginary animals appears to emerge, first in illuminations, in the second quarter of the 15th century in Shiraz and Herat simultaneously. By the early 16th century the style was embraced by the court artists in Tabriz and soon as almost epitomized the decorative arts of the time. Animals on these carpets are drawn in the style favoured at the court of Shah Tahmasp in the mid-16th century and possibly the works of these court artists were the original inspiration for the animal motifs seen on these carpets. With the accession of Shah Abbas I in 1587 a subtle change occurred in the style of decorative arts. Animal style gave way to more abstract designs.  
  
The style of spiraling tendrils and animals on carpets continued to develop, creating variant groups. This carpet fits well with a variant group that can be distinguished by the addition of a medallion, the increase and dominance of animal representation, the retreat of floral elements (palmette) and spiraling tendrils, and the total disappearance of the cloud bands.

b9813c91-11bd-5dfd-8733-543744724e66.name: Kilim, *paws*
b9813c91-11bd-5dfd-8733-543744724e66.description: The earliest preserved Pirot kilims date from the late 18th century. Early Pirot kilims were decorated with the so-called *endless pattern*, by repeating the same motif on the whole surface of the kilim. The motif of *paws* (*kostenice*) was used most often for the *endless pattern* creation. Early examples of kilims decorated with the *endless pattern* didn’t have a border. The border on the kilim indicates that it dates from the later period. The colours used are: red, blue, green, violet, yellow, orange and white.

ba073291-56dc-5c61-928a-6aa29df0d409.name: Carpet with compartments; so-called ‘Clam-Gallas’ carpet
ba073291-56dc-5c61-928a-6aa29df0d409.description: Towards the end of the 16th century, figural depictions went out of fashion. Since the quality of the carpets was adapted to international buyers both in Europe and India, pieces with less dense knotting were produced. The middle field is mirrored in quarters around a centre, which is – unobtrusively – formed by a darker quatrefoil element. Chinese-inspired cloudbands, pairs of birds and blossom combinations, appearing like beds in a geometrically laid out garden, are featured on the variously adorned fields of shields and quatrefoils. Unfortunately, no complete carpet whose field design constitutes a parallel to the MAK Collection’s carpet has been preserved. Despite the dating to the late 16th century, the compartment system is reminiscent of carpets that are depicted on Timurid miniatures at the close of the 15th century. Numerous Indian Mughal carpets produced afterwards exhibit a comparable grid system.

ba6c8502-cadb-520d-9309-2837470156db.name: Yağcıbedir rug
ba6c8502-cadb-520d-9309-2837470156db.description: This rug is an example of a “Yağcıbedir” rug named after a semi‒nomadic tribe called the “Yağcıbedir”. These rugs were mostly woven in Sındırgı and Bigadiç, villages of Balıkesir province. The motifs for this type of rugs are varied and have a nonverbal communication property. This rug is decorated with stylized apple and apple blossom motifs. According to the early Anatolian beliefs, these are symbols of plenty. Key motifs are symbolic of marriage. It is believed this carpet was woven by a young lady presaging a life of prosperity.

ba8fded9-1679-518f-9ec9-6179d462f308.name: Prayer rug
ba8fded9-1679-518f-9ec9-6179d462f308.description: The composition of the central field recalls the triple-arch design of certain Ottoman court rugs; only this time the lateral niches are merely suggested and the columns are made up of decorative floral bands. The column bases also feature floral patterns, and, instead of the lamp evoking Sura An-Nur (“The Light”), a flower garland is hanging from the apex of the centre niche. The main border of alternating palmettes and rosettes is reminiscent of classical carpet borders (16th–17th centuries). Compared to these, the layout of the present rug is lacking in accuracy, which accounts for the incomplete motifs in the bottom left corner. The rug is however remarkable for the balanced palette of warm and cool hues and its exquisite workmanship, qualities not to be found in later Kula carpets which will resort to a more subdued colour range and a rather coarse weave.

bb57306e-d345-5a2a-8cde-6b5779e15174.name: Chequerboard carpet
bb57306e-d345-5a2a-8cde-6b5779e15174.description: The Ottoman province of Syria had historic textile production at its disposal, to which this carpet also attests. Approximately 30 so-called chequerboard carpets are known, one-third of these are of a small size like the Viennese example. Although they are related to 16th-century Mamluk carpets in technique, as they likewise show asymmetric knots, a chronological classification of them is problematic. This piece was purchased in 1966 for the MAK from the Kuefstein family of Lower Austria and is said to originate from the estate of Count Johann Ludwig of Kuefstein (1587–1657), who was an imperial envoy at the Sublime Porte in Istanbul between 1627 and 1630.

bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.name: Painted wall-hanging: The Day of Judgement (*Ruz-e mahshar*)
bb7952b6-4d91-5465-865c-1ced864ef922.short_description: A painted wall-hanging depicts the *Day of Judgement* from a Shi'ite perspective in Isfahan. The main theme is the reward given in paradise to the martyrs who fell at Kerbala on 10 October 680, corresponding to the Islamic date 10 Muharram 61, and the agonies of their enemies on Judgement Day. Elements of Christian iconography are present. There is the trumpeting angel who blows into the bugle at the Last Judgement; the receiving of the arisen into heaven; the two angels who attend to the weighing scale of the souls; the chosen ones who await their entry into paradise; the blood witnesses who in advance enjoy the delights of paradise; and finally those of different faiths and traitors, who, already condemned, stand before the infernal ground. There are also new elements: the prophet of Islam is now an established, important figure, and Christ, the judge of the world, assumes the part of a precursor-prophet.

bbc8f1e6-fdee-507b-9bb8-8b0201e8ff87.name: Recycled prayer rug
bbc8f1e6-fdee-507b-9bb8-8b0201e8ff87.short_description: On this recycled Moroccan prayer rug, a prayer niche indicates the direction of prayer towards Mecca. A mosque lamp makes reference to the verse of light in the Qur'an: "God is the light of heaven and of earth. His light [comes] as if from a niche, in which a lamp stands." (Sura 24, Verse 35). Two stylised hands indicate to those praying where their hands should come to rest. Uppermost is the invocation to God: "Allahu akbar" – "God is the greatest". The open hand symbolises the five fundamental obligations of Islam (confession of faith, prayer, charity, fasting, pilgrimage). At the same time, the hand provides protection against negative influences and evoke happiness and fertility.

bbe7d049-a410-50d4-89a8-2edb4f6c0c59.name: Carpet
bbe7d049-a410-50d4-89a8-2edb4f6c0c59.description:
The imagery and the Latin inscription suggest that this carpet might have been intended for use as a tomb cover or as a temporary coffin cover during a funerary service. On a delicate blue and white patterned ground reminiscent of fifteenth-century Renaissance silks, five medallions bear motifs associated with death and resurrection: skull and crossbones, and a phoenix rising from flames. The Latin inscriptions around the phoenix read: EX MEMET I(PS)O RENASCOR (from myself I shall regenerate) and VICTORIA DOCTIS (Victory to the learned). What today appears as a date of 1520 above the phoenix is the result of repair; "1520" probably was IPSO (by itself/myself).  
  
In Greek mythology, a phoenix is a long-lived bird that is cyclically regenerated or reborn. Associated with the sun, a phoenix dies by fire and obtains new life by arising from the ashes of its predecessor. The phoenix was subsequently adopted as a symbol in Early Christianity.  
  
A carpet with funerary iconography is rare. There are only two known examples, this carpet and another one in the Victoria and Albert Museum in London. Both of these carpets are more finely and tightly woven than the most Mudejar carpets. Although the design on this carpet is austere, its colours and delicate lace-like designs on the main field and borders achieve graciousness in one hand, and splendour and dignity on the other.

bc4ce7a2-a8d5-50c0-b880-c483d4c2dbc7.name: Carpet of floral arabesque type
bc4ce7a2-a8d5-50c0-b880-c483d4c2dbc7.short_description: This highly sophisticated design of spiral tendrils connecting symmetrically arranged flower blossoms and buds, leaves, palmettes and cloudbanks was popular in Iranian carpet-weaving from the second half of AD 16th through 17th century. Some carpets of this type today are attributed to imperial workshops of Isfahan. The rich and vibrant colour palette of the carpet is based on the deep red tone of the background. Contrasting dark blue ground of the main border renders integrity to the whole composition.

bc59de19-bbdc-5a37-9345-b5cc0f2969e3.name: Landscape *verdure* with hunting scenes
bc59de19-bbdc-5a37-9345-b5cc0f2969e3.description: Landscape *verdure* tapestries with hunting scenes were often woven in Flemish workshops. Central scene of this tapestry shows a company of noblemen and ladies hunting in a hilly landscape. In the foreground, hunters on horseback and on foot, with the help of dogs, hunt the water birds. Landscape is a characteristic feature of Flemish tapestries and an important mean of figural compositions structure, especially in the scenes of battles and hunt. The figures in the scene are dressed according to the fashion of the late 16th and early 17th century. A border is framed both on the outside and the inside by the strips filled with a flower vine. Outer strip on the lower side is missing. The border is filled with balustrades and pavilions, formed by the use of columns, surrounded by vases with floral arrangements and grotesque motifs. The figural motifs on the upper and lower side of the border are identical, while the motifs along lateral sides of the border are different, but symmetrically distributed.

bc7e3eae-5354-5ec9-bfb6-2bdb12fdb9ce.name: Gördes Prayer rug
bc7e3eae-5354-5ec9-bfb6-2bdb12fdb9ce.description: Gördes, in the Manisa Province, Anatolia was an important rug producing town during the 17th and 18th centuries. The name “Gördes knot” was coined for the symmetrical knot technique after the fame and popularity of the region’s rugs. However, the “Gördes knot” technique is older than the town and wide‒spread geographically. This example is a prayer rug. The niche corners are decorated with two trees of life. The head band is composed of rose and rosebud motifs. Various flowers motifs are used on the borders as an expression of heavenly gardens.
bc7e3eae-5354-5ec9-bfb6-2bdb12fdb9ce.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

bcb08e82-a842-5d85-bc9a-00e84a746ec1.name: Dragon Sileh (Zili) rug or Verneh (Varni) Cover
bcb08e82-a842-5d85-bc9a-00e84a746ec1.description: This rug, originally intended as a cover, was woven in two pieces and sewn together in the middle. Also known as "Dragon Zili" rugs, these carpets were mainly woven in the Jabrail District of Artsak (Nagorno-Karabagh), using the soumak technique. Their characteristic pattern consists of stylized dragons in the shape of an "S" aligned in horizontal and vertical rows. The colour of the dragon alternates; their bodies are filled with tinier "S" motifs; the spaces in between with human, animal, and geometric patterns. In Azerbaijan and Russian literature, such items are called *Verneh* (Varni) covers. Its speciality lies in the fact that the direction of the "S"-shaped dragons in the bottom row of the right side is opposite the rest.

bd1c3a89-e57d-52fe-b67b-0a03bc4408ee.name: Tent band
bd1c3a89-e57d-52fe-b67b-0a03bc4408ee.description: Nomads of Central Asia wove bands for a variety of purposes. Bands joined parts of the wooden construction of dwellings and fixed felt covers to the dome and wooden trellis of the yurt; fringed and tasselled bands decorated the portable dwellings, both inside and out, and; with the help of bands, bags were secured to the backs of the beasts of burden. Bands were produced using many kinds of weaving techniques including knotted pile and flat weave. This band is woven in warp-faced and warp-float techniques and decorated with a long braided fringe.
bd1c3a89-e57d-52fe-b67b-0a03bc4408ee.bibliography: Mashkora, V.G., *Carpets of the People of Central Asia*, Tucson, AZ: George W. O’Bannon, 1996.

bd798e4f-1b55-5cb8-8ca8-e4112c802d5b.name: Pile carpet fragment
bd798e4f-1b55-5cb8-8ca8-e4112c802d5b.description: These five fragments comprise the lower left section of a large carpet, as is indicated by the width of the main border (19-20 cm.). The decoration is simple and probably involved the use of a cartoon as it contains no errors or distortions: this is particularly apparent in the impeccable rounded dots on the straight twin-coloured bands, the perfectly formed lozenges, the delicate ornamentation and the change of direction of the pattern at the corners of the carpet. The combination of linen, wool and cotton, the chromatic harmony, the impeccable relationship between pattern and colour and the notable craftsmanship all contribute towards the superb quality of this carpet.
bd798e4f-1b55-5cb8-8ca8-e4112c802d5b.method_for_datation: It belongs to a group of fragments attributed to Egypt and their dating between the 8th and the 11th century
bd798e4f-1b55-5cb8-8ca8-e4112c802d5b.method_for_provenance: Factors that determine the provenance: 1. The use of linen, which is the basic Egyptian fibre, for both warps and wefts; 2. The left-twisting (S) spin of the materials is also an Egyptian feature. Linen warps S-spun, Z-plied are found in Coptic fabrics of the 9th-10th century. Right-twisted spinning (Z) is rarely found in Group A; 3. The technique of weaving with cut-pile loops which continues the long-standing Egyptian tradition of weaving with a pile made of loops; 4. The pattern, colouring and techniques of this group fragments bear a close resemblance to contemporaneous Coptic textiles. 5. The fragments display similarities to certain inscribed and non-inscribed fragments from Fustat.
bd798e4f-1b55-5cb8-8ca8-e4112c802d5b.bibliography: Published in Theologou, J., Ozoline, A., Sartzetakis, Y., "Fustat Carpet Fragments", *Hali*, 156 (summer 2008): 65-71.
