keywords: Fustat fragment; geometric; linen; wool; cotton

bda5705e-f3c7-5961-8499-8ce968a1356b.name: Carpet '*shedde*'
bda5705e-f3c7-5961-8499-8ce968a1356b.short_description: This picturesque "*shedde*" carpet dating from the early 18th century is an outstanding piece of Azerbaijan art. *Shedde* or *shadda* is one of the most complex types of pileless weaving. In addition to warp and weft threads, various coloured threads are interwoven into the “body” creating an intricate and highly spectacular pattern. The museum keeps a rare kind of figurative *shedde* carpet. Produced by masters of Garabagh, the region where cattle-breeders dwelled from the time immemorial, the museum *shedde* features rich zoomorphic and anthropomorphic imagery. The composition of the central field consists of two kinds of broad horizontal bands. One band features a caravan of camels moving from the left to the right. It alternates with the band depicting the procession of riding hunters with falcons and dogs, moving in the same direction. Each procession is guided by a man. The combination of the two themes in a single composition (the camel caravan theme popular in Garabagh carpets and the shah falconry theme well-known from the miniature painting and stone carving) is considered unique.
bda5705e-f3c7-5961-8499-8ce968a1356b.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis by L. Kerimov (examination, 1954, date and origin).
bda5705e-f3c7-5961-8499-8ce968a1356b.method_for_provenance: According to the entry in the old Museum Inventory Register (1925-1946).

be3d15c9-0b3c-5c76-b571-476211bfa7ab.name: *Bei der Kupplerin (The Procuress)*
be3d15c9-0b3c-5c76-b571-476211bfa7ab.description: A large area of this painting is taken up by a carpet. Owing to the clearly recognisable pattern, it is possible to identify this carpet as coming from Uşak, a town in western Anatolia with a long and rich history of carpet production. On account of the dark blue ground and the red, onion-shaped central medallion, it is possible to date this carpet to the first half of the 16th century. Vermeer presents a seemingly light-hearted, quiet scene in which the objectionable aspect of the situation is not immediately apparent. Nevertheless, he leaves us in no doubt that this is a scene of procuration: the fashionably dressed suitor is paying money while with his left hand he touches the breast of the young woman.

bef82deb-d132-5484-9771-21ba888224d0.name: 'Lotto' Carpet
bef82deb-d132-5484-9771-21ba888224d0.short_description: Carpets displaying this striking design of stylised vegetal arabesques in yellow on a red ground are often called Lotto carpets after a famous altarpiece by Italian Renaissance painter Lorenzo Lotto that depicts a similar carpet. Early examples of Lotto carpets exhibit borders like this one. Thought to derive from the rectilinear form of *kufic* script, this type of interlaced border is characteristic of many early Turkish carpets.

bf068376-c382-587a-944f-2a4ebb1194c4.name: Rug (*julkhyrs*)
bf068376-c382-587a-944f-2a4ebb1194c4.description: In Central Asia these long-pile rugs are called *julkhyrs*, meaning “bearskin.” They are spread on the floor or on a low platform, which the family uses when having meals, doing housework or napping. Their long and shaggy pile makes them as soft and warm as the fur they are named for. Julkhyrs are woven with symmetrical pile knots tied around alternate warps; a warp thread is left between each knot so that the warp-weft structure becomes solid and thick. Like many nomadic weavings, they are woven in strips on a narrow horizontal loom; up to seven bands can be sewn together to make a rug of a required width. They are attributed to both Uzbek and Arab communities of Central Asia, which in many areas have lived side by side for centuries. This rug is made from three strips featuring squares and triangles; it has long tasseled fringe on both ends.

bf0b422e-0d99-5efb-bef3-a8f127757b0b.name: Konya Rug
bf0b422e-0d99-5efb-bef3-a8f127757b0b.description: Carpets with dragon motifs form an important group of Anatolian carpets. They are very rare and most of them are dated to 14th ‒ 15th centuries. The use of dragon motifs indicates the cultural influence of Asiatic Turkish traditions in Anatolia. The dragon motif, originated in the Far East, represents a mythological creature believed to be the master of air and water. It is also the guard of the tree of life. The battle of the dragon and phoenix is the representation of a common mythological theme: meeting of earth and heaven or the mother goddess and god. It is used to symbolize the fertile rains of spring. Dragon motifs are frequently found on various art objects such as wood and metal works or architectural arts in Anatolian Turkish art.

c0c780b7-bc1e-5c06-ace4-ef7fefd9fa80.name: Fragment of a [wall?] hanging
c0c780b7-bc1e-5c06-ace4-ef7fefd9fa80.description: This wool fragment from the Umayyad dynasty (AD 661–750) is adorned with a medallion depicting an eagle in shades of blue, green and yellow. The inside of the medallion’s dark-green border is dotted with 20 scrolls, while another series of scrolls topped by floral designs provides its outline. Geometric and plant motifs are visible in the corners. Ecru scrolls, topped in their case by red and orange flowers, figure on the main border, which has a brown ground. A wide band of ecru is enhanced by a rectangle with red, green and yellow geometric patterns. Here the floral designs consist of palmettes and rosettes. The depiction of medallions embellished with figures is derived from Persian silks; the decorative motifs within such medallions are characteristic of Sasanian decorative arts.

c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.name: *Eine junge Frau beim Ankleiden (Young Woman at her Toilette)*
c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.description: A young lady is seated at a table with a mirror in front of her; she is about to adjust her hair with the hairpin she has in her mouth. This seems to have been prompted by the open letter, which presumably announces the imminent arrival of a male visitor. The silver jewellery box, the bed with the heavy curtain and the dog on the woman's lap-which can be understood as a sleepy defender of virtue-would seem to indicate the amorous content of the letter. Van Mieris depicts the various textures in the painting with an impressive richness of detail and exceptional precision: the silvery gloss of the lady's satin dress, the honey coloured wood of the lute, the soft fur of the red velvet jacket and the heavy, deep-pile oriental carpet with its broad gold fringe. All these expensive items also indicate the wealth of the subject, although they can also be interpreted as symbols of vanity and extravagance.
c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections
c0f84326-ca73-50c0-aa89-a6fa1be73b81.method_for_datation: Artist signatures: "Mieris Anno 1667" and "Anno 1667. Juny. Lud. Bat. F. van Mieris fecit"

It was mentioned for the first time in the inventory drawn up between 1722 and 1728, where it was described as "in the manner of Metsu".

c0f8bfaf-f9ca-5ac0-84ba-67ebfcaf39e4.name: Tablecloth (*dastarkhan*)
c0f8bfaf-f9ca-5ac0-84ba-67ebfcaf39e4.description:
A *dastarkhan* is a thin white *palas* (a kind of traditional, flat-woven carpet popular in Azerbaijan) that functioned as a tablecloth for Azerbaijanis and other Turkic peoples. The central field of Azerbaijani *dastarkhans* was rectangular, usually plain, and the borders spotted vivid decoration in contrast with the *dastarkhans* produced in Central Asia that boast elaborate designs. A *dastarkhan* denoted a sacred meaning, as its ornaments protected the food and the breadwinner and brought abundance to the family.  
In the central field of this artifact, there are inscriptions in the old epigraphic alphabet, stylized images of birds (symbolizing protection), butas (symbolizing different abilities bestowed on a person) and branches (symbolizing blessings). Images of arrows on the *dastarkhan's* border symbolize honour, prosperity and blessings.
c0f8bfaf-f9ca-5ac0-84ba-67ebfcaf39e4.method_for_datation: By stylistic and comparative analyses with related material

keywords: tablecloth; dastarkhan; flat-woven; wool; Azerbaijan
materials: Wool pattern yarn for the warp, cotton yarn for the weft; interweaved, wrapped.

c13c410a-cc43-5e8b-8251-2f9bd6a4319e.name: Kula Rug
c13c410a-cc43-5e8b-8251-2f9bd6a4319e.description: Kula, Manisa Province was an important rug producing centre. During the 18th and 19th centuries they supplied the demand of international rug companies. Most Kula rugs, including this example are prayer rugs. The main component of prayer rug decoration is the *mihrab* and can be described as a stylized arch surrounding the prayer area. This is a double *mihrab* Kula rug with band stairs on both sides. In double *mihrab* rugs there are two *mihrab*s, one at the bottom of the image and the other at the top. This Kula rug with a double *mihrab* has eight borders, four wide bands and four narrow bands. It is decorated with an image of flowers in a vase.

c13e07a9-25e9-500c-a2eb-4f7568251a1e.name: Qajar Carpet -Hunting Scene
c13e07a9-25e9-500c-a2eb-4f7568251a1e.short_description: The pictorial carpets of Qajar Iran illustrate royals and famous people in various scenarios. This Persian Kashan wool rug displays a hunting scene with a portrait of a king or a nobleman sitting on a chair embellished with crowns, drinking and holding a copper ewer in his other hand, and a wide variety of animals and plants. The phoenix above the nobleman, a popular creature in Persian mythology, represents immortality. Hunting dogs symbolize honour and glory, while the gazelle symbolizes innocence. The imagery of water is significant, denoting purity and the source of life, and in which the fish embody undying love. The cypress tree signifies Persian perseverance and pride.

c1ccddeb-c544-52d8-b3fa-3eea219bbe3c.name: Star Medallion Carpet
c1ccddeb-c544-52d8-b3fa-3eea219bbe3c.description:
Much worn, this enormous carpet is actually a fragment of an even larger example: the side borders are complete, but the upper and lower sides are missing their borders altogether. The grand design therefore continued even further, lengthways. This was purchased in 1894. Perhaps surprisingly, the V&A museum also owns another fragment originally from the very same carpet, donated in 1959 by the scholar collector Joseph McMullan, who spotted the connection.  
  
The design is dominated by a magnificent star-medallion, with reciprocal cartouches radiating out from a central octagon at its nucleus. Along the central axis of the carpet, smaller cartouches stack above and below this star-medallion, all against a red main field. Two superimposed systems of spiralling scrollwork fills this red field, dotted with lotus flowers and beautifully-rendered palmette motifs in black and pale blue. The main border is a larger scale half-palmette scroll, punctuated with large blowsy lotus flowers outlined in leaves.  
  
Few extant carpets are attributed with total confidence to before the start of Safavid rule (in 1501), although it is certain that a mature craft technology was at work before then: the dated carpets of the initial Safavid decades are highly-accomplished, confirming at least a generation of professional skilled craftsmanship in this medium. Many other fine examples similar to this enormous fragment are known, demonstrating a similar ambition to render two-plane leafy scrollwork for example, and with the same somewhat angular result (once described as “severe austerity”). By contrast, the palmette and half-palmette motifs here (often in black outlined in light blue) are rendered with neat precision, in tight curls. This is a craft tradition adjusting to new demands for more curvilinear pattern – most probably drawing from contemporary arts of the book.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O67292/carpet-unknown/)
c1ccddeb-c544-52d8-b3fa-3eea219bbe3c.method_for_datation: Carpets in this group are arguably dated around the late fifteenth and early sixteenth century, and have often been attributed to northwestern Iran, and Tabriz in particular. This hypothesis would associate the group with the Aq Qoyunlu court in Tabriz, but no inscribed or dated examples survive.
c1ccddeb-c544-52d8-b3fa-3eea219bbe3c.obtention: Purchased in 1894. In 1959, a second smaller fragment from the same carpet was donated to the V&A by Joseph McMullen (V&A T.267-1959).

c2097e9b-56b2-56db-8332-8b268a5e48e1.name: Gördes double niche carpet
c2097e9b-56b2-56db-8332-8b268a5e48e1.description:
The rug-weaving areas of Anatolia are conventionally divided into western, central and eastern regions. Western Anatolian centres such as Uşak, Gördes, Kula and their vicinity have a long tradition of carpet and rug production. Carpets from these centers were very popular in Europe. Ghiordes is an Anatolian town northwest of Uşak. Rugs in this area have been woven at least since the 18th century and perhaps long before.  
This type of rug is often called Kiz Gördes. *Kiz* is a Turkish word for a girl or a bride, so these types of rugs were intended as a gift from a bride to her husband on their wedding day. In the central field there is a double niche with central hooked diamond medallion on a red background. Spandrels are fields with diagonal rows of florets on a light blue background. Above and beneath the arches there are two oblong fields with cloud band shaped flowers. The central field is framed with three borders. The main border is decorated with large motifs of flowers and leaves. The inner border is decorated with geometrical motifs. The outer border is the leaf and blossom meander border.

c466c19a-6e61-556b-a637-4712a73de575.name: Three fragments of woven fabric decorated with female figures carrying rose water bottles
c466c19a-6e61-556b-a637-4712a73de575.description: These silk weavings once framed a large blanket with an embroidered middle section and have been remounted to the original fabric sheet. Depicted on the background, which used to be gold, are young women in elegantly curved stance holding rosewater bottles in their arms. Curved blossoming plants emerging from a rise in the ground are visible in the spaces between the figures. The décor is arranged in offset horizontal rows: the direction of the women’s gaze switches in each row and the colouring of the garments is repeated after every fourth row. Miniature paintings were often used as templates for silk weaves during this era. An especially delightful detail is the circlet-shaped feathered headdress with a long scarf that falls behind the back and is elegantly ruffled. This type of headdress was common until c. 1620 and is defining for the time in which this silk weaving was created.

c47d93ec-a5cc-5bc4-9584-cadaac01d6bc.name: Carpet.
c47d93ec-a5cc-5bc4-9584-cadaac01d6bc.description: A fragment of a carpet, sewn together from several smaller fragments. It features a relatively rare design sometimes referred to as the 'four-lobed star-medallion' pattern, in which the corners of large cross-shaped motifs are linked by knots to smaller rectangular motifs, creating spaces in which horizontal or vertical lozenges are placed. This pattern is thought to pre-date the well-known 'star Uşak' pattern, as similar medallions can be seen on carpets depicted in miniature paintings from 15th-century Iran. Other details suggesting an early date include the knots joining the motifs at their corners and the latticework structure running between the medallions, creating a sense of a continuous composition. There are about twenty carpets surviving with this pattern, but the present example is the best preserved.
c47d93ec-a5cc-5bc4-9584-cadaac01d6bc.short_description: A fragment of a larger carpet, itself sewn together from smaller fragments. The design is an early and relatively rare variation on the famous ‘star Uşak’ pattern. Similar patterns are seen on carpets in AH 9th- / AD 15th-century paintings from Iran.
c47d93ec-a5cc-5bc4-9584-cadaac01d6bc.dates: Late hegira 9th/ AD 15th to AH 11th / AD 17th century.
c47d93ec-a5cc-5bc4-9584-cadaac01d6bc.method_for_datation: Based on comparisons with other carpets and with carpets appearing in manuscript illustrations; scholars have dated this piece to as early as 1450 and as late as 1625.
c47d93ec-a5cc-5bc4-9584-cadaac01d6bc.method_for_provenance: 'Uşak' carpets are associated with the town of that name in western Anatolia, but were not necessarily all made there.

c4d9a7c5-a59a-53c3-aaaa-19bb4d5320bd.name: Dragon carpet
c4d9a7c5-a59a-53c3-aaaa-19bb4d5320bd.description: The so-called dragon carpets are the oldest preserved group that can be localised to the South Caucasus production area. The Chinese symbol of power, the dragon, which became popular in Iran during the Ilkhanid dynasty (13th/14th century), was carried through by the art of the Timurids and Safavids into remote regions. In knotted executions, the dragons became noticeably more geometric. In total, three pairs of geometrised yellow dragons are to be seen in the carpet, yet, since they are difficult to distinguish, the exemplar is dated to the late 17th, or the early 18th century respectively. One can clearly recognise the head and tail in the MAK Collection’s dragon carpet; the originally lambent flames on the legs, however, were stylised into geometrised, tendril-like forms. Today, the carpet’s place of origin is presumed to be the Karabakh region, where Shah Abbas I (r. 1587–1629) had established manufactories.

c791fd67-b769-5838-8662-48cd1f3c7839.name: *Mafrash* (Bedding Bag) End Panel
c791fd67-b769-5838-8662-48cd1f3c7839.description:
Certain textiles from Anatolia, covers and containers made by nomads, semi-nomads and villagers for their own use known as the Caucasus and Iran, first came to the attention of consumers in Europe, in the final third of the 19th century. Although the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts purchased its first nomad and village flat-woven textiles at the turn of the 19th/20th century, this carpet was a donation by Prof. Ottó Fettick (1946, followed by his bequest in 1954) that laid the real foundations of the Museum's woven carpet collection. The 104 items included textiles of a kind that were new to the Museum: 19th-century woven Caucasian and North Iranian soumak, palas, verneh and jajim rugs, containers and covers, and Anatolian, Iranian and Balkan kilims. Professor Fettick (1875–1954) was a veterinary surgeon, bacteriologist and art collector and probably started building his collection of 19th-century flat-woven nomad carpets and other textiles in the early 20th century. The end panel of a Shahsevan *mafrash* (bedding bag) presumably from the Moghan-Savalan region is from the Fettick collection. Its ornament is comprised of three broad horizontal bands. The dark brown central band has offset rows of hooked hexagons; one row in alternating colours between two rows of white half hexagons. The upper and lower secondary broad bands contain right-facing peacocks standing in line on a yellow ground, each with a stylized "cock" motif on its back.  
  
Originally the side panel selvedges were sewn together with a blue and brown rope-like overcasting which remained on three edges of the end panel when the *mafrash* was taken apart. The cut edge of the long side panel is visible on the lower third of the left side under the frayed overcasting.  
  
There is a *mafrash* end panel of almost identical pattern in the Charles Grant Ellis Collection.

c89d2c27-b0d1-53f6-93b8-2aa06db62666.name: Carpet
c89d2c27-b0d1-53f6-93b8-2aa06db62666.description:
Woven by a Yomut woman with supreme knowledge of her artistic heritage, thorough understanding of design making and colour combinations, and full control over technical aspects of her art, this carpet probably was a prized possesion of a Turkmen family. In a Turkmen household, this type of carpet meant that female members of the household were exceptionally skillful weavers of textiles, which was considered an asset for the family. The fine weaving also illustrated that the family had enough surplus money and time to invest in creating textiles of this size and visual power.  
  
The purpose of this large carpet was to establish the status of the head of the family in the tribal society as well as to honor a guest. Invited or uninvited, guests in Turkmen society were considered “God sent” and always welcomed in the tent and given refreshments.  
  
Carpets woven by the nomadic Turkmen tribes in Central Asia are usually patterned by rows of small medallions called *göl* on a deep red ground as seen in this richly coloured carpet; one of the oldest of its type. Few other tribal textiles rival the best Turkmen weavings in quality of material and excellence of weave. A masterpiece of Yomut weaving, this soft lustrous pile carpet blends the traditional stylized and geometrized form of *göl* with more naturalistic floral forms seen in the long end panels, all of which are clearly drawn. Another striking aspect of this carpet is the appearance of the gracefully and realistically drawn, multicolored flowering plants in the aprons.

c9f822c3-3474-5596-90db-ee77387c77fd.name: *Cintamani* carpet
c9f822c3-3474-5596-90db-ee77387c77fd.description:
The *cintamani* carpet is one of the most impressive objects of the National Museum in Kraków collections and not just for its artistic features, but because of its huge dimensions (10m x 4m) as well. The central field is decorated with *cintamani* motifs: two golden wavy stripes combined with three white balls. In the background are small dark-blue multi-leaf medallions ornamented with “leaf” and “shield” palmettes grouped around the rosette motif. Medallions as well as *cintamani* motifs are arranged in net-like patterns – such a composition makes an impression of harmony. In the main border are white shields with bouquets of roses; among them are delicate, sinuous tendrils with palmettes interwoven with cloudbounds. Colouristically, the composition is balanced: the red ground contrasting with the white, yellow, blue and green pattern.  
Cairo was already a well-known carpet-weaving centre in the 15th century during the Mamluk dynasty. In 1517, the Ottomans captured the city and the style of the carpets woven there changed. The influence of the Turkish Tabriz and the Anatolian workshops became visible. This *cintamani* carpet, probably made in the second half of the 16th century, combines the graceful floral motifs of Persian-style carpets with a *cintamani* pattern characteristic of Ottoman Turkey. The *Cintamani* symbol originates from the Buddhist tradition. Adopted by the Timurids, it was known as the “Badge of Timur”. In the Ottoman Empire the *cintamani* motif was widely used in the decoration of everyday objects, i.e. garments, carpets, ceramics, symbolising the power derived from the pattern of the leopard- and tiger skins worn by rulers. The high artistic and technical quality of this carpet allows us to presume that it could have been made in one of the sultan’s court workshops.  
This *cintamani* carpet comes from the Corpus Christi church in Kraków. It was certainly used for the decoration of the church, probably on the floor. Oriental art was very popular in Poland during the 16th and 17th centuries, and textiles served to decorate both secular and sacral interiors.
c9f822c3-3474-5596-90db-ee77387c77fd.method_for_datation: Stylistic features, as well as the technique of execution (the asymmetrical, so-called “Persian” knot) allow us to suggest Cairo as the possible place of production

ca6b30ce-d3b7-5a14-b7ed-7fa66415cbc6.name: Carpet
ca6b30ce-d3b7-5a14-b7ed-7fa66415cbc6.description:
Field: Rectangular rug with a brown background that is based on an ogival network of vegetable stems, with blue-green schematic pine cones with yellow outlines. The ogives are joined by pearly rings.  
Border: The border is delimited by two yellow fine lines, with opposing serrated leaves, whose stems are joined to a sinuous S shape with an inner serrated line and small leaves on the outside.  
The warp is made of two ropes of raw wool, twisted in the Z direction and spun in the S, Z2S direction. The weft consists of three woollen threads, with no apparent twist, between each row of knots. The knot density is 1800 knots / dm, 40 knots / dm -horizontal- and 45 knots / dm -vertical.  
This carpet belongs to the series of Brocades or "guadamecí work", the name by which it is archived within the inventories. The name is derived from its imitation of Renaissance and guadamecí fabrics. They are usually two colours, or two shades of the same colour. The border is somewhat archaic with respect to other more elaborate designs with Renaissance glasses and grotesques, as well as decorative scrollwork and S shaped valances.  
The use of brown and blue colours is unusual.  
The density is typical of a quality known in Spanish as "entrefina" or medium-fine.  
This piece is attributed to the workshop of Alcaraz, but it should be noted that the field is also similar to the carpets of Cuenca, an association which can be attested by the numerous Cuencan fragments with a similar decoration and colours. Despite this, there is still doubt as to this carpet's place of production.

cb646540-71b4-53fd-9b5d-065a402f6c3b.name: 'Hortus Conclusus' church tapestry
cb646540-71b4-53fd-9b5d-065a402f6c3b.description: In our time, people who want to improve their logic skills might do a Sudoku while commuting on the urban railway. In medieval times, people would spend their time decoding the immense iconographic programme of the Catholic Church, which included not only Biblical figures and saints, but also legendary creatures with no religious connotations. The creator of the “Enclosed Garden” that can be seen on a precious tapestry from the chapel of Ried in what is today the canton of Schwyz drew on the early Christian natural history treatise known as the Physiologus, which states that a unicorn can only be captured by a virgin. From a Christian viewpoint, the virgin is Mary and her touching the unicorn’s horn is an allusion to the immaculate conception. Interpreting this scene correctly was tricky, but within the capabilities of medieval churchgoers. In contrast, they were less adept at understanding written letters and numbers.

materials: Tapestry, weft: wool, silk, gold and silver lamella, warp: linen

The quatrefoils themselves are interesting because they are similar to the design of the eastern cloud collar, a decoration found on eastern apparel.

cda5bcaf-49fc-5e8b-918d-5bb074a35a1b.name: Seljuq Rug
cda5bcaf-49fc-5e8b-918d-5bb074a35a1b.description: This rug, found in the Konya Aladdin Mosque exhibits the richness of motif and colour of the Seljuq rugs. It is unique from others in the “Konya Group” because of its background colour and octagonal decoration. The characteristic *kufic* border is evidence of its origin. The main border is framed with a thin border of blue and brown lines. Pairs of stylized *kufic* letters in white are in the main border on a red background. Octagon shapes on the red background go to infinity. The inside of the motifs are dark red. The camel’s foot motif inside the octagons are made with a dark contour.

cda75f5a-42cf-52df-85ce-82bce8d75236.name: Carpet
cda75f5a-42cf-52df-85ce-82bce8d75236.description:
Three fragments mounted on machine-sewn burlap.  
Field: The decoration corresponds to a carpet of crowns. Within its corners it presents a pinkish flower as a defining feature and also contains floral cluster or vegetal motifs. In the corners a geometric floral set of three branches is visible. The background utilises reddish hues and the plant motifs are in dark and light shades of green along with a yellow outline.  
Border: The carpet fragment shows a narrow border of Franciscan knot that separates the field and the central border by yellow stripes. The Franciscan knot is of a single end and is outlined in yellow, the knots of the major and minor sides being different. The preserved decoration of these fragments allows us to perceive that the central border is formed by candlestick motifs on a light green background. The dark green motifs outlined in yellow also act as a potent contrast.  
The warp utilises wool with its natural colour and the weft utilises red dyed wool. The decorative aspects of the carpet consist of red, dark green and light green wool.

cdb915c1-3659-5399-a392-93205b57fd30.name: Carpet
cdb915c1-3659-5399-a392-93205b57fd30.description:
Following the 1834 abolition of Portuguese religious institutions, most of their portable heritage was transferred to the Portuguese State. The incorporation of textiles, including carpets, into State property is particularly relevant to the history and the creation of national museums and collections such as the National Museum of Ancient Art. This carpet, which has been in the NMAA’s collection since 1888, comes from the former convent of Estrela for which it had been commissioned by Princess Maria I (r.1777‒1816) after the birth of her son.  
Although building began in 1779, well after the date of this carpet’s production, its incorporation in the convent can be attributed to two reasons: as an offering from the Royal Portuguese House, owner of an impressive collection of Oriental carpets, to encourage offers from other donors, or even a transfer from another religious institution.  
The lack of documentation makes it difficult to ascertain its original function. These carpets were much appreciated and used as important decorative furnishings both in sacred and profane interiors, where they were meant to define spaces. One such example of physical delimitation lay in the use of carpets to cover the stairway and higher elevated daises that became an Iberian tradition within the female universe and lasted well into the 19th century.  
This carpet has undergone several restorative interventions, with its original size having been approximately a metre larger than at present; of almost eight-metres in length, this carpet shows a very balanced design and colour. It presents the classical ornamental motifs characteristic of this category, along with the field filled with “vine scrolls” alternating with palmettes and S-shape cloud scrolls (*tchi*). It also exhibits the characteristic contrast of colours between the field and the border (red/blue), both filled with palmettes and chinar leaves.

cdc27ae7-3a64-5545-a795-1006d1e99c9e.name: Gördes Prayer Rug
cdc27ae7-3a64-5545-a795-1006d1e99c9e.description: This rug is an outstanding example of a Gördes prayer rug. The knot technique is not well suited for such detailed decorations. Nevertheless, complex stylized floral motifs are skilfully woven on the *mihrab* corners and borders expressing heavenly gardens. In contrast, the *mihrab* area is decorated simply.

d04a23e2-0c3a-5d55-be53-ebac7989ba2d.name: Gördes prayer rug
d04a23e2-0c3a-5d55-be53-ebac7989ba2d.description:
This prayer rug was made in Gördes, one of the best-known carpet production centres in Anatolia. Rugs from Gördes were very much appreciated in the West as well, because of their high quality and splendid, vivid colours. The rug preserved in the National Museum in Kraków is a fine example.  
At the centre of the Kraków rug, a bright-red *mihrab* indicates the direction of the Kaʽba in Mecca. A horseshoe arch is supported by the two delicate columns constructed from diamond shapes. Elegantly shaped ewers with flowers rising from them serve as the bases of columns. The vessels are another religious reference to recall the ablutions preceding prayers. In the capitals another significant motif from Islamic art is recognisable in the *cintamani*, meaning power and happiness.  
The ornamental and colouristic composition of the carpet is balanced. The most striking feature is the plain-red niche under turquoise-blue spandrels, which is filled with a scrolling ivory vine with contrasting red buds. The cross-panel above the *mihrab* is decorated with small palmettes much differentiated in colour (ivory, yellow, blue and red), against a dark-indigo background. The border is also highly decorative. The central, wide, dark-indigo border is filled with a rhythmical composition of large roses and palmettes, surrounded by smaller roses and carnations on leafy stems. The central border is flanked by the thinner ivory borders decorated with tendrils with flowers.  
Similar rugs are preserved in Austrian collections, the Wawel Royal Castle Kulczycki Collection and in the Ballard Collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York.
d04a23e2-0c3a-5d55-be53-ebac7989ba2d.method_for_datation: The floral ornaments that decorate this rug are rather realistic and elaborate, with a soft, fluent line; the presumption is that it dates from the 17th century

d096b05d-8793-528f-8807-6caadc794855.name: Kazak (fragment)
d096b05d-8793-528f-8807-6caadc794855.description: Roughly two-thirds of this Kazak's original total size is preserved. Most notably, the border is almost entirely missing on three sides – the central field is for the most part preserved. The fragment is striking for its wonderfully preserved, fleshy wool pile. In addition to diamond and hook designs, there are depictions of animals and humans among the varied scattered motifs. A numerical inscription is highlighted on a white ground, legible against the grain of the carpet. The numbers 1323 are most likely Hejira dating, which seems credible in light of the piece's overall impression. According to our calendar, the carpet would thus have been woven in 1905. Even though the fragment is not one of the outstanding pieces of the Dresden carpet collection in terms of classical, qualitative aspects, it was shown in 2018 in the Dresden exhibition "Museum of Untold Stories" of the Dresden State Art Collections. Discovered by a carpet enthusiast in 1980, during GDR times, dirty on a building site and left to the museum, it refers to a piece of contemporary history and is quite presentable. Such finds from bulky waste containers or demolition sites in the GDR are still called "container carpets" by their collectors today.
d096b05d-8793-528f-8807-6caadc794855.holder: Museum für Völkerkunde Dresden (Ethnological Museum Dresden), Dresden State Art Collections
d096b05d-8793-528f-8807-6caadc794855.obtention: Purchased 1980 from a Dresden collector, Friedrich Uhlemann, who afore found this piece thickly covered in dirt on a private building site where it was used as a mat. Uhlemann was very much engaged in helping Dresden painter Wilhelm Müller (1928–99) to secure oriental carpets, rugs and flat weaves of rural and nomadic tradition that were still on the territory of the DGR with building up a collection for the Ethnographic Museum of Dresden, mainly between 1979 and 1986.

d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.name: Prayer rug.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.description: A prayer rug that is typical of those produced in Ladik, a village near the city of Konya in central Anatolia. The rug has a red, central niche surrounded by three decorated frames. In the centre of the niche is an abstract tree-of-life motif springing from a stylised water-vessel. Above the vessel there is a rectangle with illegible text; above the tip of the niche there are a crescent and another rectangle with the date according to the hegira calendar, '1217' (1802) woven sideways. Made by the women in the village on a domestic handloom, the design for this type of prayer rug is inspired by the columned, court prayer rugs of the AH 10th–11th / AD 16th–17th centuries. The women also reared the sheep, sheered the wool, spun it and dyed it. Ladik lay on the main pilgrimage route from north to south, and these rugs were made to supplement the villagers' income, and were, subsequently, presented to mosques and shrines in the area and beyond as pious offerings. One such rug appears in a 17th-century European painting, a still life by Nicolaes van Gelder, dated 1664.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.short_description: This prayer rug is an example of those produced in the village of Ladik near Konya in Anatolia. Made by the women in the village, on a domestic handloom, the rugs were sold to pilgrims who passed through on their way to Mecca. They in turn donated them to mosques and shrines on their return.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.method_for_datation: Woven into the rug is the date according to the hegira calendar, '1217' (1802) positioned in a rectangle above the tip of the crescent on top of the niche.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.method_for_provenance: Artistic analysis and comparison with other prayer rugs made in Ladik.
d0bee2a2-2f3b-5679-b3ad-433e3664ca0a.obtention: Part of the collection given to the City of Glasgow by Sir William and Lady Burrell in 1944.

d123fde5-10b9-5cf8-aa5b-fe0e83c23dd3.name: Fachralo Kazak
d123fde5-10b9-5cf8-aa5b-fe0e83c23dd3.description:
Kazak rugs were made in the south central Caucasus, between Tbilisi in Georgia and Erivan in Armenia. The area is bordered by the Ganja area on the northeast and Karabakh area on the southeast.  
Fachralo or Fekhraly is a town 40km southwest of Tbilisi. This decagon medallion is one of the most common Kazak motifs and it is often found in the prayer rug format.  
The central field has a double niche on a red background. The double niche is surrounded with a white zig-zag border and in the centre there is a *fachralo* medallion on a blue-green background. The decagon *fachralo* medallion has another decagon medallion inscribed. The outer one is decorated with a small white geometric pattern on a red background and the inner one with small blue and red geometric motifs on a white background. In the centre of the white decagram there is a *kaikalak* (four opposing ram's horns) motif. The central field is covered with stylized human figure filler motifs. There are also, on the right side of the carpet, two animal motifs. Double niche is surrounded with a *kochak* (ram's horns) pattern border on a red background. Three borders surround the central field. The main border is the common Caucasian "leaf and calyx" border on a white background. Minor borders meander on dark blue and light blue backgrounds.

d26f9efa-6f6e-5edd-adc2-beece4c2fe8a.name: Medallion Carpet with Angels
d26f9efa-6f6e-5edd-adc2-beece4c2fe8a.description:
This much-worn medallion carpet belongs to a remarkable category of sixteenth-century carpets from Iran. Often named “Sanguszko” carpets after the aristocratic Polish family who owned one example (today in the Miho Museum in Japan), this group is well-known for the human figures and animals in their complex designs. Here, the red central field features a dramatic yellow central medallion with smaller cartouches and pendants along the central vertical axis. At the corners are four quarter-medallions in dark blue. The border has a cream ground, with large leafy scrolls and flowers. The red field is filled with hunting creatures, drawn with great detail and fluency: tigers and leopards hunting down deer, lurking wolves and fiery supernatural creatures also in combat. Less easy to detect are the single faces peering out from the surrounding lotus flowers: angelic white faces with beauty spots, and snarling lion faces. At the very centre, the radiating design of the medallion is also packed with interlacing foliate scrollwork, and further animals, birds and fish packed into cartouches.  
The most lyrical part of the design lies in the four corners, inside the quarter-medallions: against a dark blue ground, three winged angels gather, surrounded by curling clouds. One is seated and seems to hold a wine-cup, while the other two are carrying a peacock and a small deer: this seems to be a celestial version of a court reception scene.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O67221/carpet-unknown/)
d26f9efa-6f6e-5edd-adc2-beece4c2fe8a.method_for_datation: The figural style in this (and other carpets in the same group) matches manuscript-painting dateable to later sixteenth century Iran, but there are no surviving dated examples.
d26f9efa-6f6e-5edd-adc2-beece4c2fe8a.method_for_provenance: This carpet group was tentatively attributed to Kirman on the grounds that the technical structure was similar to the Kirman “Vase technique” group. However a Kirman provenance has not been proven.
d26f9efa-6f6e-5edd-adc2-beece4c2fe8a.obtention: Purchased in 1883 by the South Kensington Museum (today the V&A) from the art-dealers A. Myers, New Bond Street, London. This was the first Safavid-era Iranian carpet bought by the museum.

d27da85e-f180-5ec8-90d7-7fdfc02299ee.name: Kırşehir Multiple‒niche prayer rug
d27da85e-f180-5ec8-90d7-7fdfc02299ee.description: This is a rug from Kırşehir Province, an important rug producing centre famous for its prayer rugs. This type of prayer rug ‒ locally called *saf*‒ has multiple niches that are side by side allowing three or more people to communally pray. There are examples of *saf* carpets as early as the 15th century. They were produced all around the Muslim world, but they were never in high production so they remain very rare.

d2a1fca5-7efb-5323-927c-0aaad478f6c1.name: Transylvanian prayer rug
d2a1fca5-7efb-5323-927c-0aaad478f6c1.description:
Turkish rugs arrived in Transylvania through trade. Almost all types of small-format Turkish classical rugs can be found in this region. The most numerous are the so-called “Transylvanian” group – prayer rugs with an undecorated field are widely dispersed throughout Transylvania. The term Transylvanian prayer rug is mostly used by Romanian authors such as Stefano Ionescu, Mircea Dunca, Andrei Kertesz and Alexandra Zigura, since it avoids specific reference to any weaving centre.  
The Transylvanian prayer rug from the Museum of Arts and Crafts is one of the oldest rugs in the museum collection. In the central field of the carpet there is an undecorated red *mihrab* (prayer niche) field. Delicate floral ornaments appear at the edge of the upper part of the *mihrab*. Spandrels are decorated with flowering-stems on ivory ground. The main border is in Ottoman style with rosettes and pine cones on yellow ground. Minor borders are vegetal on blue and red ground.

d3abd1eb-d054-57dc-92dc-e1b2ea8806d5.name: Carpet
d3abd1eb-d054-57dc-92dc-e1b2ea8806d5.short_description: Rugs and carpets are an essential artwork category within the Islamic culture. In the late 19th century, Oriental carpets became collectible and valued art objects. The Museum of Islamic Art’s collection of carpets is one of the most important in the world. It was started in 1904 with the gift of 21 carpets from Wilhelm von Bode. The important carpet no 1 burned partially 1945 and was restored partially with fragments later. This specific artwork was created in the North West of Iran before the middle of the 16th century and shows an animated scene featuring animals and trees.

d3f2eecd-74e3-5813-bb0c-4a2756c30701.name: Khotan Pomegranate Tree Carpet
d3f2eecd-74e3-5813-bb0c-4a2756c30701.description:
A 19th Pomegranate Tree carpet from north-east Central Asia, from Khotan or Yarqand, East Turkistan (today in Xinjiang Uyghur Autonomous Region, China). This silk pile carpet has as dark blue background in its centre-field and a predominantly red border. The centre-field is dominated by a wine-red, ivory and green pomegranate tree that grows out of a small ivory vase at the base of the field. The tree branches out upwards in an abstracted symmetrical layout. Both along the main stem of the tree and on the tips of its horizontal branches are hanging pomegranate fruits that have been depicted with their seeds showing. Small buds and leaves grow on the threes stems and branches. The carpet’s border comprises of three bands of geometric patterns: the outer and inner bands are made up of pink coloured “T”-shaped elements, angled at right angles in association with each other, creating a continuous geometric decorative frame. The centre border-band holds a blue repeat chain of swastikas on a red background.  
  
The depiction of a pomegranate tree growing out of a vase reminds of the ancient tree of life or tree of knowledge that appears on the arts of many ancient civilisations in Asia. Here it is believed to be an invocation of the three-of-life in the Islamic tradition which grows out of the font-of-life in Paradise.  
  
The swastika motif in this carpet is almost as ancient a symbol as the tree of life. In Asian cultures it is seen as an auspicious symbol. On this carpet it has been applied as a decorative motif inherited from the region’s Buddhist heritage.

d4980b80-93b5-5bd1-ad00-c7a801b5aa8e.name: Rug (*gadjari*)
d4980b80-93b5-5bd1-ad00-c7a801b5aa8e.description: In Central Asia, rugs of this kind were used as floor coverings, wall hangings and horse blankets. This rug is sewn from 22 narrow strips woven in warp-float and warp-faced technique on a horizontal loom used by weavers in pastoral communities in Afghanistan. The strips woven from wool and cotton were cut into sections, sewn together, and embellished around the perimeter with narrower bands of contrasting colours. The strips are patterned with stepped diamonds, triangles with pendants, V-shaped figures, checkered sections, hooks, hooked bars and other geometric and abstract patterns in red, dark blue, green, yellow and white colours. Tassels are attached to the bottom of the rug.

d6e29c37-877d-59fc-ba89-0136adddb6e7.name: Wedding portrait of King Aleksandar and Queen Draga of Serbia
d6e29c37-877d-59fc-ba89-0136adddb6e7.description: At the end of the 19th and during the first decade of the 20th century Pirot kilims served as unavoidable decor in public buildings and in important public manifestations. An official wedding photo of King Alexander Obrenović of Serbia and Queen Draga, shows a royal couple standing on the Pirot kilims, used as floor coverings in this solemn occasion as distinguished national products. The official photograph, taken on 4 August 1900 by the court photographer Milan Jovanović, was issued on a poster by the bookstore of Sreten J. Djordjević and printed by the State Printing House of the Kingdom of Serbia.

d709dc46-d56e-5b96-833d-47202bfed1b4.name: Prayer rug
d709dc46-d56e-5b96-833d-47202bfed1b4.description: A lamp stands out against the indigo field of the prayer niche (*mihrab*) shown on this high-pile rug. Featuring a foliated scroll pattern, the olive-green spandrel is supported by two columns. Carnations decorate the upper level of the niche. A series of rosettes and palmettes interspersed with arabesques covers the ivory ground of the main border. This rug, which has 4,200 symmetrical knots per square decimetre, was made in Turkey during the first quarter of the 20th century. Positioned facing Mecca, the rug ensures the purity of the place of worship and creates a separate space for praying. Long ago, Muslims kneeled down and prostrated themselves on palm-frond mats or sheepskins. The field of a prayer rug usually shows a stylized representation of a *mihrab*, a niche made in the wall of a mosque indicating the direction of Mecca, towards which the faithful turn to pray.

d75b8026-c7bc-5c73-aacc-00b073b4d618.name: Double niche ‘Transylvanian’ rug
d75b8026-c7bc-5c73-aacc-00b073b4d618.description: The term “Transylvanian” rug designates 17th- and 18th-century rugs preserved in Transylvanian Saxon churches, which, once considered being of Transylvanian origin, were in fact made in western Anatolia. Some have a *mihrab* design, typical of prayer rugs, while others feature two opposing arches. Here, the red ground of this double niche is decorated with stylised floral motifs connected by geometric scrolls. A mosque lamp is featured at one end of the central field. Scalloped edge cartouches on ivory-white ground decorate the main border. At an early stage, the bright colours of this surprisingly well-preserved rug raised doubts about its authenticity. Still, a few other carpets from Transylvanian churches display a similarly vivid colour range; at the same time, over the past 100 years (ever since it was sent to Moscow in 1916) the rug has only been exhibited once, in 1994, which explains its excellent state of conservation.

d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.name: The *Annunciation*
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.description:
Initially composed of four panels, this piece was originally of a different size. Recent tests have proved that its lower section has been cut on both sides. Prior to this recent modification, the work underwent further changes. The Virgin Mary is represented in the second condition of the Angelic Colloquium of the Mystery of the Annunciation, by Friar Roberto Caracciolo de Lecce (1425‒1495). That is to say, this is the moment of *cogitatio* or reflection, in which the Virgin considers the Angel’s words and demonstrates her prudence.  
Similar to other paintings alluding to this theme, the work bears witness to symbolism characteristic of representations of the Annunciation: the book that lays opened before Mary; the vase with lilies; the Angel’s sceptre; the bed, topped by its canopy and with its prominent front curtains, upon which the knots are formed; the column between the two characters, and the mat on which Mary is found standing.  
In recent years, the study of textiles through paintings, in its manifold categories, has proved to be very useful. Aside from documental sources and extant objects, paintings provide important visual evidence concerning an object’s trade and usage throughout time. In this particular painting, representing a Portuguese domestic interior, the Virgin Mary stands on a mat. Following the Islamic presence in the Iberian Peninsula, which stretched well into the 16th century, floors were commonly covered with mats, mainly in the summer, when they replaced carpets.  
Although this mat could be of Portuguese manufacture (Lisbon, Oporto or the Algarve) it has been associated with the mats woven with palm fibre and decorated with geometric patterns from sub-Saharan Africa, particularly those from the Congo (and Benin and Niger).
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.holder: Museum of Portuguese Decorative Arts – Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva Foundation
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.method_for_datation: Authorship was attributed to the Lourinhã Master (active between 1500 and 1540) by Luís Reis Santos in his work dedicated to this artist and published in 1963. This attribution has been rejected in more recent studies, thus it is classified here as the work of a follower of the master.
d8518639-1ed2-5598-8b01-7b8bd53b00f0.obtention: This was one of Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva's first pieces towards his collection of primitive artworks; donated by Ricardo do Espírito Santo Silva in 1953.

d9fa7933-6825-5e1f-b45e-93db471e8c19.name: Vine scroll carpet
d9fa7933-6825-5e1f-b45e-93db471e8c19.description: In addition to North India, the Deccan Plateau, the region of the Indian subcontinent lying south of the Indo-Gangetic Plain, was an important centre of Indian carpet production. Many carpets of this group were produced for export; numerous exemplars have survived in Japanese collections. This example is regarded as one of the finest; it strongly borrows stylistic elements from 17th-century Iranian carpets due to its vine scrolls. Not only the enlargement of the tendrils, but even more the emphasis of the lance or *saz* leaves also evokes Ottoman models of the 16th century.

db2c46e8-d98a-5553-bcb2-dbc6c45d28f6.name: The Salting Carpet
db2c46e8-d98a-5553-bcb2-dbc6c45d28f6.description:
Dating from late sixteenth-century Iran, this is an extremely fine and beautiful carpet, with an intricate floral design filled with wild creatures, and verses of Persian poetry all around the borders, highlighted in metal brocade. The lines quote the great Iranian poet Hafez (d.1389), and they describe a blissful world of gardens, nightingales, roses and wine. This poetry was certainly chosen to suit the design and intended purpose of the carpet itself, to be a beautiful place to sit together with friends, in a private garden, reciting romantic verses: “Call for wine and scatter roses: what do you seek from Time?/ Thus spoke the rose at dawn. O nightingale, what say you?” The verses are emphasised by the scale of the fine calligraphy, by the use of silver brocade lettering against a dark red background, and by the distinctive formatting: each half-verse is placed in a cartouche, laid against a green border. The central medallion repeats the red and pink background, with a leafy design also overlaid with gleaming metal brocade.  
  
The central field of the carpet is filled with a rich floral landscape, organised in spiralling plant stems, with wonderfully large lotus flowers and leaves, all against a dark blue background. These are depicted to a more minute scale than the Persian poetry borders, and seem almost cramped. Among the foliage, there are perching green parrots and brown birds – these are presumably the nightingales from the poem. On closer inspection, the garden also contains Chinese-style dragons and lions (located in the four corners), and curling clouds which again echo Chinese design. One further detail rewards the careful observer: within many of the great blossoms and stems, the designer has hidden single animal heads.  
  
The carpet is attributed to the late sixteenth century, and the Safavid court of Iran (which was then based in Qazvin). At this time, carpet weaving had reached an extraordinarily high standard of design and technique, and the Safavid shahs commissioned the finest carpets as pious shrine donations, personal furnishings and suitably impressive diplomatic gifts to other states. This carpet has been linked with a very large group of royal gifts, sent by Shah Tahmasp to congratulate the newly-enthroned Ottoman Sultan Selim, in 1567. If confirmed, this account could explain an Istanbul provenance for this carpet, and many others like it.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O54294/the-salting-carpet-carpet-unknown/)
db2c46e8-d98a-5553-bcb2-dbc6c45d28f6.type: Carpet; medallion carpet with Persian inscriptions in metal brocade
db2c46e8-d98a-5553-bcb2-dbc6c45d28f6.method_for_datation: This famous carpet belongs to a larger carpet group which has long been debated by art historians. A diverse set was collectively named “Salting Carpets”, named after this example in the V&A, although they are now understood as a more complex cluster with a wider date-range. Today, scholarly consensus attributes the central group to late sixteenth-century Iran, on the basis of style and technical structure, and by association with recorded diplomatic gifts from Safavid Iran to the Ottoman Empire, including an embassy sent in 1567. Two carpets are known to have been in European collections (in Poland and Spain) by the seventeenth century, but the majority were not published until after the 1878 international exhibition in Paris: then the art-dealer Albert Goupil displayed several at his Galerie Orientale loan exhibition. George Salting bought this carpet from the London-based art-dealers Murray Marks and Durlacher Brothers, between 1880 and 1883. Although not proven, it is suggested that by 1878, these carpets had very recently come from Istanbul, having been sold out of the Ottoman palace stores. One explanation for this was the sudden instability in the city, which was under threat of the Russian-Turkish war of 1877-78: the British press certainly noted a sudden influx of other Turkish textiles on the art market as a direct result of that civilian fear. These carpets are exceptionally significant though, as Safavid court products of late sixteenth-century Iran.
db2c46e8-d98a-5553-bcb2-dbc6c45d28f6.method_for_provenance: The carpet is attributed to Iran because of its design and technical structure, which fits with late sixteenth-century production under the Safavids.
db2c46e8-d98a-5553-bcb2-dbc6c45d28f6.obtention: This carpet was initially on long term loan to the South Kensington Museum (today called the V&A), from 1883, and it would be over twenty years before the museum officially acquired it, in 1910. At that time, the owner was the art-collector George Salting, who loaned so much art (particularly Chinese porcelain) to the museum, that a dedicated gallery was organised just to display his collection. After Salting’s death in 1909, the collection was bequeathed to the V&A on a permanent basis. The carpet was discussed as “the Salting Carpet” in later scholarship (see above), but it was not the only carpet in the Salting Bequest.
db2c46e8-d98a-5553-bcb2-dbc6c45d28f6.bibliography: Mills, John, “The Salting Group: A History and a Clarification”, in Eiland, Murray L., and Pinner, Robert (eds.), *The Salting Carpets, Oriental Carpet and Textile Studies*, vol. 5, part 2, Danville, Ca: International Conference On Oriental Carpets, 1999: 1-17.

db2d3701-1c33-5bd1-b783-0045462bde9a.name: Carpet
db2d3701-1c33-5bd1-b783-0045462bde9a.description:
Carpets were one of the most important expressions of Persian art, especially during the reign of Shah ‘Abbas (1587‒1629), when they achieved the height of technical perfection and creative design. Made in leading workshops located in Tabriz, Kashan, Kerman and Isfahan, their floral and arabesque patterns with central medallions and figural scenes featuring animals contrasted with the geometric-designs that had characterised previous Persian carpets, as well as the Spanish and Turkish examples, which up until the mid-16th century had prevailed in Europe.  
These carpets were very expensive and usually had bigger dimensions when compared to their counterparts. This is the case for the large carpet fragment seen here, once part of a wide and impressive example measuring nearly six metres in length. Even though the two ends are now missing (they were cut off), the carpet still stands out for its extraordinary technical and artistic quality. One of its ends is currently in the Textile Museum in Washington, DC (Inv. No. R.33.4.6), after it was gifted by George Hewitt Meyers (1875‒1957); he, in turn, had purchased it from its previous, famous owner, the Armenian dealer of Islamic art, Dikran Kelekian (1868‒1951).  
The design of this “tree and animal” carpet combines the concept of the Persian pleasure garden with that of the royal hunting park. In addition, its wide-ranging palette, comprising 17 colours in total, shows the influence of Persian miniature painting. With a composition organised symmetrically, along its two centre lines, the field is made up of a small central medallion, with tall trees and flowering bushes inhabited by exotic birds and animals such as light brown lions and deer, blue *quilins* and multicoloured parrots. This is set against an elaborate network of scrolling vines, palmettes, blossoms, buds and leaves, on a red ground, which contrasts with the carpet’s emerald-green border.

dc216834-83df-57ab-85b5-a6e096fe4d23.name: Brocade Rug
dc216834-83df-57ab-85b5-a6e096fe4d23.description:
The decorations on 17th-century Cuenca rugs were inspired by patterns from 16th-century silk textiles and rugs. The Spanish rug in the Museum of Applied Arts’ collection belongs to the Brocade series. The field contains large, stylised palmettes in an axially symmetrical arrangement/composition on a blue ground. A vertical series of palmettes, each surmounted by a crown, runs along the central axis of the long, narrow rug and is enclosed by inclined palmettes. These are decorated with ivory, orange, light blue and green floral elements on a pale-yellow ground. The blue ground of the field is filled with a row of tiny, four-petalled rosettes. The border contains a chain created by horizontal "S" motifs connected by rings on a pale-yellow ground.  
  
At one time, lawyer Alfréd Perlmutter (1867–1929) also owned similarly decorated Spanish rug in Budapest. The whereabouts of the 520cm x 220cm rug are unknown; an photo of a detail of the rug can be found in the archives of the Museum of Applied Arts.  
  
A more richly patterned and larger version of this rug type can be found in the National Museum of Decorative Arts in Madrid (see Related Objects).

ddaf3343-7f3f-5a06-be2a-81bea6057953.name: Hunting Carpet with wild animals and lotus scrollwork
ddaf3343-7f3f-5a06-be2a-81bea6057953.description:
The design of this beautiful carpet follows a vertical symmetry, with right and left sides mirroring each other. The central field is dark red, and filled with two dynamic elements: pairs of wild animals and spiralling leafy stems of huge lotus flowers. The animals are depicted with a vibrant fluency, and include prowling tigers, crouching leopards, running wolves and more. Lions pin down bulls, while leopards pounce on mountain goats. More magical creatures are also to be found, with close inspection, hidden within the stylised plant forms. The surrounding border is on a white ground, with a series of single lotus flowers outlined in green, joined by a red half-palmette scroll. These bold motifs are filled with tiny details, including further flowers, Chinese-style clouds and animal heads.  
  
This belongs to a well-known group of carpets and carpet fragments from Iran, today dispersed in public and private collections around the world, usually called Hunting Carpets. These share the same structure, and often the same design cartoon. They are closely related to an exceptional pair of carpets known as the “Emperor Carpets” (in New York Metropolitan Museum and Vienna Museum für Angewandte Kunst), which are inscribed with Persian verses dedicated to “the king of the world”.  
Carpets like this confirm the design correlation with the arts of the book in Safavid Iran: these wild creatures all spring from the landscape scenes, border illumination and album-drawings of the sixteenth century, in which a minute and precise draughtsmanship was rated the height of skill. For virtuoso performance, Safavid painters such as Sultan Muhammad concealed miniature figures within the natural world, by painting tiny faces in rock formations and even tinier animal combats in the clouds. A similar delivery occurs in this carpet, where red-eyed lions and serpentine dragons crouch in the flower-heads.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O98838/carpet-unknown/)
ddaf3343-7f3f-5a06-be2a-81bea6057953.method_for_datation: Carpets in this group are usually attributed to the second half of the sixteenth century, because their refined designs relate to contemporary manuscript-painting, and because the group fits a proposed chronological development of Safavid carpets. None of this group is dated, however.
ddaf3343-7f3f-5a06-be2a-81bea6057953.method_for_provenance: The carpet is attributed to Iran because of its design and technical structure, which fits with sixteenth-century production.
ddaf3343-7f3f-5a06-be2a-81bea6057953.obtention: Purchased in 1894 from Jane Brunton. Despite its well-ordered appearance, this is a composite carpet, formed of three sections cut down from a much larger carpet. In 1890, the original carpet had been damaged in a fire, that occurred while it was being commercially cleaned, after which the owner sued the firm responsible. Parts of the carpet were then restored in late 1891 by Chiswick School of Arts and Crafts, and the composite carpet (the current object) was placed on loan at the South Kensington Museum (today the V&A). Later (in 1894) the owner finally sold it to the museum. She had already donated one other fragment to the museum, from the same damaged carpet, in 1892.

de2acd45-1832-5e18-b0aa-c9d4ba0f4467.name: The Schwarzenberg Paradise Park Carpet
de2acd45-1832-5e18-b0aa-c9d4ba0f4467.description:
This elaborately designed textile is known as a “Paradise Park” carpet due to its motifs including garden and animal imagery. Persian literature and art has long referenced the idea of heaven on earth, where a garden with water would bear lush plants and trees, often alongside animals both mythical and real. In this case, the term “Paradise Park” refers to a group of Persian carpets in particular that specifically combine motifs such as these in addition to a central medallion. High quality carpets from this group would have been made for members of the upper class in 16th-century Iran.  
With a central medallion followed by a cartouche and pendant on either end, this carpet is divided into four quarters with mirroring imagery. Flowers and vegetation including cypress trees cover the field of the carpet, while animals such as leopards, lions, birds and phoenixes additionally inhabit the space. Ducks appear within the central medallion while a pair of peacocks fill each cartouche. The border consists of birds, flowers and cloud band motifs.  
Two complete examples of similar “Paradise Park” carpets include the Mackay carpet in the Los Angeles County Museum of Art, and the Mantes carpet in the Louvre.

de8ab6ff-2c61-5ad0-8bc9-34983de3832a.name: Carpet with sickle leaf design
de8ab6ff-2c61-5ad0-8bc9-34983de3832a.description: In the 16th century, medallion carpets of Safavid Persia were much sought after, but by the century’s end and toward the beginning of the 17th century, floral motifs, spirals and palmettes began to gain appreciation. This long, narrow, “vase technique” carpet was probably produced in a Kerman (within southern Persia) workshop, during the reign of Shah ‘Abbas I (1571‒1629). Its field is made up of a dark-blue background, upon which is spread out an exuberant and dynamic vegetal pattern. This pattern is itself composed of several different planes of floral motifs in rich polychrome, palmettes and large sickle-shaped leaves. Compared to other examples of this type it has a narrower ground border, decorated with a frieze with spirals and flowers. In the centre of the field, there is an almost imperceptible inscription, probably the weaver’s signature, which is an extremely rare find in carpets from this period.
de8ab6ff-2c61-5ad0-8bc9-34983de3832a.obtention: Purchased by Calouste Gulbenkian in London in 1921

ded02074-f1e4-5a9b-ac59-eb95827bc2a3.name: *Afshari* carpet
ded02074-f1e4-5a9b-ac59-eb95827bc2a3.description:
Little is known about the rural rugs of Kirman so authors often describe them as *afshari* only for convenience and not as a precise label. The Afshari appear to be a minority population, although they may be the most important. They are a Turkic tribe with groups in the Caucasus, Turkey and Iran south of Kirman.  
Afshari products are seldom larger than about 170 x 200cm and they tend to be slightly more square-shaped. Some pieces have a striped kilim band at the ends. There are great variations in design, and many motifs found elsewhere are given a fresh approach, such as *boteh*, lozenge-shaped panels and medallion designs with flowers.  
In the central field on blue ground there are six “dragon palmette” motifs, six stylized floral motifs and numerous *boteh* and floret motifs. The “dragon palmette” motif is thought to derive from the “dragon and phoenix” motif of ancient Chinese origin. The palmette shape evolved from animal to vegetal. *Boteh* is the universal oriental rug design element. *Boteh* is Persian for “bush” and *buta* is Hindi for “flower”. It is thought to have originated in Kashmir in its curvilinear form. The form and content of *boteh*s are often distinctive for particular attributions and may be valuable clues to the origin of a weaving. The central field is framed with three borders. The main border resembles a floral meander on the blue background. The minor borders are also floral meanders on a white background. On the narrow sides the carpet has kilim finishes.
ded02074-f1e4-5a9b-ac59-eb95827bc2a3.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Persia; Afshari
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

e1cf8f81-916a-549e-812c-671899736546.name: Prayer rug
e1cf8f81-916a-549e-812c-671899736546.description: The prayer niche is merely suggested here by two diagonals that do not meet. The field of the niche features two hands and above them, a floral motif, which is repeated all over the purple ground of the spandrels. The spandrels and the three narrow borders with a rich decoration of *boteh*s or tiny flowers connected by scrolls are in sharp contrast to the large beige *mihrab* field. Popular belief associates the hand motif with the hand of Fatima, daughter of the Prophet Muhammad, and as such, it is often used to decorate talismans. Sometimes, the hand motif also appears on prayer rugs, mostly on Caucasian and Baluch rugs.

e1e13e80-ab15-5b9d-9fee-0d34b2a99f7f.name: *Die Madonna des Basler Bürgermeisters Jakob Meyer zum Hasen (Madonna of the Burgomaster of Basle, Jakob Meyer zum Hasen)*
e1e13e80-ab15-5b9d-9fee-0d34b2a99f7f.description: Oriental carpets appeared on paintings from the early Renaissance period onward, first on works of Italian and later of Dutch provenance. In most cases they served to focus attention on saints and holy figures. In this case, these are the Madonna and Child, at whose feet is a valuable, probably Anatolian woven carpet. The donor-the Mayor Jacob Meyer zum Hasen-and his family also kneel on the carpet, so that they also share in the atmosphere of holiness. At the same time, the carpet can be interpreted as signifying the wealth and status of the prosperous, influential mayor. The purely geometric pattern on the carpet shown here is so characteristic that the term "Holbein carpet" has become established as an art historical term.
e1e13e80-ab15-5b9d-9fee-0d34b2a99f7f.holder: Gemäldegalerie Alte Meister (Old Masters Picture Gallery), Dresden State Art Collections
e1e13e80-ab15-5b9d-9fee-0d34b2a99f7f.obtention: This altarpiece came into the Dresden Gallery from the collection of Zuan Delfino in Venice in 1743, when it was purchased by Francesco Graf Algarotti as an original painting by Holbein. During the Dresden Holbein exhibition in 1871 and the subsequent "Holbein Dispute", it was established that this painting is a forgery after the original painting known as the Darmstadt Madonna (now held in the Würth Collection, Schwäbisch Hall). The Dresden Madonna was painted by Bartholomäus Sarburgh in the years 1635-37.

e1e280d9-a6bf-5ed3-ad03-670c3679b743.name: 'Transylvanian' Double Niche Rug
e1e280d9-a6bf-5ed3-ad03-670c3679b743.description:
A characteristic type of Ottoman rugs is the "Transylvanian" double niche carpet. Several variants of the type fashionable for over two centuries are known. Its common feature is the hexagonal medallion filling the central field created by mirroring the original *mihrab* (prayer niche) of the traditional prayer rug across the central axis. This rug of symmetrical design was particularly popular in Transylvania where it was used as table or bed cover and wall hanging. The name "Transylvanian" refers to the place of frequent occurrence and not to the place of origin.  
  
This is a representative of the second period of "Transylvanian" double niche rugs. Its red field is filled by an ornate floral-foliate scroll typical of the early (First) period, with a mosque lamp decorating each peak of the 'Transylvanian' double *mihrab* niche). What makes this rug special is its border. Unlike other "Transylvanian" rugs, this consists of triangles of alternating orientation and colour on a white field. Unlike other "Transylvanian" rugs, this consists of triangles of alternating orientation and colour on a white field.

e201681f-2ba1-5a3b-83d3-a717dc315fb0.name: Caucasus *soumak*
e201681f-2ba1-5a3b-83d3-a717dc315fb0.description:
*Soumak* weaving is a form of weft-wrapping. The weft thread goes forward in front of a group of warp threads and then backward behind a smaller group. The weft forms a colourful pattern.  
*Soumak*s include large pieces intended for floor use as well as small saddlebags and animal trappings. Most of the Caucasian soumaks were made in northern Caucasus. Red-field *soumak*s in a relatively narrow range of designs, with two, three, or four medallions, were woven in the Kuba district.  
This northern Caucasus soumak is one of the three soumaks in the Museum of Arts and Crafts holdings. It is a red field soumak with three large double octagram medallions. Inner octagrams have three small octagons with a star motif on the blue background. Outer octagrams have various motifs (S, star and small circles) on light blue, green and dark blue backgrounds. Between large medallions there are pairs of small square medallions with geometric motifs on a yellow background. The leaf and calyx main border is common through the Middle East. It is a universal border and it also may be called, “leaf and wine glass”. Minor borders are *laleh abbasi* (Abbasi tulip, very common minor border through the Mideast), octagrams on a white background and running dog (the weave form of this motif has various frequencies and amplitudes; the Vitruvian scroll described it as “running dog” and it was often used in ancient Roman architecture) on a dark blue background.
e201681f-2ba1-5a3b-83d3-a717dc315fb0.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: soumak; Caucasus; medahil
materials: Wool; soumak weaving

e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.name: The *Annunciation*
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.description:
The beginning of the second quarter of the 16th century marks the emergence of the representation of “Lotto” knotted carpets in Portuguese painting. These carpets, their name derived from the Venetian artist Lorenzo Lotto, who represented them in his paintings, are characterised by their geometrical, angular aesthetics lined up in a repetitive scheme. The Lotto carpets of Turkish origin probably reached the high-end Portuguese market through the Venetian export trade.  
The presence of these carpets in Portuguese interiors is mostly evidenced through representations in paintings, in particular those of the court painter Gregório Lopes (active 1513‒† 1550). In this representation of the *Annunciation*, the Virgin Mary stands on a Turkish carpet with a yellow, meandering arabesque pattern on a red field and a pseudo-*kufic* border. It’s relevance in the painting is reinforced by the artist, for he captures the very moment when the Archangel, as if suspended in time, places one foot on the carpet, and thus enters the sacred domain of the Virgin Mother. As such, the carpet is used as a device in the painter’s masterful depiction to mark the passage from one space to another, as though through a gateway.  
Interestingly, the opposing end of the same carpet is represented in another of Gregorio Lopes’s paintings, the *Presentation of the Head of Saint John the Baptist*, of around 1539 to 1541, a painting encompassing a ceremonial banquet in an aristocratic setting. In the *Annunciation* the artist takes the contrary approach, emptying the space of the splendour of the banquet, and replacing pageantry with a bare, peaceful interior befitting of the unfolding scene.
e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.method_for_datation: Technical information provided by José Alberto Seabra de Carvalho

e2e87d5b-1f57-5af5-9864-f84516f62cdb.author: Ana Kol
keywords: painting; Annunciation; Portugal; Gregório Lopes; Lotto carpet
materials: Oil on oak panel

e438f7f3-f994-5b2c-ac3c-df61c9c9dbff.name: Vertical fixed-heddle loom
e438f7f3-f994-5b2c-ac3c-df61c9c9dbff.description: A simple loom composed of two bars between which the warps are stretched. This type of loom is called a “back strap loom” because one bar is attached to a fixed object, and the other to the weaver usually as a strap around the back. The weaver leans back and their body weight is used to provide tension on the loom. To open the shed, the weaver relaxes tension on the warps and raises the heddles. The other shed is opened by simply drawing the shed roll toward the weaver. Both simple and complex textiles can be woven on this loom.
e438f7f3-f994-5b2c-ac3c-df61c9c9dbff.method_for_datation: Early 20th century treadle loom weavers from Syria and Palestine settled in Jordan. They produced rugs, saddle bags and other textiles.

e4957137-fe26-5b45-a98b-c7918535c481.name: Textile fragment
e4957137-fe26-5b45-a98b-c7918535c481.description: Textiles constitute a major part of the Montreal Museum of Fine Arts’ collection of Islamic art. The decorative arts had great symbolic and social importance in the Islamic world. The skills of the weavers of the time have rarely been equalled, and this fragment is among the pieces that demonstrate the complexity and innovation of their techniques. Figurative designs, which were extremely popular in 16th-century Persia, appeared on garments and palace furnishings, as well as in religious and funeral ceremonies. In this fragment of reversible double cloth depicting “Boats at Sea”, two fabrics have been produced simultaneously, one over the other, following a repeat pattern of remarkable detail: sailing boats with four sailors alternating with simple rowing boats carrying three figures, all on a sea filled with fish and ducks. The vertical masts create the impression of stability, while the diagonal placement of the rowing boats suggests a rocking motion. The red motifs lay on a silver-thread ground.

e5774d57-ae8b-5789-8ba3-a24fe78f0b1f.name: Mudéjar carpet
e5774d57-ae8b-5789-8ba3-a24fe78f0b1f.description:
This carpet is a fine example of the production of workshops of southern Castile and which were most probably sold in Alcaraz. Manufactured in the 15th century by weavers of the Mudéjar population (i.e. the Muslim population living in Spain after the Reconquista), these carpets were integrating Renaissance and Byzantine designs with already known Islamic designs.  
This specific carpet is missing one of its original edges, which explains its irregular shape.  
It is composed of three octagonal roundels decorated with stylised designs of arabesque, what has become in the 20th century the "Holbein design". Such name was given in reference to the well-known paintings of Hans Holbein the Younger and paintings of various 15th- and 16th- century artists where Anatolian and Syrian carpets of this kind were represented.  
A decorative band of geometrical patterns surrounds the central motifs. The bottom part bears a band of repeating animals, maybe lions.  
Spanish carpets demonstrate, with other objects produced in the 15th century, the trade expansion in the Mediterranean, which designs were influenced by textiles and ceramics from western Anatolia. Moreover, Spanish carpets were exported to France and Italy from the 13th to the 15th century.
e5774d57-ae8b-5789-8ba3-a24fe78f0b1f.method_for_datation: This carpet has been dated based on stylistic comparisons with other known Mudéjar carpets from the same period
e5774d57-ae8b-5789-8ba3-a24fe78f0b1f.method_for_provenance: This carpet has been stylistically attributed to Alcaraz, Spain based on comparisons with further examples
