e6710518-4898-5028-a985-a35bd74bd8a8.name: Konya prayer rug with pelt
e6710518-4898-5028-a985-a35bd74bd8a8.description: Rugs with animal skins are a specialised category within Turkish carpet weaving. The earliest examples are seen in Anatolia from the 17th century. This rug has three borders. The first and third borders are identical. A sequential hooked “s” motif on white ground fills the interior. The main border is in the form of a band, with blue *Rumi* on red ground arranged in two winding rows. The branches of these *Rumi* are enriched with tiny palmettes. The animal pelt is stretched in a way to form the prayer niche of this rug with a red main ground. A ram’s horn motif on the top part of the spotted pelt design is on white ground that resembles red and brown panther spots. The same motif is found on the bottom short edge of the prayer rug.
e6710518-4898-5028-a985-a35bd74bd8a8.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts
e6710518-4898-5028-a985-a35bd74bd8a8.method_for_datation: The analyses of the material and the technique used for weaving the rug and the motifs seen on main ground and borders.

e6e39016-a178-5040-afd2-919c26cefc8e.name: Fertek‒Niğde Prayer Rug
e6e39016-a178-5040-afd2-919c26cefc8e.description: There are several towns around the Niğde Province including Taşpınar, Maden, Yahyalı, Yeşilhisar, Karapinar, Karaman, Bor and Fertek which were important rug production centres. Niğde was the regional market place, and rugs produced in these towns became known as “Niğde rugs”. This is an excellent example of a Fertek rug. It is distinguished from other Niğde rugs by simple but nice looking floral motifs. The head band of the prayer rug is decorated with stylised tulips. Eight point star motifs appear on the niche corners.

e781ed99-0334-5a17-84a6-d65ff343a949.name: *Allegory of Sight* (Venus and Cupid in a Picture Gallery)
e781ed99-0334-5a17-84a6-d65ff343a949.description:
From a series of paintings called the “The Five Senses”, this painting by Jan Brueghel the Younger is known as *The Allegory of Sight*. It displays a virtual treasure trove of Paintings, Sculpture, Scientific tools and more. At the center of the piece is Venus examining herself in a handheld mirror. A beautiful Turkish Carpet is draped over the table to the left of Venus. The fact that such a carpet is displayed among such a treasure trove of expensive and exquisite objects shows its importance.  
This painting shows an imaginary collection of art, scientific instruments, and curiosities of nature. It belongs to a popular genre of pictures developed by Antwerp artists in the 1600s that portray the cabinets, or rooms, collectors filled with art and wonders. The inclusion of Venus examining herself in a mirror reveals that this scene also doubles as an allegory of sight, and was part of a series of works depicting the five senses.  
Though an allegory, the scene contains artwork and objects based on real examples, including paintings by famous Flemish artist Peter Paul Rubens (1577–1640) and Jan Brueghel’s father, Jan Brueghel the Elder. The ancient and modern sculptures as well as the array of vessels, jewels, coins, measuring instruments, and shells strewn around the room can be matched with surviving items.  
The remarkable works depicted by Jan the Younger illustrate the types of objects the well to do collected in the 1600s to demonstrate their status and knowledge. Within the space around you are works of art and nature that represent the varied categories of collecting popular at this time.

e787c7a9-3757-59d5-b969-eea67ff8bc13.name: Arraiolos carpet
e787c7a9-3757-59d5-b969-eea67ff8bc13.description:
Throughout the 17th century, the oriental pattern that characterised the pieces from the early production of Arraiolos carpets was progressively replaced by a traditional standard, though one that also derives from the Persian medallion- and animal-based carpets. Known as “animal pattern” carpets, due to the preponderance and protagonism of their animalistic motifs, this type of carpet best divulges and characterises the Arraiolos carpet-weaving industry of the 18th century.  
In this carpet, the large central, triple, concentric, and radiant medallion stands out, being that the last frame, with its blue background, is decorated with small cocks and Caucasian palm flowers. In the remaining field, organised according to a quarter-plan layout, the decoration is made up of vases of carnations and various animals. At each corner of the central field are grandiose and colourful peacocks, holding flowering branches in their beaks. In front of these elements appear rabbits, whereas above them there are deer, flanked by cypresses. Other small animals – parrots, ducks, birds of paradise and small dogs and cockerels – and tinted flowers fill the remaining space.  
With a green background, the border is decorated with continuous and zigzagging branches, whose stalks sprout small flowers and leaves, upon which are poised miniscule birds.

e7a1a909-9452-5c02-be6a-c958cd0e8d05.name: Chelaberd (fragment)
e7a1a909-9452-5c02-be6a-c958cd0e8d05.description: Although the Chelaberd is clearly a type of rug from the Karabagh region, it is still sometimes referred to today as the so-called Sunburst Kazak - a trade name that alludes to the neighbouring Kazak region. The Dresden fragment is dominated by a massive medallion that fills the field. At the top, facing the head, the base of another medallion can be seen. A narrow-dotted line runs horizontally between the two. In contrast to numerous pieces with three or more medallions, no secondary motifs fill the field, the border here is narrow, and the wool and colours are of outstanding quality. It is a powerful piece, probably made for personal use. It is entirely plausible that this carpet originally had no more than two medallions, although it cannot be said with absolute certainty. In the 1920s, Heinrich Jakoby already pointed out similarities between the characteristic Chelaberd medallion ("sunburst medallion") and medallions on large-format Caucasian workshop carpets of the 18th century. Later on, the design-historical forerunner of the rural-village Chelaberd was identified in it.
e7a1a909-9452-5c02-be6a-c958cd0e8d05.holder: Museum für Völkerkunde Dresden (Ethnological Museum Dresden), Dresden State Art Collections
e7a1a909-9452-5c02-be6a-c958cd0e8d05.obtention: Purchased from Dresden painter Wilhelm Müller (1928–99) from his private Collection in 1978. About 10 years from 1979 onwards Müller collected oriental rugs, carpets and flat weaves for the Ethnographic Museum of Dresden in the Dresden-Leipzig-Berlin region to secure remaining rural and nomadic textiles from the 19th and early 20th century. Textiles were acquired from private households, private and state shops and even from demolition sites or waste containers.

e8943284-2319-51c2-91bf-636b5313c45d.name: ‘Transylvanian’ prayer rug
e8943284-2319-51c2-91bf-636b5313c45d.description: The term “Siebenbürger” or “Transylvanian” rug recurs frequently in Oriental carpet literature. It is used to designate 17th- and 18th-century rugs preserved in large numbers in the Saxon churches of Transylvania, whose provenance has not been yet definitively established. Certain experts have indicated Transylvania as a possible source, whereas according to more research that is more recent they were produced in western Anatolia. Many “Transylvanian” rugs feature the *mihrab* design, typical of prayer rugs; in most cases though, the niche becomes a purely decorative element devoid of its original meaning, a fashionable motif popular with carpet buyers outside the Islamic world. This rug is a fine example of exquisite craftsmanship. The white field of the *mihrab* is decorated with floral motifs intertwined with geometric scrolls; a mosque lamp is hanging from the apex. Above the red spandrels decorated with similar geometric scrolls, a narrow rectangular panel features alternating tulips and cypress trees. Polygonal cartouches alternating with octagons fill the main border.

e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.name: Panel of *azulejos* with a carpet composition
e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.description:
The use of patterns in 17th-century Portuguese *azulejos* allowed a number of solutions for covering the architectural surfaces of palaces, convents and churches. Because the Portuguese used *azulejos* to cover surfaces in all areas, including vaults and ceilings, it was necessary to create larger modules for patterns otherwise people below would only be able to see smudges of colour instead of the motifs in the patterns.  
This panel of *azulejos* shows how the patterns were used with frames, which emphasise the proximity between them and the carpets that sometimes inspired them. However, in a panel like this one, we can see the advantage of *azulejos* over textiles: the bright reflection of its surface, the eternal shine of its colours that never fade and the clever solutions to adjusting to the architectural surfaces it was covering. The module of this pattern is a 4 x 4, which implies that 16 *azulejos* are required in order to achieve a single motif that can be repeated to infinity. In this case, the decoration is composed of a four-lobe design motif with acanthus leaves at the corners, which allow a connection with the other *azulejos*. The frame of this composition is achieved by two different solutions: a half *azulejos*, in Portuguese known as a *friso* or frieze, with a “saw’s teeth” motif, positioned in the extremities of the frame. The second element is a double *azulejos* element, known in Portuguese as a *barra* or stripe, with the decoration known as “hammers”, which composes the larger area of the frame and gives a dynamic structure to the panel.
e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.method_for_datation: Stylistic analysis: in 17th-century production of *azulejos* in northern Portugal, the colours tend to be denser, with harsh greyish blues and a less bright yellow with an orange hue.
e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.method_for_provenance: The National Tile Museum holds a large number of *azulejos* of unknown origin, many gathered during the period of the destruction of the convents and palaces in the late 19th century, in the aftermath of the abolition of the religious orders in 1834.
e8b0644e-e003-52a3-99a3-463ef49e34cd.obtention: Probably salvaged during demolition of an unknown building where they had once been applied

e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.name: Niche carpet
e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.description: This carpet is among the most famous in the Berlin collection. As early as 1871 it was acquired by Wilhelm von Bode for the painter Heinrich von Angeli, but it was not until 1905 that Bode was able to buy it from his heirs and donate it to the Museum. Von Angeli and some of his colleagues depicted this carpet several times. The charm of this carpet lies in its depth of colour, its high, dense pile and the impressive sheen of the wool. On a dark blue ground, two red-ground spandrels are separated in the form of niches by a strong white line. Unusually, the spandrels blend into each other at their tops. The lower half of the niche field is filled with a light blue cloud band, in whose arc a large blossom forms a fixed point. This cloud band is reminiscent of delimitations in the so-called keyhole or Bellini carpets. Their often angular arch forms are associated with fountains, which were needed for the ritual cleansing before prayer. Because of the Persian appearance of the blossoms, the origin of the cloud band from East Asian cultures, and the use of depressed warps, this carpet has occasionally been ascribed to Persia. However, not only the colour palette and the reference to the keyhole motif, but also the use of a symmetrical knot, speak in favour of a location in Turkey.
e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.holder: Museum of Islamic Art at the Pergamon Museum
e9c5dea2-d0d2-56ce-8e1a-0301e49ff152.method_for_datation: The carpet has been radio carbon dated. The carpet has been dated on stylistic analysis of its pattern, due to its colours and knot-technique

e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.name: Prayer rug with a row of niches.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.description:
This is one of three 'row' carpets of an early date in the collection of the Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts which have survived from the 9th / 15th century to the present day. The composition has been organised into *mihrab* niches which provide a distinct space for worshippers in the mosque to pray in well-defined rows. It has survived as a fragment; the original dimensions of the complete rug are not known. The ground is white (cream). Within the sections outlined by dark-blue borders are five *mihrab* niches, two of them green and three dark-blue. The influence of the monumental *kufic* borders of AH 7th- / AD 13th-century Konya rugs of the Anatolian Seljuq period can be seen in the design of the rug's *mihrab*s. Each of the *mihrab* niches are crowned with a stylised ram's-head motif, while their corners have corner-pieces with dark-blue chequer patterns and red 'stalactites' hanging off them. In each *mihrab* there are three mosque-lamp motifs, one in the centre and two at the sides, hanging downwards. Four of the *mihrab* niches have diamond-motifs in their lower section, ornamented with motifs like arrowheads pointing in four directions. In contrast, the central niche has a diamond-motif in its lower section which is plain, as if the element of symmetry is meant to show the centre of the prayer rug.  
  
The pattern reminiscent of a double ram's-head in blue on a red ground, while it makes up the main border, is at the same time used to separate the rows from each other.  
  
The motifs on the narrow yellow-ground border which surrounds the main border resemble a chain of plaited yellow and blue rosettes. The geometric motifs carry on Seljuq tradition, especially their arrowhead-like corners which resemble *kufic* script. These, as well as the mosque-lamp and eight-pointed star motifs, prepare the way for the transition to Ottoman prayer rugs.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.short_description: The earliest Ottoman prayer rugs with multiple niches are dated to the AH 9th / AD 15th century. They were produced for use in the mosque to help the congregation to pray in straight lines. The prayer rugs (*seccade*) of this period with their geometric compositions and *kufic* borders are a transition to classical Ottoman prayer rugs.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.method_for_datation: Chemical analysis carried out on the original dyes used for this rug, together with analysis of the motifs and composition, point to a date of production in the 9th / 15th century.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.method_for_provenance: Rug-making is not widespread in the Eskişehir-Sivrihisar region. Moreover, in this period Konya was the most important centre for rug production, and since this example continues the Seljuq tradition, it is thought that it was woven in the Konya region.
e9f4c38d-048f-5665-96a4-f4e9444dc22f.obtention: The rug was transferred from the Sheikh Baba Yusuf Mosque in 1911 as a result of a countrywide initiative to collect up artworks in order to prevent theft and plunder. The aforementioned mosque was built in 903 / 1498 in Sivrihisar, one of the first large sites settled by the Turcomans (Türkmen). Sheikh Baba Yusuf (d. 918 / 1512) was a religious scholar descended from Haci Bayram Veli (753–834 / 1352–1430), founder of the Bayramiyya branch of Sufism.

ea0d55a7-8624-5566-bd62-40cadfcf4f89.name: A 'Lotto' rug probably Ushak
ea0d55a7-8624-5566-bd62-40cadfcf4f89.description: A particular group of the endless repeat patterned early Ottoman pieces is represented by the “Lotto” carpets, named after an Italian painter Lorenzo Lotto (1480–1557). The "Lotto" design was a development of the "small pattern Holbein" design, opening it up to become an overall pattern. The design possibly developed from the much earlier Turkish tradition of two-tone overall lattice carpets, such as those of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries. The largest examples with this border design tend to have complete cartouches in the border while the medium sized and smaller examples have the part-cartouches, as seen here. Ch. G. Ellis distinguishes three main trends of the "Lotto" pattern: 'Anatolian', 'Kilim' and 'Ornamented'. This "Lotto" carpet was in the property of a noble Italian family.
ea0d55a7-8624-5566-bd62-40cadfcf4f89.provenance: West Anatolia, Turkey; Possibly received as a diplomatic gift by Pope Alexander VII and then by descent

ea2151d0-0e88-5675-84d3-bf755cc53b12.name: The 'Simonetti' Carpet
ea2151d0-0e88-5675-84d3-bf755cc53b12.short_description: The Simonetti Carpet, so named for its twentieth century Italian owner, was woven in Cairo toward the end of Mamluk rule or shortly after the city’s Ottoman conquest in 1517. The use of insect-derived red, blue, green, and yellow dyes with little or no undyed white, together with the s-spun wool, rarely found outside of Egypt, points to Mamluk production, although the precise date of production is not known. The five compartment design makes this carpet one of the largest of its type. Known for dazzling visual effects produced by jewel-like tones, geometric forms and radiating designs, Mamluk carpets bear motifs such as three-petalled flowers, cypress trees and papyrus plants that resemble tiny umbrellas. Carpets like this one figured significantly in Mediterranean commerce and appear in Venetian paintings as early as the sixteenth century.

eb467c80-2eef-577d-9d53-c8374d7eff59.name: Central Anatolian carpet
eb467c80-2eef-577d-9d53-c8374d7eff59.description:
Anatolian rug-weaving areas are conventionally divided into western, central and eastern regions. The central region spans from Konya to Shivas and includes great central Anatolian high plains north of the Toros Mountain. It is one of the main areas of carpet production in Turkey and the main weaving centres are in Konya, Ladik, Kirşehir, Mucur, Karapinar, Taşpinar and Sivas.  
Compared to rugs from the western part of Anatolia, less is known about the early rugs from central Anatolia. The spread of common design features makes it at times difficult to determine which pieces are from this region.  
In the central field, on a red background there is one-and-a-half large medallions and four smaller rectangular medallions. One half of the central octagon as well as four rectangular medallions are decorated with hooks and ram's horns. The central field is framed with two borders, and a stripe at the top and the bottom. The main border is a geometric serrated leaf quatrefoil border on a white background. This formal geometric border of four-leaf cluster is probably related to leaf and calyx border on Caucasian rugs and carpets. The stripes resemble a lappets border which is common throughout Anatolia. Europeans term this motif “lappets” after ear flaps on caps. The lappet border has been linked to battle pennants. Most frequently it occurs as strips at the top and bottom of long rugs and yastiks outside the regular border.

ebe4dfb5-2c91-5b48-9947-a44e4359f085.name: Daghestan Prayer Rug
ebe4dfb5-2c91-5b48-9947-a44e4359f085.description:
A 19th century Caucasian prayer rug with a knotted pile. Its directional design consists of a single-plane lattice design crowned by an angled arch with a pointed summit, laid out on an ivory-coloured background and framed by a wide red and blue border.  
  
The lattice design of the centre field contains diamond-shaped compartments, each of which holds a single multi-coloured flower. The horizontally arranged rows of multi-coloured flowers contain repeats of three flowers, symmetrically distributed. The flower repeat arrangement is staggered across the succeeding rows, creating a diagonal uniformity of colour and shape distribution. Below the right edge of the prayer niche arch, and to the right side of the centre-field, near the edge of the border, is a figure of a quadruped, possibly a dog, rendered in pink and yellow with black outlines. This little animal, with its long curled up tale and long stretched back ears, has been inserted in place of a flower.  
  
The border of the carpet consists of a dark green/blue background overlaid with a red scroll of Arabesque design – a version of the Caucasian border scrolls inspired by Arabic *kufic* script.  
  
Such carpets are made for use in performing the daily prayers in Islamic culture. The arch end of the carpet indicates the side upon which the worshiper lays his forehead in prostration.

ed3194db-de43-56cf-8454-e27c827fa5ec.name: Masnad
ed3194db-de43-56cf-8454-e27c827fa5ec.description:
The carpets used at Islamic courts were most often produced by court workshops and intended to convey very different messages from those found in private homes. Court carpets belonged to the whole ensemble of objects that helped assert the right to rule and shaped the ruler’s public image, namely the throne, crown, royal ceremonial robe, regal standards with their pennants, scepter, and ring.  
  
Spread either in front of or beneath the ruler or religious leader, a carpet, like a throne, served to designate the privileged space around the most highly esteemed individual and to present him regally to his audience. As a special object, it helped to maintain the dignity and authority of the ruler enthroned upon it.  
  
Through its design, a carpet is clearly isolated from its surroundings by its well-defined borders. It immediately creates an independent space within its own environment. Thus the design of the carpet frames and emphasizes the individual who sits on it and serves almost as an aura filling the immediate space around him.  
  
Stepping on this carpet was possible only with the ruler’s permission and was regarded as a great honour, an act of mutual confidence, obedience, or the subject's unconditional support of the ruler. In some cases it recalls the act of bestowing a robe of honour upon the most loyal subject.
ed3194db-de43-56cf-8454-e27c827fa5ec.method_for_datation: Stylistic analyses, comparative materials, and historical documentary evidence.
ed3194db-de43-56cf-8454-e27c827fa5ec.method_for_provenance: Design analyses and comparison with carpets sharing similar design and structural characteristics.

ed3415be-acc6-52c8-ac71-5af9793c367b.name: Medallion carpet fragments
ed3415be-acc6-52c8-ac71-5af9793c367b.description:
Two 16th century Safavid pile carpet fragments from a very large classic Persian medallion carpet, showing parts of the centre-field and part of one of the long borders of the carpet. The background colour of the field is a wine red. Imposed on it is a vegetal network of floral arabesque stem patterns baring rosettes and palmettes. Over this vegetal stem network are placed multi-coloured medallions, with a large yellow one dominating the centre, and smaller ivory coloured and dark-blue coloured pendent-like cartouches at either end of it. The large yellow medallion holds a red star-shape cartouche in the centre and turquoise blue and dark blue cartouches radiating out. All the cartouches are filled with multi-coloured vegetal-stem-and-palmette arabesque compositions. The border has a dark blue background and is decorated with two intertwined leaf-stem scrolls, one turquoise and one yellow.  
  
The smaller of the two fragments, no. 9.28, consists of two large lobed cartouches, one with a dark blue background and one with a turquoise background, on a the yellow field of the central medallion. Each of the dark and light blue and the yellow areas is filled with a vegetal network of multi-coloured floral arabesque patterns baring rosettes and palmettes.  
  
The large yellow medallion and its pendant cartouches is reminiscent of the “shamsa” medallions painted in illuminated manuscripts and on book covers. The term shamsa, from the Arabic shams, which means sun, here used to name this type of radiating arabesque medallion.

ee5decc1-7f36-5e2a-8dd2-1ecc8f338d3d.name: Carpet
ee5decc1-7f36-5e2a-8dd2-1ecc8f338d3d.description:
Carpet of the Brocade series.  
Field: It is separated from the outer border by a narrow line.  
Border: It has only one border linked by vegetal motifs and with winged characters of a classical nature  
This carpet consists of a woollen warp and weft along with knots in dark blue, light blue, red, green, white and yellow.  
It is a heraldic carpet, *repostero* kind, made with the Spanish knot technique and belongs to the Brocade series. Despite the presence of classical and vegetal motifs linked to the Renaissance period, the production of the carpet was most likely carried out in a non-sophisticated workshop, since the insertion of the heraldic motif in the field is not properly solved. The coat of arms seems to imitate that of the knights of the Order of Santiago due to the presence of scallops as well as the cross-sword attributed to the order that appears behind the edges.  
If we analyse the composition of the field through its axis of symmetry, we can see that the individual decorative elements, whilst similar, are not identical -neither in size, form, nor colour. The change in colour in the upper third of the carpet does not respond to any decorative criteria and makes us think that there was a failure in the workshop itself when the wool of the red and blue colours was finished, being replaced by other colours. This is the most reasonable explanation for such an aggressive colour change, but if it were disassembled it could also perhaps be said that it was due to being composed of different fragments.  
The motif of the winged children that decorates the border is one linked to the art of the European Renaissance and is unusual in Spanish textiles. In addition to this, the high knot density and the central heraldic motif shows that the carpet was commissioned for a certain person. However, carelessness in its design and execution emphasises that it did not belong to the production area of the Kingdom of Murcia, which at this time maintained a high standard for carpet production. However, there may be influences in workshops in the nearby Levantine area of the Iberian Peninsula.  
It does not retain the original selvedges and is clearly defaced on its lower side. It comes from the old Weissberger collection.

ee8b65ca-2c80-547f-8baa-4663f8cc8a85.name: Pashmina carpet
ee8b65ca-2c80-547f-8baa-4663f8cc8a85.description:
The Mughal emperors were keen patrons of the arts who demanded extremely high standards of workmanship from the artists who worked for them. Such rigour was present in the Imperial palace itself, which had several workshops for paintings, carpets, textiles and decorative arts in general.  
Artists both from Persia and of European origins were called to work in these workshops. Documentary references to Indian carpets frequently appear in the writings of European chroniclers and travellers who had passed through this territory since the 16th century.  
Examples of such individuals include the Portuguese writer Duarte Barbosa (1480‒1521), the Dutch trader and the Portuguese Viceroy and secretary in Goa, Jan Huyghen van Linschoten (1563‒1611), between 1583 and 1588, and the French navigator François Pyrard de Laval (1578‒1623).  
Although this object is a fragment, which consists of less than half of a carpet, it is the largest known piece and one of the most important examples of its type, made with pashmina wool and silk. The use of luxury materials such as pashmina and silk, which enabled weavers to execute minute detailing, places this variety of carpet among the finest of those produced in the Kashmiri and Lahore workshops within the first half of the 17th century. Aware of the carpet’s importance and, also, because of its fragility, the connoisseur and collector Calouste Gulbenkian had long exhibited it protected behind glass in his Paris house next to the cabinets containing Iznik pottery. Like other Indian carpets, this piece, with its swirling arabesque pattern, reveals a Persian influence. This is made evident in the polychrome floral decoration and scrolling vines, themselves set upon a cherry-red field, and in the yellow border also decorated with arabesques and flowers. This said, the naturalistic flower designs, the strong colours and the large differently coloured segmented leaves that fill the field, remain characteristically Indian.

eed63784-ee48-5fbc-bc2a-5f2e487f3db3.name: Vase Carpet
eed63784-ee48-5fbc-bc2a-5f2e487f3db3.description:
This splendid carpet is laid out with a floral design of surprising complexity, against a pink-red field. The overall design is a triple-plane lattice, composed of three independently-composed trellis grids of different colours: blue-black, thorny white and leafy blue. These three grid systems are not immediately apparent because of the grand scale of the multiple flowerheads and medallions along each trellis. Furthermore, “behind” the three trellis systems are flowering plants and shrubs, also distracting the eye. This ordered design is greatly enlivened by the wonderful detail and variety in the colourful flowers and plants. Towards the top of the central axis, the white trellis features a striped vase of flowers, also repeated in the lower borders as “half-vases”: this motif gives its name to the wider category of Vase Carpets. The upper border is missing, and the original carpet was certainly even longer.  
  
The carpet belongs to a well-known group generally attributed to Kirman in southeast Iran, and to the seventeenth century. These are referred to as “Vase technique” carpets, as they often include a vase motif in their complex lattice designs, but more uniformly, the group shares the same triple-weft technical structure. There are many examples of Kirman vase carpets (and fragments) in national collections across the world. This carpet was bought in 1897 from the estate of the British designer, poet, craftsman and socialist William Morris, who supported the South Kensington Museum (today the V&A) with collections advice over many years, and was a formidable influence on the institution. During his lifetime, Morris had kept this large carpet hanging lengthways on the wall of his home, with the top section overhanging from the ceiling rather like a medieval canopy. He enjoyed it as one of his household furnishing, but more specifically, the complex planar design must have pleased him as a designer.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O98834/carpet-unknown/)
eed63784-ee48-5fbc-bc2a-5f2e487f3db3.method_for_datation: “Vase technique” carpets only very rarely include dated inscriptions in their woven designs. Importantly, one very fine example was accessioned to the royal palace of Jaipur in August 1632, according to the palace archives. This valuable piece of data allows scholars to attribute to the whole group to the seventeenth century, with confidence.
eed63784-ee48-5fbc-bc2a-5f2e487f3db3.method_for_provenance: This carpet group was attributed to Kirman on the grounds that the unusual technical structure was still in use by Kirmani weavers, suggesting a direct continuity in this specific craft practice.
eed63784-ee48-5fbc-bc2a-5f2e487f3db3.obtention: Purchased in 1897 from the estate of William Morris.

eeefe08e-b05d-5b9e-a805-c6fd43d4fe03.name: Rug.
eeefe08e-b05d-5b9e-a805-c6fd43d4fe03.description:
An Ushak carpet of the AH 10th / AD 16th century; the warp and the weft of which are of wool. The weaving technique used is the 'Turkish double knot', known as the Gördes knot. The rug is in two pieces.  
  
On a red ground, arranged on a zigzag axes, are motifs known as *chintamani* or *pelenk* (leopard-spots or tiger-stripes motif). Black and dark-blue *chintamani* motifs with blue contours are arranged together with yellow tiger stripes with black contours, according to the principle of infinity. These motifs have Buddhist roots and show Far Eastern influence; they appear on the clothing of figures in the caves at Turfan in the Xinjiang province of China, probably painted in the AH 1st–3rd- / AD 7th–9th -century.  
  
The *chintamani* or *pelenk* motifs were used as symbols of power and authority, entering Ottoman palace art with the capture of Tabriz, following the victory won at Chaldiran in AH 920 / AD 1514 by Sultan Selim I (r. AH 918–27 / AD 1512–20). From the AH 10th–12th / AD 16th–18th century the motifs are seen in all the decorative arts made by artists directed by the Ottoman court, seen especially in textiles, ceramics, book-bindings and woodwork; they were most popular under Sultan Selim II (r. AH 974–82 / AD 1566–74).  
  
The perimeter of this carpet has two narrow borders and one broad border. The first narrow border consists of a dark-blue ground between an orange-red strip, with blue and red dots and a red line. It is filled with tulip and carnation motifs between interweaving red stems. The main border is decorated with enormous lotuses, rose-petals, and stylised flower and leaf motifs in light- and dark-red with brown contours. The outermost border is filled with dark-blue, blue, and cream-coloured tulip and carnation motifs amid interweaving stems on a red background.
eeefe08e-b05d-5b9e-a805-c6fd43d4fe03.short_description: This rug was woven at Uşak for the Sultan Selim Mosque in Konya. *Chintamani* motifs (leopard spots), symbols of power and the sultanate of Far East origin, and *hatayi* (peonies), tulips and carnations were also used in tiles, textiles and woodwork between the AH 10th and 12th / AD 16th and 18th centuries.
eeefe08e-b05d-5b9e-a805-c6fd43d4fe03.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
eeefe08e-b05d-5b9e-a805-c6fd43d4fe03.method_for_datation: It is thought to have been either ordered, made specially, or donated as a pious gift to the Sultan Selim Mosque in Konya, which was begun when Sultan Selim II was governor of Konya (i.e. before he had ascended the throne) but completed in the same year he became sultan, AH 973 / AD 1566. During the Ottoman period it was traditional for the sultan to have made as furniture for the mosques he was commissioning carpets, Qur'an stands and other fine artefacts, The carpet's decorative motifs, together with the date of construction of the mosque it came from, lead us to date it in the 10th / 16th century.
eeefe08e-b05d-5b9e-a805-c6fd43d4fe03.method_for_provenance: In the 10th / 16th century the most important centre for carpet production was Uşak and its vicinity. The composition and motifs on this carpet's main border, in particular, pertain to the region of Uşak and suggest that the carpet was woven there.
eeefe08e-b05d-5b9e-a805-c6fd43d4fe03.obtention: The rug was transferred from the Sultan Selim Mosque in Konya to the Museum in 1911 as a result of the countrywide initiative to collect together artworks in order to prevent theft and plunder.

ef21b96c-da0c-528c-bc8d-e3d1e18531f7.description: Loom weights are made from a roll of clay twisted and shaped into spheres, flattened cylinders, or conical shapes. They are used to keep the warp threads of the loom taut and provide even tension in order to weave with ease.

ef2d21d6-b9e0-51ab-bff3-a705b97fdd8b.name: Caucasian carpet
ef2d21d6-b9e0-51ab-bff3-a705b97fdd8b.description:
In the Caucasus there is great variety of motifs due to artistic exchange among the ethnic groups. Different classifications of carpets are based on weaver's ethnicity, geographic origin of the carpet or the carpet structure. No system of classification is based on design or motifs. Therefore, for this peculiar carpet, it is difficult to establish its origin.  
The central field is decorated with polychrome floret and octagons with star motifs on red ground. Three borders frame the central field. The main border is floral. Minor borders are decorated with chain of S shapes on a blue background.
ef2d21d6-b9e0-51ab-bff3-a705b97fdd8b.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Caucasus; small filler elements
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

ef3f5411-9570-5d33-a16b-8b8be01931be.name: Karabagh Medallion and Sickle Leaf Rug
ef3f5411-9570-5d33-a16b-8b8be01931be.description:
It has a well-proportioned pattern of two full medallions on a dark blue field and a partial medallion at the upper and lower ends. The medallions have hooking, lancet-leaf ivory arms and are linked by fringed ivory palmettes. The remaining area of the field is filled with rosettes, flowers and leaves.  
  
Ellis includes it among the rare blue field carpets he proposes as analogues of a late 17th or early 18th century Shirvan or Karabagh rug with multiple medallions held by the Art Institute, Chicago, describing it as, "a rather small and narrow example on a blue ground". The rug was determined to be 17th century Armenian by Károly Gombos in 1983. Jennifer Wearden published it in connection with Azerbaijan embroideries as an "early 18th century Caucasian or Armenian Floral Carpet".
ef3f5411-9570-5d33-a16b-8b8be01931be.obtention: In 1940, the Museum of Applied Arts registered the rug as on deposit from the Budapest art collector Dr Emil Delmár (1876‒1959), former co-proprietor of the Danube Dredging Company. After 1951, the rug was treated as part of the museum’s own holdings, and in 1987, it was added  to the collection as the gift of Dr Bálint Füzéky and Mrs István Gömöri.

ef7eaa24-b781-58f3-a09b-1025af24d6ba.name: Carpet
ef7eaa24-b781-58f3-a09b-1025af24d6ba.description:
Spanish carpet from the Holbein series.  
Field: With a continuous field decoration on a red background containing twelve frames arranged in three vertical columns divided into four rows. Each frame contains a central inscribed octagon, framed by concentric bands in blue and red; In the centre of the octagon appears a stationary wheel with flower blooms. The spandrels, between the squares and octagons, contain stepped dots and coloured stripes. The strips that separate the squares are decorated with motifs of meanders and stylised chains.  
Border: The smaller outer borders have a decoration of oblique and parallel branches from which red and blue leaves bloom. A lot of the larger border is not preserved, but in areas where it is partially preserved, linked knots can be distinguished.  
This series is referred to as the Holbein series, referring to carpets of these same characteristics that were made popular through the court paintings of Hans Holbein (1497- 1543) and were largely produced in Anatolia.  
Those carpets represented by the painter Holbein are later than carpets of this series produced in the Kingdom of Murcia, which at this time had already gone out of style within the Iberian Peninsula.  
  
A similar piece can be found in: FERRANDIS TORRES, José: Catalog Exhibition of Spanish Carpets (Madrid, 1933) page 106.  
Published by Ferrer, Andrés: Alfombras antiguas de la provincia de Albacete. Lámina XXXV. According to Campana (Campana, M, 1966: Tappeti d´occidente, p. 38) this carpet is similar to oriental productions, known as the Holbein series. A similar copy is presented in the catalogue of the Washington Textile Museum (Plate XVI). It is safe to say that it is related to carpet number two in the acquisitions record, despite slight differences in measurement. The carpet has been photographed for possible reproduction. In Spain very few copies of this series are preserved, with a well preserved copy in the convent of Santa Clara de Medina de Pomar which has considerable differences in colour.

f073f1fe-e470-5070-abe1-8c53d486f903.name: Printed and painted cotton hanging
f073f1fe-e470-5070-abe1-8c53d486f903.short_description: *Carpe diem!* Seize the day! advises the Roman poet Quintus Horatius Flaccus (65–8 BC), known in the English-speaking world as Horace. Make the best out of your life and take it as it comes, since you never know when you will die. An identical incitement to exchange the fearful concentration on the future for the enjoyment of the present, before one crumbles into dust in no time, is found a thousand years later at the other end of the world, in a four-line poem ascribed to the Persian poet Omar Khayyam (1048–1131 AD), which decorates a late 19th century qalamkar fabric.

f2184f11-1f51-5514-8416-c8a8dc45cdec.name: Kerman Carpet
f2184f11-1f51-5514-8416-c8a8dc45cdec.short_description: Originating from Kerman, a region known for a wide range of designs utilizing natural dyes in a broad colour palette and asymmetrical knots, this Iranian carpet depicts a human with the body and wings of a bird, which demonstrates a closeness to God and divine protection. Colourful patterns featuring the damask rose frame the central scene in earth tones representing honesty, support and trustworthiness. The Zoroaster symbol stands out at the top while Darius I, commonly known as Darius the Great of Persia, is sitting on the throne uplifted by eight men. As a pyramid-like hierarchy, the Achaemenid Empire ruled over eight countries from the Ancient World. These territories included Lydia, Babylon, Persia, Palestine, Egypt, Sindh, Libya, and Macedonia.

f3dbf7ea-0203-52c4-bde7-025357b75c96.name: *Puppenfiguren aus Volksmärchen (Puppets from Folk Tales)*
f3dbf7ea-0203-52c4-bde7-025357b75c96.description:
The oblong tapestry shows in its central part a number of characters as they appear in common German fairy tales, the most well-known story collection being Grimm’s *Children’s and Household Tales*. The figures are sewn onto the ground in a patchwork, using fabric of many different colours and patterns. The darker coloured fields above and beneath the figures show flowers and birds.  
The artwork was created by an artist and acquired for the state by the Sekretariat für Kunstausstellungen des Bezirkes Dresden \[Dresden secretary for Fine Art Exhibitions\] in 1980. This was standard procedure in the German Democratic Republic (GDR) since even art production was scheduled in the socialist economy plan and the government took seriously its role as the main supporter of the country’s artists. Government-owned artworks were considered public property and as such were installed in public places for everybody to see. This was the case for the tapestry discussed here, which furnished a kindergarten during the 1980s. One can imagine that the children might have guessed the figure’s names and the corresponding fairy tales. Furthermore, the figures resemble the typical hand puppets from the GDR, which could have been a prop in retelling the figures’ stories.  
The artist Agathe Böttcher was born in Bautzen in 1929. She studied textile design beginning in 1947 in Dresden and later on in Berlin-Weissensee (post-graduate study from 1954–57). In 1954, she married the painter and film maker Jürgen Böttcher (Strawalde). Through her husband, she became acquainted with artists of the Dresden artist group *Erste Phalanx Nedserd*. In 1958 she took up a job as lecturer at the Technical University of Dresden, which she held more than 20 years. Since 1979, she has been working as a freelance artist with temporary lectureships. Agathe Böttcher lives in Dresden (2017).

f3dc702b-3b10-5fee-ae0f-1ee4b2bb97e7.name: Dragon Rug
f3dc702b-3b10-5fee-ae0f-1ee4b2bb97e7.description: This 18th century Dragon Rug is a unique expression of artistic achievement. This is the only known Dragon carpet that is woven in the Persian style of *Sehna* knotting. It was made by what is assumed to be a migratory craftsman. This assumption stems from the fact that the last 12 inches of the carpet were woven in the opposite direction than the rest, suggesting that it was taken off the loom before completion and then placed back on later. It features the standard dragon carpet layout with decadent patterns of symmetrical floral and leaf motifs. The frame consists of an interlaced pattern, while the field of the carpet includes dragon, animal, and floral motifs.

f3f71340-4ba9-56b9-bb2e-aa39656b9630.name: The *Annunciation*
f3f71340-4ba9-56b9-bb2e-aa39656b9630.description:
Aside from the *Annunciation*, the *Mass of St Gregory* is one of the most common and important painting subjects in which representations of carpets can be found. Into one of the crucial moments of Christian iconography, artists transposed aspects of the typical Portuguese feminine interior spaces of the 16th century, with the marked presence of the female dais (*estrado*). Its use appears associated with the context of Islamic presence in the Iberian Peninsula during the Middle Ages.  
In this painting, the Virgin Mary appears kneeling on a mat: this, along with other similar representations bear witness to the past presence in Portugal of these types of small carpets that are non-existent in collections today. Such is the case of these “mats”, used during the summer as an alternative to the dense knotted carpets of the winter months, as well as of the tapestries, which alternated in the summer period with the *guadamecis*.  
The artist’s decision to include a mat, rather than an Oriental carpet, may be down to the painting being commissioned for a convent of the Order of Saint Claire, where the strict rules called for austerity. This appears in opposition to Gregório Lopes’s painting intended for a wealthy clientele.  
In addition, it all goes to prove the absorption and influence of African artistic production in Portuguese contemporary life and art since the 15th century, when mats, but also other objects such as saltcellars and ivory spoons, began to be imported to Portugal from Benin.

f3fdf942-da01-5816-9d0f-f6a44c2afba1.name: Shirvan carpet
f3fdf942-da01-5816-9d0f-f6a44c2afba1.description:
The Shirvan district is an area south of the Greater Caucasus and east of the Ganja area, but in earlier times – as a khanate dependent upon Persia – it included the Apsheron Peninsula, where the city of Baku is located. Shirvan design motifs are from all over the Caucasus and even Persia.  
This carpet was purchased from Ladislav Lata Mihalović, a member of the old Zagreb nobility whose family members were important figures in Croatian political life. He was also a patron and art lover who carefully took care of the family's art collection. The interior of his apartment was lavishly furnished with oriental carpets and cushions among which numerous were Caucasian carpets.  
The central field of this carpet has a polychrome *afshan* (“scattered” in Persian) pattern on dark blue ground. The *afshan* motif consists of right-angle flower calyxes, palmettes and rosettes. The roots of this design lie in various seventeenth and eighteenth-century Indian and Persian floral rugs. A common Shirvan design results from elongating the arabesque leaves and orienting them at right angles so that the branches run parallely to the sides of the rug. The main border has a *kufic* pattern on red ground and it is often used with these field repeats. The *kufic* motif is thought to derive from a specific Arabic script termed “*kufic*”. The script has elongated angular letters with serifs. The *kufic* border is used on rugs of Shirvan and other Caucasian rugs. Minor borders or *afshan* borders have a floral meander pattern on white ground. These borders and also often used with *afshan* field repeat motifs.

keywords: Caucasus; Shirvan; Afshan
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; symmetrical knots

f445365e-28d3-5b5f-869c-11cd87fe18f8.name: The *Circumcision*
f445365e-28d3-5b5f-869c-11cd87fe18f8.description:
We are witnessing the representation of one of the most important episodes of Jesus’ childhood, in which, according to Jewish law, the Child gains its identity.  
The scene has been re-created in the interior of a Renaissance-style temple where the Holy Family and several figures cluster around the table where a priest is about to carry out the circumcision.  
Covering the altar there is a white towel, in turn, this covers a carpet, of which only the border, filled with “vine scrolls”, palmettes and foliage, is visible. This variant in the use of carpets in a painting makes this a very interesting document.  
Alongside its use as a floor-cover in paintings, when its symbolism is associated with dignity and spatial boundaries, carpets were used widely as a cover for altars in churches as well as in civil settings as furniture covers, as several Portuguese inventories attest.  
In the *Circumcision*, a so-called knotted “Holbein” carpet can be seen. It is put to the same use here as the carpet represented by Hans Holbein, the Younger (1497/8‒1543), in his famous portrait *The Ambassadors*, which thereafter gave this specific compositional structure the name “Holbein”.

f4ea69e8-9de2-5382-aca9-484c574fcf53.name: Konya Prayer Rug
f4ea69e8-9de2-5382-aca9-484c574fcf53.description: This rug is known as the “prayer rug with a high estrade”.It was woven specifically for the midday religious service in mosques on Fridays. The Kaʽba and its surrounding  buildings are portrayed. Kaʽba  motifs and foot marks at the bottom side indicate the direction of the prayer, as one must turn his/her face to the Kaʽba during prayer. There are hanging candle motifs symbolizing the holy (eternal) lights of the prophet along the right and left side of the Kaʽba motifs. The floral decoration on the borders are typical for its origin and date.

f50bd176-bda6-5419-b0f2-72d317a0f0f5.name: Prayer rug
f50bd176-bda6-5419-b0f2-72d317a0f0f5.description: At the centre of this prayer rug there is a *mihrab*, which indicates the *qibla* ‒ the direction of the Kaʽba in Mecca. The Kraków example is especially attractive because of its vivid colours: a warm-red niche, closed with an arch of bizarre shape, contrasts with yellow borders. Inside the white spandrels is a black arabesque ornament. In the cross-panel there are rosettes inscribed in lozenges. The most striking feature is a wide border with a pattern of rhythmically turned rosettes and pomegranate motifs. Such a border reflects the style of Ottoman court rugs attributed to Bursa. Similar rugs can be found in many churches in Transylvania.
f50bd176-bda6-5419-b0f2-72d317a0f0f5.method_for_datation: Geometrisation of the motifs as well as simplification of the design dates this rug to as late as the 18th century

f52af067-edfe-5f5e-95b7-9a131fd3f4f1.name: Kula prayer rug
f52af067-edfe-5f5e-95b7-9a131fd3f4f1.description:
This prayer rug was probably made in Kula. It is decorated with a terracotta-red *mihrab* closed with a stepped arch, the spandrels of which are light blue. The bordure, which consists of 23 thin stripes, is divided into three colouristic areas of green and yellow, ivory and dark-brown, and red and blue. Every space of the carpet is filled with minute motifs: four-petal rosettes in the niche, upside down tulips in the spandrels, and flowers on leafy stalks in the bordure. The big red, yellow and ivory carnations in the cross-panels beneath and above the niche, contrast with the other flora. The colouristic and ornamental composition gives an impression of delicacy and lightness.  
Carpets made in Kula were strongly influenced by the Gördes production, but the multi-striped borders can be more often found in Kula rugs. In addition, the choice of minute floral motifs is very characteristic of this production centre. It is worth noting just how differentiated the floral motifs used to decorate the carpet are, especially in terms of the colour scheme.  
Prayer rugs were very popular among the 17th- and 18th-century nobility in Poland. Taste for Oriental art was one of the characteristic features of Polish culture at the time, and prayer rugs were widely used for interior decoration.  
The Kula rug was obtained by the very famous Polish collector Feliks Jasieński ‒ called Manggha (1861–1929) ‒ and formed part of his extensive and precious collection. Part of this collection was donated to the National Museum in Kraków in 1929, according to Jasieński’s last will and testament.

f5d52aac-d406-5fea-b100-03be2aa59694.name: *Tekke Ensi*
f5d52aac-d406-5fea-b100-03be2aa59694.description:
This carpet was made by the Turkoman nomad tribe Tekke. The term *ensi* refers to a decorative *yurt* (tent) door hanging, in which many elements of the ornamental design functioned as protective symbols to ward off evil spirits.  
The central field is divided into three panels along the vertical axis. The upper and lower panels have the same decoration. The central column divides the panels into quarters. The column is decorated with “curled leaf” motifs separated by vertical bands with *bovrek* (bud) motifs. Each quarter is filled with a *gush* (bird) pattern arranged in horizontal rows. The central horizontal panel is decorated with “curled leaf” motifs separated by horizontal bands with *kochak* (ram's horns) motifs. The upper transverse band is intercepted in the middle by the *mihrab* (prayer niche) arch flanked by straight lattice design of oblongs and triangles. Above this transverse band there is another one with the variation of *kelle* (head) motif. The central border is decorated with variation of the *gapyrga* (ribs) motif. The inner border is decorated with *kochak* motifs. The outer border is decorated with the *sainak* motif. This type of border is a very common outer border on *ensi*s. The minor border is the soldat border or guard stripe, a very common minor border. The base panel carries a small geometrical design.
f5d52aac-d406-5fea-b100-03be2aa59694.obtention: Purchased from Nikola Buchsbaum, Zagreb, Croatia
f5d52aac-d406-5fea-b100-03be2aa59694.author: Andrea Klobučar
keywords: Turkmenistan; Tekke; engsi
materials: Wool; knotted carpet; asymmetrical knots

f64702ac-9f88-5cc3-82c2-e16ebbc1cc14.name: Chair seat cover
f64702ac-9f88-5cc3-82c2-e16ebbc1cc14.description:
The whole picture created on this carpet presents a quiet and leisurely scene of a lotus pond in summer with an egret among the large lotus leaves on delicate stems.  
The lotus blossom, when first introduced into the Chinese artistic repertoire, symbolized the Buddhist notion of purity. It is a beautiful, spotless white flower which grows from the muddy bottoms of ponds. This characteristic of growing out of mud unstained would have played a role in the Buddhist meaning of the flower.  
The picture on this small carpet, however, forms a rebus that plays upon the sounds of Chinese written characters. The egret standing in a pond with lotuses can be “read” as “wishing you success in an ever upward path”. Designed to cover the seat of an elegantly carved large wooden chair, the size and format of this rug were determined by its intended use.

f6de5b7e-2072-57cf-8c8c-0a705ded20d8.name: Dragon Carpet
f6de5b7e-2072-57cf-8c8c-0a705ded20d8.description:
A 17th century Caucasian pile carpet, better known as a Dragon carpet for its iconic design. Its red-background is dominated by a lattice system of two wide vegetal stems in ivory and in blue, overlapping each other in a drop-repeat directional layout. Covering each of the intersections of the lattice system are large multi-coloured palmettes of various designs. In the diamond shaped voids, or compartments, enclosed by the lattice are positioned a variety of animals including two rows of yellow “S” shaped dragons (hence the carpet’s name), three rows of pairs of deer fawns, two rows of pairs of flaming lion-and-chi-lin in combat. On the blue lattice branches are illustrated pheasants above ducks. The carpet’s narrow border has an ivory-coloured background decorated with a multi-coloured scroll of flowers.  
  
Considered to be of one of the earliest types of Caucasian carpets, a product of a cottage industry, this carpet’s design is thought to be based on earlier, and much less abstracted, Iranian prototypes. These Caucasian versions were made for the trade and its many routes.

f7879232-ae13-54c3-8e2a-b4f64e92dbd7.name: Uşak carpet (Bergama).
f7879232-ae13-54c3-8e2a-b4f64e92dbd7.description:
This is a carpet woven in the region of Western Anatolia in the AH 10th / AD 16th century. Both warp and weft are of wool. The weaving technique used is the 'Turkish double knot', known as the Gördes knot. The carpet is divided into five compartments: three pairs of octagons alternate with large rectangles on a dark-yellow ground and within a border of rosettes. Within the rectangles, which have red backgrounds, concentric octagons make up the primary motif. At the centre of each octagon is a six-armed star rosette. Around the inner octagon, resembling a floral rosette because of the hook and interlace motifs around the central star, the field is filled by a group of stars with stylised red and white leaves among them. The main octagon is completed by yellow and blue interlace motifs, while corner-pieces made up of hook motifs complete the large rectangle. Two narrow borders with chain and leaf motifs are in turn surrounded by the main border, which has groups of stylised *kufic* script on a dark-blue ground. The imitation *kufic* interlace motifs, which are white, yellow, green, and blue with red contours, are made to contrast with the contrary colours placed between them.  
  
Turkish carpets, which had an important place in Ottoman trade, were exported in large numbers to European markets beginning in the AH 8th / AD 14th century. As an expensive export ware, these carpets met with great demand from noble families, church officials, and the wealthy middle classes who engaged in trade. These groups were also highly interested in painting, and they had the valuable carpets they owned painted into the portraits of themselves with which they adorned their churches and palaces.  
  
These paintings, produced by many European artists beginning in the AD 15th century, have played an important role in establishing the dates and typology of carpets. Some carpets, known as 'Holbein' carpets, appear in paintings by the German artist Hans Holbein (AD 1497–1543), while some are known in carpet terminology as 'Holbein' carpets even though they do not appear in any paintings. The present work is judged to be part of the group known as 'Holbein IV'.
f7879232-ae13-54c3-8e2a-b4f64e92dbd7.short_description: This woollen rug was woven with Turkish double knots (Gördes knots) in Bergama in the AH 10th / AD 16th century. These rugs with rectangular frames and geometric and stylised floral motifs came to be known as 'Holbein' carpets after the German painter Hans Holbein, who included them in his paintings.
f7879232-ae13-54c3-8e2a-b4f64e92dbd7.holder: Museum of Turkish and Islamic Arts.
f7879232-ae13-54c3-8e2a-b4f64e92dbd7.method_for_datation: The carpet is dated to the 10th / 16th century on the basis of the characteristics of the motifs and composition as well as paintings in which similar carpets appear.
f7879232-ae13-54c3-8e2a-b4f64e92dbd7.method_for_provenance: It is well known that there was a thriving carpet-making industry in Bergama and Ushak in the 10th / 16th century. The presence of particular motifs and a style based on geometric division, both of which are still found on carpets produced in Bergama today, suggests that the carpet was woven in Bergama rather than Ushak.
f7879232-ae13-54c3-8e2a-b4f64e92dbd7.obtention: The carpet was transferred to the Museum in 1911 from the Shaykh Baba Yusuf Mosque in Sivrihisar as part of the initiative begun in the 19th century to collect up artworks from all over the Empire.

f7ed68df-d80f-52d6-89b8-e4a57d8f8085.name: Triple-arch prayer rug
f7ed68df-d80f-52d6-89b8-e4a57d8f8085.description:
Triple-arch rugs, sometimes also described as six-column rugs, were very popular in Transylvania – there are several interesting examples preserved in the collections at the Budapest Museum of Applied Arts and the Brukenthal National Museum in Sibiu, and in a number of Austrian collections as well. It is very probable that in this case the niche doesn’t represent the *mihrab*, but derives from mosque architecture.  
The red niche at the centre of the rug is divided into three pointed arches supported by six columns, on bases in the form of polygonal turrets, with the so-called “precious stones” decoration. The large carnation flower is suspended from the pick of the central arch, and much smaller flowers hang from the lower arches. The dark-blue spandrels are decorated with a mainly yellow ornament of rosettes, and lanceolate leaves flanking them. The main, wide border, filled with an ornament of hexagonal cartouches enclosing lozenges with carnations rising from them, is placed between two narrower borders with flower ornament. The main colours of the carpet are red, yellow and dark-blue, with details in white, red and blue.  
Some characteristic features distinguish the Kraków carpet from other examples of this type: the ornaments are rather simplified, and a clear, precise outline is almost lost especially in the spandrels; the paired central columns rise from the bases as one column, which is quite an unusual solution. Worthy of note also are the delicate, small flowers rising from the central part of the columns. The left arch has a bizarre shape, which is probably the result of an error made by the maker.
f7ed68df-d80f-52d6-89b8-e4a57d8f8085.method_for_datation: The composition of the rug and also its stylistic features prove that it belongs to the group of triple-arch carpets traditionally connected with the Anatolia workshop of the 17th century
f7ed68df-d80f-52d6-89b8-e4a57d8f8085.method_for_provenance: Both composition and technique suggest that it could have been made in Ladik, Anatolia

f85d9f00-4083-5a27-a359-1b0775ec55d5.name: Carpet fragment
f85d9f00-4083-5a27-a359-1b0775ec55d5.description: In the Middle East, woven fabrics served not only as seating, storage bags, curtains, bed linen and covers for objects and animals, but also as decorative floor coverings. The literature, artifacts and European paintings of the 16th and 17th centuries all testify to the trade in carpets, which fostered the spread of designs and beliefs across cultures. The designs, colours and shapes of textiles bore an implicit message of protection. This carpet fragment, in which onager (wild ass), deer and lion motifs are placed around a cypress, is a variation on what is known as the Garden of Paradise design that was widely used in northern and northwestern Iran in the Safavid period (1501–1722/36). Abiding features in Iranian thinking for thousands of years, gardens and the search for paradise were prominent themes in poetry, literature and painting. Carpets were viewed as reflections of the heavenly garden and as the ideal means for artistic expression that were easy to carry during the seasonal moves between winter and summer quarters. The most magnificent Garden of Paradise-design carpets were reserved for the nobility, and few examples of them from the Safavid era have survived to this day. Fragments of carpets datable from the 16th to the 18th century have been sold since the mid-19th century in order to satisfy demand among Western collectors. A large fragment of this 17th-century carpet is in the collection of the Cleveland Museum of Art (1953.128).

f949b89d-44f8-53f5-9176-1e600c351147.name: Bergama rug
f949b89d-44f8-53f5-9176-1e600c351147.description:
Bergama is a town in western Anatolia. Rugs woven there are usually square, and their design geometric. Most are decorated with five medallions: square, rectangular or polygonal in the centre and four others near the corners of the central field. Such a composition is a distant reflection of the so-called “Holbein” carpets from the 15th and 16th centuries.  
The Kraków Bergama rug is woven from wool using a very warm colour palette, predominantly shades of ochre and yellow, with the addition of light-orange, yellowish green, dark-blue and greyish violet. The fleece is high and adds an impression of softness to the geometric ornament. In the centre of the ochre field there is an octagonal white medallion surrounded by hook motifs with a colourful rosette inside. The white surface of the medallion is decorated with a meander-like ornament, which looks engraved – an effect achieved by the light-brown fleece being cut lower than the white fleece. In the corners rest smaller medallions with ornamental crosses constructed of triangles. Between the medallions are leafy stalks with tulips. Small roses and other minute designs, difficult to recognise, also appear on the main field. The main border is filled with tulips inscribed inside squares. The Kraków rug is an attractive example of the style typical of the Bergama carpet-weaving centre.
f949b89d-44f8-53f5-9176-1e600c351147.method_for_datation: The ornament is very characteristic of “Bergama” carpets

fbde1ba4-0cc0-547e-9260-e7d47c092d47.name: Picture postcard, *Greetings from Pirot*
fbde1ba4-0cc0-547e-9260-e7d47c092d47.description: A picture postcard with the Cyrillic inscription *Pozdrav iz Pirota* (*Greetings from Pirot*) shows a woman from Pirot weaving a kilim, with a child standing by her side. Pirot, a town in south-eastern Serbia, was an important centre of kilim weaving in the Balkans. Pirot kilims were woven on vertical looms (as the one shown in the picture) with a slit weave technique (*klečanje*), which renders both front and back of a weave even and identical. It took one to ten weavers to weave a kilim, depending on its dimensions. The kilims were made of fine, thinly and evenly spun wool which, until 1880’s, was exclusively processed at homes. One of their major characteristics are the studied coloristic effects, achieved by choice and distribution of colours. Natural herb dyes were replaced by the aniline ones at the beginning of the 20th century.

fbffece3-0074-5895-9c10-cd61fb31f7d9.name: Tent bag
fbffece3-0074-5895-9c10-cd61fb31f7d9.description: Nomads of Central Asia made a variety of storage and carrying bags of different sizes. They were hung on a wooden trellis of the yurt and, during migration, carried on the back of horses and donkeys. They were woven in a variety of techniques, often a combination of knotted pile and flat weave. This bag is notable for its colours of extreme richness and clarity.

fd9909b2-4573-5acb-ac97-18b27b9f7074.name: Qashqa´i
fd9909b2-4573-5acb-ac97-18b27b9f7074.description: The carpet's base is formed by two dark blue diamonds set vertically on top of each other and cut to the borders. Each of them is inscribed with a striking, ivory-coloured row of hooks in a clearly narrower rhomboid. A Memling gul appears at the centre of each hooked diamond, with emblematic octagonal motifs placed at the corners of the diamonds. As medallions, these hooked diamonds constitute the central motif of the carpet. The remaining spandrels and triangles (semi-rhomboids) of the central field are contrastingly designed with alternating red and yellow backgrounds. All areas are lavishly filled with small motifs in many variations. The major border is designed in the same colour as the base. Because midnight blue and ivory are predominant here as well, the contrast to the adjacent bright red and yellow areas is repeated. In the minor borders, however, shades of red and yellow dominate. This is a very well-balanced and gorgeous carpet – quite finely woven, of outstanding wool quality and a relatively small format, which is certainly reminiscent of the finer examples of the pile-woven saddlebags (*khorjin*) of the Qashqa´i.

fe134b50-319c-5411-b2af-fb5d9bcfd6cf.name: Ladik Prayer Rug
fe134b50-319c-5411-b2af-fb5d9bcfd6cf.description: Ladik town of Konya Province was one of the most important rug producing centres of Anatolia. From the 17th to the 19th centuries many kind of carpets including large ground rugs, hall rugs, floor mats and cushions were produced in Ladik. Prayer rugs from the region are the most famous group. The distinctive feature of a Ladik prayer rug is a *mihrab* with a triple niche and stylized columns. Ladik prayer rugs are popular in Transylvania. Rugs were exported to the region and this type became known as a “Transylvanian rug”.

ff573f89-f67a-5394-a12a-08edfa8872a9.name: Silk Carpet with metal thread
ff573f89-f67a-5394-a12a-08edfa8872a9.description:
This relatively small carpet is produced with a luxurious combination of silk knotted pile design against background areas of metal brocade, creating a shimmering combination. Today the colours are reduced to light blue, pale green, cream and other light pastels, with some dark blue details: it is possible that the silk pile has faded over the centuries. This lightness conceals the refined complexity of the design itself, which is folded across a horizontal and a vertical axis – a quartered design of calculated symmetry. Ordered around a central point, two lobed pendants mirror each other at the upper and lower side. Each features a striped central roundel, embedded in floral surrounds and scrollwork. Half-medallions meet the sides of the carpet design, with large bisected lotus flowers.  
  
Very fine carpets such as this were woven in Isfahan, Iran’s capital under the Safavid dynasty from 1598 until the fall of the Safavids in 1722. Throughout the seventeenth century, international traders from across Asia and Europe were attracted to Isfahan to buy raw silk, following an economic policy introduced by Shah ‘Abbas I. Silk carpets brocaded with precious metal thread, such as this, made impressive diplomatic gifts, as well as trading goods: examples were sent to courts and trading corporations alike, in Venice, Copenhagen and many other centres. Examples survive in international collections to this day.  
  
[V&A online catalogue link](http://collections.vam.ac.uk/item/O67211/carpet-unknown/)
